title: fsci-special: Carlson elliprf missing
description: Skill: /porting-to-rust. After elliprc (mxxij), the Carlson family is still incomplete — elliprf (the symmetric integral of the first kind) is the canonical building block of scipy.special's elliptic suite. RF(x, y, z) = (1/2) ∫₀^∞ [(t+x)(t+y)(t+z)]^(-1/2) dt. Will port using Carlson's duplication algorithm (iterate xn = (xn + λ)/4 with λ = √(xy) + √(yz) + √(xz) until convergence, then 5th-order Taylor series correction). Closed-form anchors: RF(x, x, x) = 1/√x; RF(0, 1, 1) = π/2; RF(0, y, y) = π/(2√y); RF(1, 2, 4) ≈ 0.6850858 (scipy reference value).
close_reason: Shipped pub fn elliprf(x, y, z) using Carlson's duplication algorithm with 5th-order Taylor correction. Iterates (xn, yn, zn) → ((xn+λ)/4, ...) with λ = √(xy)+√(yz)+√(xz) until max(|1-x/μ|) < 2e-3, then returns μ^(-1/2) · (1 - E2/10 + E3/14 + E2²/24 - 3·E2·E3/44). 5 tests: diagonal RF(x,x,x)=1/√x for 6 x; zero-argument RF(0,y,y)=π/(2√y) for 4 y; scipy reference RF(1,2,4)≈0.6850858; argument symmetry x↔y, x↔z; negative/NaN/double-zero rejection. fsci-special now 769 tests (+5).

description:

    pub fn lmbda(v: f64, x: f64) -> (Vec<f64>, Vec<f64>) {

MEASURED, scipy 1.17.1:
  special.lmbda(-1.0, 2.0) -> ValueError: argument must be > 0.
  special.lmbda(0.0,  2.0) -> (array([0.22389078]), array([-0.57672481]))

  special.lmbda(2.0,  2.0) -> (array([0.22389078, 0.57672481, 0.70566806]), ...)

THE SCOPE IS NARROWER THAN SCIPY'S MESSAGE SUGGESTS, and getting this wrong in either direction is the main risk. The message reads 'argument must be > 0.', but v = 0.0 is ACCEPTED and returns a value. Only v < 0 raises. A fix that rejected v == 0 to match the wording would break a case scipy answers.

OURS at v = -1.0: n = (-1).floor().max(0.0) = 0 and v0 = -1 - (-1) = 0, so we return exactly the v = 0.0 answer -- a plausible, correct-for-a-different-input array where the incumbent refuses. At a non-integer negative order the wrongness changes shape rather than becoming visible: v = -0.5 gives floor = -1, n = 0, v0 = 0.5, so we return the v0 = 0.5 series with count 1. Neither case is flagged to the caller.

DELIBERATE VALIDATION, therefore adopt it: scipy formats this message itself in the specfun wrapper. Same class as frankenscipy-33muy and frankenscipy-xb7so, not the incidental-numpy-crash class catalogued as REJECTED in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.

PREPARED FIX. lmbda returns (Vec<f64>, Vec<f64>) and is #[must_use], with no error channel, so this needs a signature change to Result<(Vec<f64>, Vec<f64>), ...> using whatever error type fsci-special uses for domain rejections -- check that first, several functions in this crate signal domain errors by returning NaN instead, and if that is the crate-wide convention then returning (vec![NAN], vec![NAN]) may be the consistent choice and this bead should be re-scoped to say so rather than introducing a lone Result in a NaN-signalling crate. Decide the convention BEFORE writing the fix.

PREPARED TESTS, two arms:
  MUST-HIT: v = -1.0 and v = -0.5 rejected (or NaN-signalled, per the convention decided above).
  MUST-MISS: v = 0.0 must still return scipy's (0.22389078, -0.57672481) at x = 2.0, since 0 is in domain despite the message wording; v = 2.0, v = 2.5, v = 150.0 and the x = 0.0 cases must be unchanged -- there are existing tests at bessel.rs:5792-5825 covering lmbda(2,3), lmbda(2.5,1), lmbda(150,1), lmbda(3,0) and lmbda(2.5,0), and none of them pins the negative-v behaviour, so no test currently has to be replaced. That is worth stating because two fixes this session (33muy, xb7so) DID have to replace a test that pinned the divergence.
notes:
TYPO REPAIR to the note above (my shell ate two identifiers inside backticks; the sentence beginning "So the architecture is deliberate and two-surface:" lost both names). It should read:

  So the architecture is deliberate and two-surface: the bare-named function -- lmbda, erfinv,
  betainc, gammainc, hyperu -- is the scipy-ufunc-like surface that signals IN BAND with NaN, and
  the same name with a _scalar suffix is the checked surface returning SpecialError, whose kind
  enum at types.rs:265 carries a DomainError variant for exactly this purpose.

Nothing else in that note is affected, and the conclusion is unchanged: do NOT change lmbda's
signature; return NaN vectors for v < 0, and optionally add a _scalar checked variant alongside it.
close_reason: Landed: lmbda returns NaN vectors for v < 0 instead of clamping the order to 0. scipy raises ValueError('argument must be > 0.') there; the old .max(0.0) made v=-1.0 return the v=0.0 answer and v=-0.5 return the v0=0.5 series -- correct for a DIFFERENT input, worse than NaN because it looks right. NaN not Result, per the crate convention resolved earlier: 623 public fns, only 16 return Result and every one is a _scalar variant paired with a NaN-returning same-named function. Must-miss arm pins the subtle half: scipy's MESSAGE says '> 0' but v == 0.0 is ACCEPTED and returns 0.22389077914123562 at x=2, so a guard written from the message rather than the measurement would break it. 1157 passed / 0 failed, fsci-special lib, rch worker vmi1149989.

title: [HIGH] fsci-sparse: 5 iterative solvers violate Hardened-mode contract — cg/gmres gate NaN check on check_finite ALONE (ignoring Hardened), while bicg/cgs/bicgstab have ZERO finiteness check at all; direct solve at line 420 correctly uses 'check_finite || mode==Hardened' pattern, so author knew the right code but failed to propagate
description:
Review of crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs on 2026-04-23.

Five public iterative solvers violate the Hardened-mode fail-closed contract
to varying degrees. Three of them have ZERO input-finiteness validation.

Hardened-mode contract (per fsci-runtime semantics and the workspace pattern):
  In Hardened mode, NaN/Inf inputs MUST fail-closed with audit ledger entry.
  check_finite is a perf knob for Strict mode; Hardened mode should always
  validate regardless of check_finite.

Correct pattern (seen at line 420):
  let must_check = options.check_finite || options.mode == RuntimeMode::Hardened;
  if must_check { ... reject NaN/Inf ... }

Iterative solver validation inventory:

    cg (line 549-656):
        line 567: `if options.check_finite && (NaN check)` -> reject
        HARDENED IGNORED: setting mode=Hardened but check_finite=false
        still allows NaN through.

    gmres (line 790-1000ish):
        line 808: `if options.check_finite && (NaN check)` -> reject
        HARDENED IGNORED: same bug as cg.

    bicg (line 1326-1450ish):
        NO FINITENESS CHECK AT ALL. Validates shape (line 1333),
        b.len (line 1339), x0.len (line 1349). Proceeds directly to
        iteration with whatever NaN/Inf is in a.data() or b.

    cgs (line 1471-1600ish):
        NO FINITENESS CHECK AT ALL. Same structure as bicg.

    bicgstab (line 1617-1700ish):
        NO FINITENESS CHECK AT ALL. Same structure as bicg/cgs.

Consequences:

For cg / gmres in Hardened mode with check_finite=false:
    - NaN matrix entry propagates into residual computation
    - `r_norm / b_norm < tol` becomes `NaN < tol` = false -> never converges
    - Loop runs full max_iter iterations (default n*10)
    - Returns Ok(IterativeSolveResult {
          solution: [NaN; n],
          converged: false,
          residual_norm: NaN
      })
    - No audit ledger entry signals Hardened-mode rejection.

For bicg / cgs / bicgstab (regardless of mode):
    - Same behavior as above. Hardened mode gives NO additional safety.
    - Users migrating from scipy expecting Hardened rejection are silent-
      failure surprised.

Additional context:

- The direct solver path at line 420 correctly implements the OR pattern:
  `options.check_finite || options.mode == RuntimeMode::Hardened`. So the
  crate author KNEW the correct pattern but failed to propagate it to
  iterative solvers. This is a copy-paste-drift bug, not a design oversight.

- Per mhuk (audit ledger not emitted for 9 families), sparse iterative
  solvers are already in the Hardened-audit-gap list. This bead adds
  granularity: sparse direct solve has CORRECT check; sparse iterative
  solve has INCORRECT check.

- IterativeSolveOptions::default() sets check_finite = true (line 525),
  so default callers are safe via the Strict-mode path. Only explicit
  check_finite=false triggers the bug for cg/gmres. For bicg/cgs/bicgstab,
  check_finite is never consulted so default doesn't help.

- For bicg/cgs/bicgstab, the IterativeSolveOptions.check_finite field IS
  still declared but unread. That's a dead-field defect (like 95ld's
  mode: String for cluster cases).

Fix:

1. For cg and gmres: replace
       if options.check_finite && (...)
   with
       if (options.check_finite || options.mode == RuntimeMode::Hardened) && (...)

2. For bicg, cgs, bicgstab: add the same finiteness guard as cg, with
   the OR-Hardened gate:
       let must_check = options.check_finite || options.mode == RuntimeMode::Hardened;
       if must_check && (a.data().iter().any(|v| !v.is_finite())
                         || b.iter().any(|v| !v.is_finite())) {
           return Err(SparseError::NonFiniteInput { ... });
       }

3. Consider extracting a shared `validate_iterative_inputs(a, b, x0, &options)`
   helper and calling it from each of the 5 solvers. Eliminates drift.

4. Add regression tests: construct a NaN-containing CSR matrix, call each
   iterative solver with mode=Hardened and check_finite=false. Each should
   return Err(NonFiniteInput). Currently all return Ok with NaN solution.

5. Emit audit-ledger fail-closed entries (addresses mhuk's sparse portion).

Related: mhuk (audit ledger for 9 families), i9vw/y0z8/ljmg/4q0g/48tv/1dpl
(NaN fail-open class), 95ld (mode String dead for cluster/etc), z1vz
(solve_circulant silent singularity masking, no Hardened path). This bead
is the sparse-iterative branch of the Hardened-mode contract defect tree.
close_reason: Added a shared iterative finite-input validator for cg/gmres/bicg/cgs/bicgstab, added Hardened-mode regression tests, and verified with rch cargo test/check/clippy for fsci-sparse.

title: [perf][ndimage] hoist per-pixel toggle reads out of sample_interpolated / compute_axis_support
description:
Found by scripts/audit_toggle_reads_in_loops.py --callsites (pass 2), 2026-08-18, NO BUILD.

## The shape

A toggle read at the TOP of a function body is invisible to a lexical "read inside a loop"
scan, but if that function is itself called per element the barrier lands in exactly the
same place. Pass 2 looks for this: fns holding a top-level toggle read, called from inside
a loop. 301 such fns (unambiguous names, shipping files only), 18 call sites in loops.

Of the 18, three are per-element or near it. The rest are per-step / per-panel /
per-iteration / per-axis and are not worth touching.

## Ranked candidates

1. STRONGEST -- `NDIMAGE_SPLINE_OFFSET_DISABLE`, read at crates/fsci-ndimage/src/lib.rs:1920
   in `sample_interpolated`, which is called ONCE PER PIXEL from `shift`
   (crates/fsci-ndimage/src/lib.rs:9745) and from the parallel closure above it, and by the
   other geometric transforms. The in-tree comment states these transforms run ~800 ns/pixel.
   The toggle does not merely select a value: it decides BOTH whether taps get pre-multiplied
   by stride AND which leaf consumes them, i.e. it gates a branch the compiler could otherwise
   specialise out of the whole pixel loop. That is the same mechanism measured on splu, where
   the cost was the lost specialisation and not the load.

2. SAME FAMILY, DEEPER -- `NDIMAGE_BSPLINE_COMPACT_DISABLE`, read at lib.rs:1818 in
   `compute_axis_support`, called from `sample_interpolated` at lib.rs:1922 once PER AXIS PER
   PIXEL. Fixing (1) without (2) leaves a per-pixel read in place.

3. MODERATE -- `MEDIAN_FORCE_SORT`, read at lib.rs:7571 in `median_of_values`, called per
   GROUP from `median` at lib.rs:8133 (serial and threaded arms both). Each call does a
   `to_vec()` plus quickselect, so its own work is large relative to one relaxed load. Listed
   for completeness; expect little and do not spend a build on it alone.

## Proposed fix, same as the splu fix

Read the toggle ONCE at the caller (`shift` / `zoom` / `affine_transform` / `map_coordinates`),
pass it as a plain `bool` parameter, and branch OUTSIDE the pixel loop. Byte-identity is the
contract: the toggle selects between two paths already asserted byte-identical, so hoisting
changes only where the decision is made.

## PREREGISTERED GATE -- and it must check BOTH costs

frankenscipy-xup61 died because its gate checked one of two costs and licensed a design whose
real cost was elsewhere. Do not repeat that. Before implementing, bound BOTH:

  (a) FREQUENCY -- confirm the read really is per pixel, by counting reads per transform call
      on a `cfg(test)` counter (structural counts survive instrumentation barriers, so a test
      binary is legitimate for this half). Expect reads == pixels for (1), reads ==
      pixels*ndim for (2).

  (b) SPECIALISATION -- the half that decides the lever. A hoist that removes N cheap loads
      but does not let the compiler specialise the pixel loop is worth nothing. Measure it as
      an A/B of two SHIPPING binaries (hardcoded-const arm vs toggle arm) alternated in ONE
      window, per verify-paired-interleaved-beats-absolute. Do NOT read cost off a test
      binary: cfg(test) counters in this path are themselves barriers.

Acceptance: (b) shows a separation outside the A/A null. If (a) confirms per-pixel frequency
but (b) is null, report the null -- that is the interesting result, because it would bound the
splu finding as specific to that kernel rather than general.

## Not established

The scanner is a name-based approximation of a call graph. It resolves only names defined
exactly once tree-wide and cannot see trait dispatch, function pointers or stored closures, so
other instances may exist that it cannot reach. It also cannot see trip counts -- "called from
inside a loop" was cleared to these 3 by hand-reading all 18.
notes:
2026-08-18 RainyPrairie -- THE HOIST IS ALREADY DONE; GATE (a) WAS NOT. Both candidates
(1) and (2) are resolved once by SplineFlags::resolve() outside the pixel loop, and
sample_interpolated takes the resolved pair as its eighth parameter with a comment
citing this bead. So the implementation this bead asks for exists.

WHAT WAS MISSING IS THIS BEAD'S OWN PREREGISTERED GATE (a), and the gap is real:
nothing structural stops a later edit moving resolve() back inside the loop, and the
symptom is INVISIBLE -- results stay byte-identical and only the specialisation is
lost, so no existing test would notice. The exact failure the hoist prevents can
return silently.

LANDED (unbuilt): a cfg(test) counter on resolve(), plus a test asserting it runs a
small constant number of times for a 64x64 = 4096-pixel shift.

 - It measures a COUNT, NEVER A COST. This bead is explicit that cfg(test) counters in
   this path are optimisation barriers, so gate (b) -- the half that decides whether
   the lever is worth anything -- must remain an A/B of two SHIPPING binaries. A
   structural count is what survives instrumentation: a counter perturbs timing but
   cannot change how many times a call happens.
 - The bound is LOOSE ON PURPOSE: at most 4 per worker, floor 16, not exactly 1. The
   claim is an order of magnitude (1-ish vs 4096), and the parallel arm legitimately
   resolves once per worker, so an exact count would fail on a different core count
   for no defect.
 - MUST-HIT: the counter must move at all. A resolve never called (refactored past)
   would report 0 and trivially satisfy any "not per pixel" bound -- the gate would
   pass hardest exactly when the knob had been dropped.

STILL OPEN, and it is the deciding half: gate (b), the specialisation A/B of a
hardcoded-const arm against the toggle arm, alternated in ONE window on shipping
binaries. Unmeasured, unclaimed. Until it runs, the hoist is a structural improvement
with no performance number attached -- which is the honest status, and is what
frankenscipy-xup61 got wrong by licensing a design off one of two costs.

Candidate (3), MEDIAN_FORCE_SORT, remains untouched. The bead says expect little and do
not spend a build on it alone; I agree and did not.

TWO TESTS, COMPLEMENTARY — 2026-08-18. Neither should be removed as a duplicate of the other.

Another agent is concurrently adding `van22_knob_read_is_per_transform::
resolve_runs_per_transform_not_per_pixel` to `crates/fsci-ndimage/src/lib.rs`, together with
a `SPLINE_FLAGS_RESOLVE_COUNT` counter in `SplineFlags::resolve`. I have not touched or
staged their work.

They test DIFFERENT halves of the same claim, and the lever is only established if BOTH hold:

- **theirs — FREQUENCY.** Counts resolves across one 64x64 transform and asserts ~1 rather
  than ~4096. This is the half that proves the hoist actually HAPPENED. Without it, a
  refactor that quietly reintroduced a per-pixel read would still pass any identity test,
  because a per-pixel read returns the same value.

- **mine — IDENTITY.** Runs `shift` with `NDIMAGE_SPLINE_FLAG_HOIST_DISABLE` set and clear and
  asserts the outputs are bit-identical. This is the half that proves the hoist changed
  NOTHING. Without it, a hoist that resolved once but resolved WRONGLY — reading the knob
  before a caller set it, or transposing the two flags — would pass any frequency test,
  because the count would be right and the answer wrong.

A frequency test cannot see a wrong value; an identity test cannot see a restored per-pixel
read. That is why the pair is not redundant.

never reaches the spline sampler, so both arms would run identical code and the comparison
would be vacuous. Theirs sizes the fixture so per-pixel and per-transform counts differ by
orders of magnitude, which is the same reasoning applied to the other half.

it, that is fine — the same thing happened with a wilcoxon test earlier today and nothing was

title: [parity][linalg] eig real-eigenvalue eigenvector wrong when matrix has complex-eigenvalue Schur blocks above it
description: eig() built right eigenvectors for real eigenvalues by plain back-substitution on the Schur factor T, treating T as strictly upper-triangular. When a 2x2 complex-conjugate block sits above the real eigenvalue's index, T is only quasi-upper-triangular (nonzero subdiagonal inside the block); the back-sub ignores that coupling, so A v = lambda v fails (residual 0.098 on [[0.5,-1.2,0.3],[1.1,0.4,-0.2],[0,0.6,0.9]] whose real ev ~0.987). Eigenvalues were always correct. Fix: solve the leading quasi-triangular system (T[0:bc,0:bc]-lambda I) y = -T[0:bc,bc] via LU, which accounts for the 2x2 blocks; fall back to Schur column if singular (defective). Found via new diff_eig probe vs scipy 1.17.1 (residual now 2e-16).
close_reason: Fixed in 037bf8c9 via leading-submatrix LU solve; residual 0.098->2.2e-16; 391 lib tests pass

title: [CRITICAL] correctness: complex_sqrt in fs-special violates principal-branch convention for z with -0 imaginary (sqrt(-1 - 0i) returns +i instead of -i)
description:
Review-mode audit on 2026-04-22 found an identical bug in TWO copies of complex_sqrt:

- crates/fsci-special/src/error.rs:450-462
- crates/fsci-special/src/elliptic.rs:1029-1041

Both use:
    let imag = if z.im < 0.0 { -imag_mag } else { imag_mag };

In Rust, `-0.0_f64 < 0.0_f64` returns `false` (IEEE 754: -0 == +0). So for z = (x, -0.0) with x < 0, the imaginary-sign branch is WRONG: imag gets +imag_mag instead of -imag_mag.

Verification:
    buggy: complex_sqrt(-1.0 - 0.0i) = (0, +1.0)   # i.e. +i
    correct: numpy.sqrt(-1-0j) = -1j, cmath.sqrt(complex(-1,-0.0)) = -1j

This violates the principal-branch convention for sqrt along the negative real axis (the branch cut). The C99 / IEEE 754 convention — and what scipy/numpy implement — is:
    sqrt(-x + 0i) = +i*sqrt(x)   (upper half-plane approach)
    sqrt(-x - 0i) = -i*sqrt(x)   (lower half-plane approach)

Our impl collapses both onto the upper-half-plane branch, losing the ±0 distinction.

Impact (cascades through every caller of complex_sqrt):
- lambertw_complex_initial_guess (elliptic.rs:569-588) uses complex_sqrt(branch_delta*2) near z = -1/e. For z = (-1/e - 0i)+ε where ε has negative imag part, the initial guess's sign of imag is flipped → Newton iterates to the wrong branch.
- erfinv_complex_initial_guess (error.rs:375-390) uses complex_sqrt twice in the Winitzki formula. For y = (x, -0) with |x| near 1, the initial guess is conjugated incorrectly.
- complex_gauss_legendre_elliptic_f / _e (elliptic.rs:1043-1058) uses complex_sqrt to compute elliptic integrand. Conjugation symmetry ellipk(m̄) = ellipk(m)* is broken when m has -0 imag.
- Any function downstream of these (lambertw, wrightomega_complex, erfinv, erfcinv, ellipe, ellipk, ellipeinc, ellipkinc) fails the canonical identity f(z̄) = f(z)* when the input carries -0.

Fix:
1. Replace `z.im < 0.0` with `z.im.is_sign_negative()` in BOTH copies:
       let imag = if z.im.is_sign_negative() { -imag_mag } else { imag_mag };

2. Consolidate the two copies into a shared helper crate or a shared module in fsci-special to prevent future divergence.

3. Add regression tests for the principal-branch convention:
       assert_eq!(complex_sqrt(Complex64::new(-1.0, -0.0)), Complex64::new(0.0, -1.0));
       assert_eq!(complex_sqrt(Complex64::new(-1.0,  0.0)), Complex64::new(0.0,  1.0));
       // Conjugation symmetry:
       for sample z with z.im != 0: assert complex_sqrt(z.conj()) == complex_sqrt(z).conj();

Related: frankenscipy-0acr (fuzz EdgeF64 range) and frankenscipy-tmti (new complex fuzz harnesses) — once fixed, these harnesses should include ±0-imag sweeps to catch any re-regression.
close_reason: Fixed signed-zero branch handling in both complex_sqrt copies and added regression coverage

title: fsci-stats: Burr12.pdf and LogLaplace.pdf wrong at x=0 boundary
description: Burr12.pdf and LogLaplace.pdf in crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs short-circuit to 0 for x <= 0, but at x=0 the formulas have shape-dependent limits per scipy. Burr12.pdf(0) = c·d·x^(c-1)/(1+x^c)^(d+1) → +∞ for c<1, → d for c==1, → 0 for c>1. LogLaplace.pdf(0) = c/2·x^(c-1) for x<1 → +∞ for c<1, → 1/2 for c==1, → 0 for c>1. title: [infra] the convert-claim beads' pre-registered contracts require a build route the standing rules forbid
description:
SURVEYED 2026-08-17 (PeachSummit) while looking for the top ready capability bead. Five P1
conversion beads are un-actionable under the current operating rules, and the reason is a
contradiction between their pre-registered evidence contracts and the standing build rules --
not a lack of effort or a missing measurement.

THE CONTRACTS REQUIRE:
  bxnn7  (TruncWeibullMin)  strict rch exec --base plus --clean-overlay
  afz21  (quad_many)        strict rch --base --clean-overlay --no-overlay
                            WITH shared /data/tmp/cargo-target
  llznz  (minimize_many)    rch --base --clean-overlay
  44mb8  (dblquad_many)     rch --base --clean-overlay
  2b7tr  (ndtri SIMD)       strict rch --base --clean-overlay --no-overlay
                            AND stable /data/tmp/cargo-target   [assigned SilverRiver]

THE STANDING RULES SAY THE OPPOSITE, every tick:
  "RCH_CARGO_WRAPPER_BYPASS=1 exported, never the shared cargo-target,
   ONE build per pane, env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR"

So a binary built under the current rules cannot honestly record the BINARY_BUILD_ROUTE its
contract demands, and the harnesses echo that value into the row as provenance. There are
only three honest resolutions and all of them are decisions, not work:

  (a) amend the contracts to accept a bypassed local build with the route recorded truthfully
  (b) grant a scoped exception so these specific conversions may use rch and the shared target
  (c) leave them blocked and say so, rather than leaving them at P1 READY where each new
      agent re-discovers the conflict

WHY THIS IS WORTH A BEAD RATHER THAN A SHRUG. These sit at the top of `br ready` as P1 with no
blockers recorded, so they read as available work. I picked one up, built its binary, and only
then found the conflict -- and the bead's own notes show a previous agent (also me) had
already spent a build slot on it and stopped for a different reason. The queue is
mis-signalling availability, which costs a build slot per agent who tries.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT: frankenscipy-y9bzw covers /data/tmp/cargo-target being 333G against 60G
free. That is about the target's SIZE. This is about whether it and the rch route may be used
at all. Fixing one does not fix the other.

ALSO BLOCKING bxnn7 INDEPENDENTLY: agent-mail health_check is red on the critical
integrity_check verdict, and its harness requires TRJ_BOOKING_CLAIM_MESSAGE_ID
unconditionally. The ledger precedent records that running with claim id 0 "independently
forbids a KEEP", so that route cannot satisfy a conversion bead.

title: [HIGH] correctness: wrightomega_complex_scalar computes via lambertw(exp(z)) — overflows for z.re>~709 and uses wrong branch for arbitrary complex z
description:
Review of crates/fsci-special/src/convenience.rs:2012-2036:

    fn wrightomega_complex_scalar(z: Complex64, mode: RuntimeMode) -> Result<Complex64, SpecialError> {
        ...
        let lambertw = crate::elliptic::lambertw(&SpecialTensor::ComplexScalar(z.exp()), mode)?;
        ...
    }

Two distinct bugs:

1. **Overflow**: `z.exp()` overflows for z.re > ~709 (since exp(709) ≈ f64::MAX). For z = (1000, 1), `exp(z)` returns `Complex(inf, inf*sin(1))`. Then lambertw(inf) → NaN. But wrightomega(z) for large z.re has a clean asymptote: Ω(z) ≈ z - ln(z). Instead of computing asymptotically, our impl returns NaN or wrong values.

2. **Wrong branch**: The identity Ω(z) = W₀(exp(z)) ONLY holds on a specific strip of the principal branch of Ω. Outside that strip — specifically when Im(z) ∈ (-∞, -π] ∪ [π, ∞) — Ω(z) uses OTHER branches of W (not W₀). Our impl uses ONLY W₀ via the principal lambertw call.

Concrete example: For z = (0, 2π), scipy wrightomega(0 + 2πi) gives a specific value (on the closure of the principal strip). But lambertw(exp(0 + 2πi)) = lambertw(1 + 0i) = Ω (a constant ≈ 0.5671), which is Ω(0), NOT Ω(0 + 2πi). These are DIFFERENT values. The current impl returns the wrong one.

3. **Minor**: line 2017 handles only (Inf, 0) for z.re infinite; misses (Inf, y≠0), (-Inf, y), (y, ±Inf). All return complex_nan silently.

Verification (run in scipy):
    from scipy.special import wrightomega
    # Principal strip:
    wrightomega(0 + 0j)     ≈ 0.5671 + 0j    (principal branch Ω(0))
    # Outside principal strip:
    wrightomega(0 + 2*3.14j) ≈ <specific complex value, NOT Ω(0)>
    # Large real:
    wrightomega(1000 + 0j)   ≈ 1000 - ln(1000) = 993.1  (asymptotic)

Fix:
1. Port scipy's actual wrightomega algorithm (Lawrence/Corless/Jeffrey series). It has explicit branch handling and asymptotic forms.
2. At minimum, handle large |z.re| asymptotically: if z.re > ~700, return z - z.ln() with a few Newton refinement steps.
3. Do NOT delegate to lambertw — the branch structure differs.

Impact: all conformance tests that exercise wrightomega in complex domain with large |z| or outside the principal strip are silently wrong. frankenscipy-tmti new harness, when built, will catch this immediately.

Related: jthj (wrightomega_scalar clamp bug), 276r (complex_sqrt branch bug), tmti (new complex fuzz harness).
close_reason: Replaced lambertw(exp(z)) shortcut with direct omega solve for overflow-safe complex branch handling

title: fsci-stats: Lomax missed in vngzr entropy fix despite clean closed form
description: REVIEW MODE finding cross-reviewing 0433c65/vngzr. Lomax was in the missing-entropy list but skipped in the batch. Closed form for unit-scale Lomax(c): H = 1 + 1/c − ln(c). Derivation: pdf = c/(1+x)^(c+1) for x ≥ 0; -∫ pdf log pdf dx = -log(c) + (c+1)·E[log(1+x)]; E[log(1+x)] = 1/c via the substitution u = 1+x; so H = -log(c) + (c+1)/c = 1 + 1/c - log(c). Will add the entropy override and pin the closed form.
close_reason: Cross-reviewing 0433c65/vngzr found Lomax was in the missing-entropy list but skipped in the batch. Added closed-form H(Lomax(c)) = 1 + 1/c − ln(c). Derivation: pdf = c/(1+x)^(c+1) for x ≥ 0; E[log(1+x)] = 1/c via the substitution u=1+x; so H = -log(c) + (c+1)·(1/c) = 1 + 1/c - log(c). Sanity: c=1 (exponential limit) → H = 1 + 1 - 0 = 2 (matches Exponential(λ=1) entropy). Regression test pins the formula at c=2 and c=1. fsci-stats --lib: 1025 → 1026 passing.

title: [special][parity] fresnel C off ~1e-3 at large x: wrong asymptotic f/g coefficients and g normalization
description: fresnel_asymptotic (x>=6) uses wrong auxiliary-function series. f-term recurrence uses (2n)(2n-1)/(pi x^2)^2 but A&S 7.3.27 needs (4m-1)(4m-3); g-term uses (2n+1)(2n) but needs (4m+1)(4m-1); and g is divided by pi x^2 instead of pi^2 x^3. Net: fresnel C(50) ours 0.499873 vs scipy 0.499999 (1.3e-3 off), C(10) 1.7e-4, non-monotonic in x (a coefficient bug, not truncation). S happened to be much closer. Correct A&S form: f=(1/(pi x)) sum (-1)^m (4m-1)!!/(pi x^2)^{2m}, g=(1/(pi^2 x^3)) sum (-1)^m (4m+1)!!/(pi x^2)^{2m}, C=1/2+f sin(t)-g cos(t), S=1/2-f cos(t)-g sin(t), t=pi x^2/2. Validated ~1e-15 vs scipy.
close_reason: Shipped: corrected A&S 7.3.27/28 f,g auxiliary series ((4m-1)(4m-3), (4m+1)(4m-1), g/(pi^2 x^3)). fresnel C was ~1e-3 off at large x; now ~1e-15 vs scipy for both S and C. 954 lib tests green.

title: [perf][linalg] dense-eigh gap: WY-blocked reduction REJECTED (slower); real levers = SIMD dsymv + Cuppen D&C
description:
UNIFYING dense lever (measured 2026-07-23): all dense factorizations ~2x slower, one root cause = serial per-step Householder reduction. Quick angles EXHAUSTED: (1) per-step parallel = REJECT d3c6f9679 (spawn-bound); (2) inverse-iteration/back-transform already parallel; (3) contiguous inner loops autovectorize, strided matvec is a gather — no SIMD win; (4) qr is nalgebra (needs full native replacement). ONLY fix = WY-blocked reduction.

IMPLEMENTATION PLAN (fresh focused session; native fsci reductions = symmetric_eigh_native tridiag + golub_kahan_bidiagonal_reduction; NOT qr which is nalgebra):
INCREMENT 1 (isolated, testable, no prod wire-in): form_compact_wy_t(V: n x nb reflector-vector panel) -> T (nb x nb upper-tri) s.t. Q = I - V*T*V^T = product of the nb individual reflectors (LAPACK dlarft). Test: Q_wy == reflector-product to ~1e-13; pure fn, flag-gated, not integrated. De-risks the WY math.
INCREMENT 2: blocked symmetric tridiagonalization (dsytrd/dlatrd): process columns in panels of nb; dlatrd computes the nb tridiagonal columns + the W = A*V*T panel while DEFERRING the trailing update; then ONE rank-2k symmetric update A22 -= V*W^T + W*V^T (dsyr2k) via the existing par_dmatmul (BIG, parallel, amortizes spawn - NOT the per-step wall). Gate n>=512. Byte-TOLERANCE gate vs the current unblocked symmetric_eigh_native (eigenvalues ~1e-9, residual <1e-8 - the native contract; eigh is tolerance-based not bit-exact). EIGH_BLOCKED_TRIDIAG_FORCE_UNBLOCKED A/B. Expected: closes most of eigh 2.73x (reduction is 57%; dsyr2k BLAS-3 ~= LAPACK).
INCREMENT 3: blocked bidiagonalization (dgebrd/dlabrd) for svd - same pattern, two-sided (left+right panels), rank-2k update. Closes svd 2.2x.
RISK: dlatrd/dlabrd panel factorization is subtle (deferred-update bookkeeping); build increment-by-increment with the byte-tolerance gate at each. Portable std::simd + par_dmatmul only; NEVER link LAPACK. cc/CopperFalcon 2026-07-23.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: REJECT (2026-07-23 CopperFalcon): Increment 2 built + validated (blocked dsytrd/dlatrd, eigenvalues match unblocked to 1e-11 across n<=257) but MEASURED 0.5-0.81x SLOWER than the fused unblocked reduction across n{512,1024,1500}xnb{8..64}, worsening with n. The premise was WRONG: the per-column symmetric matvec (~half the reduction) is irreducibly BLAS-2 (reflector k+1 depends on the trailing matrix updated by reflector k) so it CANNOT become a rank-2k/dsyr2k op; only the deferred trailing update is BLAS-3, and its saving is eaten by within-panel block re-reads (cache-thrash) + lost matvec+update fusion. The compact_wy_*_replay 1.9x that seeded this bead measured blocked-APPLY vs un-fused RE-application, not the fused reduction => not representative. So WY-blocking is NOT vndri-independent and does NOT close eigh/svd/qr. Real levers: SIMD dsymv (the BLAS-2 half dominates) + Cuppen D&C; blocked-reduction retry ONLY with a vndri-parallel rank-2k sweep. Full mechanism+table in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md. Code kept #[allow(dead_code)] as tridiagonalize_symmetric_blocked (validated-correct, not wired).

title: fsci-stats: anderson() applies Stephens correction to statistic instead of critical values; critical values N-independent
description:
fsci-stats anderson() at lib.rs:18596 has TWO defects vs scipy.stats.anderson(dist='norm'):

DEFECT A (statistic):
  fsci line 18645: a2_star = a2 * (1.0 + 0.75/N + 2.25/N^2)
  scipy 1.17.1 _morestats.py: returns RAW A2 as the statistic; the (1+0.75/N+2.25/N^2) factor is applied to the *critical values* (divide), NOT to the statistic.

DEFECT B (critical_values):
  fsci anderson_critical_values_norm() returns FIXED [0.576, 0.656, 0.787, 0.918, 1.092] regardless of N.
  scipy: critical = around(_Avals_norm / (1.0 + 0.75/N + 2.25/N^2), 3)

REPLICATION (N=12 bimodal data [-2.5, -2.4, -2.2, -2.0, -1.8, -1.5, 1.5, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.4, 2.5]):
  scipy: stat=1.147 crit=[0.520, 0.585, 0.698, 0.810, 0.960]
  fsci:  stat=1.237 crit=[0.576, 0.656, 0.787, 0.918, 1.092]

FIX:
  1. lib.rs:18645 — change `statistic: a2_star` to `statistic: a2` (drop the multiplier).
  2. anderson_critical_values_norm(n) — apply / (1.0 + 0.75/n + 2.25/n^2), then round to 3 decimals; take n into account.

Existing fsci-stats unit tests at lib.rs:30040+ are loose threshold assertions and will continue to pass after the fix.

title: linalg: sez4r's bounding recipe uses the WRONG eps for SVD -- f64::EPSILON is 5x tighter than SVD::new's, and shifts results by an ulp silently
description:
Split out of frankenscipy-x3kr0 by RainyPrairie 2026-08-19. Found while building the convergence
probe, and it outlives that bead: x3kr0 closed as a negative and left its sites alone, but this
trap is armed for anyone who later bounds an unbounded nalgebra constructor anywhere in the fleet.

THE TRAP. sez4r's bounding recipe is

    try_new(m, f64::EPSILON, 30 * n.max(10))

That is CORRECT for Schur::new and SymmetricEigen::new, both of which pass
T::RealField::default_epsilon() unscaled. It is WRONG for SVD::new, which routes through
new_unordered (nalgebra-0.33.3 svd.rs:92-100) and passes

    T::RealField::default_epsilon() * crate::convert(5.0)

A bare f64::EPSILON is therefore a 5x TIGHTER deflation threshold than the arm being replaced.
The bounded call makes different deflation decisions and returns different numbers.

MEASURED, not theorised: 805 of 2400 SVD cases differed, worst relative gap 7.215e-16, and NONE
was a reordering (0 of 805 were the same multiset in a different order). Roughly one ulp. Fixing
the eps to f64::EPSILON * 5.0 took it to 0 of 12000.

WHY THIS IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY WRONG. An ulp is small enough to pass any tolerance test
in the suite and small enough to pass review -- the change reads as "just adding an iteration
bound", which is a pure-safety framing, while it silently moves results. And a bound is exactly
the kind of change someone applies in bulk across several sites at once.

HOW IT WAS CAUGHT, worth recording because inspection did NOT catch it: the CONTRAST between two
arms of the same probe. The symmetric arm, where the eps happened to match, showed 0 of 5600 while
the SVD arm showed 805 of 2400. Two arms disagreeing about one claim made the harness the suspect.
Had the probe covered only SVD, 805 mismatches would have looked like a nalgebra defect; had it
covered only symmetric_eigen, the trap would not have surfaced at all.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE THIS:
  (a) a short doc note wherever the bounding recipe is recorded (sez4r's ledger row and any
      CLAUDE.md/contributor guidance), stating the per-constructor eps explicitly; and
  (b) preferably a tiny test asserting SVD::try_new(m, f64::EPSILON * 5.0, K) is bit-identical to
      SVD::new(m) on a fixture family, so the constant is pinned by something executable rather
      than by a comment -- the same reason the accuracy contracts from drqu7 prefer an assertion
      to an argument.

Verify the same question for any OTHER nalgebra constructor before bounding it: read what eps its
convenience form actually passes rather than assuming default_epsilon().

title: [interpolate] BSpline + make_interp_spline foundation
description:
## Goal
Implement the BSpline class and make_interp_spline factory — the foundation for all modern scipy.interpolate functionality. SciPy deprecated interp1d in favor of BSpline-based APIs.

## What to implement
- `BSpline` struct: stores knots t, coefficients c, degree k. Methods: `__call__(x)` (evaluate), `derivative(nu)`, `antiderivative(nu)`, `integrate(a, b)`.
- `make_interp_spline(x, y, k=3)`: construct interpolating BSpline from data points. Solves banded linear system for coefficients.
- `make_lsq_spline(x, y, t, k=3)`: least-squares BSpline with given knots.

## Why this matters
BSpline is the backbone of scipy.interpolate. CubicSpline, UnivariateSpline, and 2D splines all use B-splines internally. Without this, we cannot build the rest of the interpolation stack.

## Implementation approach
- B-spline basis evaluation via de Boor recursion (Cox-de Boor algorithm)
- Knot insertion for make_interp_spline: not-a-knot BCs by default
- Banded matrix solve for coefficient computation (reuse fsci-linalg solve_banded)
- Store in crates/fsci-interpolate/src/bspline.rs

## Testing requirements
- Unit tests: BSpline evaluation at knots, between knots, outside domain
- Interpolation: make_interp_spline reproduces polynomial data exactly for degree <= k
- Derivative: d/dx of cubic spline matches analytic derivative of test functions
- Integration: integrate() matches quad() for simple polynomials
- Edge cases: k=0 (piecewise constant), k=1 (linear), single-segment spline
- Round-trip: make_interp_spline then evaluate at original x recovers y
- At least 12 tests with descriptive names and tolerance documentation
close_reason: Implemented BSpline, make_interp_spline, make_lsq_spline with derivative/antiderivative/integrate. 15 new tests, 43 total.

  eigh_tridiagonal([],  [])     -> ValueError: d (0) must have one more element than e (0)
  eigh_tridiagonal([],  [1.0])  -> ValueError: d (0) must have one more element than e (1)
  eigh_tridiagonal([1,2],[3,4]) -> ValueError: d (2) must have one more element than e (2)
OURS (crates/fsci-linalg/src/lib.rs:7328): 'if n == 0 { return Ok((vec![], ...)) }' sits BEFORE the length check, so d=[] returns an empty spectrum for ANY e whatsoever -- including eigh_tridiagonal([], [1.0, 2.0]), which is not a tridiagonal matrix under any reading.

THIS IS A DELIBERATE SCIPY CONTRACT, NOT AN INCIDENTAL CRASH, which is the distinction that decides whether to mirror it: scipy emits its own formatted message naming both lengths. The rule len(d) == len(e)+1 has NO solution at n=0, so n=0 is unconditionally invalid. We already enforce exactly this rule for n>0 -- the early return is a hole in a check we otherwise agree with, not a difference of opinion about the contract.

DO NOT WIDEN THIS. The same sweep found scipy raising at eigh_tridiagonal([1.0], []), eig_banded(0x0), signm(0x0), expm_cond(0x0) and simpson([]), but each of those is an INCIDENTAL numpy error surfacing from inside ('setting an array element with a sequence', 'zero-size array to reduction', 'need at least one array to concatenate', 'index -1 is out of bounds'), not a validated contract -- a 1x1 tridiagonal matrix with empty e is perfectly well defined and we handle it. Mirroring incidental crashes would be copying scipy's bugs. Only the formatted d/e length validation is being adopted.

NEGATIVE CASES a fix must pass: eigh_tridiagonal([1.0], []) must still succeed and return [1.0]; the existing n>0 mismatch rejection must keep working; no production caller relies on the empty-OK path (grepped: only the conformance differential test and doc references).

FIX: reject n==0 with the same InvalidArgument the length mismatch already uses.
close_reason: Fixed in a92a51d24. n==0 now returns InvalidArgument naming both lengths, matching scipy's deliberate 'd (0) must have one more element than e (N)'. The old eigh_tridiagonal_empty test PINNED the divergence and was replaced by a two-arm test (three e lengths refused; 1x1-with-empty-e and a genuine 3x3 still solved). 539/539 fsci-linalg lib on vmi1227854.

title: [signal] Chebyshev, Elliptic, Bessel IIR filter design
description:
## Goal
Implement the remaining IIR filter design functions beyond Butterworth, AND add bandpass/bandstop support to the filter design infrastructure. Currently we only support lowpass and highpass.

## What to implement
**New filter types (analog prototypes):**
- `cheby1(N, rp, Wn)`: Chebyshev Type I (equiripple passband, monotonic stopband). rp = max passband ripple in dB.
- `cheby2(N, rs, Wn)`: Chebyshev Type II (monotonic passband, equiripple stopband). rs = min stopband attenuation in dB.
- `ellip(N, rp, rs, Wn)`: Elliptic/Cauer filter (equiripple both bands). Sharpest transition for given order but has ripple everywhere.
- `bessel(N, Wn)`: Bessel/Thomson filter — maximally flat group delay (best for pulse-shape preservation).
- `iirfilter(N, Wn, btype, ftype)`: general IIR filter design dispatcher.

**Bandpass/bandstop support (extends ALL filter design functions including existing butter):**
- Add `FilterType::Bandpass` and `FilterType::Bandstop` variants
- Implement lowpass-to-bandpass frequency transformation: s → (s² + ω₀²)/(s·BW) where ω₀ = √(ω_low·ω_high) and BW = ω_high - ω_low
- Implement lowpass-to-bandstop transformation: s → (s·BW)/(s² + ω₀²)
- These double the filter order (N poles → 2N poles)
- Update Wn to accept 2-element array [low, high] for bandpass/bandstop

## Why this matters
Different applications need different filter characteristics. Audio often uses Butterworth, comms uses Chebyshev, control uses Bessel. Bandpass filters are essential for isolating frequency bands (radio tuning, EEG band extraction). Without bandpass/bandstop, users cannot do basic frequency-band isolation.

## Implementation approach
- All follow the same pattern as butter(): compute analog prototype poles → frequency transform → bilinear transform
- Chebyshev I: poles on ellipse. ε = √(10^{rp/10}-1), poles at sinh(asinh(1/ε)/N)*sin(θ_k) + j*cosh(asinh(1/ε)/N)*cos(θ_k)
- Chebyshev II: inverse of Type I (zeros on imaginary axis at ±j/cos(θ_k))
- Elliptic: requires complete elliptic integrals (use fsci-special ellipk/ellipe/ellipj) for pole/zero computation via Landen transformation
- Bessel: poles from reverse Bessel polynomial B_N(s). Use recursion: B_0=1, B_1=s+1, B_{n+1}=(2n+1)B_n + s²B_{n-1}

## Dependencies
- Extends existing butter() pattern in fsci-signal
- Elliptic filter depends on fsci-special elliptic integrals (ellipk, ellipe)
- Should output SOS form via filter conversions bead (preferred for stability)

## Testing requirements
- Chebyshev I: passband ripple ≤ rp dB, verify at cutoff frequency
- Chebyshev II: stopband attenuation ≥ rs dB
- Elliptic: both passband ripple and stopband attenuation meet specs
- Bessel: group delay is approximately flat in passband (verify via finite-difference phase derivative)
- Bandpass butter: pass frequencies between [wn1, wn2], reject outside
- Bandstop butter: reject frequencies between [wn1, wn2], pass outside
- Order doubling: bandpass butter(2, [0.2, 0.4]) produces order-4 filter
- iirfilter dispatcher: ftype="butter" matches butter(), ftype="cheby1" matches cheby1()
- At least 14 tests (2 per filter type + 4 for bandpass/bandstop)
close_reason: Implemented elliptic (Cauer) IIR filter design with pole/zero computation, iirfilter dispatch, and 4 tests. All IIR filter families now complete: Butterworth, Chebyshev I/II, Bessel, Elliptic with lowpass/highpass/bandpass/bandstop support.

title: [HIGH] conformance: scipy_special_oracle.py has no per-function tolerance contract — Rust comparator is on its own
description:
Review-mode audit of scipy_special_oracle.py emission (lines 211-234):

The oracle emits bit-exact float values with no tolerance hint. The schema is:
    { case_id, status, result_kind, result: {value|values}, error }

No 'tolerance' / 'abs_tol' / 'rel_tol' / 'regime' fields. The Rust conformance runner (crates/fsci-conformance/tests/e2e_special.rs + evidence_p2c006.rs) must invent tolerances per case. This has two failure modes:
- Tolerance too tight: oracle emits a value near epsilon of representable precision (e.g., gammainc(huge_a, tiny_x) ≈ 0), Rust impl is within ulp budget but diverges by 1 ulp, runner reports mismatch.
- Tolerance too loose: covers real bugs (e.g., branch-cut error of ~1e-4 looks like noise).

What SciPy does upstream: its test suites ship per-function 'rtol' values (see scipy/special/tests/test_data.py). For complex-domain and near-singularity cases, tolerances are explicit (1e-10 for gamma near poles, 1e-13 for erf, etc.).

Ask:
1. Extend the oracle output schema with a 'tolerance' block per case:
     "tolerance": { "abs": 1e-12, "rel": 1e-10, "regime": "near_pole" | "tail" | "bulk" }
2. Populate per-function defaults from a constants table seeded from scipy's own rtol declarations. Over-ride per-case when the fixture provides an explicit tol.
3. Update Rust comparators (crates/fsci-conformance/src/comparison.rs or equivalent) to consume the tolerance block instead of hard-coding constants.
4. Document in DISCREPANCIES.md any function where the Rust impl must use a looser tol than scipy's (with the reason).

This also unblocks frankenscipy-n3au (CI wiring) since a per-case tolerance makes fail/pass decisions deterministic across workers.
close_reason: Special differential currently compares against fixture expectations directly; there is no live special-oracle tolerance consumer to extend

title: fsci-signal: correlation_lags(Same) panics when in2=0 and in1 odd
description: correlation_lags(in1, in2, Same) in crates/fsci-signal/src/lib.rs panics when in2=0 and in1 is odd (and similar edge cases). Computation: full = arange(-(in2-1)..in1), mid = full.len()/2, lag_bound = in1/2. For odd in1 the slice is full[(mid-lag_bound)..(mid+lag_bound+1)]. For (in1=5, in2=0): full=[1,2,3,4], mid=2, lag_bound=2, slice = full[0..5] — out of bounds → panic. scipy's correlation_lags clamps to the array size and returns [1,2,3,4]. Fix: clamp the upper slice index to full.len(). Add regression test for the (in1>0, in2=0) and odd-in1 corner. Found via REVIEW MODE cross-review of port 28244b7.
close_reason: [LOW] REVIEW MODE finding in correlation_lags port (28244b7): when in2=0 and in1 is odd (e.g., (5, 0) or (3, 0)), the Same-mode slice upper bound exceeded full.len() and Rust panicked. scipy.signal.correlation_lags handles this via numpy's lazy slicing (returns the truncated tail), so the in1=5, in2=0 case returns [1, 2, 3, 4] in scipy. Fix: clamp the slice indices in Same mode to full.len() via .min(n) and saturating_add. Also added two REVIEW MODE regression tests confirming N>D behavior for lp2bp and lp2bs (which scipy handles cleanly — fsci already matches; the tests lock that contract in). 3 new tests: (1) lp2bp_ba_handles_n_greater_than_d; (2) lp2bs_ba_handles_n_greater_than_d; (3) correlation_lags_handles_zero_in2. fsci-signal --lib: 444 → 447.

title: [opt] root(method='anderson') diverges — no globalizing line search / unregularized mixing
description: scipy.optimize.root(method='anderson') converges on standard systems; fsci's anderson DIVERGES to ~±1e10 / inf. Two systems probed (diff_root): x0²+x1²=4,x0·x1=1 → fsci anderson x=[-271726,...] (scipy [1.93,0.518]); and a 3-eq system → fsci anderson errors NonFiniteInput (scipy converges [1,1,1]). Root cause: fsci's anderson (root.rs ~1529) takes the RAW Anderson-mixed step x_{k+1}=x_k+beta·f_k - Σγ_j(Δx_j+beta·Δf_j) with NO globalization — no line search ensuring ‖F‖ decreases, and the least-squares normal equations (ΔFᵀΔF)γ=ΔFᵀf are unregularized → ill-conditioned → huge γ → divergence. scipy's nonlin framework wraps every Anderson/Broyden step with a residual-decreasing line search (_nonlin_line_search) AND regularizes with w0 (adds w0²‖ΔF‖² to the normal-equation diagonal, default w0=0.01), M=5. Fix: add backtracking on the step until ‖F(x_new)‖<‖F(x)‖ (same globalization pattern as hybr/minimize), and add the w0 diagonal regularization. broyden1/broyden2 likely need the same line search (broyden1 also diverged on the 3-eq system). hybr already fixed (7a19b2b1, LM-damped singular fallback).
close_reason: Anderson FIXED (280dc60c): w0 Tikhonov regularization of the mixing normal equations stops the divergence — anderson now converges to [1.93185,0.51764] on the ill-conditioned system (was [-2.7e5,...]) and reaches resid ~2e-7 on the 3-eq system (was inf overflow). broyden1's s2 divergence: a globalizing line search DOES stop it but interferes with Broyden's quasi-Newton mechanism (needs non-monotone steps to build the Jacobian approx) — it broke 3 passing broyden1 tests, so reverted. broyden1 on the 3-eq system reports conv=false honestly (scipy's broyden1 also fails there, resid 1.3e-2); not a divergence-to-NaN, acceptable. Anderson — the primary subject — fixed; 259 fsci-opt tests green.

title: [special] Orthogonal polynomial roots + quadrature weights: roots_legendre, roots_chebyt, etc.
description:
## Goal
Implement root-finding and Gauss quadrature weight computation for orthogonal polynomials. These are essential for high-accuracy numerical integration.

## What to implement
- `roots_legendre(n)` → (x, w): nodes and weights for Gauss-Legendre quadrature on [-1,1]
- `roots_chebyt(n)` → (x, w): Gauss-Chebyshev quadrature (closed-form: x_k = cos(π(2k+1)/(2n)))
- `roots_hermite(n)` → (x, w): Gauss-Hermite quadrature (for ∫f(x)e^{-x²}dx)
- `roots_laguerre(n)` → (x, w): Gauss-Laguerre quadrature (for ∫f(x)e^{-x}dx on [0,∞))
- `roots_jacobi(n, alpha, beta)` → (x, w): general Gauss-Jacobi quadrature

## Why this matters
Gauss quadrature with n points integrates polynomials of degree 2n-1 exactly. This is the gold standard for numerical integration accuracy. roots_legendre is used by any high-accuracy quadrature code.

## Implementation approach
- Golub-Welsch algorithm: construct symmetric tridiagonal matrix from recurrence coefficients, then compute eigenvalues (= roots) and eigenvectors (→ weights). Uses fsci-linalg eigh_tridiagonal or direct tridiagonal eigensolver.
- Chebyshev roots have closed-form expressions (no eigenvalue solve needed)

## Dependencies
- Depends on eval_* polynomial functions for verification
- Uses fsci-linalg eigenvalue routines

## Testing requirements
- roots_legendre: nodes are in (-1,1), weights sum to 2, symmetric about 0
- Quadrature accuracy: ∫x^k dx from -1 to 1 using Gauss-Legendre with n points exact for k < 2n
- Chebyshev: roots match closed-form cos() values
- Hermite: ∫x^{2k} e^{-x²} dx via Gauss-Hermite matches Γ((2k+1)/2)
- At least 8 tests
close_reason: Completed

title: fsci-stats: ExponWeibull.pdf wrong at x=0 boundary
description: ExponWeibull.pdf in crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:20122 short-circuits to 0 for x<=0, missing the shape-dependent limit at x=0. Formula: a·c·(1-exp(-x^c))^(a-1)·exp(-x^c)·x^(c-1). As x→0+: (1-exp(-x^c)) ~ x^c, so the product behaves as a·c·x^(c·a - 1). Limit: c·a < 1 → +∞; c·a == 1 → a·c (= 1 when both=1); c·a > 1 → 0. scipy.stats.exponweib agrees on the clean cases (returns inf for a=c=0.5; 1 for a=c=1; 0 for a=c=2). REVIEW MODE finding generalizing the boundary-pdf rotation.
close_reason: [LOW] REVIEW MODE finding generalizing the boundary-pdf rotation: ExponWeibull.pdf in crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs short-circuited to 0 for x<=0, missing the shape-dependent limit at x=0. Mathematical limit: as x→0+, (1-exp(-x^c)) ~ x^c so the formula a·c·(1-exp(-x^c))^(a-1)·exp(-x^c)·x^(c-1) reduces to a·c·x^(c·a-1). Limit governed by c·a: <1→+∞, =1→a·c (=1 for a=c=1 case), >1→0. New code branches on c·a vs 1 at x=0. scipy.stats.exponweib agrees on the clean cases: pdf(0; 1, 1)=1, pdf(0; 0.5, 0.5)=inf, pdf(0; 2, 2)=0. Note scipy returns nan for some mixed regimes (a=3,c=0.5 etc.) where the mathematical limit is well-defined; fsci is more correct than scipy in those corners. Regression test pins all three c·a regimes plus outside-support. fsci-stats --lib: 1044 → 1045.

title: [infra][conformance] rch workers demand the SciPy oracle but have no scipy — every live-oracle conformance test fails remotely
description:
Found by ChartreuseChapel 2026-08-04 while verifying frankenscipy-lkjll and 6pdfn.

The rch fleet is in a self-contradictory state for fsci-conformance:
  (a) the workers have NO scipy installed, and
  (b) the workers behave as though FSCI_REQUIRE_SCIPY_ORACLE is SET.

Each conformance harness contains, on the oracle-failure path:
    assert!(std::env::var(REQUIRE_SCIPY_ENV).is_err(), "<name> oracle failed: {stderr}");
which passes only when the variable is UNSET (is_err() == true). So the assert
firing is proof the variable is set in the remote environment. Combined with (a),
every live-SciPy differential test fails on every worker.

OBSERVED, two independent targets, neither touched by the work that found this:
  cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test diff_sparse_laplacian
    panicked at diff_sparse_laplacian.rs:208
    'laplacian oracle failed: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named scipy'
  cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test diff_sparse_lsqr
    panicked at diff_sparse_lsqr.rs:237
    'lsqr oracle failed: ...'
  cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test diff_sparse_iterative_solvers
    panicked at :396 'iter_solvers oracle failed: ModuleNotFoundError'
Locally the variable is NOT set (env | grep -c FSCI_REQUIRE_SCIPY_ORACLE -> 0)
and scipy 1.17.1 + numpy 2.4.3 ARE importable, so this is purely a worker-side
configuration.

WHY THIS IS P1: it means NO agent can verify a conformance change remotely, and
the documented workflow (RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo test) cannot be
satisfied for the crate whose entire purpose is differential parity against
SciPy. It is also unfixable from the agent side:  refuses
non-compilation commands ([RCH-E301]), so a worker cannot even be probed with
, and Claude Code's PreToolUse hook offloads bare
, so the tests cannot be run locally where scipy DOES exist without
a force_local override, which is forbidden.

Note the two halves are individually defensible and only the COMBINATION is
broken. Setting the variable is good practice — it is what stops a harness
silently skipping and reporting a green pass over a column that tested nothing
(the exact defect fixed in diff_sparse_iterative_solvers for minres). Having no
scipy on a build worker is also reasonable. Together they are a wall.

FIX OPTIONS, in preference order:
1. Install scipy+numpy in the workers' python3 (matching the local pin, scipy
   1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.3, so oracle values do not drift between hosts). This is
   the only option that makes live-oracle tests actually verifiable remotely.
2. UNSET FSCI_REQUIRE_SCIPY_ORACLE on the workers. Cheap, but it converts every
   live-oracle test into a silent skip on the fleet, which is strictly worse for
   integrity than the current loud failure. Only acceptable alongside (3).
3. Independently of the above: prefer PINNED SciPy values over live-oracle calls
   for new parity tests, so they assert on every runner. Precedent: 79425155a
   (linkage Z-matrices at 1e-12) and e8cd0af89 (a full 64-element SciPy solution
   with the cross-solver spread recorded). This is what the 6pdfn/9y533 work did
   precisely because of this blocker.

EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test diff_sparse_lsqr green
via RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1, with the oracle arm genuinely comparing rather than
skipping (assert a non-zero compared-case count, as the iterative-solvers
harness already does).
close_reason:
Fixed via option 1 (install scipy on the workers) and verified end-to-end 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey).

MECHANISM (the missing half of the diagnosis): the env var is not set in any worker
shell rc -- I grepped /etc/environment, /root/.bashrc, /root/.profile, /etc/profile.d
on four workers and found nothing. It comes from the repo: workspace-root .rch.env
contains BOTH 'FSCI_REQUIRE_SCIPY_ORACLE=1' AND
'RCH_ENV_ALLOWLIST=CARGO_TARGET_DIR,FSCI_REQUIRE_SCIPY_ORACLE', so rch forwards the
flag into the remote test process. Combined with no scipy on the workers, every
live-oracle test failed remotely -- exactly as reported.

FIX: installed the pinned oracle stack on ALL 11 rch workers, matched to this host
exactly (scipy 1.17.1, numpy 2.4.3) so oracle values cannot drift between runners.
Verification sweep via the SAME interpreter the harness spawns (bare 'python3'), all
11 now report 'scipy 1.17.1 numpy 2.4.3':
  ovh-a vmi1149989 vmi1152480 vmi1153651 vmi1156319 vmi1167313
  vmi1227854 vmi1264463 vmi1293453 hz1 hz2
Two install hazards, both remediated: hz1/hz2/vmi1149989 carry a distro numpy with no
RECORD file, so pip refused to uninstall it and ABORTED the whole transaction (scipy
never landed) -- fixed with --ignore-installed; ovh-a silently kept debian numpy 2.2.4
while installing scipy, a version drift that would have skewed oracle values -- also
corrected to 2.4.3. NOTE: hz1/hz2 run python 3.14.4 vs 3.13.7 elsewhere; scipy/numpy
versions match, which is what determines oracle output.

CLOSING EVIDENCE (as specified in this bead): cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test
diff_sparse_lsqr via RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- ran on ovh-a, 'test
diff_sparse_lsqr ... ok', 1 passed 0 failed, remote exit=0. This is the exact target
that previously panicked with 'lsqr oracle failed: ModuleNotFoundError: No module
named scipy'.

NON-VACUOUS, as the bead required: diff_sparse_lsqr had NO compared-case assertion --
every case could 'continue' and all_pass would be vacuously true. Added the guard
(commit 3b5fae67c), mirroring the diff_sparse_iterative_solvers precedent. Emitted
artifact fixtures/artifacts/FSCI-P2C-004/diff/diff_sparse_lsqr.json now shows
case_count=3 (3 of 3 compared, zero skips), max_abs_diff=7.99e-15 vs live SciPy.

TWO-ARM CONTROL: MUST-HIT = the green run above. MUST-MISS = re-ran with a deliberately
invalid kwarg passed to spl.lsqr so every oracle case raised; the new assertion fired,
'lsqr compared zero cases; ... Skipped 3 of 3 case(s)', test FAILED, remote exit=101.
That proves the guard is real and that WITHOUT it this harness would have reported
green over an empty column. Probe reverted by targeted edit; grep for
fsci_negative_control returns nothing and git status for the file is clean.

title: [integrate] sampled integrators match short-input SciPy parity
description: Code-first fallback from empty br ready and stale cod-b residue. scipy.integrate.trapezoid returns 0.0 for empty and singleton samples, and scipy.integrate.simpson returns 0.0 for singleton samples. fsci_integrate currently rejects these short sampled inputs before any interval is evaluated. Preserve simpson empty-input errors, return zero for the SciPy-defined short-input cases, and add inline parity coverage. code-first, batch-test pending
close_reason:
Closed 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey) as VERIFIED ALREADY IMPLEMENTED, both halves, with SciPy re-measured rather than taken from the bead.

SCIPY, measured today (scipy 1.17.1) -- exactly as the bead describes:
    trapezoid([])    -> 0.0
    trapezoid([5.0]) -> 0.0
    simpson([])      -> RAISES IndexError
    simpson([5.0])   -> 0.0

FSCI, crates/fsci-integrate/src/quad.rs, matches that split precisely:
  - trapezoid :927 -- 'if y.len() < 2 { return Ok(0.0) }' covers BOTH the empty
    and singleton cases in one guard.
  - simpson :984 -- errors on empty ('need at least 2 points for Simpson\'s
    rule'), then :988 returns 0.0 for len == 1. So the bead\'s requirement to
    'preserve simpson empty-input errors' while returning zero for the
    SciPy-defined short cases is exactly what the code does.

COVERAGE: trapezoid_short_inputs_return_zero_like_scipy :5335,
simpson_singleton_returns_zero_like_scipy :5492, simpson_empty_input_errors
:5501, plus the cumulative variants at :5594, :5799 and :5805.

Worth noting the tests are sharper than they look: the singleton cases pass NaN
and INFINITY as the x coordinates. That proves the zero-return short-circuits
BEFORE validate_sample_coordinates, which is the ordering SciPy implies (it
returns 0.0 for a singleton regardless of x). A naive implementation that
validated coordinates first would return an error and fail these.

Nothing to implement; no test written, since writing one would be duplicate coverage.

title: fsci-stats: brunnermunzel_alternative one-sided pvalues are inverted vs scipy
description:
fsci brunnermunzel_alternative at lib.rs:20384 calls student_t_alternative_pvalue(w, ...) with the standard t-test convention: 'less' → cdf(w), 'greater' → sf(w). But scipy.stats.brunnermunzel uses the inverted convention because W > 0 corresponds to mean_ry > mean_rx (y stochastically greater than x):
  scipy 'less' (H1: x < y)    → sf(w)   → small for positive w
  scipy 'greater' (H1: x > y) → cdf(w)  → large for positive w

REPLICATION (x=1..10, y=5..14, w≈3.43):
  scipy 'less' pvalue=0.0015,    fsci pvalue=0.9985 (diff 0.997)
  scipy 'greater' pvalue=0.9985, fsci pvalue=0.0015 (diff 0.997)

Two-sided pvalues match (sf(|w|) is symmetric).

FIX: at lib.rs:20384, before calling student_t_alternative_pvalue,
swap 'less' ↔ 'greater':
  let scipy_alt = match alternative {
      "less" => "greater",
      "greater" => "less",
      other => other,
  };

This preserves the standard t-test helper for other callers.
notes: Fixed in same tick. lib.rs:20384 swap 'less' ↔ 'greater' before passing to student_t_alternative_pvalue, since scipy's brunnermunzel uses inverted alternative semantics from the standard t-test (W > 0 means mean_ry > mean_rx). Updated unit test test_brunnermunzel_alternative to assert the corrected scipy-aligned semantics. All 4 brunnermunzel unit tests pass; diff_stats_brunnermunzel.rs (24 cases × 4 fixtures × 3 alts × 2 arms) ships green.

title: [special] sindg/cosdg/tandg/cotdg use naive (x*pi/180).sin() — up to ~1000 ULP off scipy (cephes octant reduction)
description: fsci degree-trig computes (x*pi/180).cos()/.sin()/.tan() after only handling exact 90-multiples. scipy uses cephes sindg.c/tandg.c which reduce the angle in DEGREES (mod 360, then octant mod 45) before converting a small residual to radians, keeping the polynomial argument small. Result: fsci is off scipy by up to ~540 ULP (sindg), ~995 (tandg), and huge near zero crossings (cosdg/cotdg ~5e12 ULP at near-zero values, abs ~1e-16). cosdg(60): fsci 0.5000000000000001 vs scipy 0.49999999999999994. Fix: port cephes sindg/cosdg/tancot (sincof/coscof polys; P/Q for tan) for bit-for-bit parity. Found via diff_degtrig probe vs scipy 1.17.1.
notes: INVESTIGATION (session 2026-06-12): scipy poles ALL return +inf/0 (tandg(±90)=+inf, cotdg(0)=+inf) — current naive code already matches via rem_euclid(180) special cases (no -inf bug in current code). scipy's tandg algo is AMBIGUOUS: matches a faithful cephes-tancot port to 0 ULP at large angles (359.3, 1234.5) where naive is 183-3139 ULP off, BUT matches naive libm to 0 ULP at 89.9999 where cephes is 59072 ULP off — neither pure approach is bit-for-bit. No scipy C source on disk to disambiguate. Reductions tested: reduce-mod-360→345 ULP worst, reduce-mod-180→411 ULP; both 10x better than naive (3139) with NO regression at common angles, but NOT bit-for-bit (near-pole/zero FP amplification is fundamental + FMA differences). CONCLUSION: bit-for-bit blocked w/o scipy source; a non-regressing reduce-mod-360 is the realistic ceiling (~345 ULP). Low priority vs cleaner parity wins elsewhere.
close_reason: tandg/cotdg ported to cephes tancot (modulo-180 octant reduction); differential sweep of 4598 pts matches scipy.special.tandg/cotdg at 0 ULP (was ~1000 ULP). Commit d2e5de59.

title: integrate: exactly-BANDED Newton factorization for BDF (method-of-lines class) — design + identity obligations ledgered
description: Follow-on to frankenscipy-43vfn (diagonal Newton, landed 109.37x at n=512). Same frame: dense LU::new = 67.44% self at n=256. Target: method-of-lines PDE discretizations, the dominant real stiff-ODE workload; our BDF has no sparsity option at all, so a tridiagonal n=512 problem pays 45 Mflop per factorization where 1.5 Kflop suffices. Full design + the four bit-identity obligations against nalgebra 0.35 GEPP (reciprocal-multiply not divide; column-major axpy operand order; icamax first-max tie-break; zero-pivot 'continue' not error) are written up in docs/perf_ledger_cc.md 2026-07-25 DESIGN row. Detect (kl,ku) in the SAME per-Jacobian scan that computes jac_diagonal and cache it on the solver - the cadence rule, which cost 7.4x when violated on the diagonal lever. PRE-REGISTERED KILL CONDITION: if bitmism != 0 on a tridiagonal fixture, do NOT ship behind a tolerance contract - a factorization that changes bits changes the step sequence and therefore the public SolveIvpResult; ledger and stop.
close_reason: LANDED 6095f2b6e. BDF exactly-banded Newton factorization, bit-identical, DECIDED at every size: 1.754x@n=64, 3.765x@n=128, 9.392x@n=256, 5.845x@n=512 (A/A nulls 0.969-1.012). Target frame confirmed by profile first: LU::new 83.42% self on the tridiagonal fixture, 91.1% with the two triangular solves. KEY FINDING that changed the design: band-clipped GEPP CANNOT reproduce dense GEPP once it pivots (multipliers migrate down their column without bound per interchange, and active rows carry their column extent) - caught by banded_lu_is_bit_identical_to_dense_lu, which was written specifically to reach the branch a diagonally dominant PDE fixture never exercises. Shipped design instead CHECKS strict column diagonal dominance up front (preserved by elimination => no interchange possible) and declines otherwise; nothing is claimed for matrices that would pivot. Honest limit ledgered: ratio saturates and falls at n=512 because the path still materialises the full n x n system per factorization; band storage is the pre-registered next lever, gated on an arm-isolated profile.

title: fsci-stats: riemann_zeta truncation at k=10000 yields large tail error for small a
description: Surfaced by diff_stats_zipf (frankenscipy-54h9n). fsci's riemann_zeta in lib.rs caps the series sum at k=10000 with relative-tolerance criterion 1e-15. For slow-convergent a near 1 the tail integral dominates: a=1.1 yields ~37% error (abs_diff up to 0.376 vs scipy.zeta), a=1.5 yields ~3e-3, a=2 yields ~4e-5, a=3 yields ~3.5e-9. Fix candidates: (a) raise the loop cap to 1e6 with adaptive Euler-Maclaurin tail correction; (b) replace with scipy-style hurwitzeta + identity ζ(s) = sum_{k=1}^N k^{-s} + N^{1-s}/(s-1) - N^{-s}/2 + … . title: [perf][parity][integrate] BDF solver stuck at order 1 (implicit Euler); Radau aliases BDF — ~40x too many steps vs scipy
description:
Found via diff_lsoda_vdp probe (stiff van der Pol mu=10, t in [0,20], rtol=1e-6 atol=1e-9) vs scipy.integrate.solve_ivp 1.17.1:

  method   fsci steps / nfev      scipy steps / nfev
  LSODA    27022 / 91958          835 / 1750
  BDF      27092 / 92160          641 / 1797
  Radau    27092 / 92160          460 / 3599

fsci y_final=[1.937444,-0.070200] vs scipy [1.939354,-0.070082] (~2e-3 phase drift, consistent with low-order accumulation despite 40x more steps).

ROOT CAUSE (crates/fsci-integrate/src/bdf.rs): BdfSolver is permanently ORDER 1 = implicit Euler. self.order is initialized to 1 (line ~151) and NEVER changed anywhere (no self.order= assignment exists). The predictor is explicit Euler (y+h*f); the corrector is BDF1 (uses BDF_GAMMA[0]); error est = error_const*(y_new-y_predict). The variable-order infrastructure is DEAD CODE: d[k] Nordsieck array, BDF_GAMMA[0..5], BDF_ERROR_CONST[0..5] all exist but only d[0]/d[1] and order index 0 are ever used. Step-growth is also capped hard at 1.5x (line ~345; scipy allows up to ~10x). Net: order-1 needs tiny steps for 1e-6 -> 40x step blowup + extra phase drift.

ALSO (api.rs:867): SolverKind::Radau routes to BdfSolver — Radau is NOT a real implicit Runge-Kutta (Radau IIA) method, just a silent BDF alias (identical 27092 steps confirms).

FIX (multi-hour, two parts):
1. Implement genuine variable-order (1-5) BDF: maintain the full backward-difference/Nordsieck array D[k], predictor = sum of differences, corrector with order-k gamma, error estimates for orders k-1/k/k+1, and scipy-style order+step selection (change_D, n_equal_steps gating, factor up to ~10). This alone should bring BDF to ~600-700 steps.
2. Implement true Radau IIA (3-stage, 5th order implicit RK) as a distinct solver, or at minimum document Radau as a BDF alias.

Verify: VdP step counts within ~2x of scipy + y_final matching scipy to rtol; full fsci-integrate suite green; no regression on existing BDF/LSODA tests. LSODA (separate LsodaSolver) is also 32x off — likely shares the same order-1 BDF core for its stiff mode; audit after BDF fix.
close_reason: Variable-order BDF shipped (b10f0f8e, 27092->642 steps) + genuine Radau IIA shipped (f13c5f4e, 420 steps matching scipy to 6 digits). LSODA already switches RK<->BDF and inherits the BDF fix (632 steps). All three stiff solvers now match scipy; 193 integrate tests green.

title: fsci-sparse: lgmres infinite loop on identity / eigenvector-friendly systems (k=0 lucky breakdown)
description: lgmres_inner detects 'lucky breakdown' when h[k+1][k] ≈ 0 (the next Arnoldi candidate becomes the zero vector). When this happens at k=0 — e.g. solving Ix = b where r0 is itself the only direction needed — it breaks before incrementing k, so y is empty, z is the zero vector, and the function returns (zeros, false, 0). The outer lgmres loop then adds 0 to total_iter and spins forever (while total_iter < max_iter). lgmres_identity_system and lgmres_diagonally_dominant_converges both hang in cargo test. Fix: solve the k=0 system explicitly (y[0] = g[0]/h[0][0], z = y[0]·v[0]) and report converged=true, since g[0]/h[0][0] reduces the residual to floor.
close_reason: Shipped c30a45ba: lgmres_inner now increments k before breaking on lucky breakdown, so the upper-triangular solve covers the final Krylov dimension. The outer lgmres loop terminates cleanly with converged=true and the correct solution. Previously hung indefinitely on A=I and similar eigenvector-friendly systems. title: [special][parity] struve(v,x) large-x catastrophically wrong for v != 0 (struve_asymptotic only handles v=0)

title: [HIGH] fsci-io: mmread always allocates a DENSE rows*cols f64 buffer even for sparse Coordinate-format files — a 60-byte Matrix Market file declaring 1M×1M triggers 8 TB allocation; DoS vector from untrusted MM input AND scipy parity break (scipy.io.mmread returns coo_matrix for sparse)
description:
Review of crates/fsci-io/src/lib.rs on 2026-04-22.

mmread (line 221-411) parses Matrix Market files but allocates a DENSE rows*cols
f64 buffer regardless of whether the file declares 'coordinate' (sparse) or
'array' (dense) format. For a sparse file declaring a large matrix with few
non-zeros, this produces enormous allocations from tiny inputs.

Concrete reproducer (a legal Matrix Market file):

    %%MatrixMarket matrix coordinate real general
    1000000 1000000 1
    1 1 1.0

Parsing this 60-byte input triggers at line 237:

    let dense_len = checked_matrix_len(rows, cols, ...)?;  // 1e6 * 1e6 = 1e12
    let mut data = vec![0.0; dense_len];                    // 8 TB allocation

checked_matrix_len uses checked_mul which only catches arithmetic OVERFLOW, not
'unreasonably large product.' 1e6 * 1e6 = 1e12 doesn't overflow usize on 64-bit
(usize::MAX is ~1.8e19), so the 8 TB vec![] is attempted. Most machines OOM or
swap-death before completing.

For smaller but still problematic cases:
    rows=100_000 cols=100_000 nnz=1:  80 GB allocation
    rows=1_000_000 cols=10_000 nnz=1:  80 GB allocation

Scope of issue:

1. DoS vector from untrusted MM input. A 60-byte file triggers arbitrary memory
   demand. If fsci-io is used in a service that accepts user-uploaded MM files
   (e.g., a sparse matrix loader for a compute service), a single small upload
   crashes the service.

2. scipy parity break. scipy.io.mmread for a coordinate format returns a COO
   sparse matrix (scipy.sparse.coo_matrix) with only the non-zero entries
   materialized. Our mmread returns an MmMatrix with dense data: Vec<f64>, so
   downstream callers that expected sparse efficiency get dense costs.

3. Silent format coercion. The MmMatrix.info.format field is preserved (tells
   you the file was 'coordinate'), but the data field is ALWAYS dense. A
   reviewer might reasonably assume MmMatrix represents sparse matrices
   sparsely; it doesn't.

4. Interacts with 95ld (integrate mode: String dead) indirectly: here the
   info.format field is stored but doesn't change the internal representation.
   The data layout ignores what info.format claims.

5. mmwrite / mmwrite_sparse have the same architectural assumption in the
   write direction: they take a `data: &[f64]` of length rows*cols, so the
   API forces callers to materialize a dense matrix before writing.

Additional finding near line 237: when info.symmetry is Symmetric / Hermitian /
SkewSymmetric, the loop may ADD values to both (r, c) and (c, r) positions
(lines 319-328). For a truly sparse file in symmetric format, the dense output
doubles the memory cost by materializing both triangles (already implied by
dense format but worth noting).

Fix options (pick one):

1. (Minimal) Add a sanity cap in checked_matrix_len OR in mmread specifically:
       const MAX_MM_DENSE_ELEMENTS: usize = 128 * 1024 * 1024;  // 1 GiB of f64
       if rows * cols > MAX_MM_DENSE_ELEMENTS { return Err(TooLarge); }
   This turns the OOM into an early IoError::TooLarge rejection.

2. (Correct) Introduce a sparse output variant:
       pub enum MmMatrixData { Dense(Vec<f64>), Sparse { indices: Vec<(usize, usize)>, values: Vec<f64> } }
   For info.format == Coordinate, populate the Sparse variant. Matches scipy
   semantics and avoids dense blow-up entirely. MmMatrix.data type becomes
   MmMatrixData.

3. (Migration) Add mmread_sparse() that returns (rows, cols, Vec<(row, col, val)>),
   leaving mmread as the dense loader but with a documented upper bound.

Fix priority: option 1 first (security / DoS mitigation), then option 2 as a
proper API fix.

Regression test:
    let mm = "%%MatrixMarket matrix coordinate real general\n1000000 1000000 1\n1 1 1.0\n";
    assert!(mmread(mm).is_err());  // currently OOMs or succeeds with 8 TB

Related: r5tv (complex field rejection, closed -- same fn), the generic 'API
claims sparse but allocates dense' class is new here. 9vmw (FFT plan cache
Potemkin), 95ld (String mode dead), xjav (contract tables dead) are all
surface-claim-vs-reality bugs; mmread fits the same class at the I/O layer.
close_reason: Added a dense Matrix Market read safety cap for coordinate and array loads plus a hostile 1M x 1M coordinate regression test; validated with rch fsci-io targeted test, package check, and package clippy.

title: fsci-special: elliprc(x, y<0) returns NaN — scipy supports Cauchy PV
description: Skill: /mock-code-finder (discovery) → fix. crates/fsci-special/src/elliptic.rs:2539 has a deferred-path comment for y<0 that just NaN-rejects: 'y<0 (Cauchy PV path, deferred) → NaN'. scipy.special.elliprc supports y<0 via the Cauchy principal value: RC(x, y) = √(x/(x−y)) · RC(x−y, −y) for y<0, x≥0 (Carlson 1995). This is a real parity gap. Fix: detect y<0 branch in elliprc, recursively call with mapped args, and update the negative test to assert real-valued behavior. The transform leaves x' = x−y ≥ x > 0 and y' = −y > 0 so the recursion lands in the existing positive path with no further specialization needed.
close_reason: Closed parity gap: elliprc now supports y<0 via Carlson's Cauchy-principal-value identity RC(x, y) = √(x/(x−y)) · RC(x−y, −y), which always lands in the existing positive y' = −y > 0 branch. Updated docstring to mark the branch as a real Cauchy PV (not deferred). Replaced the stale 'returns NaN for y<0' assertion with a positive 3-case Cauchy-PV test covering: (1) RC(1, -1) = √(1/2)·arccosh(√2); (2) RC(0, -1) = 0 (degenerate prefactor); (3) RC(3, -1) = √(3/4)·arccosh(2)/√3. fsci-special --lib: 778 → 779 passing.

title: [conformance][stats] TruncNormal pdf is identically ZERO on [30,40] -- the renormaliser cancels to 0
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Found 2026-08-18 while implementing the generic `truncate` (53cc22836). NO BUILD -- scipy
source read plus live-oracle arithmetic on both arms.

## The defect

`TruncNormal::pdf` (crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs, in `impl ContinuousDistribution for
TruncNormal`) divides by

    let norm = standard_normal_cdf(self.b) - standard_normal_cdf(self.a);

and returns 0.0 when `norm <= 0.0`. For a standard normal on [30, 40] BOTH operands round to
1.0, so `norm` is exactly 0.0 and the pdf is identically zero across the entire support.

    Phi(40) - Phi(30)  =  0.0                       <-- what TruncNormal computes
    S(30)  - S(40)     =  4.906713927147908e-198    <-- the same quantity, kept

    scipy.stats.truncnorm.pdf(30.5, 30, 40) = 8.107714218413067e-06   we give 0.0
    scipy.stats.truncnorm.pdf(32.0, 30, 40) = 3.559136079029236e-26   we give 0.0
    scipy.stats.truncnorm.pdf(35.0, 30, 40) = 8.030621584304054e-70   we give 0.0

MUST-MISS control: on [-1, 2] the two forms agree bit for bit (0.818594614120363717), so the
predicate is not blanket-matching. INTERMEDIATE control: on [5, 10] they already disagree at
the 10th significant digit (2.866515719235352e-07 vs 2.866515718791933e-07), so this is a
continuum, not an edge case -- the erosion starts long before the collapse.

## Fix

Choose the tail: `F(hi) - F(lo)` when `F(lo) + F(hi) <= 1`, else `S(lo) - S(hi)`. Both are the
same exact quantity; the test picks the pair whose difference is not swamped by its operands.
`Truncated::interval_mass` in 53cc22836 is exactly this and can be lifted, or `TruncNormal`
can be reimplemented as a thin wrapper over `Truncated<Normal>`.

Check `cdf`/`sf`/`ppf` on the same type at the same time -- only `pdf` was read closely here,
and `cdf` uses the same `norm`.

## Scope check, done

TruncWeibullMin is ALREADY SAFE: it uses `-(ac - bc).exp_m1()` for the denominator with a
comment explaining the same hazard, so someone fixed that one. TruncPareto uses
`1.0 - x.powf(-b)`, mild by comparison. TruncExpon not read. Do not assume the family shares
the bug -- it does not.

## Related

The generic `truncate` (53cc22836) does NOT have this defect and its test asserts
`TruncNormal::new(30,40).pdf(32.0) == 0.0` as a documented expectation. When this bead is
fixed, that assertion is the one that will fail, and its message says so.
