comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
FIXED in e26949566 (UNBUILT -- disk throttle at the 42G brake, no cargo of any kind).

Seven sites -- pdf, cdf, mean, var, entropy, skewness, kurtosis -- each formed
`standard_normal_cdf(b) - standard_normal_cdf(a)` independently. They now all route through one
private `TruncNormal::mass()` delegating to `interval_probability`, so they cannot drift apart
again.

`cdf` needed TWO changes, not one: its NUMERATOR `Phi(x) - Phi(a)` is also an interval mass and
cancels for the same reason.

Added `sf`, which did not exist -- the trait default had been subtracting, and the upper part of
the interval is exactly where that has already lost its digits. Previously unreachable value now
covered: `scipy.stats.truncnorm.sf(32, 30, 40)` = 1.11114702924630903e-27. `ppf`/`isf` still use
the trait defaults, which now invert a correct `cdf`/`sf`.

The regression guard is the more important test: `[-1, 2]` and `[5, 10]` are pinned to 1e-11
against scipy. A fix that repaired the extreme case while perturbing ordinary use would be a
worse defect than the original, and nothing else in the suite would have caught it. The premise
is asserted on the real arithmetic (`Phi(40) - Phi(30) == 0.0`) so a future pass for a different
reason is distinguishable.

The generic-wrapper suite's expected-failure assertion has been converted rather than deleted:
`Truncated<Normal>` and `TruncNormal` must now AGREE to 1e-12 on the same three points. Two
independent constructions agreeing is a stronger statement than either against scipy alone.

Scope checked, not assumed: `TruncWeibullMin` was already safe (uses `-(ac - bc).exp_m1()` with
a comment about this hazard); `TruncPareto` uses `1.0 - x.powf(-b)`, mild by comparison. Neither
touched.

NEEDS A BUILD before this bead can be closed.

title: [HIGH] fsci-signal: kaiserord / chirp / DLTI::new all use unguarded 'foo <= 0.0' predicates on f64 parameters (ripple, width, t1, dt) — NaN and Inf both pass validation; extends workspace-wide NaN-fail-open class (i9vw/y0z8/ljmg/4q0g); contrast with fsci-special/fsci-fft/fsci-opt/fsci-cluster which correctly use is_finite/is_nan guards
description:
Review of crates/fsci-signal/src/lib.rs on 2026-04-23, extending the
4q0g/i9vw/y0z8/ljmg NaN-fail-open chain into fsci-signal.

Workspace-wide sweep identified at least FOUR public sites in fsci-signal that
use the unguarded `foo <= 0.0` or `foo < 0.0` predicate on f64 parameters from
user input, all vulnerable to NaN fall-through:

Site 1 -- kaiserord (line 5247-5257):
    pub fn kaiserord(ripple: f64, width: f64) -> Result<(usize, f64), SignalError> {
        if ripple <= 0.0 { return Err(...); }
        if width <= 0.0 || width >= 1.0 { return Err(...); }
        ...
    }
    For NaN ripple: NaN <= 0.0 is false -> not rejected.
    For NaN width: NaN <= 0.0 is false AND NaN >= 1.0 is false -> BOTH branches false,
                   not rejected.
    Downstream: ripple is used in beta = 0.1102 * (a - 8.7) etc. For NaN,
                comparisons at lines 5262-5268 all false, beta = 0.0.
                Then numtaps computation uses width (NaN) -> NaN result silently.

Site 2 -- chirp (line 5617):
    pub fn chirp(t: &[f64], f0: f64, t1: f64, f1: f64, method: ChirpMethod)
                 -> Result<Vec<f64>, SignalError> {
        if t1 <= 0.0 { return Err(...); }
        if method == ChirpMethod::Logarithmic && (f0 <= 0.0 || f1 <= 0.0) { return Err(...); }
        ...
    }
    For NaN t1: not rejected -> line 5631 `k = (f1 - f0) / t1` = NaN -> output all NaN.
    For Inf t1: not rejected -> k = 0 -> output is constant cos(2pi*f0*t), misleading.
    For NaN f0 or f1 (non-Log): not caught at all -> passthrough to computation.

Site 3 -- DLTI::new (line 7825):
    if dt <= 0.0 { return Err("sampling period dt must be positive"); }
    Same pattern. NaN dt and Inf dt pass, stored in self.dt, used in eval_at_freq
    where angle = omega * self.dt -> angle = NaN, cos(NaN) = NaN silently.

Site 4 -- find_peaks_cwt / chirp / other spots in the 86KB lib.rs grep likely
to reveal more. This bead groups the three confirmed sites; a full audit may
find 2-4 more.

Fix is the same pattern as fsci-opt::approx_fprime (line 40):

    if !foo.is_finite() || foo <= 0.0 { return Err(SignalError::InvalidArgument(...)); }

or refuse Inf too where it's not legit:

    if foo.is_nan() { return Err(...); }
    if foo <= 0.0 { return Err(...); }

Regression tests:
    kaiserord(NaN, 0.1)          -> Err
    kaiserord(0.1, NaN)          -> Err
    chirp(&[...], 1.0, NaN, 2.0, Linear)      -> Err
    chirp(&[...], NaN, 1.0, 2.0, Logarithmic) -> Err
    DLTI::new(vec![1.0], vec![1.0], NaN)      -> Err

NaN fail-open chain now spans 5 beads across 3 crates:
  i9vw (fsci-integrate validate_first_step/max_step/tol)
  -> y0z8 (fsci-integrate quad/quad_vec/cubature epsabs/epsrel)
  -> ljmg (fsci-integrate BdfSolver unvalidated + RkSolver is_finite guard)
  -> 4q0g (fsci-ndimage gaussian_filter sigma)
  -> THIS BEAD (fsci-signal kaiserord/chirp/DLTI)

Workspace-wide counter-examples (crates that do it correctly):
  - fsci-special (gamma.rs/beta.rs/elliptic.rs -- is_nan() first, then <= 0.0)
  - fsci-fft (validate_finite_complex/real at 2123-2141)
  - fsci-opt (approx_fprime line 40)
  - fsci-cluster dbscan/mean_shift (line 770/1310 -- !foo.is_finite() || foo <= 0.0)

Recommendation: add a clippy lint (or a regression test that scans source) that
flags `if PARAM <= 0.0` on function parameters of type f64 without a preceding
`PARAM.is_finite()` or `PARAM.is_nan()` check. Prevents future drift.

Related: i9vw, y0z8, ljmg, 4q0g (NaN class), wofb / sf() default (precision
loss), s9tt (stringly-typed errors). All symptoms of 'scipy port treats float
parameters as if they're never NaN/Inf' — a workspace-wide cultural gap.

title: [signal] FIR filter design: firwin, firwin2, kaiserord
description:
## Goal
Implement FIR (Finite Impulse Response) filter design functions. FIR filters are guaranteed stable and can achieve exact linear phase — essential properties for many applications.

## What to implement (core)
- `firwin(numtaps, cutoff, window, pass_zero)`: window-based FIR filter design. Creates lowpass/highpass/bandpass/bandstop FIR filters by windowing the ideal sinc response.
- `firwin2(numtaps, freq, gain)`: FIR filter with arbitrary frequency response specification via frequency-sampling method.
- `kaiserord(ripple, width)`: estimate Kaiser window parameters (numtaps, beta) for given specifications.

## Stretch goal (if time permits)
- `remez(numtaps, bands, desired)`: Parks-McClellan optimal equiripple FIR filter design via Remez exchange algorithm. This is significantly more complex than firwin (iterative minimax optimization) and can be deferred.

## Why this matters
FIR filters are the default choice when linear phase is needed (audio, biomedical, communications). firwin is one of the top-5 most used scipy.signal functions. The window method is simpler but remez gives optimal (minimax) designs.

## Implementation approach
- firwin: generate ideal lowpass impulse response (sinc function), multiply by window, normalize for unity gain at DC (lowpass) or Nyquist (highpass). For highpass: spectral inversion. For bandpass: difference of two lowpass filters. For bandstop: spectral inversion of bandpass.
- firwin2: evaluate desired frequency response at DFT frequencies, inverse FFT to get impulse response, multiply by window.
- kaiserord: empirical formulas from Kaiser-1974 relating transition width δ and ripple A to (numtaps, beta). A = -20*log10(δ), beta from Kaiser formula.
- Use existing window functions (hann, hamming, blackman, kaiser) and sinc from fsci-special

## Dependencies
- Uses existing window functions from fsci-signal
- Uses sinc from fsci-special/convenience

## Testing requirements
- firwin lowpass: magnitude at cutoff ≈ -6dB, passband flat, stopband attenuated
- firwin highpass: verify passband at high frequencies
- firwin bandpass: two cutoff frequencies respected
- firwin bandstop: notch at center frequency
- firwin2 arbitrary: matches specified magnitude points
- kaiserord: estimated numtaps reasonable for typical specs (ripple=60dB, width=0.1 → numtaps≈37)
- Linear phase: verify impulse response is symmetric (h[n] = h[N-1-n])
- At least 10 tests
close_reason: Implemented firwin (lowpass/highpass/bandpass/bandstop), firwin2 (arbitrary freq response), kaiserord. 12 new tests, 86 total.

description:
fsci cvm_cdf at lib.rs:17722 returns the asymptotic CDF via the Bessel-K series for ALL n. scipy 1.17 uses a Csörgő-Faraway finite-sample correction at small n that gives noticeably different tail probabilities.   (b) Document the asymptotic precision floor in cvm_cdf docstring and bump cramervonmises tolerance in tests to ~1e-2 for small n.

title: [CRITICAL] correctness: complex_jv_scalar and complex_iv_scalar produce INFINITY for negative-integer orders via Γ(v+1) pole instead of using J_{-n}(z) = (-1)^n J_n(z) identity
description:
Review of crates/fsci-special/src/bessel.rs:2501-2578:

Both complex_jv_scalar and complex_iv_scalar compute the series:
    sum = (z/2)^v / Γ(v+1) * Σ terms

via:
    let log_first = v_c * log_half_z - crate::gamma::complex_gammaln(Complex64::new(v + 1.0, 0.0));
    let mut sum = log_first.exp();

For negative-integer v = -n (n ∈ ℕ), this evaluates complex_gammaln(Complex64::new(1 - n, 0.0)) — a Γ pole. Per frankenscipy-d218, complex_gammaln returns (−∞, φ) silently at such poles. Then:
    log_first = v * log(z) - (-∞) = +∞
    sum = exp(+∞) = ∞

But the correct identity for integer v is J_{-n}(z) = (-1)^n * J_n(z) and I_{-n}(z) = I_n(z), both finite for finite z.

Verification (scipy):
    jv(-1, 1+0j) = -0.4401 - 0j  (our impl returns ~∞)
    jv(-2, 1+0j) = +0.1149 + 0j  (our impl returns ~∞)
    iv(-1, 1+0j) =  0.5652 + 0j  (our impl returns ~∞)

Impact:
- ANY complex-domain call to jv/iv with negative-integer order produces INFINITY instead of the correct finite value.
- yv and kv (at 2583 / 2674) may have similar patterns; audit recommended.
- No fuzz target currently exercises this path (order is treated as f64 and the existing harnesses don't pick negative integers specifically).
- Conformance fixture cases with negative-integer orders in complex domain would expose this — but per v2tz, such cases either don't exist or can't be oracled.

Fix:
1. In complex_jv_scalar: if v < 0 and v.fract() == 0.0 (integer), compute as sign * complex_jv_scalar(-v, z) where sign = if (-v as i64) % 2 == 0 { 1 } else { -1 }.
2. In complex_iv_scalar: if v < 0 and v.fract() == 0.0 (integer), just compute complex_iv_scalar(-v, z) — I_v symmetric under v → -v for integer v.
3. Audit complex_yv_scalar (line 2583) and complex_kv_scalar (line 2674) for similar Γ-pole hazards.
4. Add regression tests:
       assert_close(complex_jv_scalar(-1.0, C(1,0)), C(-0.44005, 0), tol=1e-14);
       assert_close(complex_jv_scalar(-2.0, C(1,0)), C(0.11490, 0), tol=1e-14);
       assert_close(complex_iv_scalar(-1.0, C(1,0)), C(0.56516, 0), tol=1e-14);

Related: d218 (complex_gammaln pole bug — underlying cause), tmti (new bessel_base complex fuzz harness catches this immediately), v2tz (oracle gap means this would slip past conformance).
close_reason: Fixed negative-integer-order handling in complex_jv_scalar/complex_iv_scalar and added regression coverage

title: [signal] Filter conversions: tf2zpk, zpk2tf, tf2sos, sos2tf, zpk2sos, sos2zpk
description:
## Goal
Implement the filter representation conversion functions. These are the plumbing that connects all filter design and analysis functions. SciPy users routinely convert between transfer function (b,a), zero-pole-gain (z,p,k), and second-order sections (sos) forms.

## What to implement
- `tf2zpk(b, a)` → (zeros, poles, gain): find roots of numerator/denominator polynomials
- `zpk2tf(z, p, k)` → (b, a): expand zeros/poles into polynomial coefficients
- `tf2sos(b, a)` → sos: convert to second-order sections (cascade of biquads) — this is the numerically preferred form
- `sos2tf(sos)` → (b, a): expand SOS back to transfer function
- `zpk2sos(z, p, k)` → sos: pair zeros/poles into biquad sections
- `sos2zpk(sos)` → (z, p, k): extract zeros/poles from SOS
- `SosSection` struct: [b0, b1, b2, a0, a1, a2] for one biquad section

## Why this matters
SOS form is essential for numerical stability of high-order filters. Without tf2sos, users cannot safely implement filters above order ~8. Every signal processing textbook recommends SOS form for implementation.

## Implementation approach
- tf2zpk: use companion matrix eigenvalue approach (polynomial root finding via eigenvalues of companion matrix)
- zpk2tf: use polynomial multiplication from roots
- zpk2sos: pair complex conjugate poles, pair with nearest zeros, sort by distance from unit circle for numerical stability
- SOS is a Kx6 array where each row is [b0, b1, b2, 1, a1, a2]

## Testing requirements
- Roundtrip: tf → zpk → tf, tf → sos → tf, zpk → sos → zpk (all within tolerance)
- Known filter: butter(4, 0.3) should give same sos as SciPy reference values
- Stability: tf2sos for high-order filter (order 10+) should preserve magnitude response
- Edge: first-order filter (odd-order sections), purely real zeros
- At least 10 tests
close_reason: Implemented tf2zpk, zpk2tf, tf2sos, sos2tf, zpk2sos, sos2zpk with companion matrix eigenvalue root finding and proper SOS pairing. 11 new tests, 60 total. Unblocks freqz, sosfilt, and advanced IIR beads.

title: [signal] iirnotch and iirpeak: second-order notch/peak filters
description:
## Goal
Implement notch and peak IIR filters used for removing/isolating specific frequencies (e.g. 60Hz hum removal).

## What to implement
- `iirnotch(w0, Q)`: Design second-order notch filter. w0 = frequency to remove (normalized 0-1), Q = quality factor.
- `iirpeak(w0, Q)`: Design second-order peaking filter. Same parameters but boosts instead of rejecting.

## Implementation
- Notch: H(z) = (1 - 2cos(ω₀)z⁻¹ + z⁻²) / (1 - 2r·cos(ω₀)z⁻¹ + r²z⁻²) where r = 1 - BW/2
- Peak: same structure with zeros and poles swapped
- BW = ω₀/Q (bandwidth)

## Testing
- Notch at w0: response at w0 should be near zero
- Peak at w0: response at w0 should be maximum
- At least 4 tests
close_reason: Implemented iirnotch and iirpeak second-order IIR notch/peak filters. Fixed cos(2w0) → cos(w0) bug during testing. 4 tests, all 165 signal tests passing.

title: [parity][special] ncfdtr missing — non-central F CDF not implemented
description: fsci-special lacked scipy.special.ncfdtr(dfn, dfd, nc, f), the non-central F CDF. Implemented as the Poisson(nc/2)-weighted mixture of central regularized incomplete beta values: sum_j e^{-lam} lam^j/j! * I_y(dfn/2+j, dfd/2), lam=nc/2, y=dfn*f/(dfn*f+dfd), summed outward from mode j0=floor(lam) (mode weight in log space). Reuses existing btdtr (regularized incomplete beta). Verified vs scipy 1.17.1 over 500 cases (nc up to 300), max abs err 9.7e-14. Inverses ncfdtri/ncfdtridfd/ncfdtridfn/ncfdtrinc still missing (root-finding, follow-up).
close_reason: Implemented in 9b2a2c25: ncfdtr via Poisson-weighted mixture of central incomplete-beta (btdtr), mode-centered. Verified vs scipy 1.17.1 over 500 cases (nc<=300), max abs err 9.7e-14.

title: [HIGH] fsci-ndimage: gaussian_filter + gaussian_filter_nd use unguarded 'sigma <= 0.0' predicate — NaN sigma returns array-of-NaN silently; Inf sigma triggers vec![0.0; usize::MAX] = 147 EB allocation / OOM; empirically verified NaN and Inf both bypass the reject branch; same class as i9vw/y0z8/ljmg
description:
Review of crates/fsci-ndimage/src/lib.rs on 2026-04-23.

Two public Gaussian filter functions use the unguarded `sigma <= 0.0` predicate
that NaN and Inf silently pass, producing OOM or silently-corrupted output:

Site 1 -- gaussian_filter (line 683-721):

    pub fn gaussian_filter(input: &NdArray, sigma: f64, mode, cval) -> Result<...> {
        if sigma <= 0.0 {
            return Err(...);
        }
        ...
        let radius = (4.0 * sigma).ceil() as usize;
        let ksize = 2 * radius + 1;
        let mut kernel_1d = vec![0.0; ksize];
        ...
    }

Site 2 -- gaussian_filter_nd (or similar, line 2177):

    for (axis, &sigma) in sigmas.iter().enumerate() {
        if sigma <= 0.0 {
            continue;  // skip this axis
        }
        let radius = (4.0 * sigma).ceil() as usize;
        let ksize = 2 * radius + 1;
        let mut kernel_1d = vec![0.0; ksize];
        ...
    }

Empirically verified (rustc probe, 2026-04-23):

    NaN <= 0.0 = false   (NaN sigma NOT rejected)
    Inf <= 0.0 = false   (Inf sigma NOT rejected)

Consequences:

NaN sigma path:
    radius = (4.0 * NaN).ceil() as usize = 0 (NaN saturates to 0 in f64-as-usize cast)
    ksize = 1
    kernel = [exp(-0 / (2 * NaN^2))] = [exp(-0/NaN)] = [exp(NaN)] = [NaN]
    total = NaN
    kernel /= total = [NaN]
    convolve input with [NaN] -> output is all NaN
    Returns Ok(output) with silently-corrupted NaN array.

Inf sigma path:
    radius = (4.0 * Inf).ceil() as usize = usize::MAX (saturating cast)
    ksize = 2 * usize::MAX + 1
      - debug build: panics at arithmetic overflow
      - release build: wraps to usize::MAX
    vec![0.0; usize::MAX] on release tries to allocate 147 EB
      - immediate OOM on any machine
      - DoS vector from a single f64::INFINITY argument

The fix is the same pattern fsci-opt::approx_fprime uses correctly (line 40):
    if !sigma.is_finite() || sigma <= 0.0 { return Err(...); }

For site 2 (multi-sigma), replace continue with return Err(...) OR explicit
is_finite guard, since NaN/Inf should never silently skip an axis vs. legit
zero (which intentionally skips).

Compounds with the general NaN-fail-open chain (i9vw / y0z8 / ljmg in
integrate). Same architectural failure in ndimage.

Scope:

- gaussian_filter is a heavily-used scipy function; any caller passing a
  user-controlled sigma (CLI arg, config value, API parameter) can trigger
  OOM with sigma=Inf or silent NaN output with sigma=NaN.
- Downstream callers in fsci-signal (via scipy_fft_oracle-like usage) may
  propagate NaN through further signal-processing pipelines, masking the
  root cause.

Fix:

1. Replace both sites with is_finite-first predicate.

2. Add regression tests:
       gaussian_filter(input, f64::NAN, mode, 0.0)      -> Err
       gaussian_filter(input, f64::INFINITY, mode, 0.0) -> Err
       gaussian_filter_nd(input, &[1.0, f64::NAN])      -> Err

3. Do a repo-wide audit for the same `foo <= 0.0` / `foo < 0.0` pattern
   on float parameters — this is the fourth appearance of the class:
   - i9vw (validate_first_step / validate_max_step / validate_tol)
   - y0z8 (quad / quad_vec / cubature epsabs/epsrel)
   - ljmg (RkSolver is_finite guard lumps Inf with NaN)
   - THIS bead (gaussian_filter sigma)

Related: i9vw (validate_* NaN fail-open), y0z8 (quad NaN fail-open), ljmg
(BDF/RK asymmetry), 42z1 (mmread DoS), l15l (procrustes divergence).
Pattern: public API surfaces that accept f64 parameters without
is_finite() guards form a workspace-wide class defect.
close_reason: Added finite sigma guards in gaussian_filter and gaussian_filter_multi_sigma plus non-finite regression tests; validated with rch fsci-ndimage non_finite_sigma tests and package check. Package clippy remains blocked by preexisting fsci-spatial warnings unrelated to this bead.

title: [bug] complex loggamma uses principal log(Gamma), off by 2pi*k vs scipy analytic continuation
description: complex_gammaln Re(z)<0.5 reflection branch (ln(pi)-ln(sin(pi z))-lnGamma(1-z)) yields the PRINCIPAL log of Gamma(z), clamping Im to (-pi,pi]. scipy.special.loggamma is the ANALYTIC CONTINUATION whose Im winds by 2pi per unit of negative Re(z). Verified vs scipy 1.17.1: loggamma(-3-1j) ours Im=-2.84 vs scipy +9.73 (off by 4pi); -5: 6pi; etc. Fix: replace reflection with upward recurrence loggamma(z)=loggamma(z+n)-sum_{k}log(z+k) (principal logs accumulate correct winding). gamma/rgamma use exp(+/-loggamma) so unaffected (exp ignores 2pi*i). File exp1 complex ~8.6e-6 accuracy as separate.
close_reason: Fixed: complex_gammaln Re(z)<0.5 now uses upward recurrence loggamma(z)=loggamma(z+n)-sum log(z+k) (principal logs accumulate winding) instead of reflection. Oracle-verified vs scipy 1.17.1: complex loggamma maxrel 1.236 -> 2.68e-15. gamma/rgamma unaffected (3.5e-15, exp ignores 2pi*i). Added complex_loggamma_winding_matches_scipy (6 scipy golden rows). 117 gamma tests pass, clippy clean.

SCIPY, re-measured today (scipy 1.17.1, equal_var=False):
    [1]   vs [2]     -> statistic NaN, pvalue NaN, df 1.0

title: [conformance][sparse] GMRES lucky-breakdown test is absolute: a scaled system gets a FALSE converged=true
description:
Found 2026-08-15 (RainyPrairie) while fixing frankenscipy-degwi, which was the same defect in cg().

crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs:2534 (and the sibling arm at :2881) tests the Arnoldi subdiagonal for breakdown with 'h[j+1][j].abs() < f64::EPSILON * 100.0' — an ABSOLUTE floor on a quantity that carries the scale of A and of b. h[j+1][j] is ||w|| after modified Gram-Schmidt, so it scales linearly with ||A||*||v_j||.

This is MORE severe than the cg() case (degwi), because the branch does not report failure — it declares a lucky breakdown, calls update_solution(), and 'return Ok((true, iters))'. A caller sees converged=true. So for a system where A and b are scaled down (multiply both by 1e-8 and the solution is unchanged), GMRES can stop early on a subspace that does NOT contain the solution and report success with an inaccurate x. A false GREEN, not a spurious RED.

Fix direction: same as degwi — scale the test by the magnitude it is guarding against. The textbook Arnoldi criterion compares the post-orthogonalization norm to the PRE-orthogonalization norm of w (i.e. ||A v_j||): breakdown iff h[j+1][j] <= eps_factor * ||A v_j||. That is invariant to scaling of A and b. Do NOT reuse cg_curvature_floor; the operands differ.

NEGATIVE CASE any fix must pass: (1) an honest lucky breakdown must still be detected — a system whose solution lies exactly in a Krylov subspace of dimension < restart must return converged=true in that many iterations, not run to max_iter; (2) a well-conditioned system with A and b both scaled by 1e-8 must return a solution whose RELATIVE residual ||Ax-b||/||b|| meets the requested tol, verified against the unscaled solve — the current code passes tol at the flag while failing it on the iterate.
close_reason: Fixed in d63ee05a6. Harness: 'cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib' via 'RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec'; worker vmi1227854; 465 passed, 0 failed, 4 ignored. Cited probes: gmres_lucky_breakdown_is_invariant_to_problem_scaling and lgmres_lucky_breakdown_is_invariant_to_problem_scaling (both negative-case clause 2 of this bead: A,b x1e-15, asserting the RELATIVE residual and agreement with the unscaled solution rather than the flag), and honest_lucky_breakdown_still_stops_at_the_first_step (clause 1: A=I is still detected on the first step, <=1 iteration). Scope was larger than the bead described: the absolute Arnoldi floor at :2534/:2881 was one of FOUR absolute floors on scale-carrying quantities in this path -- also the update_solution pivot floor (which left y holding undivided numerators), the LGMRES outer projection clamp dot(az,az).max(EPSILON), and the lgmres_inner entry test r_norm < EPSILON. Fixing only the Arnoldi one left the measured false green in place at 2.09e-9 vs tol 1e-10. Filed frankenscipy-jtzr8 for spsolve_relative_residual, whose silent absolute fallback made the first version of these assertions pass vacuously.

title: [lint][stats] 78 clippy errors in the restored fsci-stats lib (97 all-targets) block the documented gate
description:
Filed by RusticCarp 2026-08-05 while reconciling fsci-stats (frankenscipy-gur9n, restore landed in 5fafe6a0a).

cargo clippy -j2 -p fsci-stats --lib --no-deps -- -D warnings   -> 78 errors
cargo clippy -j2 -p fsci-stats --all-targets --no-deps --keep-going -- -D warnings -> 97 errors

CAUSE, stated plainly: the reconciliation brought back ~14,000 lines that 3a4493248 had deleted. That code was written before several newer clippy lints existed, and its perf bins had not compiled since June, so nothing had linted it in months. This is NOT a behaviour regression — the restored code is byte-for-byte what earned the original measurements — but it DOES make the documented workspace gate fail for this crate, and that has to be paid.

Same shape as fsci-signal, where the equivalent debt was 15 errors and was fixed inline as part of the reconciliation (5eb7d4536). fsci-stats is roughly 6x the volume, which is why it is split out rather than rushed: the dominant class in the other crates was needless_range_loop, and 78 index-to-iterator rewrites in statistical kernels at low attention is how a silent off-by-one gets introduced.

METHOD: get the full list with --keep-going (a plain run stops at the first failing target and hides the rest). Fix in small batches, running cargo test -p fsci-stats --lib between batches — the 2054 lib tests are the safety net, and they include bit-identity gates such as goodness_of_fit_many_match_serial_loop_bit_for_bit that will catch a rewrite that perturbs a numeric loop.

DO NOT blanket-allow a lint class to clear this. Where an allow IS the right answer (flat-buffer numeric kernels tripping too_many_arguments, for example) follow the existing workspace convention — 41 such allows already exist — and give each one a reason.

EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: cargo clippy -p fsci-stats --all-targets --no-deps -- -D warnings exits 0 and cargo test -p fsci-stats --lib stays at 2054 passed / 0 failed.

Measured 2026-08-16 (RainyPrairie), harness 'rch exec -- cargo clippy -j 1 -p fsci-stats <target> -- -D warnings' on RCH_WORKER=vmi1149989: '--lib' exits 0 (Finished, zero errors) and '--all-targets' exits 0 (Finished, zero errors). This bead recorded 78 lib errors and 97 all-targets; both counts are now zero, so its closure condition is met by work a peer landed rather than by anything I did. Closing on that cited evidence rather than leaving a green gate tracked as a blocker, which is its own kind of wrong signal -- an agent reading the ready queue would keep seeing fsci-stats listed as ungateable.

comments.text:
PROGRESS: 78 lib clippy errors => 44. Two batches landed, each its own reviewable slice, suite at 2054 passed / 0 failed throughout.

  ee5c54621  23 cleared: 15 excessive_precision + 8 redundant_closure/contains
  5d1aed5fd  11 cleared: type_complexity, via one `StatPValueMatrices` alias

I deliberately took only the classes with NO behavioural risk, and I am stopping before the rest rather than pushing on at the end of a very long session. The remaining 44 are led by exactly the class this bead warns about.

ONE JUDGEMENT CALL WORTH REVIEWING (ee5c54621): the 15 excessive_precision hits were ALLOWED with a reason, not truncated. They are coefficient tables transcribed verbatim from scipy (KS Stirling series) and Cephes (the exp rational approximation in the KDE path). Every literal parses to exactly the same f64 as its shortest form — verified, so the allow hides no numeric change. They are kept because two are load-bearing as documentation: 9.999_999_999_999_999_999_1e-1 parses to exactly 1.0 and 2.000_000_000_000_000_000_1e0 to exactly 2.0, and shortening them to `1.0`/`2.0` would make the block look like a different, simpler polynomial than Cephes specifies, and stop it being diffable character-for-character against upstream. If a reviewer disagrees, truncating is bit-safe — it is a documentation argument, not a correctness one.

REMAINING 44, by class:
   11  needless_range_loop family (k over w/r/y/wmat/chol, dimension over
       whitened, kk over r, j over w) — THE RISKY ONE. These are inside
       numeric kernels: whitening, Cholesky, weight matrices. An
       index-to-iterator rewrite here is exactly where a silent off-by-one or a
       transposed index hides, and the 2054 tests will catch some but not all
       of those. Do these ONE AT A TIME, reading each loop's bounds, with the
       suite between.
    5  chunks_exact / chunks_exact_mut with constant size => as_chunks::<N>().
       Safe and already done several times elsewhere in this series; note
       as_chunks returns a (chunks, remainder) tuple, so remainder handling has

title: perf: theilslopes/siegelslopes O(n^2)->O(n log^2 n) — band-enumerate collect_theil_slopes_in_interval
description: ROOT CAUSE (profiled, n=4000 105ms, O(n^2) scaling): theilslopes_fast's collect_theil_slopes_in_interval (fsci-stats/lib.rs ~43351) does a nested for i { for j } over ALL n^2 pairs to gather band slopes in (lower,upper] + the 'below' count. The rest of the fast path (sampling, interval estimate, count_le via TheilSlopeOrder inversion count) is already O(n log n) — this final collection scan is the only O(n^2) step. FIX: replace with a CDQ divide-and-conquer (or 2D range-reporting / merge-sort-tree) enumeration of the 3D dominance {i<j in x-sorted order : U_j<=U_i AND L_j>L_i} where U=y-upper*x, L=y-lower*x (slope<=upper <=> U_j<=U_i; slope>lower <=> L_j>L_i). 'below' = inversions in L (count slope<=lower). Band size is bounded by candidate_limit (~O(n)), so enumeration is O(n log^2 n + band). BIT-IDENTICAL: collects the EXACT same slope f64 values ((y_i-y_j)/(x_i-x_j), order-independent) -> select_nth picks the same kth -> same result; verify vs current theilslopes_materialized to exact equality on random data (handle x-ties: exclude vertical pairs, match THEIL_SLOPE_MIN_X_GAP). Beats scipy (also O(n^2)). ~200 lines, multi-turn. Reuse kendall_strict_inversions for the below count.
close_reason: done

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: IMPLEMENTING: replaced collect_theil_slopes_in_interval's O(n^2) nested scan with CDQ divide-and-conquer band-enumeration (theil_cdq_collect): recurse on x-order, merge collects cross pairs (U_b<=U_a AND L_a<L_b) via U-descending sweep + BTreeSet-by-L prefix enumeration. below/upper_count via count_non_strict_inversions_sort. Guards: no-near-x-tie + |x|,|y|<1e150 (else exact O(n^2) scan fallback, kept as collect_theil_slopes_in_interval_scan). VERIFIED BIT-IDENTICAL: test theil_cdq_collect_matches_scan_and_fast_eq_materialized asserts collect_fast==scan (below + slope .to_bits()) AND full theilslopes==theilslopes_materialized (all 4 fields .to_bits()). PERF: n=4000 105->24ms (4.4x). REMAINING: n>=8000 still falls back because select_theil_slope_ranks's SAMPLE-based interval estimate bails (estimated_span>candidate_limit) BEFORE collect — follow-up = iterative count_le binary-search to narrow [lower,upper] until span<=limit, then the now-cheap CDQ collect handles all n.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: DEAD END — CONFIRMED NOT BIT-EXACT-ABLE, do not re-attempt. The CDQ/inversion approach reformulates slope(a,b)=(y_b-y_a)/(x_b-x_a)<=lambda as L_b<=L_a (L=y-lambda*x). Mathematically equal but NOT bit-identical in floating point at the boundary: the scan uses DIVISION then compare; the L-form uses mul/sub/compare — they disagree for pairs whose slope is within rounding of the threshold. The existing test interval_enumeration_matches_full_sort_for_open_closed_bounds picks bounds EXACTLY at pair slopes and asserts the 'below' count bit-exactly -> my CDQ gave below=129 vs 128 (off by one boundary pair). FUNDAMENTAL: a division-based per-pair slope predicate cannot decompose into a per-element key for O(n log n) counting bit-exactly. Implemented + reverted. theilslopes stays O(n^2) (matches scipy, which is also O(n^2)). Closing as wontfix-bit-exact.

IMPLEMENTATION: check_COLA (crates/fsci-signal/src/lib.rs:16314) and check_NOLA (:16332) both route through overlap_add_binsums, which calls validate_real_values_finite(window, 'COLA/NOLA window samples must be finite') at :16288 -- after the nperseg/noverlap/length checks and before any accumulation.     check_COLA(nan) -> False    check_NOLA(nan) -> False
    check_COLA(inf) -> False    check_NOLA(inf) -> True
SciPy returns a bool and never raises. Worth flagging that SciPy returns TRUE for NOLA on an infinite window, which a caller reads as 'safe to invert' -- arguably a worse outcome than an error, and a point in favour of fsci's stricter choice rather than against it.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
CONTRACT CLASSIFICATION BEFORE WRITING ANY GATE (RusticCarp 2026-08-06). This corrects this bead's premise and must be read before implementing it.

The bead — and the instruction that prompted it — asks for "bit-identity gates" for all 53 undriven toggles. THAT IS WRONG FOR 12 OF THEM, and writing a to_bits() assertion there would fail. The failure would then invite exactly the wrong repair: loosening the assertion until it passes.

Classified all 53 by the contract stated in their own doc comment:

  41  claim BYTE-IDENTICAL / BIT-IDENTICAL  -> to_bits() gate is correct
  12  claim WITHIN-ULP / tolerance          -> to_bits() gate would FAIL
   0  with no stated contract

The 12 tolerance levers:
  BHATTACHARYYA_FORCE_SERIAL   CANBERRA_FORCE_SERIAL
  CHEBYSHEV_FORCE_SERIAL       CITYBLOCK_FORCE_SERIAL
  DESCRIBE_REDUCE_FORCE_SERIAL EXPECTILE_FORCE_SERIAL
  GMEAN_W_FORCE_SERIAL         MINKOWSKI_FORCE_SERIAL
  NANSUM_FORCE_SERIAL          PEARSONR_FORCE_SERIAL
  SQEUCLIDEAN_FORCE_SERIAL     TVAR_PAR_FORCE_SERIAL

WHY THEY DIFFER — worked example. SQEUCLIDEAN_FORCE_SERIAL does NOT select serial versus parallel. It selects a 1-accumulator left fold versus a 4-way-unrolled chunk sum. Those REASSOCIATE the additions, so the last bits legitimately differ. Its own doc says so: "the ORIG exact 1-accumulator fold, byte-identical to map(..).sum(); default false fans a 4-way-unrolled chunk sum ... WITHIN per-op ULP tolerance". This is the k-accumulator lever recorded in project memory as explicitly NOT byte-identical.

So the correct deliverable for this bead is A RUNNABLE A/B PER TOGGLE AT ITS OWN STATED CONTRACT, not a uniform bit-identity gate:
  - 41 byte-identical levers  -> assert to_bits() equality
  - 12 tolerance levers       -> assert agreement within the per-op ULP bound the
                                 doc claims, and NEVER silently widen that bound
                                 to make a test pass. If a tolerance gate fails,
                                 that is a finding about the lever, not about the
                                 test.

That distinction is the whole value of doing this carefully. A uniform to_bits() sweep would have produced 12 red tests and enormous pressure to weaken them, which is how a real reassociation defect would get papered over.

SECOND POINT, on sizing. Every gate must be sized ABOVE the lever's work gate or it is vacuous — below the gate both arms take the same path and the comparison proves nothing. The gates are not uniform either; JENSENSHANNON uses JS_MIN_PER_THREAD = 200_000 (so n >= 400_000), while others gate on different constants. Read each one; do not assume a shared threshold.

RECOMMENDED ORDER: do the 41 byte-identical ones first — they are unambiguous and the assertion is exact. Take the 12 tolerance levers last and individually, because each needs its claimed bound read out of its doc and honoured rather than invented.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
HEADER — READ BEFORE WORKING THIS BEAD. Two standing rules and one active hazard.

1. EVERY BYTE-IDENTICAL CLAIM IS A HYPOTHESIS THE EXACT GATE IS TESTING, NOT A FACT.
   The 41-exact / 12-tolerance split was derived from doc comments, and one entry
   was ALREADY WRONG (logsumexp: the static's doc claimed byte-identity while the
   inline comment in the function it gates correctly said within-ULP). Each lever
   has two sources of truth that can disagree silently — the static's doc, which
   is what people read, and the inline comment plus the code, which is what
   ships. The split stays PROVISIONAL until frankenscipy-yq1k8 audits the rest.

   METHOD: apply the EXACT gate first and let it surface disagreements. When one
   fails, the finding is about the DOC or the LEVER — fix whichever is actually
   wrong and record WHICH. Never widen the gate to accommodate the disagreement.
   Do not pre-emptively soften a gate because a drift seems plausible.

2. "IT PASSED" IS WEAKER THAN "IT CANNOT DIFFER". Where the parallel arm merges
   INTEGER counts, or reduces with min/max, associativity makes drift impossible
   and that argument belongs in the test. Where it is a float sum split across
   chunks, a green exact gate only means this fixture did not expose a drift.
   Say which kind of evidence you have.

3. ACTIVE HAZARD — INDEX ARITHMETIC AT GATE SIZE. These levers gate at large n
   (1<<17 and 1<<18 for the histogram family, 200_000/thread for ecdf, 700_000+
   for softmax, 1_600_000 for diff, 1<<22 for maxfold). My first histogram
   fixture panicked with "attempt to multiply with overflow" because `i * 7919`
   exceeds i32 at n = 300_000 in debug.

   THAT IS NOT JUST A FIXTURE LESSON, AND THIS IS THE POINT OF PUTTING IT HERE.
   All 53 toggles in this bead are UNDRIVEN — nothing has ever exercised their
   parallel arms. A parallel arm that has never run at its own work-gate size can
   contain exactly the same class of bug: an index or offset computed in a
   narrower type, an `n * stride` product, a `chunk * nthreads` that is fine at
   test sizes and overflows at gate sizes. Debug builds panic on it; release
   builds wrap silently and produce a wrong answer.

   SO CHECK IT AS YOU GO, not only where it bites. For each lever, when you size
   the fixture above its gate, look at the parallel arm's index arithmetic for
   products and offsets in narrow types, and prefer running these gates in a
   DEBUG profile where overflow panics rather than wraps. A gate that panics on
   overflow has found a real defect in the lever, not a nuisance in the test —
   record it as such and file it rather than widening the fixture down below the
   gate to make it go away. Shrinking the fixture below the work gate would hide
   the bug AND make the gate vacuous, which is the worst of both.

      MY POSITIVE CONTROL PASSED ON THIS VERSION — it only proves the probe is

      and the positive control failed.

  v4  count references that are NOT the declaration, NOT a comment, and NOT the
      `NAME.load` gate site. Whatever remains is code manipulating the toggle —

WHAT ACTUALLY CAUGHT v2, and it is the lesson: the NEGATIVE control. Asserting that a toggle I know is UNGATED (BHATTACHARYYA_FORCE_SERIAL, still in the tolerance group, never driven) is STILL reported undriven. v2 matched everything and would have reported any codebase as perfectly covered. THE PREDICTION WAS TESTED WHERE IT COULD FAIL, AND IT HELD. Last comment named
MEAN_W_FUSE, HMEAN_W_FUSE, F_ONEWAY_FUSE and DESCRIBE_REDUCE as the remaining
float reductions and said a fifth stale doc would be among them. Those four were

  HMEAN_W_FUSE_DISABLE     FIFTH STALE DOC, the FLATLY WRONG kind. Static said
                           "Byte-identical", unqualified. Measured n = 200_000:
                           0.9102444235517904 split vs 0.9102444235518026 fused.
  DESCRIBE_REDUCE_FORCE_SERIAL  FIRST DOC IN THIS BEAD THAT WAS ALREADY RIGHT.
  MEAN_W_FUSE_DISABLE      exact, structural, PASSED
  F_ONEWAY_FUSE_DISABLE    exact, structural, PASSED

HMEAN_W's mechanism is the one already on yq1k8: a parallel split landing on a
function that ALREADY had a documented byte-identical toggle. The other two
sources of truth were correct throughout — `hmean_weighted_reduce`'s own doc
records "~1e-15 reassociation above the gate" and `hmean_weighted`'s inline
comment says "BYTE-IDENTICAL below the parallel gate". Only the static, the thing
a classifier reads, was wrong. Doc fixed, bound taken from the other two.

A REFINEMENT WORTH CARRYING: HMEAN_W is not uniformly a tolerance lever. Its five
fused FLAGS stay exact at every size — OR is associative and the precedence
(data-invalid > weights-invalid > Sw==0 > x==0&&w>0) is preserved — while only the
two sums reassociate. The test asserts the flag paths with to_bits() and gives
tolerance only to the sums. Same shape as DESCRIBE_REDUCE, whose doc already
distinguished byte-identical min/max from a within-ULP S; measured, exactly that
split held (min/max bit-identical, mean/variance/skewness all drifted, mean
1.000001022927722 vs 1.0000010229277225).

SO THE CONTRACT IS PER-OUTPUT, NOT PER-LEVER. Three of the levers gated so far
carry BOTH an exact and a tolerance claim in the same toggle. Classifying a lever
as "tolerance" and giving all of its outputs a tolerance assertion throws away
true exact claims — which is the same loss as widening a bound, just quieter.
Whoever takes the remaining 19 should check whether a lever has an exact
sub-claim (flags, min/max, counts, indices) before levelling it down.

METHOD CORRECTION FROM THE LAST SLICE, and it worked: last time an exact probe
aborted at its first failure and MASKED a later lever, so a second run was needed
and one claim was briefly unobserved. This slice probed with NON-ABORTING PRINTS,

failing assertion is a worse instrument than a print — it stops at the first
answer and hides the rest.

the toggle switches unconditionally and the "size above the work gate" rule does

Evidence class, stated honestly: MEAN_W and F_ONEWAY have a structural argument
plus a green exact gate, but no observation that distinguishes "passed because
the arms are arithmetically identical" from "passed because the toggle was

comments.author: RusticCarp
comments.text:
RECLASSIFICATION OF THE spatial.distance FAMILY, RECORDED BEFORE GATING IT — and it corrects something I said in my own previous comment. RusticCarp 2026-08-06.

I described these six as "the k-accumulator reassociation lever, not parallelism
at all". THAT IS WRONG and reading the code says so: they are BOTH. The toggle
selects a 1-accumulator `.sum()` against a 4-way-unrolled chunk sum, and above a
size gate that chunk sum is ALSO fanned across threads with `thread::scope`. Two
independent sources of reassociation stacked in one lever, not one.

TWO CORRECTIONS THAT CHANGE HOW THE SLICE MUST BE WRITTEN.

1. CHEBYSHEV_FORCE_SERIAL DOES NOT BELONG IN THE 12-TOLERANCE LIST. Its own doc
   says the opposite of what the classification says: "BYTE-IDENTICAL either way
   — f64::max is exactly associative/commutative and ignores NaN, so any grouping
   of the reduction yields the same bits (unlike the ULP-reordered parallel SUM
   siblings)". The code agrees: 4-way unrolled chunk MAX, merged with max.
   It was swept into the tolerance bucket by family resemblance — five of its six
   siblings are sums — not by its own contract.

   THIS IS THE OPPOSITE ERROR FROM THE FIVE STALE DOCS AND IT IS WORTH NAMING.
   A stale doc claims exactness the code cannot deliver, and an exact gate
   catches it. A lever wrongly placed in the TOLERANCE bucket fails silently in
   the other direction: it would have received a tolerance assertion, and a true
   byte-identity claim would have been quietly discarded — the same loss as
   widening a bound, with nothing red to notice. Only an EXACT gate applied to it
   can reveal that, which is another argument for exact-first as the default.
   CHEBYSHEV gets an exact gate in the next slice. If it fails, the
   reclassification is wrong and that is the finding.

2. THE SIZE GATES ARE NOT UNIFORM ACROSS THE FAMILY, AND ONE OF THEM IS A TRAP.
   For the five SUM levers the FORCE_SERIAL arm returns the 1-accumulator fold
   immediately and the default arm applies the 4-way unroll AT EVERY SIZE — the
   size gate only chooses serial-unrolled versus threaded-unrolled. So their A/B
   is NON-VACUOUS AT ANY n, and there are two distinct regimes worth covering:
   unroll-only below the thread gate, unroll+threads above it.

   CHEBYSHEV IS THE EXCEPTION: `if CHEBYSHEV_FORCE_SERIAL || n < (1 << 22) {
   return serial(); }`. Below 1<<22 BOTH arms take the naive fold and the toggle
   proves nothing. Sizing this family uniformly — the obvious move for six
   sibling functions — would leave exactly one of the six vacuous, and it would
   be the one whose result (an exact pass) looks most reassuring.

   Thread gates, all different, none inferable from the others:
     BHATTACHARYYA 1<<17   CANBERRA 1<<17   CITYBLOCK 1<<20
     SQEUCLIDEAN   1<<20   MINKOWSKI 1<<16  CHEBYSHEV 1<<22 (and vacuous below)

So the standing rule "every gate must be sized ABOVE its own lever's work gate"
needs a companion clause: READ EACH GATE, because sibling functions with
near-identical docs do not share one. Family resemblance is what put CHEBYSHEV in
the wrong bucket and it is what would have made its fixture vacuous.

comments.author: RusticCarp
comments.text:
PROGRESS: 13 of 33 remaining (23a4c49d9). Suite 2064 passed / 0 failed, green 4/4 at default concurrency. RusticCarp 2026-08-06.

A DEFECT IN THIS BEAD'S OWN HARNESS THAT FAKED A STALE-DOC FINDING, and it
outranked the levers, so it was fixed before this slice shipped.

Adding the distance slice turned `heavy_gate_levers_are_bit_identical` red:
    par_max_fold: serial 17.17081558664073 vs parallel 17.170815586640796
A max fold cannot reassociate, so that was impossible on its face — and it looked
EXACTLY like a genuine stale-byte-identity finding, the same shape as the five
this bead has already found and repaired. I would have written it up as the sixth.

It was a RACE. The perf toggles are process-global AtomicBools and `cargo test`
runs tests concurrently, so a sibling test flipped LOGSUMEXP_FORCE_SERIAL while
that test held it pinned. Diagnosed with both arms, not by inspection:
    default concurrency  ->  1 FAILED (2063 passed)
    --test-threads=1     ->  0 FAILED (2064 passed)

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE SLICE. A racing A/B is not weaker evidence, it is
evidence pointing at the wrong thing, and it points BOTH WAYS. It can invent a
drift in a lever that structurally cannot drift — which is a false stale-doc
finding, and would have produced a "doc fix" loosening a contract that was
correct. It can equally MASK a real drift by pinning the other arm to the value
you expected, which is a stale doc shipped as verified. Every claim this bead has
produced was measured on this harness.

FIX: a TOGGLE_LOCK mutex taken by every test that writes a global toggle. All 30
found mechanically and verified with both control arms (must-hit: a known
toggle-writer IS detected; must-miss: a non-toggle fn is NOT) — 30 writers, 30
guarded, 0 missing. Poisoning deliberately ignored so one genuine failure cannot
cascade into 29 poisoned ones that bury it. Cost ~2s on a ~20s suite versus ~90s
for --test-threads=1. Four toggles had multiple writers (LOGSUMEXP, MOMENT_PAR,
PAR_SUM, RANKDATA_RADIX) but the lock covers all 30, because a writer racing a
READER corrupts equally and the reader set is every function whose call path
loads a toggle.

WHAT THIS SHOULD CHANGE ELSEWHERE: this hazard is not specific to fsci-stats. Any
crate whose A/B harness drives `pub static` toggles from `#[cfg(test)]` has it,
and the six sibling crates audited on ct8n2 all drive their toggles from PERF
BINS — separate processes, so they are immune — EXCEPT wherever a crate has
in-crate A/B tests. fsci-signal has 4, fsci-cluster 4, fsci-interpolate 11,
fsci-io 5. Those should be checked for multi-writer toggles; I have not done it
and am not claiming they are clean.

THE SLICE — six spatial.distance levers, 19 -> 13.

  CHEBYSHEV_FORCE_SERIAL IS EXACT, NOT TOLERANCE, confirmed by an exact gate at
  n = 1<<22. It was in the 12-tolerance list by family resemblance only. That
  misclassification direction fails SILENTLY: a tolerance assertion on a
  genuinely exact lever discards a true claim with nothing red to notice. The
  five stale docs go the other way and an exact gate catches those by itself, so
  this direction is the harder one and is worth watching for in the remaining 13.

  The five SUM levers (BHATTACHARYYA CANBERRA CITYBLOCK SQEUCLIDEAN MINKOWSKI)
  have NO VACUOUS REGIME: the FORCE_SERIAL arm is a 1-accumulator fold and the
  default applies a 4-way unroll at EVERY size, with the size gate only choosing
  serial-unrolled vs threaded-unrolled. Both regimes are covered. CHEBYSHEV is
  the opposite — vacuous below 1<<22 — so sizing the family uniformly would have
  left exactly one of the six proving nothing. Its fixture bound is now a
  `const { assert!(..) }` so shrinking it fails the BUILD.

  All 10 sum comparisons drifted, and that count is now a permanent assertion in
  the test rather than a one-time observation: a tolerance assertion passes just
  as happily when the arms never ran as when they agreed.

REMAINING 13, all exact-claim or hoist-shaped, no float-sum reassociation left:
  DISCRETE_PPF_MANY  EXPECTILE  FLIGNER  FLIGNER_PPF  GMEAN_W  NANSUM
  OBRIENTRANSFORM  PAR_DISCRETE_MAP  RANK_TWO  ROBUST_ZSCORE_HOIST  SORT_TWO
  TVAR_FORCE_COLLECT  TVAR_PAR_FORCE_SERIAL

Of these, EXPECTILE, GMEAN_W, NANSUM and TVAR_PAR still carry a TOLERANCE claim
from the original classification. Given CHEBYSHEV, each should get an EXACT gate
first anyway — the classification has now been wrong in both directions, so the
doc is not evidence for either verdict.

Count 19 -> 13 from the naming-agnostic probe, both control arms observed passing.

    'let var = ... / (n - 1.0)', commented 'ddof=1 sample variance, matching
    scipy's np.cov(bias=False)'.
  - GaussianKdeNd, :42194 -- 'Sample covariance (ddof=1), matching
    np.cov(bias=False)'.

VERIFIED AGAINST LIVE SCIPY, not just read. scipy.stats.gaussian_kde on the
test's own d=2 dataset (a=[0.1,1.2,0.5,-0.3,0.8,1.5], b=[2.0,-1.0,0.3,0.7,-0.5,1.1])
evaluated at the same three query points returns

which are bit-for-bit the constants asserted by
gaussian_kde_nd_matches_scipy_reference_values at :71776. So the goldens are
genuinely SciPy's, not a self-recorded snapshot of fsci's own output -- worth
checking, because a golden test is only as good as whoever typed the numbers.

with a ddof=0 (bias=True) covariance -- i.e. the exact bug this bead describes --
gives 0.1373074085557181, 0.18284905732672102, 0.11919937602934806, a relative
difference of 6.54%, 12.30% and 6.78%. Against the test's 1e-12 tolerance that
regression would fail enormously, so the coverage is real and not incidental.

the divergence is 6.5-12.3%, several times larger. The covariance scale factor is
n/(n-1), so the error grows as n shrinks -- at n=6 that is 1.2x on the covariance.

title: [conformance][stats] scipy goodness_of_fit fits the normal with ddof=1, disagreeing with its own norm.fit

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Found 2026-08-19 while gating a head-to-head measurement on the two arms agreeing about the
ANSWER before any cost number was believed. That gate is what caught it.

## The divergence, measured on both arms

Data: 50 points, fixed generation rule (see `crates/fsci-stats/src/bin/perf_goodness_of_fit.rs`).

    our AD statistic, at scipy's own fitted params : 5.093638686805e-01
    scipy `_anderson_darling`, same params          : 5.093638686805e-01   (agree, 13 digits)
    scipy `goodness_of_fit(norm, ...)` reports      : 4.784847727434e-01

The formula is not in dispute -- ours reproduces scipy's `_anderson_darling` exactly. The FIT
differs:

    scipy goodness_of_fit scale : 1.7665892538552177   (np.std(ddof=1), unbiased)
    scipy norm.fit / our fit    : 1.7488341373612308   (np.std(ddof=0), MLE)
    ratio                       : sqrt(50/49) exactly

`loc` agrees exactly (0.4654) in both.

## SciPy is internally inconsistent here, which is the interesting part

`scipy/stats/_fit.py::_fit_norm` uses `np.std(data, ddof=1, axis=-1)` when both loc and scale
are free. It is reached via `_fit_funs = {stats.norm: _fit_norm}` -- a fast path registered for
the NORMAL ALONE. Every other distribution falls through to `dist.fit(data)`, which is the MLE
(ddof=0).

So within scipy:
  * `stats.norm.fit(data)`                        -> ddof=0
  * `stats.goodness_of_fit(stats.norm, data)`     -> ddof=1
  * `stats.goodness_of_fit(stats.gamma, data)`    -> ddof=0 (via gamma.fit)

## Why this is NOT simply a bug in ours to fix

Both tests are valid. The Monte Carlo null is simulated with the SAME estimator used on the
observed data, so each is internally consistent and each has correct level. What is not valid
is comparing the two statistics to each other.

Ours uses `D::try_fit` for every family, which is the crate's MLE, so ours is the
self-consistent one -- it does not special-case the normal. Matching scipy would mean making
`goodness_of_fit` disagree with our own `Normal::try_fit`, i.e. importing scipy's
inconsistency.

## Decision needed, not obvious

Options, in the order I would rank them:

1. Leave as is, document on `goodness_of_fit` that the normal's statistic differs from scipy's
   by the ddof choice and say why. Cheapest, keeps self-consistency, and the p-values remain
   comparable in the sense that matters (both tests have correct level).
2. Add an opt-in `unbiased_scale` flag so a caller who needs bit-comparability with scipy can
   have it. Honest but adds surface for an inconsistency we did not create.
3. Match scipy unconditionally. Rejected unless someone argues for it: it makes our own
   `goodness_of_fit` and `Normal::try_fit` disagree about what "fit a normal" means.

Recorded in the ledger row at docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md ("goodness_of_fit: the whole-job
advantage over SciPy is ENTIRELY import"), commit 78e527f44.

title: [stats] Discrete distributions: Binomial, NegBinomial, Geometric, Hypergeometric, Bernoulli
description:
## Goal
Implement the core discrete probability distributions and a DiscreteDistribution trait. Currently we only have Poisson with basic pmf/cdf. Discrete distributions are used everywhere in hypothesis testing, reliability analysis, and combinatorics.

## What to implement
- `DiscreteDistribution` trait: pmf(k), cdf(k), sf(k), ppf(q), mean(), var(), std(), rvs(n)
- `Binomial(n, p)`: number of successes in n trials. PMF: C(n,k)*p^k*(1-p)^(n-k)
- `NegBinomial(n, p)`: number of trials until n successes. PMF involves gamma function.
- `Geometric(p)`: number of trials until first success. PMF: p*(1-p)^(k-1)
- `Hypergeometric(M, n, N)`: draws without replacement. PMF: C(n,k)*C(M-n,N-k)/C(M,N)
- `Bernoulli(p)`: single binary trial (special case of Binomial with n=1)
- Enhance existing `Poisson` to implement the trait

## Why this matters
Binomial is used in A/B testing, clinical trials, and quality control. Hypergeometric is used in Fisher exact test. These are among the most commonly used distributions outside of the continuous ones.

## Testing requirements
- Binomial: PMF sums to 1 over k=0..n, mean=np, var=np(1-p)
- NegBinomial: PMF sums to 1, mean=n/p
- Geometric: memoryless property, mean=1/p
- Hypergeometric: PMF sums to 1, reduces to binomial in limit
- ppf/cdf roundtrip for each distribution
- Edge cases: p=0, p=1, n=0
- At least 12 tests
close_reason: Implemented DiscreteDistribution trait + Binomial, Bernoulli, Geometric, NegBinomial, Hypergeometric. Retrofitted Poisson to implement trait. 20 new tests, 136 total.

title: fsci-stats: port scipy.stats.exponpow
description: scipy.stats.exponpow(b) is missing in fsci-stats. Closed-form distribution on x ≥ 0 with shape b > 0. pdf(x) = b·x^(b-1)·exp(1 + x^b − exp(x^b)). cdf(x) = 1 − exp(1 − exp(x^b)) = -expm1(-expm1(x^b)). sf(x) = exp(1 − exp(x^b)) = exp(-expm1(x^b)). ppf(q) = (log1p(-log1p(-q)))^(1/b). Boundary at x=0 is shape-dependent: b<1 → ∞, b=1 → 1, b>1 → 0. Add 4 anchor tests verified against scipy: pdf at multiple (b, x), cdf, ppf round-trip, boundary regimes. Note: NOT to be confused with the generalized-normal a.k.a. gennorm distribution.
close_reason: Ported scipy.stats.exponpow(b) to crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs as a new ExponPow struct. Closed-form pdf/cdf/sf/ppf using the numerical-stability-friendly forms: cdf via -expm1(-expm1(x^b)), sf via exp(-expm1(x^b)), ppf via (ln(1-ln(1-q)))^(1/b) with ln_1p. Boundary at x=0 is shape-dependent: b<1→∞, b=1→1, b>1→0. mean/var inherited as NaN (no clean closed form). Note: NOT to be confused with gennorm (the generalized-normal). 3 anchor tests verified against scipy: pdf+cdf at 12 (b, x) values; boundary at x=0 across all three regimes; ppf↔cdf round-trip on the interior of support (skip when cdf saturates near 1, which is a numerical limit of any closed-form inverse). fsci-stats --lib: 1057 → 1060.

title: [linalg] add cossin — cosine-sine (CS) decomposition (scipy parity)
description: scipy.linalg.cossin(X,p,q): CS decomposition of a partitioned orthogonal matrix X = u @ cs @ vh. ANALYSIS (cc): the cs matrix (the angles) = descending SVD singular values of X11 → cosines C, S=sqrt(1-C^2), cs=[[C,-S],[S,C]] block layout — this part matches scipy EXACTLY and is trivial. The HARD part: u=diag(U1,U2), vh=diag(V1h,V2h) must match LAPACK dbbcsd's per-angle SIGN convention, which is NOT a simple svd_flip rule (tested flip_u/flip_v, neither matches) — it emerges from dbbcsd's bidiagonal QR sweep. So full parity needs porting dorcsd2by1/dbbcsd (a substantial LAPACK routine, convention-critical). NOTE: fsci-linalg is RubyWaterfall-contended (perf beads 8ty4p/psn7x in progress) — coordinate/use worktree recipe. This is the LAST remaining scipy function gap after the spline/FITPACK surface was completed.

In spectral_rolloff, spectral_centroid and spectral_bandwidth the validation is FUSED INTO THE REDUCTION PASS rather than sitting as an early return -- the code was optimised to validate while accumulating, with comments asserting the NaN behaviour is preserved byte-identically ("an invalid bin still returns NaN and a zero total still returns 0.0, exactly as the original"). A grep for a guard at the top of the function finds `return 0.0` for the empty case and nothing else, so it reads as unguarded. The guard is real, just not where a guard-shaped search looks.

That is now the SEVENTH distinct way this cohort hides its implementation from a mechanical sweep. Combined with the accept-shaped beads (increment 4) it means neither "has a guard" nor "lacks a guard" can be scored automatically.

TWO BEADS THAT LOOK LIKE ONE: t9yur and o638q both name spectral_rolloff. They are different parameters -- rolloff_percent versus the magnitude/frequency bins -- with separate guards and separate tests (:24526 and :24542). Fourth title-collision case in this pass, after nix3y/ut7rx, uw9oe/cj64b and dacm4/i650g.

TWO CONTRACTS STRONGER THAN THEIR TITLES:
  - jn1ng rejects NEGATIVE magnitudes as well as non-finite. That is load-bearing for flatness specifically: it is a geometric/arithmetic mean ratio, so a negative would produce a NaN inside the log and surface as a silently wrong number rather than a boundary rejection.
  - qsl4q test is named thd_rejects_zero_fundamental_bin_WITHOUT_HANGING. The guard is also a liveness property -- it prevents a non-terminating harmonic sweep -- not merely a value check.

comments.text:
TENTH BULK INCREMENT 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey). Four closed: a3m7m, 8w2oa, qtj06, snymc. Running total 80 of 80.

THE "WITHOUT SAMPLING" NAMING IS A REAL CONTRACT, not phrasing. Three beads in this batch carry it (a3m7m, 8w2oa, qtj06) and in every case the test passes an objective closure that PANICS if called, so a pass proves the guard short-circuits before the user function is ever evaluated. That is the same technique as gauss_legendre in 1mxfr and the neval==0 assertion in r9kzs -- three independent places in this codebase converged on it.

For anyone continuing: when a bead title says "without sampling", "before evaluating" or "before allocation", the test is asserting a SHORT-CIRCUIT property and the right check is whether the fixture can detect being called -- a panicking closure, a counter, or an assertion that the evaluation count is zero. A test that merely asserts the returned error is weaker than the bead asks for.

SHARED-GUARD FIND, consistent with the group-by-helper advice: a3m7m is served by one predicate, invalid_scalar_minimize_controls(a, b, tol, maxiter) at opt/lib.rs:3367, used by BOTH scalar minimizers. Locating that helper settled the bead in one step; searching per-minimizer would have taken two passes and risked missing one.

ADJACENT-INPUT CONTRAST worth noting on 8w2oa: pso rejects a zero ITERATION budget (NaN sentinel, no sampling) but a zero PARTICLE count falls back to a single particle (:7622). Two superficially similar degenerate inputs, two deliberately different decisions. A sweep that assumed "zero means reject" would mis-score the second.

TWELFTH BULK INCREMENT 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey). TEN closed in one pass -- jobeu, ps36w, 6fdrs, x3qom, 8xjld, lnq4e, xg0bx, bpzfl, qd01d, tfe7l -- the fsci-signal non-finite-samples cluster. Running total 96 of 96. Double the usual batch size, and the reason is worth generalising.

THE SHARED-HELPER APPROACH IS THE FASTEST YET. fsci-signal routes finite-input validation through validate_real_values_finite / validate_spectral_samples, which between them have 59 CALL SITES. One grep established that every entry point in this cluster is guarded by the same helper; then one grep of the test module by behaviour phrase ("rejects_non_finite") mapped ten beads to ten named tests. Recommended order for the remaining ~66, refining the earlier advice:
  1. grep the ERROR ENUM (best when the crate has one, e.g. fsci-integrate)
  2. grep the shared VALIDATOR HELPER and count its call sites (best when the
     crate validates through one function, e.g. fsci-signal)
  3. only then fall back to per-function or per-bead searching
Both (1) and (2) turn a cluster into a single lookup.

TWO PAIRS THAT ARE NOT DUPLICATES, continuing the running list:

ScarletWaterfall 2026-08-08, SCI40-44: sample statistics for this reconciliation, since they bear on how much of the backlog is stale rather than open.

I worked 34 beads this session across fsci-opt/sparse/fft/special/stats. Of those, 4 needed real code and 30 were ALREADY SATISFIED. That is 88 percent stale, on a sample drawn by walking br ready in priority order rather than by cherry-picking -- consistent with, and larger than, this bead's original 8-of-8 P2 sample.

The four that were real:
  7elm7  toms748 was Illinois-Regula-Falsi degrading to exact bisection (41 calls vs scipy 9); implemented Alefeld-Potra-Shi 748, now 9 calls
  mhxei  diags() stored explicit zeros where scipy's dia->csr prunes
  ykn1o  analytic_signal had no inline even-length imaginary golden
  b39yd  premise refuted, but a genuine 1-element-shape coverage gap existed

Two failure modes worth naming for whoever does the next sweep, because both cost me time and both are silent:

1. POSITIONAL CITATION ROT, already filed as defect_positional_ledger_citations_rot. The BLOCKER comments on rft2l (line 11251) and h0sb5 (line 24122) both pointed at unrelated code by the time I read them -- 11251 landed in a Planck/Zipf entropy loop, 24122 in a Laplace pdf. Content-addressing (impl block + test fn name) found them immediately. Closes I wrote cite names, not lines.

2. STALE BEAD TEXT READS AS A LIVE BUG REPORT. Six degenerate-sample beads (k9s0g xhqrv edisn 67ouq 7tb64 6e976) describe precise, plausible divergences -- 'fsci returns NaN for all n<3', 'df = -1.0 from len-1' -- none of which reproduce. Reading the source is not enough to tell, because the source looks like it could go either way; I had to append a probe, run it on the fleet, print the actual values, and strip it. Recommend that pattern over source-reading for any bead of this shape.

METHOD I used for the 30 stale ones, offered as a template: (a) find the covering test by name, not line; (b) re-run the goldens against LIVE scipy at close time rather than trusting the source comment -- all ~90 constants I checked did match, so the comments were honest, but that is a result and not an assumption; (c) where the bead names a bug class, observe the must-miss arm too (e.g. scipy's own 1-cdf gives exactly 0.0 where sf gives 5.9e-24, which is what makes the sf override demonstrably necessary); (d) state any residual gap in the close rather than rounding it to done -- I left xoqwh's 'combined test' letter unmet and recorded a 1-ulp spearmanr difference.

Not proposing a bulk auto-close. The 88 percent figure is an argument for a systematic reconciliation pass with the above evidence bar, not for trusting the ratio.

title: GAP: fsci-linalg solve_continuous_are / solve_discrete_are (3/6 → 5/6)
description:
Per fgxx audit, fsci-linalg lacks solve_continuous_are and
solve_discrete_are. Both are required by control-theory consumers
(LQR, Kalman filter covariance equations).

scipy's implementation uses the Schur decomposition of a Hamiltonian
(continuous) or symplectic (discrete) pencil, then extracts the
stable invariant subspace. fsci has the underlying schur + ordqz
primitives, so the missing layer is the pencil-construction +
stable-subspace extraction.

Acceptance:
- solve_continuous_are(A, B, Q, R[, S, E]) — continuous-time Riccati:
    AᵀX + XA − (XB + S)R⁻¹(BᵀX + Sᵀ) + Q = 0
- solve_discrete_are(A, B, Q, R[, S, E]) — discrete-time Riccati.
- Pencil construction + ordqz-based stable-subspace extraction.
- Unit tests: 3 well-conditioned problems from Benner et al.'s
  CAREX/DAREX benchmark set.
- COVERAGE.md updated (special_solve family flips from 3/6 to 5/6).

Out of scope: solve_lyapunov deprecated alias (declined in
DISCREPANCIES.md).

Related: fgxx (parent audit).

title: fsci-integrate: nquad fix in 819a64c misses NaN-propagation failure mode
description: Self-found defect via stale-rch test feedback. The recent 819a64c fix added a RefCell<Option<IntegrateValidationError>> channel, but only captures Err results from inner nquad_inner calls. The most common silent-failure mode is NaN propagation: when the integrand returns NaN, inner quad returns Ok with NaN integral (not Err). My channel sees no Err, so nquad still returns Ok with NaN result — same defect as before. Fix: also check finiteness of the inner result; capture a typed error in the channel if NaN/Inf. Update regression test (was running 60s+ because adaptive subdivision iterated maxiter times).
close_reason: Fixed the NaN-propagation gap in 819a64c's nquad fix. Pre-fix vetrv missed the case where the user integrand returns NaN: inner quad returns Ok with non-finite integral (no Err for the channel to capture), the outer adaptive loop iterates to maxiter producing NaN, and nquad returned Ok with NaN result — same silent-distortion defect the original ticket addressed. Added a post-loop finiteness guard: if !result.is_finite(), return IntegrateValidationError::QuadInvalidBounds with detail naming the failure mode. Updated regression test to use unconditional NaN integrand (was using conditional NaN that exhausted maxiter; the new test exits as soon as the first NaN propagates). cargo build -p fsci-integrate clean (23s).

title: [MEDIUM] fuzz: all existing harnesses use crash-only oracle for non-trivial kernels — no structured metamorphic assertions beyond conjugation symmetry
description:
Review-mode audit of 13 fuzz harnesses under fuzz/fuzz_targets/:

Oracle strength breakdown (per /testing-fuzzing skill, hierarchy from strongest to weakest):
- Reference implementation (strongest): NONE. No harness compares Rust output vs scipy or a trusted reference.
- Simplified shadow model: NONE.
- Inverse operation (round-trip): partial in p2c005_sparse_formats (format conversion round-trip).
- Metamorphic relation: used in p2c006_special_complex_branches for conjugation symmetry + real-axis reduction.
- Crash oracle (weakest): used everywhere else as the primary contract.

Weakness: per skill rule 'Use the strongest oracle available. A crash-only harness is acceptable only when no stronger oracle exists.' Examples:

- p2c001_validate_tol / p2c001_step_bounds: just let _ = fn(input); no oracle.
- p2c002_solve: no check that A @ x ≈ b after solve(A, b) succeeds. This is THE first metamorphic relation for any linear solver.
- p2c002_factorizations: no A ≈ L @ U invariant. Same for QR, SVD, Cholesky.
- p2c004_sparse_helpers: no invariant on output (e.g. tril(A).nnz <= A.nnz).
- p2c003_add (broken): the _properties variant had commutativity + associativity checks but the underlying fn doesn't exist (see frankenscipy-gvl2).

Per skill's strength-2 'simplified shadow model': for sparse, a BTreeMap<(usize, usize), f64> is a natural shadow. For solve, a direct naive Gaussian-elimination solver in the fuzz harness itself can serve as the reference.

Ask:
1. Add A @ x ≈ b invariant to p2c002_solve (measure residual, assert below tolerance scaled by κ(A) from fsci-linalg::cond).
2. Add A ≈ L @ U, A ≈ Q @ R invariants to p2c002_factorizations for LU, QR, SVD, Cholesky.
3. Add tril/triu idempotence and sparsity non-increase invariants to p2c004_sparse_helpers.
4. Add integer-arithmetic-style property checks (commutativity, associativity) wherever they hold mathematically for the kernel being fuzzed (e.g., sparse matrix addition).
5. For fsci-integrate quadrature: add the 'integral over [a,b] + integral over [b,c] = integral over [a,c]' metamorphic relation (fuzz [a,b,c] and check).

Every new harness added via tmti / bead plyj should include at least one strength-2+ oracle, not a bare let _ = fn(...).

title: [sparse] audit the last three EPSILON*1e6 gates (lsqr, krylov_arnoldi_eigs, svds) by recurrence replay
description:
Filed by ChartreuseChapel 2026-08-04 on closing frankenscipy-9y533.

The loose-gate defect class is now CONFIRMED FOUR TIMES, each with a measured
divergence from SciPy:
  qmr       frankenscipy-9pfja  aborted healthy solves from n=4096
  bicg      frankenscipy-9y533  tripped at iteration 19 on n=64
  cgs       frankenscipy-9y533  tripped at iteration 19 on n=64
  bicgstab  frankenscipy-9y533  tripped at iteration 13 on n=64

Three sites still use the same f64::EPSILON * 1e6 = 2.220e-10 constant. They
were deliberately NOT touched in 9y533 because there is no measured evidence
they are wrong, and changing a numerical gate blind is the mistake 9y533 exists
to correct:

  crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs:3001   lsqr
      if rho.abs() > f64::EPSILON * 1e6 { ... }
      INVERTED sense — it guards a divide rather than aborting, so tightening
      changes which BRANCH is taken, not merely when the solver bails. Treat
      exactly as bicgstab's t.t gate was treated: find SciPy's counterpart
      first. SciPy's lsqr uses its own Golub-Kahan stopping rules (atol/btol/
      conlim), so there may be no direct peer and the honest answer may be that
      this gate should not exist.

  crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs:9993   krylov_arnoldi_eigs
      if h[j + 1][j] < f64::EPSILON * 1e6 { ... }
      This is Arnoldi HAPPY-breakdown detection — h[j+1][j] going to zero means
      the Krylov space is invariant and the eigenpairs are exact. Semantically
      different from a BiCG breakdown gate, so do NOT assume eps**2 transfers.
      But h[j+1][j] is a NORM, and calling 2.22e-10 'zero' for a norm is the
      same magnitude error that made the t.t gate wrong.

  crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs:10613  svds
      if sigma > f64::EPSILON * 1e6 { ... }
      A singular-value threshold. Compare against scipy.sparse.linalg.svds and
      its ARPACK tolerance handling.

METHOD, the one that worked twice (do not skip to the fix):
1. Replay the recurrence in float64 (numpy) on a fixture the routine is
   supposed to handle, logging the min absolute value of each gated quantity.
2. Run the live SciPy peer on the identical input. If SciPy converges where the
   replay trips, the gate is the bug.
3. Read the peer's source for the actual constant AND the actual position of
   the check — 9y533 found SciPy tests |omega| one step later rather than the
   t.t denominator, so a constant swap would have been wrong.
4. Land a red-before/green-after probe pinning the SciPy answer.

A NEGATIVE RESULT CLOSES THIS BEAD. If the replay shows these gates are never
approached on realistic inputs, record the min values observed and close it as
latent. That is a successful outcome, not a failed one — do not manufacture a
change to justify the bead.
close_reason:
All three EPSILON*1e6 gates audited and ALL THREE CONFIRMED WRONG by the prescribed method (recurrence replay + live SciPy peer on identical input). Fixed in c979e3edd. Root cause is one defect, three times: an ABSOLUTE threshold (2.220e-10) applied to a SCALE-DEPENDENT quantity, so every one is a scale-equivariance break.

MEASURED, pre-fix, live oracle scipy 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.3:
- krylov_arnoldi_eigs: h[j+1][j] is a NORM carrying the operator scale. svds drives the Krylov space with AtA, so ||A||=5e-6 gives operator norm 2.5e-11, already under the gate. On diag(5,3,1)*1e-6 with k=2, fsci returned 1 eigenvalue instead of 2 (basis truncated to a 1-D subspace at j=0); scipy.sparse.linalg.svds returns [3e-6,5e-6] with unit-norm left vectors. Reproduced via eigsh on diag(1,4,9)*1e-11.
- svds sigma gate: absolute threshold exceeded EVERY singular value of a uniformly small matrix, so every left singular vector came back as the ZERO vector while sigma itself was reported correctly and nonzero.
- lsqr rho gate: gate was INERT as written — cs=rho_bar/rho and sn=beta/rho divide by rho unconditionally FOUR LINES ABOVE it, so a genuine zero rho already produced NaN before the gate was reached; it never protected a division, it only froze x and w while the recurrence advanced. Recurrence replay on A=[[4,1,0],[1,4,1],[0,1,4]]*1e-11, b=[1,2,3]: rho=2.586e-11 at EVERY one of 30 iterations, always under 2.220e-10, so the x-update never executed once and lsqr returned the ZERO vector. scipy converges in 3 iterations to relative error 4.78e-16.

FIXES: Arnoldi -> relative h[j+1][j] <= eps^(2/3)*||w_before||, with ||w_before|| recovered free from the MGS projection coefficients (Pythagoras, no extra pass). eps^(2/3) is ARPACK's eps23 and is TIGHTER than the old gate at unit scale (3.67e-11 vs 2.22e-10), so breakdown detection is not loosened. svds -> sigma > EPSILON*sigma_max (zero matrix degrades to 'sigma > 0', correct). lsqr -> magnitude gate REMOVED (scipy has none) and replaced by scipy's STRUCTURAL guard, the arnorm=alfa*beta==0 early return, here alpha==0 i.e. At b=0 where x=0 is the exact LSQ solution. Bead hypothesis that the lsqr gate 'should not exist' CONFIRMED; hypothesis that eps^2 would not transfer to Arnoldi happy-breakdown also CONFIRMED (answer is relative eps^(2/3), not eps^2).

EVIDENCE: 4 regression tests added in the same bead, ALL CONFIRMED FAILING PRE-FIX (svds/eigsh aborted on 'expected 2 eigenvalues, left: 1'), all passing post-fix: lsqr_is_scale_equivariant_for_small_magnitude_matrices, svds_is_scale_equivariant_for_small_magnitude_matrices, eigsh_is_scale_equivariant_for_small_magnitude_matrices, lsqr_returns_zero_solution_when_a_transpose_b_vanishes. Each asserts RELATIVE error so the same bound must hold at every scale, and each carries a live-scipy reference value. RCH remote (hz1, vmi1149989): cargo test -j2 -p fsci-sparse --lib -> 403 passed, 0 failed, 4 ignored. cargo clippy -j2 -p fsci-sparse --lib --all-features -- -D warnings -> exit 0. rustfmt --check clean. ubs on linalg.rs -> 0 critical.

Loose-gate defect class count is now SEVEN (qmr 9pfja; bicg/cgs/bicgstab 9y533; lsqr/arnoldi/svds here). No EPSILON*1e6 gate remains in fsci-sparse live code; the 7 remaining textual hits are comments documenting the old thresholds.

NOT FIXED HERE, filed instead: frankenscipy-5i3a9 (metamorphic_tests.rs stale csr_to_dense call) and frankenscipy-lnb7b (signal/stats perf bin feature-gate drift) both block cargo check --workspace --all-targets and are pre-existing and independent.
