title: [stats] Goodness-of-fit tests: ks_1samp, ks_2samp, shapiro, normaltest, anderson
description:
## Goal
Implement the most important goodness-of-fit tests. These test whether data follows a specified distribution — one of the most common statistical workflows.

## What to implement
- `ks_1samp(data, cdf_func)`: one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Tests H0: data comes from the specified distribution. Returns (statistic, p-value).
- `ks_2samp(data1, data2)`: two-sample KS test. Tests H0: two samples come from the same distribution.
- `shapiro(data)`: Shapiro-Wilk test for normality. The most powerful normality test for small samples (n < 5000).
- `normaltest(data)`: D'Agostino-Pearson test combining skewness and kurtosis tests (uses our existing skew/kurtosis).
- `anderson(data, dist)`: Anderson-Darling test. More sensitive to tail deviations than KS.

## Why this matters
Normality testing is a prerequisite for many parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA). KS test is the standard nonparametric goodness-of-fit test. These are among the top-10 most used scipy.stats functions.

## Implementation approach
- KS statistic: max|F_empirical(x) - F_theoretical(x)|. P-value from Kolmogorov distribution.
- KS two-sample: max|F_1(x) - F_2(x)|. Use Smirnov approximation for p-value.
- Shapiro-Wilk: requires precomputed coefficients table (Royston 1992 algorithm for n > 12)
- normaltest: combine skewtest and kurtosistest using chi-squared (already have skew/kurtosis)
- Anderson: compute statistic, compare to critical values table

## Dependencies
- Uses existing summary statistics (skew, kurtosis)
- Uses existing CDF functions from distributions

## Testing requirements
- ks_1samp: normal data + Normal CDF → high p-value; uniform data + Normal CDF → low p-value
- ks_2samp: same distribution → high p; different → low p
- shapiro: normal data → p > 0.05; uniform data → p < 0.05
- normaltest: normal data → not rejected; highly skewed → rejected
- anderson: known critical values for normal distribution
- At least 10 tests
close_reason: Implemented ks_1samp, ks_2samp, shapiro, normaltest, anderson with 18 tests

title: [CRITICAL] conformance: run_differential_test is NOT differential — 11 of 12 family runners invoke ZERO scipy oracle script; only stats wires oracle path, and its script does not exist
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs:run_differential_test (line 7671) on 2026-04-22.

The public entry point `run_differential_test` dispatches by family to 12 runner functions:
    run_differential_validate_tol, _linalg, _array_api, _special, _fft, _optimize,
    _casp, _cluster, _spatial, _signal, _stats, _integrate.

Audited each for whether it actually calls a scipy oracle script (capture_*_oracle_inner, capture_linalg_oracle, capture_oracle_for_fixture, Command::new for python script):

| Runner (line)                         | Invokes scipy oracle? | Comparator used                   |
|---------------------------------------|:---------------------:|-----------------------------------|
| run_differential_validate_tol (7719)  | NO                    | case.expected direct match        |
| run_differential_linalg (7817)        | NO                    | compare_linalg_case_differential (self-check) |
| run_differential_array_api (7869)     | NO                    | compare_array_api_case_differential            |
| run_differential_special (7956)       | NO                    | compare_special_case_differential              |
| run_differential_fft (8321)           | NO                    | compare_fft_case_differential                  |
| run_differential_optimize (7627)      | NO                    | compare_optimize_case_differential             |
| run_differential_casp                 | NO                    | compare_casp_case_differential                 |
| run_differential_cluster              | NO                    | compare_cluster_case_differential              |
| run_differential_spatial              | NO                    | compare_spatial_case_differential              |
| run_differential_signal (8136)        | NO                    | compare_signal_case_differential               |
| run_differential_stats (8044)         | **YES** (but script missing per cpgl) | compare_stats_case_against_oracle when available, else self-check |
| run_differential_integrate (8000)     | NO                    | compare_integrate_case_differential            |

Only run_differential_stats WIRES the oracle path (resolve_differential_oracle_config @ 8055 + capture_stats_oracle_inner @ 8061). Every other runner probes scipy availability purely for the `oracle_status` field in the report, then compares Rust output against HAND-TYPED `case.expected.*` fields in the fixture.

Additional traps:
- Even for stats, the default script path is python_oracle/scipy_stats_oracle.py which does not exist (frankenscipy-cpgl). probe_oracle_availability @ 10948 returns Missing (because config.script_path.exists() is false). Condition at 8058 (required || Available) is false, so oracle is not called, falls through to self-check @ 8108.
- Even if the script existed, required defaults to false (1493, 7267, 11580, 13116), so a script that exists but fails to execute also falls through silently via capture_failure_status @ 8073.
- probe_oracle_availability @ 10947 only runs `python -c 'import scipy; print(scipy.__version__)'`. It does NOT verify numpy availability, does NOT verify family-specific oracle can parse the fixture, does NOT verify fixture hash matches captured oracle (per cpn9).

The oracle-backed linalg path (run_linalg_packet_with_oracle_capture @ 5973, capture_linalg_oracle @ 6010, compare_linalg_case_against_oracle @ 6196) EXISTS but is never invoked from run_differential_test. It is called only from tests (11836, 11884) via a separate public entry.

Consequence: The word 'differential' in `run_differential_test` and every `compare_*_case_differential` is a MISNOMER. Nothing about these functions performs differential comparison against SciPy. They are self-checking comparisons of Rust output against fixture-encoded expected values. The per-case result.oracle_status field reports Available/Missing/Failed purely as metadata -- it has no effect on pass/fail.

This unifies and amplifies my prior beads:
- di9p (10 families have no oracle) -- true for ALL 12 entry points under run_differential_test
- cpgl (stats lacks scipy_stats_oracle.py) -- explains why the one wired runner silently falls back
- dvd6 (sparse oracle/fixture mismatch) -- separate issue; sparse isn't even in run_differential_test dispatch (SparseOps is in the packet_runner registry @ 11235)
- ihex ('both errored = pass') -- only affects the linalg-with-oracle path at 6196 which isn't called from the differential entry
- v2tz / r9st / m76c -- oracle dispatcher gaps, but the dispatchers aren't invoked here

Ask (priority = unblock truthful conformance reporting):
1. Rename `run_differential_test` to `run_self_check_test` or `run_fixture_check_test`. It is not differential. A new function `run_oracle_backed_test` should be the true differential entry.
2. For every family, wire the oracle path: create scipy_<family>_oracle.py (per di9p) and have the runner invoke it via `capture_<family>_oracle_inner`.
3. Default `required: true` for DifferentialOracleConfig so missing scripts fail loud.
4. Export a separate `run_fixture_check_test` that explicitly does not require the oracle -- developers can call this for local dev, but the CI conformance gate must use `run_oracle_backed_test`.
5. Flip the semantics of `probed_oracle_status`: when oracle is Missing, the CONFORMANCE result for every case should be CaseOutcome::Unjudgeable (per ihex), not Pass.

This is the single biggest conformance reporting fiction in the codebase. All 'differential_<family>_quota_and_structured_logs' tests in the runner currently certify green status without consulting scipy at all.

Related: cpgl, di9p, dvd6, cpn9, ihex, v2tz, m76c.
close_reason: Oracle dispatch by family (commit ec39c11).

title: [stats] gaussian_kde, entropy, boxcox, kendalltau
description:
## Goal
Implement kernel density estimation, entropy computation, power transforms, and Kendall correlation — important tools for exploratory data analysis and feature engineering.

## What to implement
- `gaussian_kde(data)`: Gaussian kernel density estimation. Returns an object that can be evaluated at arbitrary points. Uses Scott or Silverman bandwidth selection.
- `entropy(pk, qk)`: Shannon entropy H = -Σ p_k log(p_k). If qk provided, computes KL divergence D_KL(p||q) = Σ p_k log(p_k/q_k).
- `differential_entropy(values)`: differential entropy from sample data (k-nearest-neighbor estimator).
- `boxcox(x, lmbda)`: Box-Cox power transformation to make data more normal-like. λ=0 → log(x), λ=1 → x-1, general: (x^λ-1)/λ.
- `boxcox_normmax(x)`: find λ that maximizes normality (profile likelihood).
- `kendalltau(x, y)`: Kendall rank correlation coefficient. Counts concordant/discordant pairs.

## Implementation approach
- gaussian_kde: for each eval point, sum Gaussian kernels centered at data points. Bandwidth: h = n^{-1/5} * std (Scott rule).
- entropy: straightforward sum with log, handle p=0 case
- boxcox: apply transform elementwise, boxcox_normmax uses bracket search on log-likelihood
- kendalltau: O(n²) algorithm counting concordant/discordant pairs. Tau = (C-D)/n(n-1)/2.

## Testing requirements
- KDE: integrates to ≈ 1, peaks near modes of the data
- entropy: H(uniform) = log(n), H(deterministic) = 0
- boxcox: x=e, λ=0 → ln(e)=1; boxcox_normmax finds reasonable λ
- kendalltau: monotonic data → τ=1; reverse → τ=-1; uncorrelated → τ≈0
- At least 10 tests
close_reason: Implemented GaussianKde, entropy, boxcox (with optimal lambda), kendalltau with 14 tests

title: fsci-stats: kruskal() lacks tie correction, diverges from scipy on tied data
description:
fsci kruskal at lib.rs:14019 computes H = (12/(N(N+1))) * Σ(R_i²/n_i) - 3(N+1) but does NOT apply scipy's tie-correction divisor:
  H_corrected = H / (1 - Σ(t³ - t) / (N³ - N))
where t are the sizes of each tie group in the combined-rank pool.

REPLICATION:
  • g3_with_ties (3 groups of 5 with overlapping values 1-6):
    fsci stat=0.481, scipy=0.720, diff=0.239
  • g4_unequal_n (also has ties across boundaries):
    fsci stat=2.583, scipy=2.666, diff=0.083

g2_no_ties and g3_mixed (ties-free) pass at 1e-9 abs.

FIX:
  After computing H at lib.rs:14019, sort the combined ranks, find tie
  groups (consecutive equal values in the sorted observations), compute
  C = 1 - Σ(t³ - t) / (N³ - N), and divide H by C.

  Existing tests at lib.rs:32xxx are all on tie-free data so won't break.

REPLICATE: see diff_stats_kruskal.rs which currently scopes to no-ties
fixtures only.
notes: Fixed in same tick. Added tie-correction divisor C = 1 - Σ(t³-t)/(N³-N) at lib.rs:14019+ and divide H by C. All 4 existing fsci-stats kruskal unit tests still pass; diff_stats_kruskal.rs (12 cases × including with-ties fixture) passes at 1e-9 abs.

title: [conformance][linalg] value-range eigenvalue selection is ulp-sensitive at an exact bound
description:
Found 2026-08-16 (RainyPrairie) by a test assertion that failed and was right to fail.

Selecting eigenvalues by VALUE with a bound that lands within an ulp of an eigenvalue gives implementation-defined counts. Measured on d=[1,2,3,4,5], e=[0.5;4] with select_range=(2.0, 3.0):

  scipy select='v' returns ONE value, 2.9999999999999996
  ours returns NONE

Neither is wrong. The eigenvalue near 3 is 2.9999999999999996 under scipy's select='v' driver and 3.0000000000000004 under our routine, so against a HALF-OPEN upper bound of exactly 3.0 it falls on opposite sides. The selection rule is identical; the eigenvalue differs in the last ulp because the two implementations compute it differently -- the same class as the eigvals_only-vs-full split filed alongside 0y08i.

WHY IT IS WORTH A BEAD RATHER THAN A COMMENT: a conformance test that pins scipy's COUNT for a value range is pinning a coincidence of rounding, and will flip on an unrelated change to either eigenvalue routine. My first version of the test did exactly that. Anyone writing value-range conformance cases needs to know to keep bounds away from the spectrum.

WORK: decide and document the project's position. Either (a) state that value-range selection is exact-arithmetic-defined and that boundary cases within an ulp are unspecified, and add a test asserting only away-from-boundary behaviour; or (b) if bit-level agreement with scipy is wanted here, that requires matching its eigenvalue driver, which is a much larger commitment than this selection API.

NEGATIVE CASE for any fix: the away-from-boundary cases must keep passing unchanged -- (1.5, 4.5) selecting three values and (2.5, 3.5) selecting one are the ones currently pinned.
close_reason: RESOLVED as option (a): the position is now documented on eigh_tridiagonal_subset_by_value. Boundary semantics are exact-arithmetic-defined and selection counts at a bound within an ulp of an eigenvalue are UNSPECIFIED -- scipy returns one eigenvalue for select_range=(2.0, 3.0) where we return none, because the value near 3 falls either side of the half-open bound under the two implementations. Neither is wrong. The doc states the rule that follows: conformance tests here must keep bounds AWAY from the spectrum, since pinning a count at an exact bound pins a rounding coincidence. The away-from-boundary cases (1.5,4.5) and (2.5,3.5) remain pinned and passing, which was this bead negative case. 548/0/42 on vmi1149989.

title: [opt] Multivariate root finding: root, fsolve
description:
## Goal
Implement scipy.optimize.root and fsolve for solving systems of nonlinear equations F(x) = 0.

## What to implement
- `root(fun, x0, method)`: find root of vector-valued function using various methods
  - method="hybr": Powell's hybrid method (modified Newton with dogleg trust region)
  - method="broyden1": Broyden's first method (quasi-Newton, approximate Jacobian updates)
- `fsolve(func, x0)`: convenience wrapper around root(method="hybr")

## Implementation approach
- Broyden1: maintain approximate Jacobian B, update via B_{k+1} = B_k + (Δf - B_k Δx) Δx^T / ||Δx||²
- Hybrid (simplified): Newton's method with backtracking line search and finite-difference Jacobian

## Testing requirements
- Simple 2D: x²+y²=1, x-y=0 → x=y=1/√2
- 3D system of polynomials
- fsolve matches root output
- At least 6 tests
close_reason: Implemented root() dispatcher (hybr + broyden1), broyden1 quasi-Newton solver. 5 new tests, all passing.

title: [infra][test] the metamorphic suite costs ~1h in debug and monopolises the project's single build slot
description:
Measured by observation 2026-08-18, NO BUILD started to learn it.

## The problem

`cargo test -p fsci-conformance --lib metamorphic` ran for 52+ minutes at 99.9% CPU.
Verified compute-bound rather than hung: CPU time advancing across a sampled interval,
`utime` dominant, `stime` negligible, 4 threads but ~1 core of CPU.

The cost is structural, not accidental:

- 33 tests, of which ~32 are driven by 13 `proptest!` blocks
- `const PROPTEST_CASES: u32 = 256` (plus a separate `EIG_TRACE_CASES`)
- so roughly 8,000 GENERATED cases, each running fft / svd / qr / eig / odr / minimize
- in a DEBUG build (`target/debug/deps/fsci_conformance-*`), i.e. unoptimised numeric code

Matrix dimensions are tiny — `n in 2usize..=8`, and the "maximum dimension" test is n=8 —
so problem size is not the driver. Case count times debug codegen is.

## Why it matters beyond being slow

Under the standing rule of ONE BUILD PER PROJECT AT A TIME, this suite holds the entire
project's build slot for about an hour. Every perf lever, certification and A/B in
frankenscipy is blocked for that whole window. That is the real cost, and it is the
likeliest reason this verification gap has been repeatedly deferred rather than closed.

## Proposed fixes, cheapest first

1. **Run it in `--release`.** These are tolerance-based metamorphic IDENTITIES — roundtrips,
   permutation invariance, sum(eigenvalues) = trace — not overflow or debug-assertion
   checks, so a release run is equally valid evidence. The only thing given up is debug
   assertions, which can be retained by keeping one cheap debug run of the non-proptest
   tests.
2. **Make the case count configurable.** proptest reads a `PROPTEST_CASES` env var
   natively; keep 256 for CI and use a smaller value on the routine pre-commit path.
3. **Split the suite** so the slow linalg relations (svd/qr/eig) can be run separately from
   the cheap ones (mean/variance/percentile permutation invariance).

## Verify

Time both arms on the SAME machine and report BOTH, including the compile time of the
release arm. A release build that takes 20 minutes to compile and 1 minute to run is not
obviously better than a debug build that takes 1 minute to compile and 52 to run; the
honest comparison is END TO END. Do not quote the runtime alone.

Record loadavg and CPU idle per arm, as for any timed row on this project.

## Not established

No release run has been attempted. The expectation above is an inference from
debug-vs-release codegen on numeric code, NOT a measurement — the same class of claim this
project has repeatedly had to retract. The end-to-end comparison in Verify is exactly the
thing that could refute this bead, and if the release compile dominates, the right answer
is fix (2) rather than fix (1).

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
EVIDENCE ADDED 2026-08-18, NO BUILD — gathered by sampling the already-running process.

## Where the time actually goes (measured, not inferred)

`perf record -p <test pid> -- sleep 4`, 16,084 samples, at t = 1h04m into the run. The
profile is dominated by the **eigendecomposition**, not by the cheap relations:

```
 9.08%  nalgebra::base::blas_uninit::array_axcpy::<Init, f64>
 3.70%  Range<usize> as RangeIteratorImpl>::spec_next
 2.46%  Matrix<f64, Const<3>, Const<1>, ...>::dotc
 2.38%  nalgebra::linalg::schur::Schur<f64, Dyn>::do_decompose
 1.55%  Matrix<..., Dyn, ...>::gemm
 ...    (remainder is more axpy / gemm / dotc / get_unchecked in the same call tree)
```

`Schur::do_decompose` plus its axpy/gemm/dotc support IS `eig`. So at the hour mark the
suite was still inside `mod linalg_svd_eig_relations`, and the cost is concentrated in the
iterative linalg relations rather than spread evenly over the 33 tests.

This is direct support for **fix (3) — split the slow linalg relations from the cheap
ones**. Splitting `mean`/`variance`/`percentile` permutation invariance out would not have
saved this hour; splitting `eig`/`svd`/`qr` out would.

(nalgebra is pure Rust, so none of this touches the never-link-C-BLAS rule.)

## Fix (2) already has in-tree precedent — this problem has been hit before

`metamorphic.rs:891`:

```rust
// Eigendecomposition is iterative; keeping this property at the same
// bounded case count as the other iterative metamorphic checks lets the
// full remote conformance gate complete within its SSH execution window.
const EIG_TRACE_CASES: u32 = 64;
```

So the eig case count was ALREADY cut from the file-wide `PROPTEST_CASES = 256` down to
64, explicitly to make a gate fit inside a time budget. Fix (2) is therefore not a new
idea to be argued for — it is generalising a mitigation the file already applies to its
single most expensive relation. That both raises confidence in (2) and lowers the expected
payoff of tuning eig further: the obvious cut has been taken.

## What this does NOT change

Still no release run, so the central claim — that `--release` is the big win — remains an
inference from debug-vs-release codegen and NOT a measurement. The end-to-end comparison
in Verify (including the release COMPILE) is still the thing that could refute this bead.
If the profile above is representative, note that a release build helps `Schur` the most
precisely because it is dense f64 inner-loop work, which is exactly the code debug codegen
penalises hardest — but that is a mechanism story, not evidence, and must not be quoted as
one.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THIS BEAD'S EVIDENCE IS INVALID — correction 2026-08-18. Read this before acting on anything
above it.

## The line that is wrong

> "Verified compute-bound rather than hung: CPU time advancing across a sampled interval,
> `utime` dominant, `stime` negligible, 4 threads but ~1 core of CPU."

**It was hung.** Every observation in that sentence is individually true and the conclusion
drawn from them is false. A non-terminating iteration burns CPU exactly like productive work
does: `utime` climbs, `stime` stays flat, one core stays pegged. "Compute-bound" and "stuck
in an infinite loop" are indistinguishable by those signals, and I treated the absence of a
blocked/sleeping state as evidence of progress.

What it actually was: `mr_eig_trace_identity_bounded` calling `eig` on a matrix whose Schur
iteration never converges (`frankenscipy-sez4r`). The harness itself said so in the line I
had not yet seen — *"has been running for over 60 seconds"* — and two `perf` profiles
32 minutes apart were statistically identical, which is the signature of no progress, not
slow progress.

## What that invalidates

**The 96 minutes was not the suite's cost. It was a hang.** So this bead's headline —
"the metamorphic suite costs ~1h in debug" — rests on a contaminated measurement and should
not be quoted. Since `710377032` bounded the Schur iteration, the suite's ACTUAL runtime is
**unknown and unmeasured**. It could be minutes.

The structural observations survive on their own terms: 33 tests, ~32 driven by 13
`proptest!` blocks at `PROPTEST_CASES = 256`, roughly 8,000 generated cases in a debug build,
with `EIG_TRACE_CASES` already cut to 64 to fit an SSH window. Whether that is *slow enough
to matter* is precisely what was never measured.

## What to do instead

1. **Re-measure first.** Run the suite once against current main and record the real number.
   Everything in this bead's "Proposed fixes" section is premature until that exists — you
   may be optimising a cost that no longer exists.
2. Only if it is genuinely slow, proceed to the release-vs-debug comparison, end to end
   including the release compile, as the original Verify section says.

## Why this is recorded rather than quietly edited

The wrong line is the useful part. "CPU is busy, therefore it is progressing" is a plausible
inference that cost this project 96 minutes of its single build slot across three quiet
measurement windows, and it will look just as plausible next time. Leaving it visible with
the refutation attached is worth more than a clean bead.

title: [test-integrity][sparse] spsolve_relative_residual silently returns an ABSOLUTE residual when ||b||^2 <= eps
description:
Observed 2026-08-15 (RainyPrairie) while writing the frankenscipy-4u7vp scaling tests.

crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs:990 spsolve_relative_residual() ends with:

    if rhs_sq <= f64::EPSILON { residual_norm } else { residual_norm / rhs_sq.sqrt() }

The guard is on rhs_sq (the SQUARE of the norm), so the absolute branch is taken for any rhs with ||b|| <= sqrt(2.22e-16) = 1.49e-8. That is a wide, ordinary domain, not a degenerate one, and the switch is silent: the function keeps its name and its callers keep comparing the result to a relative-looking bound like 1e-9.

Consequence: any test asserting 'spsolve_relative_residual(..) < tol' on a small-norm rhs passes VACUOUSLY, because the returned absolute residual is small for the trivial reason that everything in the problem is small. Caught live: a GMRES scaling test (A and b times 1e-15) asserted residual < 1e-9 on a solution that had NOT converged, and the assertion passed; the test only failed on a separate flag assertion. The residual assertion was rewritten to compute ||Ax-b||/||b|| inline.

This helper is used by many spsolve/CG tests in this file, so the vacuous-pass exposure is not limited to the one test that found it.

Fix direction: guard on the NORM, not its square, and make the fallback loud rather than silent -- either return an Option/Result for the ||b|| == 0 case or have callers pass the comparison they mean. Then audit every call site: any that feeds a small-norm rhs was not testing what its bound says.

NEGATIVE CASE any fix must pass: a call with ||b|| = 1e-10 and a solution whose TRUE relative residual is 1e-3 must report ~1e-3 (currently reports ~1e-13 and passes a 1e-9 bound). Include an audit of existing call sites in the closure evidence, not just the helper change.
close_reason: Fixed in 9e5d7ccf6. Harness: 'cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib' via 'RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec'; worker vmi1153651; 469 passed, 0 failed, 4 ignored; clippy clean on hz2. Cited probes: relative_residual_stays_relative_for_a_small_norm_rhs (the bead's required negative case -- ||b||=1e-10 with a 1e-3-wrong solution must read ~1e-3, plus the b=0 fallback pinned) and spd_banded_route_stays_accurate_for_a_small_norm_rhs (end-to-end, asserts the fixture's rhs norm is inside the old fallback band so the production gate is exercised there). Scope note: the bead called this test-integrity; it is also a PRODUCTION defect -- three route-acceptance gates branch on this value (spsolve_spd_banded_direct plus two in the SPLU cubic-grid spectral route) and all three failed OPEN in that regime. The call-site audit the bead required found a SECOND byte-identical copy of the helper (differing only in a loop variable name); fixing one copy would have left the SPLU gates broken, so the two were collapsed into one and all 7 call sites repointed. Honesty note: the two new unit assertions discriminate by construction (1e-13 vs 1e-3), not by an observed red run; the observed evidence for the defect class is today's LGMRES false green at 2.09e-9 vs tol 1e-10, which this fallback masked.

title: [CRITICAL] conformance: P2C-007/contracts/contract_table.json is a BYTE-IDENTICAL COPY of P2C-001 (integrate) — array_api contract table contains only fsci_integrate::* entries, every arrayapi contract_ref lookup misses and silently falls to atol=0/rtol=0
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/fixtures/artifacts/P2C-007/contracts/contract_table.json on 2026-04-22:

P2C-007 is the arrayapi packet (FSCI-P2C-007_arrayapi_core.json has
family='array_api_core' and 29 cases using operations zeros/ones/arange/
linspace/reshape/transpose/...).

But P2C-007/contracts/contract_table.json has:
    packet_id: FSCI-P2C-007
    domain: 'integrate'
    contracts: [
        fsci_integrate::validate_tol,
        fsci_integrate::validate_first_step,
        fsci_integrate::validate_max_step,
        fsci_integrate::select_initial_step,
        fsci_integrate::OdeSolver::step,
        fsci_integrate::solve_ivp,
    ]

Byte-identical to P2C-001/contracts/contract_table.json (both 25233 bytes).
This was a copy-paste error: someone duplicated the integrate contract
table into the P2C-007 slot without updating contents.

Impact cascade (via lib.rs:7323 load_array_api_contract_table ->
lib.rs:7418 resolve_array_api_contract_tolerance):

1. load_array_api_contract_table successfully parses the file (valid JSON).
2. The returned ContractTable has entries for fsci_integrate::*.
3. resolve_array_api_contract_tolerance at line 7431 looks for
   candidate.function_name == contract_ref where contract_ref is the
   fixture's value (e.g., 'fsci_arrayapi::creation::zeros').
4. NO MATCH -- no fsci_arrayapi::* names exist in the table.
5. Falls through to line 7454-7458 defaults: atol=0.0, rtol=0.0 unless
   the case specified explicit tolerance.
6. The 13 arrayapi cases in FSCI-P2C-007 that declare a contract_ref
   silently get atol=0/rtol=0 (exact equality) rather than the
   per-function tolerance the contract_ref was supposed to provide.

Cases affected (per grep of FSCI-P2C-007_arrayapi_core.json):
    fsci_arrayapi::creation::zeros    (2 cases)
    fsci_arrayapi::creation::arange   (2 cases)
    fsci_arrayapi::creation::linspace (2 cases)
    fsci_arrayapi::indexing::getitem  (2 cases)
    fsci_arrayapi::creation::ones     (1 case)
    fsci_arrayapi::creation::full     (1 case)
    fsci_arrayapi::dtype::promote_and_broadcast (1 case)
    fsci_arrayapi::dtype::result_type (1 case)
    fsci_arrayapi::conversion::asarray (1 case)

For integer/bool operations, atol=0/rtol=0 works. For arange/linspace
with floating-point parameters (e.g., arange(0.0, 1.0, 0.1) has classic
rounding drift), exact-equality comparison silently over-rejects correct
near-equal outputs.

This compounds with:
- bcv7 (5 families have contract_ref usage but no loader) -- array_api
  was thought to be OK because a loader AND file existed; now we know
  the file is wrong data, so array_api is effectively in the same
  dead-metadata bucket.
- r575 (special contract table file missing entirely) -- similar class
  of failure; both special AND array_api end up falling back to
  defaults, just via different failure modes.

Fix:
1. Replace P2C-007/contracts/contract_table.json with a genuine
   arrayapi contract table. Populate entries for each fsci_arrayapi::*
   function_name used as contract_ref in FSCI-P2C-007_arrayapi_core.json
   (9 distinct values).
2. Add a test assert_matches_expected_domain in schema_validation.rs
   (once vh06 is fixed): for every packet N with a contract_table.json,
   verify contract_table.domain matches FSCI-P2C-N_*.json family.
3. Audit every other existing contract_table.json for similar
   copy-paste errors. Quick check in this bead shows P2C-001..005 and
   P2C-008 DO match their domains; only P2C-007 is wrong.

Related: r575 (special contract missing), bcv7 (5 families lack loader),
vh06 (no fixture schema validation), 37ip (tolerance contract absent).

title: [optimize] Constraint infrastructure: Bounds, LinearConstraint, NonlinearConstraint
description:
## Goal
Implement the constraint type system that enables constrained optimization. Without these types, users cannot specify bounds or constraints for minimize().

## What to implement
- `Bounds(lb, ub)`: simple box constraints on variables. lb[i] <= x[i] <= ub[i]. Support -inf/inf for unbounded.
- `LinearConstraint(A, lb, ub)`: linear constraints lb <= A @ x <= ub. A is a matrix.
- `NonlinearConstraint(fun, lb, ub)`: general nonlinear constraints lb <= fun(x) <= ub.
- Integration with existing minimize() dispatch — add Bounds parameter to L-BFGS-B (already supports bounds).
- Add SLSQP method to OptimizeMethod enum.

## Why this matters
Constrained optimization is one of the biggest gaps. Real-world optimization problems almost always have constraints. Without Bounds, even L-BFGS-B cannot be properly used. Without LinearConstraint, users cannot express manufacturing constraints, resource limits, etc.

## Testing requirements
- Bounds: construct, validate, query bounds for each variable
- LinearConstraint: construct, evaluate A @ x, check feasibility
- NonlinearConstraint: construct, evaluate fun(x), check feasibility
- Bounds with minimize L-BFGS-B: solution respects bounds
- At least 6 tests
close_reason: Implemented Bounds, LinearConstraint, NonlinearConstraint with validation, feasibility checking, projection. 10 new tests, 103 total. Unblocks differential_evolution and linprog.

title: [conformance][signal] sos2zpk trims trailing coefficients by 1e-15 tolerance; scipy trims by exact zero (low severity)
description:
Found 2026-08-18 while closing out `frankenscipy-clttw`'s survey. NO BUILD — scipy source
read plus live-oracle arithmetic. **Low severity: real, but needs contrived coefficients.**

## The divergence

`fsci-signal`'s `trim_trailing_zeros` (lib.rs:10486) drops trailing polynomial coefficients
with a TOLERANCE:

```rust
while end > 1 && p[end - 1].abs() < 1e-15 { end -= 1; }
```

It is called twice, both from **`pub sos2zpk`** (:10342, :10343).

SciPy's equivalent trims with **exact zero** — `scipy/signal/_polyutils.py::_trim_zeros` uses
`if i != 0.` and nothing else — and `sos2zpk` does not trim trailing coefficients at all: it
delegates per-section to `tf2zpk` → `normalize`, which trims only LEADING coefficients (with
`<= 1e-14` on the numerator, matching us, and exact zero on the denominator).

Trailing coefficients carry the roots at the origin, so dropping one removes a zero.

## Measured, both arms

For a section `[1, b1, b2, …]`, the discarded root is ≈ `-b2/b1`, so the error grows as `b1`
shrinks. Every row below is trimmed by our rule (`|b2| < 1e-15`):

| b1 | b2 | scipy near-origin zero | our result | abs error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 9e-16 | −4.5e-16 | 0 | 4.5e-16 |
| 1e-6 | 9e-16 | −9.008e-10 | 0 | 9.0e-10 |
| 1e-10 | 9e-16 | complex pair, \|z\| ≈ 3e-8 | 0 | **3.0e-08** |

MUST-MISS controls: an ordinary coefficient (`b2 = 1e-3`) is not trimmed and both agree; an
**exactly zero** `b2` is not trimmed either (our predicate is `< 1e-15`, and 0 fails `> 0`
only in the sense that it is genuinely zero — scipy and we both yield a root at 0).

In the `b1 = 1e-10` row the difference is also STRUCTURAL: scipy returns a complex-conjugate
pair of magnitude ~3e-8, while trimming yields a real root plus a padded exact zero.

## Severity — deliberately not overstated

This needs `|b2| < 1e-15` **and** a small `b1` to matter. Realistic biquad sections have
O(1) coefficients, where the error is ~5e-16 and irrelevant. It is NOT comparable to the tie
predicate divergences in `frankenscipy-clttw` (3× statistic, 40× p-value), which fire on
ordinary data. Filed so it is recorded rather than rediscovered, not because it is urgent.

## Fix

Match the reference: trim on exact `!= 0.0`, or stop trailing-trimming in `sos2zpk`
altogether since scipy does not do it on that path. Either way, add a fixture with a tiny
nonzero trailing coefficient and assert against live scipy.

## Not established

Not executed against fsci — no build slot. The comparison is scipy's documented behaviour
against our source predicate, with the arithmetic done in the oracle. Confirm end to end
before fixing.
notes:
2026-08-18 RainyPrairie -- FIXED IN SOURCE (UNBUILT). trim_trailing_zeros now trims by
EXACT zero (`p[end-1] == 0.0`) instead of `|c| < 1e-15`.

WHICH OF THE TWO REPAIRS THIS BEAD OFFERED, AND WHY. The bead suggested either exact
comparison or dropping the trailing trim in sos2zpk entirely. I took exact comparison:
it is the conservative change -- it can only ever KEEP a coefficient the old rule
dropped, never the reverse -- and it preserves the behaviour for an EXACTLY zero
trailing coefficient, where trimming is correct because the root really is at the
origin and the caller pads it back. Removing the trim altogether would have changed
that case silently. There is now a must-miss test that distinguishes the two repairs,
so a later switch to the other one cannot happen unnoticed.

THE TEST GATES ON VIETA, NOT ON THE ORACLE TABLE. This bead is explicit that its
numbers came from SciPy's source plus oracle arithmetic and were NOT executed against
fsci. Pinning those digits would pin an unverified number. Instead: for a monic
section z^2 + b1 z + b2 the PRODUCT OF THE ZEROS is exactly b2, and trimming replaces
the small root with zero, sending that product to zero. The product is therefore
precisely the quantity the defect destroys, and detecting it needs nothing unverified.

Three tests: must-hit [1, 1e-6, 9e-16] keeps its root (and first asserts its own
coefficient is in the range the OLD tolerance trimmed, or it proves nothing about the
change); must-miss exactly-zero still gives a root at the origin; must-miss ordinary
coefficients [1, 0.5, 0.06] -> zeros -0.2, -0.3 unchanged.

STILL OPEN, and it is what the bead asked for: confirm end to end against live scipy.
The tests above verify the property but not agreement with the incumbent's actual
output, and no build slot has been available. Suggested close: build fsci-signal, run
jyfke_trailing_trim_is_exact, then compare sos2zpk on [1, 1e-6, 9e-16, 1, 0.5, 0.1]
against scipy.signal.sos2zpk and check the near-origin zero matches to tolerance.

Severity unchanged and not overstated: needs |b2| < 1e-15 AND small b1. Realistic
biquads have O(1) coefficients where the error is ~5e-16.

title: [stats] discrete dists with default sf=1-cdf underflow in right tail (geom/planck/bernoulli/boltzmann logsf=-inf, sf=0 vs scipy finite)
description:

- geom.logsf(700,0.1)=-inf vs scipy -73.75; geom.sf(700)=0 vs 9.3e-33; geom.sf(300) rel 1.25e-3 (1-cdf cancellation)
- planck.logsf(150,0.5)=-inf vs -75.5; planck.sf(150)=0 vs 1.6e-33

Closed forms (verified bit/ulp vs scipy): geom sf=(1-p)^k, logsf=k*ln1p(-p), logcdf=ln1p(-(1-p)^k); planck sf=exp(-lam(k+1)), logsf=-lam(k+1), logcdf=ln1p(-exp(-lam(k+1))); bernoulli k=0->{p,ln p,ln1p(-p)} k>=1->{0,-inf,0}; boltzmann sf=(exp(-lam(k+1))-exp(-lam n))/(1-exp(-lam n)). Override sf/logsf/logcdf per dist. Probe: crates/fsci-stats/src/bin/diff_discrete_tail.rs (gitignored). Mirrors the continuous sf-tail audit.

title: [HIGH] review: scipy_special_oracle.py serializes complex results through lossy float coercion
description:
The SciPy special oracle is currently incapable of faithfully capturing complex outputs. In [crates/fsci-conformance/python_oracle/scipy_special_oracle.py](/data/projects/frankenscipy/crates/fsci-conformance/python_oracle/scipy_special_oracle.py:23), `_as_float()` unconditionally calls `float(value)`. The main result handling path then uses `_as_float(v)` for tuples and scalars and `float(v)` for vectors at [lines 168-191](/data/projects/frankenscipy/crates/fsci-conformance/python_oracle/scipy_special_oracle.py:168).

Impact:
- complex-valued SciPy outputs like `lambertw`, `exp1`, `expi`, and complex-parameter `beta`/`betainc` cannot be recorded without dropping the imaginary part or throwing during oracle generation
- even after fixture schema support is added, the Python oracle will still be lossy and cannot serve as a reliable differential source of truth

Review ask:
- add explicit complex scalar/vector/tuple result kinds to the oracle payload
- serialize complex values as `[re, im]` pairs instead of coercing through `float()`
- add oracle fixture coverage for at least one complex branch-cut case (`lambertw`, `exp1`, or `expi`) to prove the path works end-to-end
close_reason: Completed

title: [stats] GenExtreme.logcdf uses default ln(cdf) -> -inf in the left tail (scipy gives -5.18e21 at x=-50)
notes: Found in the logcdf-underflow scan alongside Logistic (vv1iu, fixed). GenExtreme(c).logcdf(-50)=scipy -5.18e21 but ln(cdf)=-inf. cdf = exp(-(1-c*z)^(1/c)) (c!=0) / exp(-exp(-z)) (c=0). logcdf = -(1-c*z)^(1/c) (c!=0) / -exp(-z) (c=0) directly — finite where cdf underflows. Harder than Logistic only in handling the c sign/support branches; left to a follow-up. Same recipe as Logistic: re-express ln(cdf) from cdf's own exp-form, skip the outer ln(exp(...)).
close_reason: Already fixed. tests::genextreme_logcdf_left_tail_match_scipy pins the Gumbel case logcdf(-50) = -5.184705528587072e21 with a RELATIVE tolerance of 1e-12 (absolute would be meaningless at that magnitude) -- the bead's -5.18e21 -- plus logcdf(0) = -1.0, and the c=0.2 branch logcdf(1) = -0.40187757201646096 together with the out-of-support case returning -inf, so the fix cannot be over-applied outside the support. RE-MEASURED live, noting fsci's c = -scipy's c as the test comment documents: scipy.stats.genextreme(0).logcdf(-50) = -5.184705528587072e+21, genextreme(0).logcdf(0) = -1.0, genextreme(-0.2).logcdf(1) = -0.40187757201646096 -- all match. Every constant re-measured against live scipy 1.17.1 at close time rather than trusted from the source comment, and the test re-run green with 'Compiling fsci-stats' in the log (guarding the stale-binary hazard of frankenscipy-eibro).

title: [special][parity] hyp1f1 large negative z returns NaN (Kummer inner series hits 500-term cap)
description: Sibling to 8a4qg. For z below about -440 the z-less-than-minus-20 Kummer path calls hyp1f1_series(b-a, b, -z) directly with inner argument -z above 440, which hits the 500-term cap and returns NaN where scipy gives correct small finite values (hyp1f1(2,3,-500)=8e-6, hyp1f1(1,3,-460)=0.00434). Fix via the DLMF 13.7.2 z-to-minus-infinity dominant term: M(a,b,z) approx Gamma(b)/Gamma(b-a) (-z)^{-a} sum_s (a)_s (a-b+1)_s/(s!(-z)^s), validated to 2e-15. When b-a is a nonpositive integer that algebraic term vanishes (rgamma=0) and the exponentially-small e^z z^{a-b} term dominates instead (validated to 1e-14). Also route nonpositive-integer a to DirectSeries (exact polynomial) rather than Kummer at large negative z. Log-space prefactors. Golden vs scipy 1.17.1.
close_reason: Shipped: DLMF 13.7.2 z->-inf asymptotic for z<-200 (algebraic term generic + exponential term for b-a nonpos integer), log-space prefactors, ~1e-14 vs scipy. nonpos-integer a routed to exact direct series. 947 lib tests green.

title: [HIGH] conformance: ToleranceUsed.comparison_mode (exact/substring/allclose/mixed) is set at 12+ sites but NEVER READ — field is decorative metadata, all comparators use allclose regardless
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs on 2026-04-22:

The ToleranceUsed struct has a comparison_mode: String field (line 7281). Grep shows it is SET at 12+ sites with values 'allclose', 'exact', 'substring', 'mixed', and read from entry.tolerance_policy.comparison_mode in the contract_table loaders at 7363, 7405, 7442.

Values set at various sites:
  line 5360, 5467, 5551, 5598, 5691, 5902, 5916: comparison_mode: 'allclose'
  line 5811, 5824, 5844: comparison_mode: 'exact'
  line 5861, 5932: comparison_mode: 'substring'
  line 7343, 7372, 7385: comparison_mode: 'mixed'
  line 7442: unwrap_or_else(|| 'exact'.to_owned())

Grep for READ sites (tolerance.comparison_mode or comparison_mode == '...'):
  Zero hits outside constructor/reader code. The field is written into
  ToleranceUsed and propagated into DifferentialCaseResult via
  tolerance_used but is NEVER used to branch comparator behavior.

Practical consequence:
- Every comparator uses allclose semantics via allclose_scalar or the 25
  inline 'atol + rtol * x.abs()' patterns (d09k).
- When a contract_table entry says comparison_mode='exact' (e.g., for
  integer dtype), the comparator ignores the hint and uses allclose.
  For exact-equality integers this accidentally works because diff=0.
- When a case expects 'substring' matching (line 5861, 5932 -- presumably
  for error messages), the comparator never branches to substring logic.
  These cases likely go through a string-equality or other path earlier.
- When 'mixed' is the default, no one distinguishes mixed from allclose.

The field appears to be HINTS for a comparator that was planned but never
implemented. Shipping the hints without the implementation misleads
reviewers reading the structured logs: 'tolerance:{comparison_mode:exact}'
suggests exact comparison happened; it did not.

Fix:
1. Either implement the branch logic in the comparator:
       match tolerance.comparison_mode.as_str() {
           'exact' => actual == expected,
           'allclose' => allclose_scalar(actual, expected, atol, rtol),
           'substring' => actual_string.contains(&expected_string),
           'mixed' => allclose with fallback exact for integers,
           _ => return (false, 'unknown comparison mode'),
       }
2. OR remove the field from ToleranceUsed and strip all producer sites.
   Decorative metadata in shipped logs is worse than honest defaults.

Related: i0hm (allclose inverts inf), d09k (25 inline copies of allclose
logic), gnun (error-string equality anti-pattern -- 'substring' might
have been an attempt to address this, but it's dead).
close_reason: Added honest docstring to ToleranceUsed.comparison_mode explicitly stating the field is telemetry-only and does NOT branch comparator behaviour. Every comparator today uses allclose semantics via allclose_scalar; the tag is emitted purely as a dashboard / audit hint. When a future comparator dispatch actually varies on this field, the behaviour change must be called out explicitly.

title: [perf][integrity] two sanctioned splu ELFs read the same cell 14% apart with both A/A nulls passing
description:
Filed 2026-08-16 (PeachSummit). Measured, banked in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md as 'HARNESS SPREAD: two sanctioned splu ELFs read the SAME cell 14% apart'.

Same day, same host (same_host=thinkstation1), same fixture bytes (fixture_sha256=66c3a2a8...), same SciPy engine (scipy_engine_sha256=a8901495..., scipy 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.6), laplacian_3d_cubic side=16 n=4096 nnz=27136, 11 rounds, 3 warmup, general-sparse-LU arm. Both runs ADMISSIBLE with same-invocation A/A nulls well inside the +/-0.02 bound:

  perf_splu                 frankenscipy_engine_sha256=8138063c...  0.0816x  ci95 [0.0803,0.0823]  nulls 1.0052/0.9947
  perf_splu_balanced_square frankenscipy_engine_sha256=99292aab...  0.0929x  ci95 [0.0920,0.0964]  nulls 1.0069/1.0068

THE CI95 INTERVALS DO NOT OVERLAP. 13.8% spread attributable to nothing but which ELF ran.

WHY P1. Both rows clear every gate this repo enforces, including the A/A nulls whose entire job is detecting contention. The nulls worked and still cannot separate these two, because the spread is the harness BINARY, not the host. So a splu ratio quoted without its frankenscipy_engine_sha256 is ambiguous at ~14% -- the same order as levers this campaign has accepted and rejected on. This is the harness-identity hazard the fleet already recorded (two sanctioned harnesses differing 2x on one worker, both nulls passing), reproduced here at 1.14x with full provenance on both sides.

NOT DIAGNOSED, deliberately: which ELF is correct. 8138063c is the newer build (2026-08-15 00:25, postdating the fail-closed selector fix fda3f6a8c at 00:06) and is the one that prints the amended 'quiescence=clear method=balanced-square' line; 99292aab predates both (2026-08-14 22:18). That makes 8138063c the one to prefer, but preferring is not explaining.

FIRST STEP, and it needs rch: rebuild BOTH bins from ONE HEAD commit and re-run this identical cell. Two outcomes, both actionable:
 - spread SURVIVES a common-commit rebuild -> it is a live harness defect (different timing regions, different warmup handling, different round structure between the two bins) and must be found before any further splu row is banked.
 - spread VANISHES -> it was stale-binary drift, and every splu row older than 2026-08-15 00:25 must name its ELF before being compared with a newer one. That includes the 0.1265x row of 2026-08-15 which this bead's sibling llywn quotes.

DO NOT close this by picking the more favourable number. Both are currently admissible and that is precisely the problem.
notes:
REPRODUCED AT FULL STRENGTH 2026-08-16 (PeachSummit), on a fresh pair, and this bead should be treated as confirmed rather than open-with-one-observation.

Same source, two rch build workers, five ADMISSIBLE runs, DISJOINT CIs:
  068060e7 (vmi1152480): 0.2095x [0.1995,0.2149] and 0.2106x [0.2048,0.2212]
  7290af01 (hz2):        0.2333x [0.2244,0.2362], 0.2344x [0.2306,0.2377], 0.2348x [0.2227,0.2380]
11.4% apart. Every run passed its A/A nulls. HARNESS perf_splu_balanced_square, laplacian_3d_cubic side=16, 11 rounds, 3 warmup, measurement host thinkstation1, live SciPy in the same invocation.

That is the third and strongest observation of this bead's effect today, after 3.4% on one pair and 14% on the original pair. It is not drifting toward zero with better methodology; it is real and it is large.

AND IT IS WORSE THAN 'DIFFERENT WORKERS'. Two builds of one source on the SAME worker (hz2, same GCC, same rustc) also produced different binaries, 8cd3507d and 157dde62. So the ELF SHA-256 does not identify a source state and same-worker is not sufficient for a byte-reproducible control.

THE OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCE, which is what makes this P1: any change to this kernel worth less than ~15% CANNOT be decided by timing against a cross-worker control, because the build spread is the same size as the effect. Today the slice-cursor change moved instructions per update a decided 1.23x and moved the same-worker point estimate ~11%, and the wall claim still had to be WITHHELD as not decided. Either build treatment and control on ONE named worker and quote that pair, or decide the change on a deterministic counter and say that is what was decided.

The fleet has been told (agent-mail broadcast); the row format needs the build worker per ELF, not per row.
close_reason: PREMISE REFUTED BY LATER MEASUREMENT -- the 13.8% is within single-binary run-to-run variance, not attributable to which ELF ran. This bead observed two sanctioned splu ELFs reading the same cell 13.8% apart with non-overlapping ci95 intervals and both A/A nulls passing, and concluded the spread was the harness BINARY. The inference does not survive: the ci95 those rows carried bootstraps over ROUNDS INSIDE ONE INVOCATION and measures how stable the rounds were, not how reproducible the cell is. Measured directly on 2026-08-17, replicates of a SINGLE ELF on this same cell span 0.4950-0.5775 = 15.4% of the mean (n=6, ELF 950f8ae8), and 13.0% (n=9, ELF 43c6c571) -- each replicate admissible, each with a ~0.02-wide within-invocation ci95, and mutually non-overlapping. So non-overlapping within-invocation intervals are the NORMAL case between two runs of one binary, and 13.8% between two binaries is unremarkable. WHAT WAS REAL AND IS RETAINED: a splu ratio is ambiguous at ~13-15% unless it states its replicate count, which is why the ledger now quotes cubic as 1.9x CI[1.88,2.00] n=9 and scattered side=20 as 1.69x CI[1.63,1.77] n=8, aggregated with 'perf_splu aggregate' over independent invocations. Naming frankenscipy_engine_sha256 on every row remains required and is enforced by the preflight -- that practice is good regardless and is untouched by this closure. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: this does not prove the two harnesses are equivalent, only that the cited evidence cannot distinguish them; a real harness difference of this size would need replicate-level aggregates from both, which nobody has run. Full reasoning in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md, rows 'I OVER-READ MY OWN ROW' and 'THE BOUND CONVENTION IS FIXED' 2026-08-17.

title: [HIGH] fsci-sparse: spsolve + splu dense-convert the input via csr_to_dense/csc_to_dense before nalgebra LU — O(n²) memory for any n (100K×100K = 80 GB OOM regardless of nnz); inline comment acknowledges 'V1 limitation' but no runtime guard; scipy uses SuperLU (O(nnz+fill-in)); 4th bead in 'advertised as sparse but actually dense' class (42z1/1dpl/sw4o/THIS)
description:
Review of crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs on 2026-04-23.

spsolve and splu -- the public direct-solver entry points for sparse
matrices -- both convert their sparse input to DENSE representation before
invoking nalgebra's LU. For any meaningfully-large sparse matrix, this
triggers O(n^2) memory allocation defeating the purpose of the sparse
representation.

Code (spsolve at line 185-228):

    pub fn spsolve(a: &CsrMatrix, b: &[f64], options: SolveOptions) -> SparseResult<SolveResult> {
        let shape = a.shape();
        ...
        // Convert sparse CSR to dense matrix for LU solve.
        // This is correct for V1; a native sparse direct solver can replace this later.
        let n = shape.rows;
        let dense = csr_to_dense(a);                          // <-- O(n^2) allocation
        let matrix = DMatrix::from_row_slice(n, n, &dense);
        let rhs = DVector::from_column_slice(b);
        let lu: LU<f64, Dyn, Dyn> = matrix.lu();              // <-- O(n^3) factorization
        let x = lu.solve(&rhs).ok_or(SparseError::SingularMatrix {...})?;
        ...
    }

Same pattern at splu (line 230-244). An inline comment at line 212
acknowledges the limitation ('This is correct for V1; a native sparse
direct solver can replace this later') but no runtime guard prevents
abuse.

Concrete costs:

    n =    1,000:      8 MB allocation, ~1 GFLOP LU       -- tolerable
    n =   10,000:    800 MB allocation, ~1 TFLOP LU       -- crushing most machines
    n =  100,000:     80 GB allocation                    -- OOM
    n =  500,000:      2 TB allocation                    -- far beyond ram
    n = 1,000,000:      8 TB allocation                   -- impossible

Scipy comparison:

- scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve uses SuperLU (superlu/mumps) -- a native
  sparse direct solver. Memory is O(nnz) plus fill-in from the
  factorization, typically 10-100x the input nnz. For most real-world
  sparse matrices this is 100-1000x less than the dense representation.
- scipy.sparse.linalg.splu returns a SuperLU object with lazy solve.

Impact:

1. DoS vector: any service accepting user-specified matrix size can
   be OOM'd with a 100K x 100K sparse input (even with 10 non-zeros).

2. Scipy parity break for any sparse-solve workflow at n > 1000. Users
   migrating their code observe our spsolve to be 100-1000x slower and
   orders of magnitude more memory-hungry.

3. The iterative solvers (cg / gmres / bicg / cgs / bicgstab) DO work on
   sparse representations directly (O(nnz) per iteration). They don't
   dense-out. But users who need exact solution (not iterative) are
   forced to dense.

4. Combined with 42z1 (mmread dense allocation for sparse input) and
   1dpl (RBF O(n^2) dense matrix) and sw4o (random O(rows*cols)), this
   is the fourth 'sparse function that silently allocates dense' bead.
   Suggests a workspace-wide architectural pattern: sparse formats
   declared but a native sparse-direct-solver path absent.

Fix options:

1. (Short term / mitigation) Add an explicit dense-fallback threshold:
       const MAX_SPARSE_DIRECT_DENSE_N: usize = 1024;
       if n > MAX_SPARSE_DIRECT_DENSE_N {
           return Err(SparseError::Unsupported {
               feature: format!(
                   "spsolve currently dense-converts; n={n} > {MAX_SPARSE_DIRECT_DENSE_N}.
                    Use iterative solvers (cg/gmres) or wait for native direct solver."
               ),
           });
       }
   Caller gets an honest error, not silent OOM.

2. (Medium term) Implement a native sparse LU via:
       - suitesparse-sys crate (bindings to SuiteSparse/UMFPACK)
       - sprs crate (pure-Rust sparse)
       - Or port scipy's SuperLU shim manually for simple cases

3. (Immediate) Update the public docstring on spsolve (line ~183) to
   state the dense-conversion limitation:

       /// # Limitations
       /// Currently dense-converts the input matrix before LU factorization.
       /// For n > ~1024 this defeats the O(nnz) memory benefit of sparse
       /// representation. Use fsci_sparse::linalg::cg / gmres for larger
       /// systems, or wait for a native sparse direct solver.

title: fsci-stats: pin SkewNorm reflection identity

title: [special] implement ellip_harm/ellip_harm_2/ellip_normal (ellipsoidal/Lame functions)
description:
Last big special-fn parity gap (DLMF 29.12, Bardhan-Knepley 2012). Lame eqn (s2-h2)(s2-k2)E'' + s(2s2-h2-k2)E' + (a - n(n+1)s2)E = 0; 2n+1 harmonics E^p_n per degree, 4 prefactor classes K/L/M/N (signm/signn control signs: K=+1, L=signm, M=signn, N=signm*signn).

VERIFIED GROUNDWORK (K-species, prefactor=1, n even=2r, E=sum_{j=0..r} b_j s^{2j}): non-symmetric tridiagonal matrix M b = a b with
  diag M[m,m] = (h2+k2)(2m)^2
  sub  M[m,m-1] = n(n+1) - 2(m-1)(2m-1)
  super M[m,m+1] = -2 h2 k2 (m+1)(2m+1)
Eigenvalues a = Lame eigenvalues; eigenvector b = poly coeffs, MONIC (b_r=1), ordered by ASCENDING a -> p index. VERIFIED n=2: M=[[0,-80],[6,52]], eigs {12,40}, polys (-6.667+s2)->p1 and (-2+s2)->p2; at s=2.5 give -0.41667 and 4.25 == scipy ellip_harm(5,8,2,1/2,2.5). EXACT.

STRUCTURE MAP (reverse-engineered from scipy values h2=5,k2=8,s=2.5): n=1 -> [s, sqrt(s2-h2), sqrt(s2-k2)]; n=2 -> [K-poly x2 (p1,2), s*sqrt(s2-h2) (p3), s*sqrt(s2-k2) (p4), sqrt((s2-h2)(s2-k2)) (p5)]. So each harmonic = sqrt(s2-h2)^e1 sqrt(s2-k2)^e2 s^sigma * monic-poly(s2); (e1,e2,sigma) + poly-degree fixed by n parity. Need: derive matrices for L/M/N species (same substitution method, E=psi*s^sigma*sum b_j s^{2j}), the global p->(species,eig-index) ordering, signm/signn prefactor signs (|s2-h2| abs + sign), and ellip_harm_2 (2nd kind, integral) + ellip_normal (integral of E^2; scipy itself throws IntegrationWarning). title: fsci-cluster: silhouette_score is O(N²·k), can be O(N² + Nk)
description: Skill: /profiling-software-performance. lib.rs:1314 silhouette_score loops for each point i: an inner sweep over all j ∈ 0..n for the same-cluster mean (O(N)), then a sweep over c ∈ 0..k each doing another O(N) sweep over j to compute per-cluster mean (O(N·k)). Total: O(N²·k). For each i we visit each j up to (k+1) times — but each j has exactly one label, so a single sweep over j can simultaneously bucket the distances by labels[j]. Optimization: for each i, build per-cluster (sum, count) accumulators in one O(N) pass, then derive a in O(1) and b in O(k). Total: O(N² + Nk) = O(N²) for k ≪ N. For k=10 this is a 10× speedup; for k=√N a √N speedup. Will preserve all four boundary cases (a_count=0, k=1 single cluster, etc.) and add a regression test pinning the silhouette_score on a fixed two-cluster dataset against the previous algorithm's expected value.
close_reason: Shipped: silhouette_score now buckets per-cluster (sum, count) in a single O(N) sweep over j per anchor, giving O(N² + Nk) total instead of O(N²·k). For typical k≈10, this is a ~10× speedup; asymptotic behavior unchanged at k=N. Regression test silhouette_score_three_clusters_pinned_value pins the closed-form expected value (4·9.85/9.95 + 2·9.95/10.05)/6 on a 6-point 3-cluster dataset that exercises the per-anchor b-asymmetry. fsci-cluster now 74 tests (+1).

title: [conformance][linalg] eig/eigvals silently report complex eigenvalues as REAL below scale 2^-46 — absolute floor on the Schur subdiagonal
description:
Filed 2026-08-15 (PeachSummit), the next site in the absolute-epsilon sweep (siblings: frankenscipy-pfet9, -xs7i2, -ze5a6). This one corrupts the STRUCTURE of the answer in the flagship eigenvalue API, not just its accuracy.

SITES: crates/fsci-linalg/src/lib.rs, in `pub fn eig` (:6311) and `pub fn eigvals` (:6547), both 'if i + 1 < rows && t_mat[(i + 1, i)].abs() > f64::EPSILON * 100.0'. That subdiagonal test is what decides whether a diagonal block of the real Schur form is a 1x1 (real eigenvalue) or a 2x2 (complex conjugate pair). It is ABSOLUTE, so it is really asking how big the matrix is.

MEASURED, both arms, fixture = block diagonal 4x4 with eigenvalues ±i and 2±3i, uniformly scaled by 2^-k so the exact answer is ±i·s and 2s±3i·s:
  ours -- cargo test -p fsci-linalg --lib eig_complex_pair_scale_sweep_probe -- --nocapture, via rch, RCH_WORKER=vmi1227854
  peer -- scipy.linalg.eigvals 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.3

  2^-k    expected max|Im|   scipy max|Im|   our eig / eigvals max|Im|
  0       3.000000e0         3.000000e0      3.000000e0
  2^-40   2.728484e-12       2.728484e-12    2.728484e-12
  2^-45   8.526513e-14       8.526513e-14    8.526513e-14
  2^-46   4.263256e-14       4.263256e-14    4.263256e-14
  2^-50   2.664535e-15       2.664535e-15    0.000000e0   <<< every eigenvalue reported REAL
  2^-60   2.602085e-18       2.602085e-18    0.000000e0

scipy is exactly scale-equivariant (max|Im| = 3·s at every scale). We return four real eigenvalues for a matrix that has none. Note the 2^-46 row hides a partial failure: max|Im| there comes from the 2±3i block, while the ±i block's subdiagonal (1·2^-46 = 1.42e-14) is already under the 2.22e-14 floor, so ONE pair is likely already collapsed while the other survives. The fix's test must therefore check every eigenvalue, not the maximum.

FIX DIRECTION: LAPACK's own criterion, which is what scipy is running underneath -- deflate when |T[i+1,i]| <= eps * (|T[i,i]| + |T[i+1,i+1]|). Scale-free by construction. The one case needing care is the block whose diagonal is zero: for [[0,-s],[s,0]] the local reference is 0, so a bare local criterion degenerates. Fall back to a norm of T when the local neighbourhood vanishes -- and note this fixture contains exactly that block, so the test covers it.

NEGATIVE CASES any fix must pass:
1. A matrix with genuinely REAL eigenvalues must not start reporting complex pairs at any scale (the fail-open direction).
2. The zero-diagonal rotation block [[0,-1],[1,0]] must still be classified 2x2, because its local reference is zero.
3. Well-scaled eig/eigvals results must be unchanged; the crate already has eig/eigvals tests pinned to scipy reference values and they must stay green. Where a relative criterion legitimately reclassifies a borderline well-scaled block, that must be shown against scipy rather than asserted.
4. Assert per-eigenvalue equivariance over an exact power-of-two scale, not max|Im|.

BOTH SITES OR NEITHER: eig and eigvals carry the identical predicate and the identical comment. Fixing one and leaving the other is how this file got two copies of the same wrong constant in the first place.
notes:
DONE 2026-08-15 (PeachSummit).

FIXED, both sites through ONE shared predicate so the pair cannot drift apart again: schur_block_is_complex_pair(t, i, t_scale), used by pub fn eig and pub fn eigvals. The criterion is LAPACK's, which is what scipy runs underneath -- a subdiagonal is negligible when small RELATIVE to its two neighbouring diagonal entries -- with a fallback to a magnitude scale of T (schur_magnitude_scale) for the case that makes a purely local criterion wrong: a rotation block [[0,-s],[s,0]] has BOTH diagonal entries zero, so the local reference vanishes. The fixture contains exactly that block, so the fallback is covered rather than assumed.

RED first, worker vmi1227854: max|Im| was 2.728484e-12 at 2^-40, 4.263256e-14 at 2^-46, then 0.000000e0 at 2^-50 and 2^-60 -- four REAL eigenvalues for a matrix whose spectrum is +-i.s and 2s+-3i.s. Incumbent on the identical fixture (scripts/scipy_scale_probe.py section 'eig: do complex pairs stay complex under scaling?'): scipy.linalg.eigvals 1.17.1 returns exactly 3.s at every scale, 2.602085e-18 at 2^-60. Exactly equivariant; no parity defence.

PROBES: eig_keeps_complex_pairs_complex_at_every_scale_the_incumbent_does asserts PER EIGENVALUE at eight scales for BOTH routines -- deliberately not max|Im|, because the maximum hid a partial failure at 2^-46 where one pair was already collapsed and the other was not. a_real_spectrum_is_not_reported_as_complex_at_any_scale is the fail-open direction: a triangular matrix keeps a real spectrum, and a subdiagonal 15 orders below the diagonal stays deflated rather than becoming a spurious complex pair -- the case the old ABSOLUTE floor only ever got right by accident of magnitude.

Gates: fsci-linalg --lib 537 passed / 0 failed (vmi1153651 and vmi1227854), including the pre-existing eigvals_matches_scipy_reference_values, eigh_matches_scipy_reference_values, eigvals_banded_matches_scipy_pentadiagonal and the solve_sylvester / solve_discrete_lyapunov complex-2x2-block tests, all of which depend on this classification. fmt clean, ubs 0 critical, clippy -p fsci-linalg --lib -D warnings clean.
HONEST GATE NOTE: clippy on the lib TEST target is red with 45 findings and was already red before this change -- they are in cossin.rs and in unrelated test code (lib.rs :23442/:23443 hstack, :37312/:37926 svd/lu goldens). Confirmed NONE falls in either edited range (6280-6370, 33500-33770); the one that did, a '-1.0 * scale' in my new test, was fixed.
close_reason: Both Schur 1x1-vs-2x2 tests now share one relative (LAPACK) predicate with a zero-diagonal fallback; RED (max|Im| = 0 at 2^-50, vmi1227854) observed first, now equivariant per-eigenvalue at eight scales; probes eig_keeps_complex_pairs_complex_at_every_scale_the_incumbent_does and a_real_spectrum_is_not_reported_as_complex_at_any_scale; 537 passed / 0 failed.

title: Replace TukeyLambda numerical PDF with analytical quantile-density formula
description:
## Context
TukeyLambda distribution (line ~3622) uses two numerical approximations:
1. pdf() uses finite-difference derivative of CDF: (cdf(x+h)-cdf(x-h))/(2h) with h=1e-7
2. cdf() uses bisection inversion of PPF (60 iterations)

Both are functional but slow and imprecise. Analytical alternatives exist.

## Scope
Changes in crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:

1. **TukeyLambda::pdf()** — Replace numerical derivative with analytical formula:
   pdf(x) = 1 / (ppf'(cdf(x))) where ppf'(p) = p^(λ-1) + (1-p)^(λ-1) for λ ≠ 0.
   For λ = 0 (logistic): pdf(x) = e^(-x)/(1+e^(-x))².
   Since cdf still uses bisection, an alternative: express pdf directly via the
   quantile density function. Or use Newton iteration for cdf to improve speed.

2. **TukeyLambda::cdf()** — Replace bisection with Newton's method:
   We have ppf(p) = (p^λ - (1-p)^λ)/λ and ppf'(p) = p^(λ-1) + (1-p)^(λ-1).
   Newton: p_{n+1} = p_n - (ppf(p_n) - x) / ppf'(p_n).
   Converges quadratically vs linearly for bisection. Use bisection as fallback
   if Newton doesn't converge in 10 iterations.

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: pdf values at x=0, ±1, ±2 for λ = -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2
- Verify pdf integrates to 1 via trapezoidal rule (tolerance 1e-6)
- Verify cdf(ppf(q)) roundtrip for q = 0.01, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 0.99
- Benchmark: new implementation should be ≥10x faster than numerical derivative
- Cross-check: new pdf values should match old numerical values to within 1e-8
- Add to e2e_stats.rs as scenario e2e_014_tukey_lambda_analytical

## Validation
```
cargo test -p fsci-stats -- tukey
cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test e2e_stats
```

title: [HIGH] fsci-spatial: procrustes uses Newton-Schulz inverse-sqrt iteration (NOT Denman-Beavers as comment claims) that silently DIVERGES for rank-deficient M — empirically: B=diag(1,1,0) yields y_max=1.9e5 after 30 iters; rotation matrix R and disparity become garbage (~10^10) with no Err signal; scipy uses SVD which handles rank-deficient correctly
description:
Review of crates/fsci-spatial/src/lib.rs on 2026-04-23.

procrustes (line 2425-2540+) uses a Newton-Schulz matrix-inverse-square-root
iteration to compute R = M * (M^T M)^{-1/2} as a replacement for the
SVD-based solution scipy uses. The iteration silently DIVERGES for
rank-deficient or near-rank-deficient B = M^T M, producing garbage rotation
matrices and nonsensical 'disparity' results — without any error signal.

Iteration (line 2491-2511):

    for _ in 0..30 {
        let y2 = mat_mul(&y, &y, d);
        let by2 = mat_mul(&mtm, &y2, d);
        let mut rhs = vec![vec![0.0; d]; d];
        for i in 0..d {
            for j in 0..d {
                rhs[i][j] = if i == j { 3.0 } else { 0.0 } - by2[i][j];
            }
        }
        let y_new = mat_mul(&y, &rhs, d);
        ... y[i][j] = y_new[i][j] * 0.5;
        if max_diff < 1e-14 { break; }
    }

This is Newton-Schulz: Y_{k+1} = 0.5 * Y_k * (3I - B Y_k^2), which converges
to B^{-1/2} ONLY when Y_0 = I is close enough (||I - B|| < 1). The code
always starts with Y_0 = I, so convergence requires all eigenvalues of B to
lie in (0, 2). For B with eigenvalues near 0 (rank-deficient) or near 2+
(large singular values of M), the iteration diverges.

Empirical reproduction (rustc probe, 2026-04-23):

    Case B = I (trivial):                  converges iter 0
    Case B = 0.5 * I (well-conditioned):   converges iter 6
    Case B = diag(1, 1, 0):                y_max = 1.918e5 after 30 iters (DIVERGES)
    Case B = diag(1, 1, 1e-10):            y_max = 9.819e4 after 30 iters (DIVERGES)

Concrete downstream consequence: when the caller provides aligned datasets
data1 and data2 where:
- data1 and data2 are orthogonal (e.g., data1 in xy-plane, data2 in yz-plane
  of 3D), or
- n < d (fewer samples than dimensions — common for small datasets),

the Procrustes computation silently produces rotation matrix R with entries
in the 10^4-10^5 range (should be orthonormal, entries in [-1, 1]), then
computes 'disparity' = sum of squared distances which is garbage on the
order of (10^5)^2 = 10^10 instead of the correct [0, 2] range. The caller
receives Ok(ProcrustesResult) with no indication of divergence.

Scipy comparison:
- scipy.spatial.procrustes uses scipy.linalg.svd of data2^T @ data1 directly.
  SVD handles rank-deficient inputs by zeroing out zero singular values.
- scipy returns correct (approximate) R even when M is rank-deficient:
  R = V @ U^T where U, S, V^T = SVD(M).

No convergence detection:
- Loop at line 2491 runs exactly 0..30 iterations. If not converged, simply
  exits with current y. No Err returned. Line 2508-2511 breaks early if
  converged, but no path signals 'hit the iteration cap without converging.'
- The 30-iteration cap with 1e-14 threshold is a heuristic; users have no
  visibility into which path their input took.

Additional concern — Denman-Beavers reference in comment (line 2484):

    // R = M * (M^T M)^{-1/2} via Denman-Beavers iteration for matrix square root inverse

Denman-Beavers is a DIFFERENT iteration (Y_{k+1} = 0.5 (Y_k + Z_k^{-1}),
Z_{k+1} = 0.5 (Z_k + Y_k^{-1}) with Y_0 = A, Z_0 = I) that actually handles
rank-deficient well but requires computing Z_k^{-1} at each step. The code
implements Newton-Schulz (explicit formula, no inverse needed, but
convergence-fragile), not Denman-Beavers. Comment misleading.

Fix options:

1. (Correct) Replace Newton-Schulz with a real SVD. fsci-linalg has svd
   functions — compute M = U S V^T, then R = V U^T. Handles rank-deficiency
   by setting zero singular values to zero in R. Matches scipy exactly.

2. (Mitigation) Detect divergence: check ||y|| after each iter; if
   growing beyond some bound (say 10x), return Err(NumericalDivergence) or
   similar. At least the caller learns the result is bad.

3. (Partial fix) Better initial guess: use Y_0 = (trace(B) / d) * I^{-1/2}
   which gives Y_0 closer to B^{-1/2} for well-scaled inputs. Reduces
   but doesn't eliminate rank-deficient failure.

4. Document the limitation in the docstring if deferring the fix:
     /// # Limitations
     /// Uses a Newton-Schulz iteration that diverges for rank-deficient
     /// inputs (M with zero singular values). For rank-deficient data,
     /// use scipy.spatial.procrustes instead.
   Not a fix, but at least honest about the trap.

Regression test:
    let data1 = vec![vec![1.0, 0.0, 0.0], vec![0.0, 1.0, 0.0]];  // xy-plane
    let data2 = vec![vec![0.0, 1.0, 0.0], vec![0.0, 0.0, 1.0]];  // yz-plane
    let result = procrustes(&data1, &data2).unwrap();
    assert!(result.disparity < 2.0);  // currently ~10^10

Related: wofb (precision loss), mvuj (btdtrc, closed), i9vw (validate NaN),
n240 (cluster fail-open). This bead is the fsci-spatial instance of the
'silent numerical failure' class — like wofb's sf() default, procrustes has
a correct-looking function signature but produces wrong answers on realistic
degenerate inputs.
close_reason: Replaced Procrustes Newton-Schulz rotation with SVD-based alignment for rank-deficient inputs

title: [special][parity] ndtri/erfcinv break in the deep tail (-inf/inf) and ~1e-8 off at 1e-10
description: ndtri(p)=sqrt2*erfinv(2p-1): 2p-1 rounds to exactly -1 for p<~1e-16 so erfinv(-1)=-inf -> ndtri(1e-50)=-inf (scipy -14.93), ndtri(1e-200)=-inf (scipy -30.2). And ndtri(1e-10) ~1.3e-8 off. erfcinv_conv(y)=erfinv(1-y): 1-y->1 for y<1e-16 so erfcinv(1e-100)=inf (scipy 15.07). Validated ~5e-16 vs scipy across p in 1e-300..0.999.

title: [perf][linalg] Recursive (communication-avoiding) LU — recast scalar panel factorization as GEMM
description: After 4amot (mixed-precision IR, 1.49x shipped baee89ed): f32 only accelerates the SIMD trailing update, so the remaining time is dominated by the SCALAR panel factorization (right-looking rank-1 column updates) + U-block triangular solve, which neither f32 nor the register-blocked trailing kernel speeds up. Lever: replace the right-looking blocked panel with a RECURSIVE LU (Toledo/CALU): split columns in half, recursively factor the left half, apply the resulting L to the right half via TRSM+GEMM, recursively factor the trailing block. This recasts most of the O(n^2*NB) scalar panel work as O(n^3) GEMM (the well-vectorized trailing kernel), shrinking the scalar critical path. Preserve first-max partial pivoting / row-permutation semantics / singular fallback / golden digest (or tolerance parity vs scipy). Stack with mixed precision (recursive f32 factor). Target solve/1000 >=2x vs current f64. Proof: golden/parity tests, same-worker baseline_solve A/B.
notes: TRAILING-GEMM CACHE-BLOCKING EXHAUSTED (workers are AVX2): jc column-panel tiling = NO-OP (within noise at n=1000 AND n=2000, U12 stays L2-resident without it; reverted); MR=4xNC=3 wider register tile = REGRESSION (12 accs of Simd<f32,16> = 24 YMM > 16 -> spills; mixed 53.8ms vs NC=1 47.9ms same-worker vmi1152480; reverted). The NC=1 register-blocked trailing kernel is at the hardware limit. REAL WIN this round came from a DIFFERENT phase: vectorized the previously-100%-scalar U-block solve in BOTH LU factorizations (SHIPPED 1d7d450b, bit-identical golden-preserved, best-of-campaign baseline_solve/1000 mixed 31.6-36.3ms / f64 54-56ms = 1.54-1.71x; helps f64 solve/inv/det too).
