title: [sparse][parity] laplacian() returns dense Vec<Vec<f64>> at HEAD but CsrMatrix before 1e12c2d6e — scipy returns sparse; validate_csgraph also dropped
description:
Found by ScarletWaterfall 2026-08-08 (SC62) while fixing the fsci-sparse perf harness for frankenscipy-sparse-rustfmt-deletion-495ga. Sibling of that bead and of frankenscipy-ct8n2, but a DIFFERENT defect class: this is not a missing symbol or a reverted perf lever, it is a public API that changed shape and lost its validation, under a commit whose subject was "fsci-sparse: rustfmt sparse linalg solvers and bench".

THE CHANGE. crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs, `laplacian`, publicly re-exported from fsci_sparse (lib.rs:151):

  BEFORE 1e12c2d6e:
    pub fn laplacian(graph: &CsrMatrix, normed: bool) -> SparseResult<CsrMatrix>
        validate_csgraph(graph)?;
        let degree = laplacian_degrees(graph);
        ...

  AT HEAD:
    pub fn laplacian(graph: &CsrMatrix, normed: bool) -> SparseResult<Vec<Vec<f64>>>
        let n = graph.shape().rows;   // no validate_csgraph
        ...

Three regressions in one signature change:

1. SPARSE IN, DENSE OUT. The whole point of a graph Laplacian on a CSR operator
   is that it stays sparse — a graph Laplacian has the same sparsity pattern as
   the adjacency matrix plus a diagonal. Returning Vec<Vec<f64>> allocates n^2
   f64s regardless of nnz. At n = 50,000 that is 2.5e9 doubles, 20 GB, for a
   graph that might have 250,000 edges. This is not a slow path, it is an
   allocation failure on any real graph.

2. PARITY. scipy.sparse.csgraph.laplacian returns SPARSE for sparse input.
   Verified live on scipy 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.3:
     laplacian(csr_matrix(...))                -> coo_matrix, issparse True
     laplacian(csr_matrix(...), normed=True)   -> coo_matrix, issparse True
   fsci now returns dense in both cases.

3. VALIDATION DROPPED. The pre-change implementation opened with
   validate_csgraph(graph)?. HEAD does not call it. Whatever that check enforced
   (shape/finiteness/structure) is no longer enforced on a public entry point.

HOW IT STAYED GREEN, and the part worth reading. The tests were ADAPTED to the
new return type rather than failing:

  BEFORE: assert!((laplacian_entry(&l, 0, 0) - 4.0).abs() < 1e-10, ...)
  AT HEAD: assert!((l[0][0] - 4.0).abs() < 1e-10, ...)

Same fixture, same expected value 4.0, same tolerance — only the ACCESSOR
changed, from a CSR lookup helper to dense indexing. The test's arithmetic
content is intact, so it reads as untouched in review, but its ability to detect
the sparse->dense change is gone. This is the golden-regeneration reflex in a
form that does not touch a single golden number: regenerate the ACCESSOR, not the
value. Worth naming, because a reviewer scanning for changed expected values
would not catch it. Same for laplacian_normed_diagonal_ones, laplacian_row_sums_zero,
laplacian_symmetric — all still pass at HEAD.

DETECTION. Invisible to every detector in this family so far:
  - ct8n2's unresolved-import scan: `laplacian` still exists and is still
    exported, so nothing dangles.
  - my symbol diff: the NAME survives, so it is not in the 110.
  - the unused-parameter heuristic: signature has no vestigial arg.
  - the test suite: adapted, green.
It surfaced only because perf_sparse.rs still calls .shape()/.nnz()/.indptr()/
.indices()/.data() on the result and therefore fails to compile — but ONLY with
--features sparse-incumbent-bench, which is off by default. 26 of the 27 errors
in that bin are this one regression.

SCOPE QUESTION FOR THE OWNER, because I am not certain which way this should go
and it is not my call to make unilaterally:
 (a) Restore SparseResult<CsrMatrix>. Matches scipy, restores scalability,
     restores validate_csgraph, fixes perf_sparse. But it is a breaking change
     for any caller written against HEAD's dense return, and the four tests need
     their accessors moved back.
 (b) Keep dense and rename to something honest (laplacian_dense), adding a
     sparse `laplacian` alongside. Larger surface, no breakage.
I lean (a): the dense return is almost certainly unintended collateral of a
rustfmt commit rather than a designed API, nothing in the repo documents it as a
deliberate choice, and the scipy peer is unambiguous. But (a) is a public API
change and should be an explicit decision, not something I slip in while fixing
a bench.

DO NOT fix this by changing perf_sparse.rs to accept Vec<Vec<f64>>. That would
make the build green by ratifying the regression — the same move that made the
unit tests green.
close_reason:
Fixed in commit 2835c7f90 by restoring 857ecbe9d verbatim. laplacian() returns SparseResult<CsrMatrix> again, along with laplacian_degrees, direct_canonical_laplacian, dense_laplacian_to_csr, LAPLACIAN_FORCE_DENSE_REFERENCE and LAPLACIAN_FORCE_SERIAL.

SCOPE QUESTION WITHDRAWN BEFORE ACTING, on evidence. I raised (a) restore CSR vs (b) keep dense and rename, and said in SC62 it needed an owner decision. I then read both commit BODIES rather than their subjects: 25f64e513 ('revert unmeasured direct CSR Laplacian') has NO body -- its objection was procedural, that a perf change lacked measurement. 857ecbe9d answers it in full: a bit-identity proof against a dense reference above the n>=512 gate, LAPLACIAN_FORCE_DENSE_REFERENCE as a same-binary A/B control, a torus bench fixture validating CSR structure against live SciPy, and an explicit 'API is a breaking return-type change (early project, OK)'. The last INTENTIONAL decision on this signature was CSR, taken with proof; HEAD's dense state was collateral from a formatting commit, not a position anyone argued. That made this a restore of landed work rather than a design call, which is why I proceeded rather than continuing to defer.

CITED EVIDENCE:
  - crates/fsci-conformance/tests/diff_sparse_laplacian.rs passes against LIVE
    scipy 1.17.1: 6 cases (4n / 5n_cycle / 3n_triangle x normed,unnormed) at
    ABS_TOL 1e-10, UNCHANGED. So the restored CSR Laplacian agrees with
    scipy.sparse.csgraph.laplacian NUMERICALLY, not merely structurally.
    'Compiling fsci-conformance' appears in the log, so this is not a stale
    binary (frankenscipy-eibro guard).
  - fsci-sparse: 410 lib tests pass, including the four laplacian tests moved
    back to CSR accessors verbatim from 857ecbe9d rather than rewritten by me;
    56 metamorphic pass including MR45 restored to csr_to_dense.
  - clippy -D warnings clean on the lib; rustfmt clean on both crates.
  - NO TOLERANCE CHANGED anywhere in the commit.
  - perf_sparse.rs now COMPILES under --features sparse-incumbent-bench. It had
    27 errors: 26 E0599 from calling CSR methods on the dense return, plus the
    unresolved LAPLACIAN_FORCE_DENSE_REFERENCE import. All resolved.

THE THREE REGRESSIONS IN THE BEAD TITLE, each reversed: sparse-in/dense-out (n^2
allocation regardless of nnz) gone; scipy parity restored and verified
numerically; validate_csgraph called again on the public entry point, since
857ecbe9d's implementation opens with it.

BOOKKEEPING CORRECTION: I had originally added the dependency backwards, making
this bead depend on frankenscipy-sparse-rustfmt-deletion-495ga, which would have
held it open until the whole 110-symbol restore finished. Wrong direction -- this
fix is independent and was BLOCKING part of that bead's harness work. Reversed
the edge before closing.

NOT CLOSED BY THIS: four perf bins still fail on unresolved
GMRES_BATCH_FORCE_SEQUENTIAL. I deliberately did not re-declare that toggle --
the parallel batch path it gated was also deleted by 1e12c2d6e, so declaring it
would give a two-arm probe with identical sequential arms. Tracked under 495ga.

ScarletWaterfall 2026-08-08 (SC63): FULL SIGNATURE HISTORY MEASURED. My core claim stands, my framing was too simple, and a source comment in the repo had the causality backwards.

MEASURED (git show at each commit, return type extracted directly):

  6df7c7c2d  08-02 04:37  -> SparseResult<CsrMatrix>       perf(sparse): build Laplacian directly as CSR
  25f64e513  08-02 04:52  -> SparseResult<Vec<Vec<f64>>>   perf(sparse): revert unmeasured direct CSR Laplacian
  857ecbe9d  08-02 07:05  -> SparseResult<CsrMatrix>       feat(sparse): return canonical CSR from graph Laplacian (no dense fill)
  1e12c2d6e  08-03 23:36  -> SparseResult<Vec<Vec<f64>>>   fsci-sparse: rustfmt sparse linalg solvers and bench
  HEAD                    -> SparseResult<Vec<Vec<f64>>>

WHAT STANDS: 857ecbe9d is a deliberate feat( commit whose subject literally says 'return canonical CSR from graph Laplacian (no dense fill)'. 1e12c2d6e silently reverted it under a formatting subject. That is the defect this bead is about and it is confirmed.

WHERE MY SC62 FRAMING WAS TOO SIMPLE: I described the dense return as 'almost certainly unintended collateral of a rustfmt commit' with 'nothing in the repo documenting it as a deliberate choice'. Not quite. CSR was reverted ONCE DELIBERATELY, 15 minutes after it first landed — 25f64e513, 'revert unmeasured direct CSR Laplacian'. Someone had explicit reservations about the CSR form on measurement grounds. 857ecbe9d then re-landed it as a feat two hours later. So the CSR return has a CONTESTED history, not a clean one, and my recommendation of option (a) has to account for that rather than presenting the restore as obvious. Whoever decides should read 857ecbe9d's justification against 25f64e513's objection; I am not going to adjudicate a dispute between two earlier commits from the outside.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE: the scalability and parity arguments are independent of that dispute. Dense is n^2 regardless of nnz, and scipy returns sparse for sparse input. Those hold whichever way the measurement question was settled.

REPO COMMENT CORRECTED. crates/fsci-conformance/tests/diff_sparse_laplacian.rs carried an explanation claiming '857ecbe9d briefly returned canonical CSR ... but 25f64e513 reverted the source as an unmeasured change'. That is chronologically impossible: 25f64e513 is 2h13m EARLIER than 857ecbe9d. Whoever repaired that test after it broke misattributed the revert, and the effect was to point future readers at the wrong commit and to make the silent rustfmt revert invisible in the one place someone would look. Replaced with the measured table above plus a warning not to adapt this file to whichever shape is current — that adaptation is exactly what kept the fsci-sparse unit tests green across the same change.

That comment also records that this churn already caused a build outage once: the test 'stopped compiling and took every other fsci-conformance test target down with it'.

title: [integrate] solve_ivp lacks a vector-system test (existing test is scalar exponential decay)
close_reason: Already satisfied; the bead's premise that the only test is scalar exponential decay is stale. tests::solve_ivp_harmonic_oscillator_system (crates/fsci-integrate/src/api.rs) integrates the 2-equation COUPLED system y' = [y1, -y0] from y(0) = [1, 0] over t in [0, 2] with Rk45 at rtol 1e-9 / atol 1e-12, and checks both components against the analytic solution at t = 2: y0 -> cos(2) = -0.4161468365471424 and y1 -> -sin(2) = -0.9092974268256817, each to 1e-6. Coupling matters here -- the two equations feed each other, so a solver that mishandled the vector path (wrong component ordering, or treating the state as independent scalars) fails rather than coincides, which a decoupled 2-vector fixture would not catch. scipy.integrate.solve_ivp converges to the same analytic solution at this tolerance, as the test comment notes. title: fsci-stats: TruncWeibullMin pdf/cdf/ppf NaN at extreme c·a^c — log-space rewrite
description: TruncWeibullMin.pdf returns NaN for extreme parameters where c·a^c is large, e.g. (c=10, a=10, b=10.1). Both exp(-a^c) and exp(-b^c) underflow to 0, denom=0, and division yields NaN. Same problem affects cdf and ppf indirectly. Fix: rewrite pdf as c·x^(c-1)·exp(a^c - x^c) / (-expm1(a^c - b^c)); cdf as expm1(a^c - x^c) / expm1(a^c - b^c); ppf as (a^c - ln1p(q · expm1(a^c - b^c)))^(1/c). This avoids the small-quantity subtraction. Found via fuzz harness frankenscipy-kin4s.
close_reason: Fixed via log-space rewrite shipped with the fuzz harness frankenscipy-kin4s. Original pdf/cdf path computed exp(-a^c) - exp(-b^c) which underflows to 0 when c·a^c is large (e.g., c=10, a=10 → a^c=1e10). Rewritten pdf to c·x^(c-1)·exp(a^c-x^c)/(-expm1(a^c-b^c)); cdf to expm1(a^c-x^c)/expm1(a^c-b^c); ppf to (a^c - ln1p(q·expm1(a^c-b^c)))^(1/c). New regression test truncweibull_min_handles_extreme_c_a_underflow at (c=10, a=10, b=10.1).

title: [special][parity] gammaincinv absolute tolerance + gammainccinv P-near-1 precision loss at small y
description: gammaincinv_scalar Newton converges on err.abs()<1e-14 (ABSOLUTE); for small y the target P~1e-10 so 1e-14 absolute is only ~1e-4 relative, stopping early: gammaincinv(2,1e-10) ~4.7e-6 off scipy. Fix: relative tolerance err.abs()<=1e-15*max(y,tiny). gammainccinv_scalar(a,y)=gammaincinv(a,1-y) computes P near 1 (abs precision 1e-16) so the small Q=1-P resolves to only ~1e-6: gammainccinv(2,1e-10) ~3e-7 off, and y<1e-16 breaks (1-y rounds to 1). Fix: Newton on Q directly via gammaincc_conv, seed = gammaincinv(a,1-y) when 1-y<1 else asymptotic fixed-point x=-ln(y Gamma(a))+(a-1)ln x. Validated machine precision down to y=1e-300.

title: [HIGH] integrate: BdfSolver::new does ZERO config validation; RkSolver::new has an is_finite() guard that makes NaN max_step SKIP validation entirely — two public solver entry points, asymmetric validation, NaN tolerances slip through and burn Jacobian iterations until StepSizeTooSmall
description:
Review of crates/fsci-integrate/src/bdf.rs + rk.rs on 2026-04-22, extending frankenscipy-i9vw.

Both BdfSolver and RkSolver are public re-exports (lib.rs:16, lib.rs:28-30). They accept a config struct with rtol/atol/max_step/first_step and are direct construction entry points for users writing custom integration loops outside solve_ivp.

Validation inconsistency:

RkSolver::new (rk.rs:452-532):
    validates rtol + atol via validate_tol                   [i9vw-broken but called]
    validates max_step via validate_max_step                 [i9vw-broken AND skipped if !is_finite()]
    validates first_step via validate_first_step             [i9vw-broken but called]

    Key defect at rk.rs:472:
        if config.max_step.is_finite() {
            validate_max_step(config.max_step)?;
        }
    This is_finite() guard wraps the validation call. is_finite() returns false for
    both Inf and NaN. For NaN max_step, the guard takes the 'Inf-is-legit' path and
    SKIPS validation entirely, meaning NaN max_step reaches the RK step controller
    without even the broken-predicate check. Inf max_step legitimately skips validation
    (Inf is the default per solve_ivp), but NaN should not be bundled with it.

BdfSolver::new (bdf.rs:80-150):
    NO validation call. rtol is copied directly to self.rtol (bdf.rs:131). atol is
    materialized as a Vec<f64> without any bounds/finite check (bdf.rs:94-97). max_step
    is stored directly (bdf.rs:130). first_step is used as-is at bdf.rs:99-110 with
    only the select_initial_step_bdf path checking NaN (internally, per existing code).

Consequences:

1. A user calling BdfSolver::new with rtol=NaN, atol=ToleranceValue::Scalar(NaN),
   max_step=NaN, first_step=Some(NaN) gets a solver instance with no objection and
   then runs steps on NaN tolerances. The step-level NaN check at bdf.rs:296 catches
   error_norm.is_nan() and halves h until h < 1e-14 -> StepSizeTooSmall error. But
   that's 47 convergence iterations (MAX_CONVERGE_ITER = 4 at new newton, MAX_STEP_ATTEMPTS)
   of wasted Newton iterations per step, plus Jacobian evaluations.

2. Performance hazard: BDF does ~O(n^2) work per step with Jacobian rebuilds. NaN
   tolerances cause MANY failed steps. A fuzz harness hitting BdfSolver::new with
   NaN inputs will run 1000x slower than with valid inputs -- unmeasured but very
   likely >1000ms per iteration, demolishing fuzzing throughput (per /testing-fuzzing
   1000 exec/s floor for stateful targets would be impossible).

3. Hardened mode unused: BdfSolver stores self.mode = config.mode but the Hardened
   code path (bdf.rs:450-ish) only uses mode to gate the 'all finite' y_new check
   at line 445. It does NOT use mode to decide whether NaN rtol/atol should fail
   closed at construction. The Hardened contract is partially implemented.

4. Asymmetry with RkSolver is itself a defect: two public solver entry points with
   different validation contracts. A user switching from Rk45 to Bdf (for stiffness)
   loses input validation silently.

5. The `if config.max_step.is_finite() { validate... }` guard in RkSolver::new is an
   anti-pattern: validation should be conditional on INPUT SEMANTICS ('is this meant
   to be treated as unbounded?'), not on whether the input happens to be Inf-OR-NaN.
   The correct predicate is: `if !config.max_step.is_nan() && config.max_step !=
   f64::INFINITY { validate... }` -- and NaN should separately fail closed.

Fix (in order of priority):

1. Add a validate_solver_config helper that's called from both BdfSolver::new and
   RkSolver::new:
       pub(crate) fn validate_solver_config(
           rtol: f64, atol: &ToleranceValue, max_step: f64,
           first_step: Option<f64>, t0: f64, t_bound: f64,
           n: usize, mode: RuntimeMode,
           ledger: Option<&SyncSharedAuditLedger>,
       ) -> Result<ValidatedTolerance, IntegrateValidationError> { ... }
   This absorbs the is_finite() guard, NaN-rejection, and mode-aware audit emission.

2. Call this helper from BdfSolver::new at the top.

3. Fix the is_finite() guard in RkSolver::new: replace with explicit NaN rejection
   + Inf passthrough:
       if config.max_step.is_nan() {
           return Err(IntegrateValidationError::NonFiniteMaxStep);
       }
       if config.max_step != f64::INFINITY {
           validate_max_step_with_audit(config.max_step, ledger)?;
       }

4. Depends on i9vw fix: the NaN fail-open in validate_* must be fixed first, otherwise
   the helper above inherits the same defect.

5. Add regression tests:
       BdfSolver::new(..., rtol=NaN)              => Err

title: [perf][linalg] eigh is a CONSTANT ~1.8-2.2x behind LAPACK dsyevd (n=512-1024) — the growth premise is refuted, Cuppen withdrawn
description:
RE-SCOPED 2026-08-16 (RainyPrairie) after the original premise was refuted by measurement. The prior description is preserved in the bead's notes; this is what the bead now is.

WHAT IT IS: `eigh` carries a real, worth-fixing CONSTANT-FACTOR deficit against LAPACK dsyevd. It is NOT an asymptotic kernel-quality wall, and it does NOT need Cuppen's divide-and-conquer algorithm.

MEASURED, RCH_WORKER=hz2 host=hetzner2, harness crates/fsci-linalg/src/bin/perf_eigh_vs_scipy.rs, elf_sha256=7b8b7c7f9ef447be7e7bc07171b9e2034cde8b1f67cc0248788ec0af3ef7dd57, incumbent decomp_sha256=3c3d1688a87b606757306eb5ed81c8e45e0b6d286792031d4ffaa8b56a773361, live scipy 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.3, interleaved in one process tree on identical matrix bytes, agreement checked before timing, all A/A nulls bracketing 1.0. Full rows in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.

  n=512   fsci  72.083ms   scipy1  39.627ms   1.8224x   ci95=[1.4636, 2.0274]
  n=768   fsci 206.966ms   scipy1  94.589ms   2.2295x   ci95=[2.0243, 2.3680]
  n=1024  fsci 441.551ms   scipy1 244.144ms   1.8144x   ci95=[1.7467, 1.9763]

THE RATIO IS FLAT. 1.82x -> 2.23x -> 1.81x. n=1024 is indistinguishable from n=512 despite EIGHT TIMES the work. Both arms scale together (fsci 2.87x then 2.13x per size step; scipy1 2.39x then 2.58x), which is the signature of two implementations of the same asymptotic order with different constants.

WHY THE ORIGINAL PREMISE WAS WRONG, and it is a reusable lesson rather than a slip. The bead read "1.32x at n=256, 2.73x at n=512, ratio GROWS, therefore asymptotic, therefore Cuppen". But `eigh` switches implementation at PUBLIC_NATIVE_EIGH_MIN_DIM = 512: n=256 ran nalgebra's symmetric_eigen and n=512 ran symmetric_eigh_native. The two points came from two DIFFERENT ALGORITHMS, so no scaling law could be inferred from them. Every size at or above 512 already uses the same implementation, so sweeping 512/768/1024 -- which needed no code change at all -- answers the scaling question directly, and the growth disappears.

Also note the magnitude moved: the banked 2.73x at n=512 came from a REMEMBERED scipy figure captured in a separate run. Measured live and interleaved it is 1.82-1.93x, worst bound at least 1.46x slower.

WHAT IS ALREADY ELIMINATED, by measurement rather than assumption -- do not re-chase either:
  - the blocked dsytrd (WY) reduction: measured SLOWER, 0.5-0.81x across n in {512,1024,1500}, kept as dead-code infrastructure (frankenscipy-2o0vp);
  - eigenvalue clustering forcing the sequential QR fallback: refuted numerically. The gate is min_gap = 1e-6 * scale over ALL n-1 consecutive gaps; measured minimum RELATIVE gap on the benchmark's own input distribution is 1.324e-03 at n=256, 2.077e-04 at n=512 and 2.441e-04 at n=1024, two-plus orders above the threshold, so the parallel inverse-iteration path always fires.

THE TWO LIVE QUESTIONS, in cost order:

1. CHEAP, AND POSSIBLY A ONE-LINE WIN: does nalgebra's symmetric_eigen beat symmetric_eigh_native at n >= 512 as well? Nothing has ever measured that -- the switch at 512 has never been justified against the alternative at the SAME size. If nalgebra wins there, raising or removing PUBLIC_NATIVE_EIGH_MIN_DIM is the whole fix and the native path should not be taken at all. Instrument written and parked in git stash: PUBLIC_NATIVE_EIGH_MIN_DIM_OVERRIDE plus an impl x size sweep in the harness, with a routing test whose must-hit/must-miss arms prove the override takes effect.

2. IF NATIVE IS WORTH KEEPING: locate the constant. Per-stage wall counters are written and parked in the same stash -- EIGH_NATIVE_STAGE_TIMING / EIGH_NATIVE_STAGE_NANOS over [0] Householder tridiagonalization, [1] tridiagonal eigensolve, [2] eigenvector back-transform plus sort -- with a three-arm test (off-by-default must-miss, nonzero must-hit, accumulation). Run at n=512 and n=1024 and attribute the ~2x before optimising anything.

A LATENT CLIFF worth its own bead if anyone wants it: the inverse-iteration gate is all-or-nothing over all n-1 gaps, so ONE near-degenerate pair anywhere drops the whole matrix onto the sequential QR path with no signal to the caller. A structured or nearly-degenerate input can therefore cost a large constant factor invisibly, while a random-matrix benchmark shows nothing. Any future eigh timing should state which arm it exercised.

CLOSING EVIDENCE: either a measured decision on question 1 (with the threshold changed accordingly), or a stage attribution from question 2 followed by a measured improvement to the dominant stage. NOT a Cuppen implementation -- that verdict is withdrawn.
notes:
2026-08-17 RainyPrairie -- CONFIRMED ON A SECOND WORKER UNDER THE PROPER PROTOCOL.
One pinned MULTI-SIZE invocation on vmi1227854 (the recipe I recorded last note),
so absolute times are comparable across sizes.

     n      impl    fsci   scipy   ratio  fsci/n^3  scipy/n^3
   512  nalgebra    62.4    36.0   1.731      62.4       36.0
   512    native    61.9    36.7   1.686      61.9       36.7
   768  nalgebra   199.2    90.7   2.197      59.0       26.9
   768    native   194.0    92.6   2.096      57.5       27.4
  1024  nalgebra   419.2   221.4   1.893      52.4       27.7
  1024    native   432.9   214.3   2.014      54.1       26.8

All six nulls=PASS, margins 4.04x-14.46x.

SciPy's normalised cost MINIMISES AT 768 on BOTH workers; ours does not:
  vmi1227854  scipy/n^3 36.0 -> 26.9 -> 27.7     fsci/n^3 62.4 -> 59.0 -> 52.4
  ovh-a       scipy/n^3 32.1 -> 23.8 -> 26.2     fsci/n^3 48.9 -> 43.1 -> 43.3

So the ratio peak at 768 is the INCUMBENT's efficiency peak, now on two workers
measured under a protocol that makes the comparison legitimate.

OUR CURVE IS THE HEALTHIER SHAPE: fsci/n^3 falls monotonically here and is
flat-to-falling on ovh-a -- we scale slightly BETTER than O(n^3) over 512-1024 while
SciPy gives efficiency back at 1024. The constant factor is the whole story and it
sits in the Householder reduction (56-62%, per the stage profile).

RATIO SHAPE REPLICATES A THIRD TIME (1.69-1.73 -> 2.10-2.20 -> 1.89-2.01). Peak at
768 now on ovh-a, vmi1293453, vmi1227854 and hz2 -- four workers.

BOUNDS UNCHANGED: n=512 >= 1.37x, n=768 >= 1.52x, n=1024 >= 1.58x.

WHERE THIS LEAVES ll0kk: the bead's re-scoped question ("where does the constant
sit") is ANSWERED -- Householder reduction, ~60% of runtime, flat share across
sizes. The size-shape question is answered too, and the answer is that there is
nothing to fix there. What remains is a single concrete lever: make the reduction
faster by some route OTHER than blocking, since blocked dsytrd is already measured
slower (0.5-0.81x) on this bead. That is a code problem now, not a measurement one.

title: [perf][sparse] splu cubic 1.60x slower CI[1.59,1.61] n=12 (was 2.08x): two levers shipped; residual is 1.74 Ir/update constant factor, updates already 98.8% of minimum
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-14 (RosePelican) with crates/fsci-sparse/src/bin/perf_splu_balanced_square.rs, live scipy 1.17.1 in the same invocation, balanced-square substrate ported from franken_networkx scripts/balanced_square_ab.py (72761094c) so it runs on a BUSY host.

TWO ROWS, both with A/A nulls inside +/-0.02 and bootstrap-median CIs:
  laplacian_3d_cubic side=16 (n=4096, nnz=27136): SciPy/FrankenSciPy = 0.0093x, CI95 [0.0093,0.0094] => 107x LOSS
  scattered_pentadiagonal side=10 (n=1000, nnz=4994): 0.7927x, CI95 [0.7860,0.7966] => 1.26x loss

THE MECHANISM, and it rules out the obvious suspect. Our fill is at SuperLU parity or better: retained factor payload 19,045,760 bytes ~= 1.19M (usize,f64) entries vs SuperLU 1,231,312 LU nonzeros on the cubic row; 87,904 bytes ~= 5.5k entries vs 5,998 on the scattered row. Same COLAMD ordering, same fill. So the fill-reducing ordering is NOT the problem — per-entry elimination THROUGHPUT is. At ~5k fill entries we sit at 0.79x; at ~1.2M we sit at 0.0093x. The loss scales with fill, not with n.

NAMED LEVER: NativeSparseLu stores l_rows/u_rows as Vec<Vec<(usize, f64)>>. Every elimination update indexes a jagged inner Vec inside the hot loop, which is the devectorizing layout this suite has already measured at 2.2-3.5x elsewhere (perf_jagged_vec_inner_loop_devectorization), on top of pointer-chasing one allocation per row. Replace with left-looking Gilbert-Peierls elimination over a DENSE scatter workspace plus a flat CSC layout (the algorithm SuperLU actually uses), then supernodal blocking if the scatter version does not close it.

CLOSING EVIDENCE: re-run both rows above with the same harness; the low-fill row must not regress and the high-fill row must move materially off 0.0093x. Do NOT re-attack the ordering.

NOTE the harness distinguishes arms: splu routes an exact cubic Dirichlet grid to CubicSpectralLu (an O(n log n) structure-specific solver, 204x vs SuperLU with ZERO fill) and SparseLuFactorization::backend_used reports NativeSparseLu for BOTH. Use the cubic_spectral_factor_hits counter, which the harness asserts against the named arm.
notes:
=== STANDING RESULTS as of 2026-08-16 (PeachSummit). The ORIGINAL description above is
historical: its title claim, both its cells, and its named container are all superseded.
Read this block, not the description. ===

and our update count is 98.8% of the theoretical minimum -- so there is NO algorithmic

current cost, and every future lever should be sized against that.

--- THE GAP IS INSTRUCTION COUNT, AND IT IS SIZED (2026-08-17, shipping binary) ---

THIS SUPERSEDES EVERY EARLIER DIAGNOSIS ON THIS BEAD. Profiling the INCUMBENT for the
first time settled what the deficit is made of:

  SuperLU   387,524,579 insn/factorization   4.05 Ir per element-update   IPC 2.04
  ours      659M - 781M                      6.9 - 8.2                    IPC 2.12

Instruction ratio 1.70-2.02x; measured time ratio 1.9x. They coincide. Both arms issue at
IPC ~2.1, so the gap is not locality, not latency, not vectorisation quality. It is WORK:
we execute about twice the instructions for the same factorization on the same fill.

TARGET: 4.05 Ir per element-update. Reproduce the baseline with
scripts/superlu_instruction_baseline.py under callgrind (full minus setup-only).

--- WHERE OUR EXTRA INSTRUCTIONS GO (side=16, shipping binary, per element-update) ---

  7.78 total
  3.92  apply_sorted_pivot_tail (inclusive)
  1.14  matched_run_length            <- column comparison, CLOSED, see below
  0.97  exact-cancellation check      <- 24.9% of the merge body, 2.04x the arithmetic
  0.81  merge_sorted_remainder
  0.67  factorize_csr
  0.34  __memcpy
  0.16  select_sorted_pivot_row
  0.16  _int_malloc

The comparison and the cancellation check together are 2.11 of 7.78 -- 27% of our work on
two things SuperLU does not do at all. Only ~15-27% of the 2x excess is accounted for; the
rest is in the merge body and per-pivot bookkeeping and is NOT yet attributed.

--- DEPENDENT-CRATE VERIFICATION OF THE SHIPPED LEVERS (2026-08-18) ---

The two levers changed apply_sorted_pivot_tail's SIGNATURE (a parameter threaded through
every call site) and flipped TWO toggle defaults, one of which is semantic. Every test run
during development was `-p fsci-sparse --lib` only. The crates that depend on fsci-sparse
were never compiled against the change until now.

  fsci-spatial                        235 passed, 0 failed
  fsci-conformance (skip metamorphic) 186 passed, 0 failed
  fsci-conformance, sparse-specific     2 passed, 0 failed

NOT RUN, and this is the honest gap: 33 metamorphic tests were filtered out. They are slow
(one exceeds 60s alone and the full suite timed out at 570s) and are linalg/SVD relations
rather than sparse ones, so they are unlikely to touch splu -- but "unlikely" is not "ran".
Whoever needs full coverage should run `cargo test -p fsci-conformance --lib metamorphic`
in a window where a multi-minute run is acceptable.

WHY THIS MATTERED: the cancellation-skip default is a SEMANTIC change -- a factorization
that cancels retains explicit zeros. A conformance packet asserting a stored pattern on a
cancelling matrix would have caught it. None did, which is evidence, not proof.

--- MEASUREMENT RULES THIS BEAD PAID FOR. Violate these and the numbers are worthless. ---

1. COST FIGURES MUST COME FROM A BINARY WITH NO cfg(test) CODE IN THE MEASURED REGION.
   The cfg(test) counters sit inside the hot path and act as optimisation barriers; they
   inflated one measured effect 34-FOLD. Three cost rows had to be withdrawn.
2. STRUCTURAL COUNTS (run lengths, churn, allocation CALL counts, prefix shares) are fine
   under cfg(test) -- barriers do not change how often a Vec outgrows its capacity.
3. CHECK THE ELF SHA-256 BEFORE EVERY PROFILE. A stale binary from a previous turn's
   temporary edit has already been profiled by mistake once and caught only by this.
4. LINE-LEVEL ATTRIBUTION IS UNUSABLE HERE (~60% of cost lands on pseudo-lines). Use
   function-level, or per-address mapped through objdump.
5. AN A/B MUST HOLD WORK CONSTANT. An arm that changes results may abort early and its
   totals then measure truncated work, not cost. Require BIT-IDENTITY of the arm, which is
   the control a skip-the-work arm can never satisfy.
6. DETECTION FLOOR: run-to-run spread on this cell is 12.8%. A lever must plausibly clear
   ~13% to be worth a certification window. Screen before measuring.


--- FIRST BUILD AFTER THE FREEZE: what is unverified, and what is not (2026-08-17) ---

Several turns of source-only work accumulated while /data sat at 100% used. Diffed
against ac8acabf0, the last commit that actually compiled (534 lib tests passed):

  ALMOST UNCHANGED: the production code path. The min|x| cancellation rewrite was applied
  and then reverted in full after the disassembly refuted it, so the three cancellation
  loops are byte-for-byte what they were when they last passed tests. Every other edit is
  a COMMENT, with ONE exception, corrected here because the earlier version of this note
  claimed "unchanged" and went stale the moment I added the counter:

    the two in-place compactions gained an `else` arm holding a single `#[cfg(test)]`
    statement. In a release build that statement is removed and the arm is EMPTY, so it
    has no effect on shipping codegen -- but the source is no longer identical, and a
    note that says "unchanged" invites the next person to skip verifying it. Verify it.

  NEW AND UNVERIFIED (the whole risk surface):
    1. test `min_magnitude_cancellation_decides_exactly_as_the_bool_scan` plus its two
       helper fns. Its logic was verified in Python -- zero disagreements over every 1-,
       2- and 3-element combination of 0.0, -0.0, NaN, +-inf, +-MIN_POSITIVE, +-5e-324,
       +-1.0 -- but it has never been compiled.
    2. perf_splu USAGE and error text: string literals only, no logic, including two
       backslash line-continuations inside string literals that have not been compiled.

  SO THE FIRST BUILD IS A PLAIN `cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib` AND NOTHING ELSE.
  Do not certify off it, do not profile off it. A measurement needs its own build in a
  window you did NOT build in, and the ELF SHA-256 checked before the profile runs.

  STILL PENDING AND STILL UNMEASURED, in priority order:
    a. how often the exact-cancellation check actually fires (structural count, valid
       under cfg(test)) -- decides whether the 24.9%-of-merge-body check earns its cost
    b. confirm merge_sorted_remainder's call count and remainder-size DISTRIBUTION in a
       SINGLE profile; the 146 Ir/call figure currently divides one run's total by
       another run's call count, which is the cross-row arithmetic this bead has been
       burned by three times
    c. the capacity-headroom knob ships at 1 and is measured at ~2% -- below the ~13%
       floor, so it is not worth a certification window on its own


--- THE CANCELLATION QUESTION, SHARPENED BY SOURCE READING (2026-08-17, no measurement) ---

The exact-cancellation check is 24.9% of the merge body, 0.97 Ir per element-update, 24%
of SuperLU's ENTIRE budget, and SuperLU does not perform it. It cannot be made cheaper by
changing the accumulator (min|x| was tried and REFUTED by the lowering: f64::min emits
vminpd + vcmpunordpd + vblendvpd, so with abs's vandpd it is four vector ops per group --
identical to the vcmpeqpd/vpor/vextractf128/vpackssdw it would replace). So the only way it
goes is by not detecting cancellation at all. Source reading establishes what that costs.

SAFE: pivot selection. `select_sorted_pivot_row` prefers the diagonal only when
`!is_sparse_zero_pivot(diagonal_abs)`, and otherwise takes the largest magnitude among
candidates. A retained structural zero therefore cannot raise a false SingularMatrix; it is
simply never chosen unless every candidate is zero, which is a genuinely singular column.

SAFE: fill growth. The tail-only branches guard with `if delta != 0.0`, so a zero
multiplier cannot insert explicit zeros into a row.

NOT FREE, and this is the part that decides the lever. A retained zero at a row's HEAD
keeps that row in the first-column bucket for that column. The row is then a candidate at
that pivot, passes the head check, forms multiplier = 0.0 / pivot = 0.0, skips the L push
(`if multiplier != 0.0`), and still runs a FULL merge that changes nothing. Retained zeros
in the interior of a row cost only storage and a slightly longer sweep; retained zeros at
the head cost an entire wasted row-update each.

SO THE MEASUREMENT MUST BE SPLIT, and counting "how often cancellation fires" alone would
NOT decide it:
    (i)  how many entries the check drops per factorization       -- the saving side
    (ii) how many of those are at a row's HEAD at the time         -- the cost side
Only (ii) converts into wasted candidate visits. If (ii) is near zero the check is close to
pure overhead and dropping it is a real lever; if (ii) is large the check is paying for
itself in avoided visits and the line closes.

Both are STRUCTURAL counts, so they are valid under cfg(test) instrumentation, unlike the
cost figures on this bead that had to be redone.

--- WHAT HAS BEEN TRIED AND CLOSED, so it is not re-attacked ---

0. COLUMN COMPARISON REMOVAL (run directory / arena family) -- CLOSED FOR GOOD. It is
   14.66% of the program, so worth attacking, BUT the comparison is between two DIFFERENT
   rows, so only a symbolic phase can establish it, and ours costs 3,008,581,116 Ir per
   factorization: 28x what it saves and 4x the entire numeric factorization. Entry
   condition to reopen: make symbolic_fill_pattern 28x cheaper first. Note this is a defect
   in OUR symbolic implementation -- SuperLU does symbolic AND numeric inside 4.05
   Ir/element-update total.


1. SUPERNODAL BLOCKING (frankenscipy-9nw95) is CLOSED WITH A MECHANISM, not abandoned. The
   structure is genuinely there -- mean width 5.24, blocks 97.2% dense, 5.08x fewer touches,
   padding tax only 1.01x -- and it still does not pay: the dense scatter has IDENTICAL
   marginal cost to the merge (15.06 vs 15.00 Ir per element-update) plus ~18M constant
   overhead, so THERE IS NO CROSSOVER WIDTH. The merge kernel is already dense inside its
   runs (96.8% of elements). Any future supernodal successor must beat 15.00 Ir per
   element-update, checkable with SUPERNODE_AB_WIDTH plus the committed workload harness.
   The code remains in-tree behind default-off toggles, deliberately not deleted.
2. BACK-MERGE: rejected, kept behind SPLU_BACK_MERGE_ENABLE (default false).
3. PARTIAL IN-PLACE: landed and shipping (SPLU_PARTIAL_INPLACE_ENABLE default true).
4. ORDERING: do NOT re-attack. Fill is at SuperLU parity on both fixtures.

--- THE ONLY LEVER LEFT: ARENA (frankenscipy-u7biq), TWO PRECONDITIONS CLEARED, ZERO GAIN
    MEASURED ---

The 53.91% of D1 read misses spent streaming target-row values cannot be reached by
restructuring the update. What remains is changing what is STORED.

  a. Index contiguity: candidate sweeps are perfectly contiguous in row index under the
     shipping ordering -- 1.00 slots per needed row (natural order reads 1.03, so the
     counter discriminates).
  b. The layout is genuinely LOST rather than already free: glibc hands the rows out 99.4%
     adjacent AS BUILT, and ONE synthetic growth per row collapses that to 5.2%.

Which names the arena's real requirement, and it is NOT "allocate contiguously": a naive
arena that grew rows on demand would reproduce the same collapse. Each row must be placed
at FINAL size and never move, which needs a per-row symbolic fill count --
symbolic_fill_pattern already computes exactly that and is in-tree, left from the closed
supernodal line. The dead phase is this lever's input.

NEITHER PRECONDITION IS A PREDICTED WIN. Two supernodal drivers already died holding
plausible mechanisms that fitted the numbers. Keep the prior disciplined.

--- THREE CAVEATS THAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THESE NUMBERS ---

1. ROUNDS-DEPENDENCE. Bounds quoted as "worst CI floor" are NOT rounds-invariant: cubic CI
   width is 0.0402 at rounds=11 and 0.0135 at rounds=41, 3.0x narrower, so the floor rises
   for the same performance. Cite every bound WITH its rounds.
2. DENSITY IS TESTED ON TWO FIXTURE FAMILIES ONLY, which differ in more than density.
3. THE 5.2% ADJACENCY FIGURE IS A STAND-IN. It comes from a synthetic growth, not from the
   elimination itself. A cfg(test) hook reading the LIVE rows at the end of factorize_csr's
   elimination loop is committed (167ba81a7) but UNCOMPILED AND UNRUN -- written during a
   host-wide build freeze. It must be built and run before its number is banked, and IF THE
   REAL ELIMINATION LEAVES THE ROWS MOSTLY ADJACENT, precondition (b) is REFUTED and the
   arena should not be written.

CLOSING EVIDENCE for this bead: re-run both families with the same harness; the scattered
family must not regress below 1.2106x and the cubic bound must move materially below 1.89x
at rounds=41.

comments.text:
RosePelican 2026-08-14, CORRECTION to the named lever in the description — the container is worse than I wrote.

I said Vec<Vec<(usize, f64)>>. That is the SHAPE OF THE FINISHED FACTOR
(NativeSparseLu.l_rows/u_rows, linalg.rs:122-131). The ELIMINATION itself does not use it. Read
NativeSparseLu::factorize_csr (linalg.rs:266+):

  let mut rows = permuted_rows_as_maps(a, p);     // Vec<BTreeMap<usize, f64>>   (linalg.rs:447)
  let mut column_rows = sparse_column_membership(n, &rows);  // Vec<BTreeSet<usize>> (linalg.rs:490)

So the working matrix during a right-looking elimination is A RED-BLACK TREE PER ROW plus a
red-black tree per COLUMN. Every fill update is an O(log nnz) tree descent through pointer-chased
nodes with a heap allocation per inserted entry, and the column-membership sets are maintained in
parallel. There is no contiguous run of doubles anywhere in the inner loop, so nothing vectorizes
and nothing prefetches.

That is a fully sufficient explanation for the two rows and for their SHAPE. At ~5.5k fill entries
(scattered, n=1000) the tree overhead is amortized against a tiny amount of real work and we sit at
0.7927x. At ~1.19M fill entries (cubic, n=4096) it dominates completely and we sit at 0.0093x. The
loss tracking FILL rather than n is exactly what a per-entry constant factor predicts.

SECOND FINDING while reading it: PermutationOrdering::Colamd does NOT run COLAMD. linalg.rs:286-301
maps every non-Natural, non-MMD request to reverse_cuthill_mckee, with a comment saying a real
COLAMD port is 'a later lever'. Our measured fill still came out at SuperLU parity on both fixtures
(1.19M vs 1.23M; 5.5k vs 6.0k), so this is NOT currently costing us anything measurable — but
ordering_used prints Colamd while RCM runs, which will mislead the next person who profiles this.
Worth its own small bead; it is a labelling defect, not a perf one.

The lever is unchanged and now better founded: left-looking Gilbert-Peierls over a DENSE scatter
workspace on flat CSC arrays (symbolic reach by DFS on the elimination graph, numeric scatter into a
dense n-vector, gather back into CSC), which is what SuperLU does before it supernodes. Expect the
low-fill row to be roughly unchanged and the high-fill row to move by orders of magnitude; both must
be re-measured together so a low-fill regression cannot hide.

crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs is exclusively reserved by ChartreuseAnchor (expires 02:10) and
reading it shows the kernel rewrite is ALREADY UNDERWAY: the elimination rows are now hash-backed
rather than BTreeMap ('Membership updates are O(1) hash operations', 'hash-backed to avoid a
red-black-tree descent for every numeric elimination update'), and the ordering mislabelling I filed
as h4yov is already fixed at linalg.rs:317-343, which now returns the EFFECTIVE ordering
(ReverseCuthillMcKee) instead of echoing the requested Colamd. I have therefore not touched the

BASELINE, live scipy 1.17.1 in the same invocation, taken on a busy host with
crates/fsci-sparse/src/bin/perf_splu_balanced_square.rs (c938555c0):
  laplacian_3d_cubic side=16   n=4096 nnz=27136  ratio 0.0093x  CI95 [0.0093,0.0094]  nulls 0.9970/0.9976
  scattered_pentadiagonal s=10 n=1000 nnz=4994   ratio 0.7927x  CI95 [0.7860,0.7966]  nulls 1.0071/1.0018
Parity gated before timing: worst relative solution diff vs SuperLU's own solution 3.9e-15 and
6.6e-16. Invocation:
  rch exec -- cargo run --release -p fsci-sparse --bin perf_splu_balanced_square \
      --features sparse-incumbent-bench -- <side> <rounds> <warmup> off <cubic|scattered>

WHAT THE BASELINE PREDICTS ABOUT THE HASH CHANGE. Fill is NOT the problem: 19,045,760 B of retained
factor payload ~= 1.19M (usize,f64) entries vs SuperLU's 1,231,312 LU nonzeros on the cubic row, and
87,904 B ~= 5.5k vs 5,998 on the scattered row. We already produce marginally LESS fill than
SuperLU with the same effective ordering. So the whole gap is per-entry elimination throughput, and
it scales with FILL rather than n. Concretely: the scattered row should barely move under the hash
change (0.79x is nearly parity already and there is almost no fill to pay for), while the cubic row
carries all 107x. If the cubic row does NOT move much after hashing, the residual constant is the
per-entry lookup itself, and the next increment is a dense scatter workspace — scatter the target
row into a dense f64 buffer, apply the pivot tail with direct indexed writes while tracking newly
created fill, gather back — so the inner loop performs no lookup at all. That is Gilbert-Peierls,
which is what SuperLU does before it supernodes.

TWO TRAPS IN THE HARNESS, both load-bearing.
(1) splu routes an exact cubic Dirichlet grid to CubicSpectralLu, an O(n log n) structure-specific
solver that is not an LU: it reports 204x against SuperLU while retaining a factor with ZERO fill.
backend_used returns NativeSparseLu for THAT path and for the general LU alike, so the field cannot
tell them apart. Always pass the 'off' arm for a kernel before/after; the harness forces
SPLU_CUBIC_SPECTRAL_DISABLE and asserts on SPLU_CUBIC_SPECTRAL_FACTOR_HITS so a row cannot name an
algorithm that did not run.
(2) perf_spsolve's bounded_preflight needs host-mean busy <= 20% across all 64 CPUs, which never
passes on this box — that gate, not analysis, is why this surface had no measurement. The harness
uses the balanced-square substrate ported from franken_networkx scripts/balanced_square_ab.py
(72761094c): arms interleaved A B B A A B B A inside each round, each arm's own first-half /
second-half ratio as its A/A null. No evidence standard is relaxed; it only stops requiring an idle
host.

STILL OUTSTANDING: these are not yet perf_ledger_cc.md rows. The ledger preflight requires
in-process physical cores / logical threads / RAM / NUMA count / pre+post quiescence, which the
harness now emits, but rch has refused every cargo-run admission for this crate since
('no admissible workers', ~40 consecutive attempts across foreground and detached launches). One
successful re-run of '-- 16 21 4 off cubic' and '-- 10 21 4 off scattered' fills both rows.

Pre-register callback-plus-native-batch mechanism and falsifiers; screen SciPy 1.17.1 default finite-difference, analytic rosen_der, and fused fun+jac public arms; materialize the best solution and full quality/work counters; require actual observed tasks, host identity, in-process ELF and SciPy engine SHA-256, strict rch --base --clean-overlay --no-overlay, dual nulls, corrected median gate, raw artifact, and chooser statement.

title: [special] noncentral inverse-parameter fns (ncfdtridfd/dfn/inc, nctdtridf/inc) need cdflib DINVR port for parity
description: scipy.special.{ncfdtridfd,ncfdtridfn,ncfdtrinc,nctdtridf,nctdtrinc} invert the noncentral F/t CDF on a distribution PARAMETER (dfn/dfd/nc/df). Forward ncfdtr/nctdtr already present. A generic monotonic bracket+bisect does NOT match scipy: inverting on the noncentrality/df parameter is ill-conditioned (CDF nearly flat in nc for large nc), so scipy's exact value is defined by cdflib's DINVR search tolerance/step heuristics, not the mathematical root. Measured: bisection vs scipy disagree by rel-err up to ~7 across the domain (both satisfy CDF=p; different nc). Faithful parity requires porting cdflib DINVR (zsearch+stinvr) with matching abs/rel tol AND the forward CDF matching cdflib's tail underflow. ncfdtridfd/ncfdtridfn/nctdtridf additionally hit non-invertible regions where scipy returns boundary sentinels (1e-100/1e+100). Scope: port DINVR as a shared root-finder; verify against scipy across sweeps incl boundary returns. Not a quick win.
notes: df-inversions BLOCKED (BlackThrush): bisection-to-cdflib-bounds fails because the FORWARD ncfdtr is itself inaccurate at extreme df — ncfdtr(5,1e-100,2,1.5)=1.0 (should be ~0) and breaks at dfd=1e100 (0.368 vs plateau ~0.62). The huge-root cases (scipy ncfdtridfd(10,0.6,5,1.2)=2.16e17) also need forward accuracy at df~1e17 fsci lacks. nc-inversions (ncfdtrinc/nctdtrinc) shipped fine because nc-range is moderate. Fixing df-inversions needs an accurate ncfdtr at extreme df first, then cdflib bound/sentinel (+/-1e100, 1e-100) replication.

title: [interpolate] RegularGridInterpolator + interpn for N-D data
description:
## Goal
Implement RegularGridInterpolator (N-D interpolation on a regular/rectilinear grid) and the interpn convenience function. This is the single most requested missing interpolation feature.

## What to implement
- `RegularGridInterpolator`: construct from (points_per_dim, values_ndarray). Methods: linear and nearest-neighbor interpolation.
- `interpn(points, values, xi)`: convenience wrapper.
- Support for bounds_error and fill_value (out-of-bounds handling).

## Why this matters
Virtually every scientific application that works with gridded data (climate models, CFD results, lookup tables, imaging) needs N-D interpolation. Without this, users cannot migrate from SciPy.

## Implementation approach
- Multilinear interpolation: for each query point, find the enclosing hypercube in the grid, then do successive 1D linear interpolations along each axis (tensor product).
- Nearest-neighbor: find nearest grid point per axis.
- Grid points must be sorted and monotonically increasing per axis.
- Store as crates/fsci-interpolate/src/ndgrid.rs

## Testing requirements
- 2D: interpolate on a 2D grid, verify bilinear interpolation matches hand-computed values
- 3D: trilinear interpolation test
- Nearest-neighbor: exact grid points return exact values
- Out-of-bounds: fill_value and bounds_error modes
- Edge: 1D grid (should degenerate to interp1d behavior), single-cell grid
- Monotonicity: non-monotone grid axes rejected
- At least 10 tests
close_reason: Implemented RegularGridInterpolator + interpn with multilinear and nearest-neighbor methods, bounds handling, fill_value, 15 tests

title: fsci-stats: port scipy.stats.planck (untruncated geometric)
description: Port scipy.stats.planck as Planck struct (untruncated geometric, discrete). One parameter lambda > 0. Support k = 0, 1, 2, .... Closed forms: pmf(k; lambda) = (1-e^(-lambda)) * e^(-lambda*k); cdf(k; lambda) = 1 - e^(-lambda*(k+1)). Mean = 1/(e^lambda - 1) (geometric mean). Var = e^lambda / (e^lambda - 1)^2. Add adjacent to Boltzmann (Planck is the N→∞ limit). 3 anchor tests at scipy 1.17.1 tol 1e-12 plus metamorphic identity Planck(lambda).pmf(k) = lim_{N→∞} Boltzmann(lambda, N).pmf(k) at large N.
close_reason: Ported scipy.stats.planck as Planck struct (untruncated geometric, discrete). One parameter lambda > 0. Support k = 0, 1, 2, .... All formulas closed-form: pmf(k; lambda) = (1-e^(-lambda)) * e^(-lambda*k); cdf(k; lambda) = 1 - e^(-lambda*(k+1)); mean = 1/(e^lambda-1); var = e^lambda/(e^lambda-1)^2 = 1/em + 1/em^2 where em = e^lambda - 1. Used numerically-stable expm1 throughout. 3 tests at scipy 1.17.1 tol 1e-12: pmf/cdf at 5 (lambda, k) anchors; mean+var at 3 lambda anchors; metamorphic identity Planck(lambda) = lim_{N→∞} Boltzmann(lambda, N) verified at N=50 with tol 1e-12 (since e^(-lambda*N) bound makes the tail negligible). fsci-stats --lib: 1119 -> 1122.

title: [conformance][sparse] sparse_norm silently returns the Frobenius norm for every ord it does not implement
description:
Found 2026-08-15 (RainyPrairie) by source-read plus differential against live scipy 1.17.1. crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs sparse_norm() ends its match with '_ => Frobenius', so ANY unrecognized ord silently yields a different norm than the one requested. The docstring says 'Matches scipy.sparse.linalg.norm' without qualification.

MEASURED on [[1,-2,0],[0,3,-4],[5,0,0]] (scipy 1.17.1):
  ord        scipy        ours (before)
  fro        7.416198     7.416198   ok
  1          6.000000     6.000000   ok
  inf        7.000000     7.000000   ok
  -1         4.000000     7.416198   WRONG (min column sum)
  -inf       3.000000     7.416198   WRONG (min row sum)
  2          5.261994     7.416198   WRONG (spectral norm)
  nonsense   ValueError   7.416198   WRONG (silently answers a question not asked)

Same class as frankenscipy-jtzr8: a silent fallback that returns a plausible number instead of the requested quantity, so a caller comparing it to a bound gets an answer that looks fine.

EMPTY ROWS/COLUMNS decided by measurement, since that is where min-norms differ from max-norms: on [[1,-2,0],[0,3,0],[0,0,0]] scipy gives ord=-1 -> 0.0 and ord=-inf -> 0.0, i.e. an entirely empty column or row counts as a zero sum and therefore wins the minimum. An all-zero matrix gives 0.0 for every ord.

SCOPED FIX (this bead): implement -1 and -inf, and stop the silent Frobenius fallback for unrecognized ords. There is exactly ONE production call site (linalg.rs:6457, which passes "1"); the other ~19 are tests, benches and conformance fixtures.

NOT in this bead, filed separately because they are API changes rather than defects: ord=2 (spectral norm, scipy computes it via svds) and converting the return type to SparseResult<f64> so an invalid ord can be REJECTED the way scipy rejects it rather than signalled numerically.

NEGATIVE CASES a fix must pass: an empty column must make ord=-1 zero (not be skipped, which would return the smallest NONEMPTY column sum instead); an all-zero matrix must give 0.0 for every supported ord; and the three already-correct ords must be unchanged, pinned to the scipy values above.
close_reason: Fixed in 3da5a21dd. Harness 'cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib' via 'RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec': full suite 482 passed, 0 failed, 4 ignored on RCH_WORKER=vmi1153651; post-amend re-verify of the named probe on RCH_WORKER=vmi1227854; clippy clean on hz1; ubs 0 critical. Cited probe: sparse_norm_matches_scipy_including_the_minimum_norms, every expectation a live scipy 1.17.1 measurement. Implemented -1 (min column sum) and -inf (min row sum); unimplemented ords now return NaN instead of the Frobenius norm. NEGATIVE CASES all held: an entirely empty column makes ord=-1 return 0.0 and an empty row makes ord=-inf return 0.0 (the case that distinguishes a correct implementation from one that sums only stored entries and returns the smallest NONEMPTY sum); an all-zero matrix returns 0.0 for all five ords; and the three previously-correct ords are pinned unchanged to scipy's 7.416198 / 6.0 / 7.0. NOT DONE, filed as frankenscipy-93plj: the return type stays f64, so an invalid ord is signalled as NaN rather than REJECTED the way scipy raises ValueError, and ord=2 (spectral, scipy gives 5.261994 via svds) is still unimplemented -- both are API changes rather than this defect, and the blast radius is measured there (1 production call site, ~19 test/bench/conformance sites in other agents' files).

title: [parity-gap] jn_nonnegative forward recurrence diverges for moderate n at small x
description:
Fourth in the Bessel forward-recurrence cancellation family ([frankenscipy-xlci0], [frankenscipy-0j009], [frankenscipy-tt2v2] handled spherical j/i and complex). The non-spherical regular Bessel jn_nonnegative (crates/fsci-special/src/bessel.rs:2459) uses forward recurrence J_{k+1} = 2k/x · J_k − J_{k-1}. For x << 2k, J_n decays as (x/2)^n / n! (super-exponential) while the prefactor 2k/x grows, so the subtraction produces catastrophic cancellation.

Verified at x=0.1:

  n   forward (broken)      true (series)
  ─   ────────────────────  ──────────────
  4   +2.5e−3               +2.6e−7         (4 orders too big)
  5   +0.20                 +2.6e−9         (8 orders off)
  6   +20                   +2.2e−11        (12 orders off)
  10  +9.7e9                +8.7e−22        (31 orders off)

Repro: jn_nonnegative(10, 0.1) → ~9.7e9 instead of ~8.7e−22.

Existing tests cover small n (n ≤ 3 at moderate x), masking the bug.

Fix: in the n ≥ 2 ∧ |x| < n regime, switch to Miller's downward recurrence  J_{k−1} = 2k/x · J_k − J_{k+1}; seed j_{m+1}=0, j_m=1e−30, with overflow rescaling, then normalize against the analytic J_0(x) computed by the existing j0_core. Mirrors the spherical-Bessel fix.

Acceptance: jn_nonnegative(10, 0.1) within 1% of (0.05)^10 / 10! ≈ 2.69e-22; existing recurrence tests still pass.

title: fsci-stats: Cauchy lacks closed-form sf override
description: REVIEW MODE finding (LOW). Continuation of h36zm/6uo0s/wofb sf-precision systemic rotation. Cauchy inherits the lossy default sf = 1 - cdf despite having a clean closed form via the arctan reciprocal identity:  sf(x) = arctan(scale/(x-loc))/π    for x > loc  sf(x) = 1 - arctan(-scale/(x-loc))/π = 0.5 - arctan((x-loc)/scale)/π    for x ≤ loc. The right tail is the precision-sensitive case; for very deep tail (e.g., x = loc + 1e30·scale) the default 1 - cdf collapses to 0 because cdf rounds to 1.0, while the closed form returns ~3e-31 directly. Will add the sf override + tail-precision regression test.
close_reason: REVIEW MODE finding extends h36zm/6uo0s/wofb sf-precision rotation to Cauchy. Pre-fix: Cauchy inherited default sf = 1 - cdf which collapses to 0 in the very deep right tail (x ≈ loc + 1e20+ scale) when cdf rounds to 1.0. Added closed-form sf override using the arctan reciprocal identity: sf(x) = arctan(scale/(x-loc))/π for x > loc; falls back to 0.5 - arctan((x-loc)/scale)/π for x ≤ loc (default precision adequate there). Regression test cauchy_sf_preserves_deep_tail_precision exercises x = 1e20 and asserts sf > 0 with rel < 1e-12 vs the closed form, plus sf + cdf = 1 near the centre. fsci-stats --lib: 1011 → 1012 passing.

title: EPIC: Linalg Matrix Functions (logm, sqrtm, matrix_power)
description:
## Background

FEATURE_PARITY.md lists logm + sqrtm + matrix_power as the #2 highest-impact missing functions (after stats.describe). fsci-linalg at 26% coverage has the core solvers/decompositions but lacks matrix FUNCTIONS: logm, sqrtm, fractional_matrix_power, matrix_power, funm, signm.

## Current State

Implemented: solve, solve_triangular, solve_banded, inv, det, lstsq, pinv, lu, lu_factor, lu_solve, qr, svd, svdvals, cholesky, cho_factor, cho_solve, ldl, eig, eigvals, eigh, eigvalsh, schur, hessenberg, expm, norm, matrix_rank. Note: expm EXISTS — so the Schur-based approach is already proven.

## Goal

Implement logm, sqrtm, matrix_power using the existing Schur decomposition infrastructure (which expm already uses).

## Success Criteria

1. logm — matrix logarithm via Schur decomposition + inverse scaling and squaring
2. sqrtm — matrix square root via Schur decomposition
3. matrix_power — integer matrix power via repeated squaring; negative powers via inv + repeated squaring
4. Unit tests: identity matrix, diagonal matrix, known-answer cases, singular input handling
5. Conformance fixtures against SciPy expected values
6. expm(logm(A)) ≈ A round-trip test for well-conditioned inputs

## Serves Project Goal

These are among the most commonly called scipy.linalg functions and are prerequisites for several downstream algorithms.

title: Implement logm (matrix logarithm)
description:
## What

Implement logm(A) — matrix logarithm via Schur decomposition + inverse scaling and squaring (Al-Mohy & Higham, 2012).

## Why

#2 highest-impact missing function. Required for computing matrix square roots, fractional powers, and geodesics on matrix manifolds.

## Implementation Notes

- Compute Schur decomposition T = Q^H A Q (already have schur() in fsci-linalg)
- Apply inverse scaling and squaring to triangular T
- Use Padé approximants for log of near-identity matrix
- Transform back: logm(A) = Q logm(T) Q^H
- Handle real matrices with complex eigenvalues (return complex result or real if possible)
- Error: singular matrix → return error, negative real eigenvalues → complex log

## Tests

- logm(expm(A)) ≈ A for well-conditioned A
- logm(I) = 0
- logm(diag(d)) = diag(log(d))
- Known-answer test for 2×2 and 3×3 matrices
- Singular matrix → error
close_reason: logm already implemented in fsci-linalg (verified in reality-check)

title: Implement sqrtm (matrix square root)
description:
## What

Implement sqrtm(A) — principal matrix square root via Schur decomposition (Björck & Hammarling, 1983).

## Why

Needed for Riemannian geometry, Fréchet distance, and matrix interpolation. Part of the #2 highest-impact missing group.

## Implementation Notes

- Schur decomposition: T = Q^H A Q
- Compute sqrt of triangular T column by column using recurrence relation
- Transform back: sqrtm(A) = Q sqrtm(T) Q^H
- Alternative: use Denman-Beavers iteration (Newton's method for matrix sqrt)

## Tests

- sqrtm(A) @ sqrtm(A) ≈ A
- sqrtm(I) = I
- sqrtm(diag(d)) = diag(sqrt(d))
- SPD matrix → real result
- Non-SPD → may produce complex result
close_reason: Added 6 tests for sqrtm: identity, diagonal, squared equals original, 3x3 SPD, negative eigenvalue returns NaN, non-square rejection. Implementation already existed.

title: Implement matrix_power (integer matrix power)
description:
## What

Implement matrix_power(A, n) — raise square matrix to integer power n via repeated squaring. Negative powers via inv() + repeated squaring.

## Implementation Notes

- n=0 → identity, n=1 → A, n=-1 → inv(A)
- Positive n: binary exponentiation (square and multiply)
- Negative n: compute inv(A) then binary exponentiation with |n|
- Non-square input → error

## Tests

- matrix_power(A, 0) = I
- matrix_power(A, 1) = A
- matrix_power(A, 2) = A @ A
- matrix_power(A, -1) = inv(A)
- matrix_power(A, -2) = inv(A) @ inv(A)
- Non-square → error
close_reason: Added 6 tests for matrix_power covering: n=0 (identity), n=1 (original), n=2 (multiply), n=-1 (inverse), n=-2 (inverse squared), non-square rejection

title: [CRITICAL] CI: ci_gates.rs manifest diverges from .github/workflows/ci.yml (G5/G6 run more tests in yaml but with '|| true' suppression, so failures never fail CI); 7 of 14 e2e families (stats/signal/interpolate/io/spatial/cluster/ndimage) are EXCLUDED from G5; G3 'Differential Conformance' runs only golden_journeys+schema (per ivg5, not actually differential); G4 'Adversarial' runs smoke, no fuzz replay
description:
Review of .github/workflows/ci.yml + crates/fsci-conformance/src/ci_gates.rs
on 2026-04-23.

Three compounding problems in the CI gate topology:

1. HARD DRIFT between the programmatic manifest and the actual workflow.

    ci_gates.rs:72 says G5 runs:
        "cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test e2e_linalg -- --nocapture"
    (ONE test)

    ci.yml:67-71 actually runs:
        for test in e2e_linalg e2e_ivp e2e_optimize e2e_sparse e2e_fft e2e_special e2e_casp; do
            cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test "$test" -- --nocapture || true
        done
    (SEVEN tests, but see item 3)

    ci_gates.rs:73-75 says G6 runs:
        "cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test perf_linalg -- --nocapture"
    (ONE test)

    ci.yml:82-87 actually runs:
        for test in perf_linalg perf_ivp perf_arrayapi; do
            ... || true
        done
    (THREE tests, but see item 3)

    ci_gates.rs is public API (GateId enum, GateId::commands()) and its
    tests at line 300-304 assert_eq that every gate has commands. These
    tests pin the STATIC METADATA, not the actual CI behavior. Readers of
    ci_gates.rs get a wrong picture of what the pipeline runs.

2. G5 and G6 use '|| true' suppression -- failures DO NOT fail CI.

    ci.yml:70:      cargo test ... "$test" -- --nocapture || true
    ci.yml:85:      cargo test ... "$test" -- --nocapture || true

    With '|| true' appended, ANY test failure in the loop is ignored. The
    outer step exit code is always 0, meaning G5 and G6 NEVER fail the CI
    pipeline. A bug that breaks e2e_ivp, e2e_optimize, e2e_sparse,
    perf_ivp, or perf_arrayapi lands on main without alarm.

    This is a form of the 'advisory gate' anti-pattern. The CI topology
    CLAIMS G5 and G6 are gates ('E2E Scenarios', 'Performance Regression')
    but operationally they are log-only steps.

3. ENTIRE FAMILIES EXCLUDED from G5 coverage.

    Family e2e tests in tree (crates/fsci-conformance/tests/):
        e2e_linalg.rs      (53K)  <- in ci.yml G5
        e2e_ivp.rs         (43K)  <- in ci.yml G5
        e2e_optimize.rs    (46K)  <- in ci.yml G5
        e2e_sparse.rs      (94K)  <- in ci.yml G5
        e2e_fft.rs         (28K)  <- in ci.yml G5
        e2e_special.rs     (28K)  <- in ci.yml G5
        e2e_casp.rs        (26K)  <- in ci.yml G5

        e2e_stats.rs      (134K)  <- NOT IN G5
        e2e_signal.rs      (86K)  <- NOT IN G5
        e2e_interpolate.rs (52K)  <- NOT IN G5
        e2e_io.rs          (47K)  <- NOT IN G5
        e2e_spatial.rs     (53K)  <- NOT IN G5
        e2e_cluster.rs     (32K)  <- NOT IN G5
        e2e_ndimage.rs     (36K)  <- NOT IN G5
        e2e_orchestrator.rs(14K)  <- NOT IN G5

    Excluded e2e tests total 454 KB of scenarios vs 318 KB included. More
    than half of the e2e test surface is never gated.

    Combined with '|| true' on the included 7 tests, the ACTUAL G5 signal
    strength is: 'no hard failure from cargo test -p fsci-conformance'
    (which is broader than what G5 was meant to check).

4. G3 'Differential Conformance' runs only golden_journeys +
   schema_validation.

    ci.yml:43-46 runs:
        cargo test ... --test golden_journeys
        cargo test ... --test schema_validation

    Per bead 6mdr (now closed or open): golden_journeys writes artifacts
    but does not read golden files (no actual differential comparison).
    Per bead ivg5 (open): run_differential_test is not actually
    differential for 11 of 12 family runners.

    So G3 'Differential Conformance' does not, in fact, test scipy-parity
    differential conformance for any family. It tests artifact-write
    (golden_journeys) + schema-field-presence (schema_validation). The
    'differential' label is unearned.

5. G4 'Adversarial Regression' runs only smoke, not any fuzz corpus.

    ci.yml:56 runs:
        cargo test ... --test smoke

    fuzz/fuzz_targets/ contains p2c001_validate_tol, p2c001_step_bounds,
    p2c002_solve, p2c002_factorizations, p2c003_add, p2c003_add_properties,
    p2c004_sparse_helpers, p2c005_sparse_formats, p2c006_special_complex_branches,
    p2c007_stats_fit_survives_nan_inf, and more. The corpus under
    fuzz/corpus/ has crash artifacts. NONE of these get replayed in G4.

    Per /testing-fuzzing skill: 'Every crash artifact becomes a regression
    test or it WILL regress.' fuzz/artifacts/ crashes are not replayed
    in CI.

6. G7 'Schema Validation' duplicates G3's schema_validation.

    ci.yml:97 runs cargo test ... schema_validation  (same test as G3 line 45).
    Running the same test in two gates doubles compute without adding
    coverage.

Consequences:

- The README and crate docs describe an 8-gate CI pipeline that provides
  differential conformance, adversarial regression, E2E orchestration,
  performance regression, schema validation, and RaptorQ decode-proof
  verification. None of these claims hold operationally:
    - G3 is artifact-write + schema presence check, not differential.
    - G4 is smoke test, not adversarial.
    - G5 loops through 7 of 14 e2e tests with || true.
    - G6 loops through 3 perf tests with || true.
    - G7 is a duplicate of part of G3.
    - G8 is RaptorQ decoder test, not parity artifacts (per the cosmetic
      decode_proof.json artifact write_parity_artifacts emits).

- Downstream 'conformance ratified by CI' claims are unbacked. Merging
  a PR passes green when half the families are untested and the other
  half can't fail CI.

Fix priority:

1. Remove '|| true' suppression from G5 and G6. If loops-of-tests are
   desired, use a single consolidated cargo test invocation that fails
   fast on first failure.

2. Add all 14 e2e_* tests to G5 (and remove the manual for loop -- use
   `cargo test -p fsci-conformance --tests` which runs all integration
   tests).

3. Add fuzz corpus replay to G4: for each fuzz target under fuzz/, run
   `cargo +nightly fuzz run <target> --runs=0` which replays artifacts
   without generating new ones.

4. Rename G3 pending ivg5 fix: either wire actual differential
   comparison OR rename G3 to 'Self-Check Conformance' in both
   ci_gates.rs and ci.yml.

5. Reconcile ci_gates.rs commands() with ci.yml. Preferably have
   ci.yml invoke `cargo test -p fsci-ci` binary that reads ci_gates.rs
   programmatically — so the manifest IS the source of truth.

6. Delete G7 (redundant) or give it distinct tests.

Regression test: add a CI workflow test that parses ci.yml and asserts
no '|| true' appears in any step. Fails today.

Related: ivg5 (run_differential_test not actually differential), 6mdr
(golden_journeys no golden files), y5bh (smoke was vacuous, now real),
9vmw / s5e2 / 8ghr (Potemkin infrastructure), 7h9o (dashboard claim
drift). The CI gate topology is the capstone of the naming-dishonesty
stack: it's the final layer at which the workspace claims 'conformance
ratified' without the evidence.

title: [conformance][stats] brunnermunzel_matrix rejects ragged samples that scipy accepts, and only on ONE side of its A/B toggle
description:
Found 2026-08-16 (RainyPrairie) by the frankenscipy-yq1k8 doc-vs-implementation audit, by reading only -- no build, filed during the /data build freeze with the fix prepared but NOT yet gated.

TWO DEFECTS IN ONE SITE, crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:44308 brunnermunzel_matrix.

(1) THE A/B ARMS DISAGREE OBSERVABLY, so the doc claim is false. The doc on BRUNNERMUNZEL_MATRIX_PRESORT_DISABLE (:44150) says 'Byte-identical either way', and the function comment repeats 'BYTE-IDENTICAL (ranks scattered to original positions; identical summation order)'. But the toggle branch returns all_pairs_two_full_matrices BEFORE the equal-length validation at :44321-44325. So on ragged input the DEFAULT arm returns Err(InvalidArgument 'all variables must have the same length') and the DISABLE arm returns Ok with a full matrix of statistics. Err vs Ok is not byte-identity. This is precisely yq1k8's class: the static's doc and the shipped code disagree, and the doc is the one people read.

(2) THE VALIDATION ITSELF IS WRONG, which is why the fix is to delete it rather than to hoist it. brunnermunzel is a TWO-SAMPLE test and nx need not equal ny. MEASURED, scipy 1.17.1: brunnermunzel([1,2,3],[2,3,4,5,6]) -> statistic 2.794002794004191, pvalue 0.033529597617504764. It does not object.

PROVENANCE OF THE BUG, which also shows it is not a deliberate choice: the identical string 'all variables must have the same length' appears at :43577, :43820 and :43974, and all three of those guard functions taking 'variables' -- correlation-style matrices, where equal length genuinely IS required because you cannot correlate unequal-length vectors. brunnermunzel_matrix takes 'samples'. Every OTHER two-sample samples-matrix in the family -- ks_2samp_matrix (:43886), mannwhitneyu_matrix (:43926), ranksums_matrix (:44121), wasserstein_distance_matrix (:43736), energy_distance_matrix (:43772) -- has no such check and accepts ragged input. ks_2samp_matrix is the closest possible comparison: same presort-once lever, same toggle shape, no length check.

THE FAST PATH ALREADY HANDLES RAGGED, so deleting the check does not paper over a latent panic. brunnermunzel_presorted (:44207) reads nx = xs.sorted.len() and ny = ys.sorted.len() independently and merges them as a genuine two-sample merge; nothing in it assumes nx == ny.

PREPARED FIX (not applied -- build freeze, and I will not commit ungated code): delete the 'let n = samples[0].len();' and 'samples.iter().any(|v| v.len() != n)' block at :44320-44326, leaving the m == 0 early return. Both arms then accept ragged input and the byte-identity claim becomes true.

PREPARED TEST, two arms as required by yq1k8's own standing rule:
  MUST-HIT: samples of lengths 3, 5, 4 -> both toggle settings return Ok, and the two matrices agree bit-for-bit via to_bits(), which is the assertion the doc has always claimed and nothing has ever checked.
  MUST-MISS: equal-length samples must be unchanged from today's values, so the fix cannot be a silent behavioural rewrite of the common case.
  ORACLE ROW: brunnermunzel([1,2,3],[2,3,4,5,6]) == (2.794002794004191, 0.033529597617504764) from live scipy 1.17.1, pinning the off-diagonal directly rather than only self-consistency between the two arms.

NOTE the toggle-race hazard when writing that test: BRUNNERMUNZEL_MATRIX_PRESORT_DISABLE is a process-global static, so an A/B test that stores into it must hold the same mutex every other toggle-writing test in this crate holds, or concurrent cargo test threads will both invent drift and mask it.

GATE WHEN THE FREEZE LIFTS (df -h /data above 70G): cargo test -p fsci-stats --lib brunnermunzel.
close_reason:
REFUTED BY ITS OWN TEST, 2026-08-16 (RainyPrairie), on rch worker vmi1227854. Both claims in the filed description are wrong. Code reverted to HEAD (stashed, not dropped: stash "m3eja REFUTED: brunnermunzel ragged-accept attempt + two-arm test"). Nothing shipped.

WHAT I CLAIMED: (1) the A/B arms of brunnermunzel_matrix disagree Err-vs-Ok on ragged input, falsifying the toggle's byte-identity doc; (2) the equal-length check is copy-paste from the correlation-matrix helpers and should be deleted, since scipy accepts unequal lengths for brunnermunzel and every sibling two-sample matrix accepts ragged input.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS. I deleted the check and wrote the two-arm test the standing rule requires. The MUST-HIT arm failed immediately at the DISABLE call, not at the default one: lib.rs:72109, the second expect(). The fallback arm rejects ragged input too, from INSIDE the shared helper — all_pairs_two_full_matrices (:43960) and all_pairs_two_symmetric_matrices (:43806) both carry the same equal-length validation.

So before my change BOTH arms rejected ragged input, they AGREED, and the byte-identity claim was never falsified. My change is what would have broken it: deleting the check left the fast arm (which routes through all_pairs_two_full_matrices_by_index, the one helper variant that does NOT validate) accepting ragged input while the DISABLE arm still refused. I would have INTRODUCED exactly the divergence I filed the bead about.

AND THE CHECK IS NOT COPY-PASTE. It is load-bearing, and brunnermunzel_matrix is the only member of the family that needs it: it is the only one whose fast arm uses the non-validating _by_index helper. ks_2samp_matrix (:43895/:43908), mannwhitneyu_matrix (:43934/:43947) and ranksums_matrix (:44129/:44142) each pass their PRESORTED samples back through the same validating helper on both arms — presorting does not change lengths — so they inherit the validation on both sides. My "every sibling accepts ragged" claim came from grepping for the error STRING and finding none in those functions, without checking what their helpers do. The string's absence meant the check was inherited, not missing.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is not a scipy conformance red. The whole two-sample *_matrix family rejects ragged input, consistently, on every arm. scipy has no all-pairs form of any of these, so there is no incumbent to conform to; the only scipy fact in play is that the PAIRWISE brunnermunzel(x, y) accepts unequal lengths, which says nothing about what an all-pairs matrix API we invented should do. It is a defensible API choice, and it is inconsistent with all_pairs_cross_matrix (:43922 comment) which documents that "two-sample distances/tests accept ragged inputs" for the CROSS variants. That inconsistency is a design question worth its own bead if anyone wants ragged support, NOT a defect, and emphatically not something to fix by deleting a validation.

THE PROCESS LESSON, which is the reusable part. The two-arm rule earned its keep here: a one-arm test (ragged input now returns Ok on the default path) would have PASSED, and I would have shipped a real A/B divergence under a commit message announcing I had fixed one. What caught it was insisting the DISABLE arm produce a value too, before comparing bits. Related to frankenscipy-yq1k8, which is where this hunt started, and it sharpens that bead's warning: reading a function body is not enough to know what it validates, because validation can live in a shared helper the body merely calls. Grep the callee, not just the caller.

title: [HIGH] conformance: FSCI-P2C-006 oracle_capture.json is stale (9 days old) — cases using recently-added dispatchers still show unsupported_function
description:
Review-mode audit of fsci-conformance FSCI-P2C-006 fixtures on 2026-04-22:

    crates/fsci-conformance/fixtures/artifacts/FSCI-P2C-006/oracle_capture.json
    ├─ generated_unix_ms: 1776101732534 → 2026-04-13 17:35 (9 days old)
    └─ scipy_version: 1.17.1, numpy: 2.4.3, python: 3.13.7

    crates/fsci-conformance/python_oracle/scipy_special_oracle.py
    └─ mtime: 2026-04-22 12:02 (today)

The oracle script has been modified 9 days after the fixture was last regenerated. Evidence of staleness:

1. oracle_capture.json contains 7/30 cases with result_kind=unsupported_function, including:
    meta_erf_plus_erfc_neg2 (function=rel_erf_erfc_identity)
    meta_gamma_recurrence_x2p5 (function=rel_gamma_recurrence)
    meta_beta_symmetry_0p75_2p5 (function=rel_beta_symmetry)
    meta_gammainc_complement_2p5_1p7 (function=rel_gammainc_complement)
    meta_jn_recurrence_n3_x2p5 (function=rel_jn_recurrence)

2. scipy_special_oracle.py:169-173 HAS these as func_map entries today. So a re-capture would produce real numbers, not unsupported_function.

3. This means any conformance test consuming oracle_capture.json is comparing its Rust output against 'unsupported_function' — always passing (or always failing) without actual SciPy comparison.

Ask:
1. Regenerate crates/fsci-conformance/fixtures/artifacts/FSCI-P2C-006/oracle_capture.json by running:
     python crates/fsci-conformance/python_oracle/scipy_special_oracle.py \
        --fixture crates/fsci-conformance/fixtures/FSCI-P2C-006_special_core.json \
        --output  crates/fsci-conformance/fixtures/artifacts/FSCI-P2C-006/oracle_capture.json \
        --oracle-root <path>
   and commit the updated JSON.

2. Add a fixture-staleness CI gate: compute blake3(oracle_script) + blake3(fixture_source) and embed in oracle_capture.json; CI fails if any artifact's recorded hash doesn't match current files. This is the /testing-conformance-harnesses PROVENANCE.md contract.
