title: [signal] Resampling: resample, resample_poly, decimate
description:
## Goal
Implement signal resampling functions for changing sample rate — a fundamental operation in audio processing, telecommunications, and multi-rate signal processing.

## What to implement
- `resample(x, num)`: resample using FFT method. Changes the number of samples in a signal using Fourier method (zero-pad or truncate in frequency domain).
- `resample_poly(x, up, down)`: polyphase resampling (rational rate change by factor up/down). More efficient and has less aliasing artifacts than FFT method.
- `decimate(x, q, ftype)`: downsample after applying anti-aliasing filter. Applies lowpass filter then takes every q-th sample.

## Why this matters
Sample rate conversion is needed whenever combining data from different sources (e.g., 44.1kHz audio to 48kHz), downsampling high-rate sensor data, or matching sample rates for cross-correlation.

## Implementation approach
- resample: FFT → zero-pad/truncate → IFFT. Handles both upsampling and downsampling.
- resample_poly: design anti-aliasing FIR filter, apply polyphase decomposition for efficiency
- decimate: apply butter/cheby1 lowpass at Nyquist/q, then slice every q-th sample

## Dependencies
- resample depends on fsci-fft (rfft/irfft)
- decimate depends on existing lfilter + butter

## Testing requirements
- resample: sine wave at known frequency survives up/downsampling (frequency preserved, amplitude scales correctly)
- resample_poly: rational rate change 3/2 of sine wave preserves frequency
- decimate: anti-aliasing prevents folding artifacts
- Energy preservation: sum(x²) ≈ sum(y²) * (len_x/len_y) for resample
- At least 6 tests
close_reason: Implemented resample (FFT method), resample_poly (polyphase FIR), decimate (anti-alias + downsample) with 8 tests

title: [CRITICAL] conformance: scipy_special_oracle.py stirling2 lambda computes WRONG values (returns comb(n,k)*k! instead of Stirling number of the 2nd kind)
description:
Review-mode audit of crates/fsci-conformance/python_oracle/scipy_special_oracle.py:144:

    "stirling2": lambda n, k: special.comb(n, k, exact=True) * special.factorial(k, exact=True) if k <= n else 0,

This formula is algebraically WRONG. It does NOT compute Stirling numbers of the second kind S(n, k).

Verification (Python):
    S(3, 2) = 3  (correct)
    oracle_S(3, 2) = comb(3,2) * 2! = 3 * 2 = 6  (WRONG, 2× high)
    S(4, 2) = 7  (correct)
    oracle_S(4, 2) = comb(4,2) * 2! = 6 * 2 = 12  (WRONG, ~1.7× high)

The correct formula is S(n, k) = (1/k!) * sum_{j=0}^{k} (-1)^j * C(k,j) * (k-j)^n, or use sympy.functions.combinatorial.numbers.stirling(n, k, kind=2). The quantity the lambda computes — comb(n,k)*k! = n!/(n-k)! — is the number of k-permutations, not Stirling numbers.

Impact:
- ANY conformance case using function='stirling2' in a packet fixture receives a systematically wrong reference value. A Rust impl that correctly computes S(n,k) would FAIL the conformance check. A Rust impl that reproduces the WRONG formula would PASS.
- Current search finds no Rust caller yet, so this is latent — but the moment someone wires up a Stirling-2 test, every pass/fail verdict will be inverted.

Fix:
1. Change stirling2 dispatcher to a correct implementation. Options:
   a) Use sympy.functions.combinatorial.numbers.stirling(n, k, kind=2) (adds sympy dep to oracle venv).
   b) Manual formula: sum((-1)**j * comb(k, j) * (k-j)**n for j in range(k+1)) / factorial(k).
   c) Remove stirling2 from func_map until a correct oracle exists; fail closed on 'unsupported function: stirling2' — matches the doctrine.

Recommended: (c) remove + reopen once a verified oracle ships (sympy preferred).

Verification after fix: assert oracle_S(3,2) == 3, oracle_S(4,2) == 7, oracle_S(5,3) == 25, oracle_S(6,4) == 65.
close_reason: Removed incorrect stirling2 oracle dispatcher and added fail-closed regression coverage

title: [interpolate] NearestNDInterpolator + griddata(method='nearest')
description:
## Goal
Implement nearest-neighbor scattered data interpolation — the simplest and most robust scattered data method.

## What to implement
- `NearestNDInterpolator(points, values)`: nearest-neighbor interpolation for scattered data. Construct from (points, values), evaluate at new points. Wraps fsci-spatial KDTree.
- `griddata(points, values, xi, method="nearest")`: convenience function using NearestND under the hood.
- Both work in arbitrary dimensions.

## Why this matters
Nearest-neighbor interpolation is the simplest method for scattered data. It always works (no convex hull restriction), handles any dimensionality, and is very fast via KDTree. It is the recommended starting point for scattered data before trying more sophisticated methods.

## Implementation approach
- NearestNDInterpolator: build KDTree from input points, query nearest neighbor for each evaluation point, return corresponding value
- griddata with method="nearest": construct NearestNDInterpolator and evaluate
- This is straightforward — essentially a thin wrapper around KDTree

## Dependencies
- Uses existing KDTree from fsci-spatial (already implemented)

## Testing requirements
- 2D scattered data: exact at data points, reasonable between
- N-D: 3D test with known function
- griddata dispatch: method="nearest" works
- Large dataset (1000 points): verify correctness against brute-force
- Out-of-bounds: still works (finds nearest even if far away)
- Empty input rejection
- At least 8 tests
close_reason: Implemented NearestNDInterpolator (KDTree-based) and griddata(method='nearest'). 8 new tests, 29 total. Unblocks LinearNDInterpolator/Delaunay bead.

title: linalg: revisit the contractual cholesky() output-buffer zero as a BUNDLE (our TSQR analogue)
description: PRIMITIVE TRANSFER BUS, consumed from franken_numpy (owner of the data-movement primitive). Their TSQR reject is DEFINITIVE and root-caused to API-SURFACE costs, not the kernel: a whole-matrix cast copy plus a second O(mn) residual pass, which get RELATIVELY WORSE as m grows (0.87x at 2e6x8). Retry needs BOTH zero-copy extraction AND dropping the residual recompute — a kernel-only speedup provably cannot close a surface-cost wall. OUR ANALOGUE: cholesky() performs an 8 MB output-buffer zero at n=1000 that exists purely to honour the documented contract 'strict upper triangle is already zero'. Measured 8.41% self after the scratch-hoist work (2026-07-22) and correctly REJECTED as sub-floor IN ISOLATION. The transfer argument is that isolation is the wrong frame: a surface-contract cost is invisible to kernel levers by construction. Bundle it with the pack (9.2%) and memmove (3.9%) data-movement block, or change the contract (e.g. return a triangular view / document the upper triangle as unspecified) — an API change, which needs owner sign-off and a conformance review because scipy.linalg.cholesky returns a full array with zeros. DO NOT re-measure the isolated memset; that row stands. Prior art: docs/perf_ledger_cc.md 2026-07-26 PRIMITIVE ADAPTATION row.
close_reason: Packed lower rows directly into the blocked Cholesky slab while retaining contractual strict-upper zero padding; added blocked public contract test.

title: [HIGH] conformance: audit ledger emission is wired for only 3 of 12 family runners (validate_tol/linalg/fft) — 9 families silently skip audit-trail capture
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs on 2026-04-22:

emit_differential_audit_ledger_for_fixture @ line 7642 is called from exactly 3 sites:
    line 7802: run_differential_validate_tol
    line 7854: run_differential_linalg
    line 8359: run_differential_fft

The other 9 family runners do NOT emit audit ledgers:
    run_differential_array_api
    run_differential_special
    run_differential_optimize
    run_differential_casp
    run_differential_cluster
    run_differential_spatial
    run_differential_signal
    run_differential_stats
    run_differential_integrate

This compounds xo4o (2.9% Hardened coverage) badly:
- Hardened mode per crates/fsci-runtime/src/mode.rs:10-13 is meant to add
  finite-check rejection and emit audit-ledger entries when rejections happen.
- For a Hardened case in fsci-stats / fsci-special / fsci-optimize / fsci-cluster
  / fsci-spatial / fsci-signal / fsci-integrate / fsci-casp, the rejection
  happens but no ledger is captured by the conformance runner.
- No downstream assertion verifies that fsci-* emitted the expected audit events.

Impact: claiming 'Hardened conformance verified' for these 9 families is HALF
a claim -- the numerical behavior might be verified (inadequately per xo4o),
but the fail-closed audit-trail contract is entirely unverified.

Also: the existing emit paths at 7802/7854/8359 check 'if !ledger.is_empty()'
before emitting. A family whose cases happen to not trigger any audit events
silently skips emission without logging empty-state. Distinguishing 'runner
never captured' from 'runner captured nothing' requires an explicit marker.

Fix:
1. Extend each of the 9 runners to instantiate a ledger and pass it through
   execute_*_case_with_differential_audit. fsci-linalg has
   linalg_sync_audit_ledger already; fsci-stats/signal/cluster/etc. need similar.
2. After the per-case loop, call emit_differential_audit_ledger_for_fixture
   unconditionally (write empty ledger if no events).
3. Add assertions to the *_quota_and_structured_logs tests: for Hardened
   cases, assert the emitted ledger contains entries of expected kinds
   (bounded_recovery, fail_closed, etc.).

Related: xo4o (Hardened coverage 2.9%), ihex (both-errored = pass),
ivg5 (runners do not invoke oracles), 3szj (shapiro bug that audit entries
might have caught).
close_reason: All 12 differential runners now emit audit ledger artifacts. Added neutral_audit_ledger() helper returning Arc<Mutex<AuditLedger>> and wired it into the 8 runners that previously passed None for the audit_ledger arg (run_differential_array_api/special/optimize/casp/cluster/spatial/signal/stats). Each runner instantiates a ledger, passes Some(audit_ledger.as_ref()) to run_case_with_panic_capture, and emits via emit_differential_audit_ledger_for_fixture at the end. title: [sparse][conformance] diags() stores explicit zeros where scipy's dia->csr prunes them
description:
Found by RusticCarp 2026-08-04 while closing frankenscipy-sg4qi. Split out deliberately rather than folded into that bead, because it is a DIFFERENT divergence with a different fix and a real scope question.

DIVERGENCE: fsci's diags() stores explicit zeros; scipy's dia -> csr conversion prunes them.

VERIFIED LIVE, scipy 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.3:
  sp.diags([np.zeros(5)], [0], shape=(5,5))            -> dia_matrix, .nnz == 5
  sp.diags([np.zeros(5)], [0], shape=(5,5)).tocsr()    -> .nnz == 0
                                                          data = [], indptr = [0 0 0 0 0 0]
  sp.diags([[1,0,2,0,3]], [0], shape=(5,5)).tocsr()    -> .nnz == 3, data = [1,2,3]
                                                          (INTERIOR zeros pruned too)

fsci: crates/fsci-sparse/src/construct.rs, diags_row_block (line 231). Every
in-bounds diagonal entry is pushed to data/indices unconditionally — there is no
value test anywhere in the row fill:

    if let Some((col, value)) = entry {
        indices.push(col);
        data.push(value);
        c += 1;
    }

So fsci's diags(zeros(5), [0], (5,5)) returns a CsrMatrix with 5 STORED zeros,
where scipy's .tocsr() peer has 0. Now that sparse_nnz correctly reports stored
cardinality (fixed in 3c3846258), this divergence is directly observable:
fsci sparse_nnz == 5 vs scipy .nnz == 0 on the same logical construction.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND nnz: stored count drives indptr/indices/data layout, so it
also changes .tocsr() round-trips, any downstream nnz-proportional cost, and
sparse_density (which divides stored nnz by rows*cols and will therefore report
a nonzero density for an all-zero diags matrix).

SCOPE QUESTION — DECIDE BEFORE WRITING CODE, and say which in the close reason:
 (a) Match scipy: prune values that are exactly 0.0 during the diags row fill.
     Cheap and local, but it is a BEHAVIOUR CHANGE to a constructor and will move
     MR27 in crates/fsci-sparse/tests/metamorphic_tests.rs:764, whose current
     expectation of 5 is correct for TODAY's non-pruning diags. MR27 would then
     need its expected value changed to 0 WITH this bead cited as the reason —
     that is a legitimate golden change, not a weakening, but it must be stated.
     Check first whether scipy prunes in diags() itself or only in tocsr(); the
     dia_matrix .nnz of 5 says the pruning happens at CONVERSION, so a faithful
     port might keep the stored zeros in a DIA-shaped intermediate and prune when
     producing CSR. fsci's diags returns CSR directly, so it has no intermediate
     to hang that on.
 (b) Keep fsci's behaviour deliberately and document the divergence. Only
     defensible if some caller relies on the explicit-zero structure being
     preserved (a fixed sparsity pattern for repeated assembly, for example).
     Grep callers before choosing this.

DO NOT pick (a) just because it makes a number match, and do not pick (b) just to
avoid touching MR27.

EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: a test pinning fsci's diags stored count against the live
scipy .tocsr() value above for BOTH the all-zero diagonal and the mixed
[1,0,2,0,3] diagonal (the mixed case is the one that catches a fix which only
special-cases the all-zero diagonal), plus cargo test -p fsci-sparse --all-targets
green, plus an explicit statement of which branch (a) or (b) was taken.
close_reason: Fixed in commit 864ef68cc, option (a) MATCH SCIPY. Scope question answered with a live check first: scipy prunes at CONVERSION, not in diags() -- sp.diags([np.zeros(5)],[0],shape=(5,5)).nnz == 5 (dia) but the same call with format='csr' has nnz == 0 (scipy 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.3). fsci's diags returns CSR directly with no DIA intermediate, so the converted peer is what it must match; the unpruned layout remains available and unchanged via spdiags, which returns a DiaMatrix like scipy's. Grepped callers before choosing: conformance/metamorphic/benches either dense-compare or are updated here, none depend on the explicit-zero structure. GOLDEN CHANGE STATED, not quiet: MR27 in crates/fsci-sparse/tests/metamorphic_tests.rs moves its expected stored nnz from 5 to 0 with this bead cited -- that expectation was correct for the old non-pruning diags and is wrong for the scipy peer. MR27's actual relation (stored vs numerical cardinality) is preserved by building the explicit-zero CSR from components, and MR33's fixture moved the same way so it does not become vacuous (it now asserts the fixture really has explicit zeros before eliminating). EVIDENCE REQUESTED BY THE BEAD: new unit test diags_prunes_exact_zeros_like_scipy_csr_peer pins BOTH the all-zero case (nnz 0, indptr [0 0 0 0 0 0]) and the mixed [1,0,2,0,3] case (nnz 3, data [1,2,3], indices [0,2,4], indptr [0 1 1 2 2 3]) against the live scipy values, plus an offset-diagonal case and the -0.0/NaN edges. NEGATIVE CONTROL observed: the pre-change tree asserted and passed nnz == 5 on the same all-zero construction. 406 lib + 56 metamorphic tests pass. Noted for follow-up: the existing conformance oracle diff_sparse_diags_kron compares DENSE values only, which is why it never caught this.

title: [CRITICAL] conformance: scipy_special_oracle.py btdtrc lambda uses '1 - betainc(a, b, x)' — catastrophic cancellation for x near 1 returns 0.0 when true value is ~4e-18; symmetry identity betainc(b, a, 1-x) preserves precision
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/python_oracle/scipy_special_oracle.py:182 on 2026-04-22:

    "btdtrc": lambda a, b, x: 1.0 - special.betainc(a, b, x),

Problem: `1 - betainc(a, b, x)` has catastrophic cancellation for x
near 1, where betainc returns values close to 1 and the subtraction
loses all significant digits. Verified with scipy:

    x = 0.999999, a = 2.0, b = 3.0
    1 - betainc(a, b, x)         = 0.0 (catastrophic cancellation)
    betainc(b, a, 1 - x)         = 4.00e-18 (correct via symmetry)

The symmetry identity `btdtrc(a, b, x) = betainc(b, a, 1 - x)` is the
standard precision-preserving formulation for the beta distribution's
complementary CDF. scipy historically shipped btdtrc directly; it was
removed/deprecated in newer scipy versions, but the correct substitution
is the symmetry identity, NOT the naive 1 - betainc formulation.

Impact:

1. Oracle-backed conformance cases with `function: 'btdtrc'` and x close
   to 1 receive oracle values of EXACTLY 0.0 when the true result is
   ~1e-18 or smaller.

2. A fsci-special btdtrc implementation that correctly uses the symmetry
   identity (preserving precision) would return 4e-18 for x=0.999999.
   The comparator reports 'mismatch: expected=0, got=4e-18'. A correct
   Rust impl fails conformance because the oracle is WRONG.

3. A wrong Rust impl that also does `1.0 - betainc(a, b, x)` would
   happen to match the oracle at x=0.999999 (both 0) but that's
   agreement in wrongness, not correctness verification.

Fixture FSCI-P2C-006 has 1 case using function='btdtrc' (per grep).
If that case's x is near 1, it's currently in the wrong-by-wrong bucket.
If x is moderate, precision loss is small but still non-zero.

Same class of issue as m9jp (stirling2 wrong formula) and pqka (optimize
oracle grad/hess mismatch) -- a hand-rolled oracle formula that's
mathematically incorrect or precision-lossy versus scipy's canonical
implementation.

Fix:

    "btdtrc": lambda a, b, x: special.betainc(b, a, 1.0 - x),

Verification after fix (sample):
    x=0.999999, a=2, b=3: 4.00e-18 (both impls now)
    x=0.9999, a=2, b=3: 4.00e-12 (both impls now)

Related: m9jp (stirling2 wrong formula, closed), pqka (optimize grad
mismatch, open), r575 (special contract table missing), eecf2a2 /
768ab7e / 77eb9ae (parallel agent's recent oracle expansion that
landed this lambda).
close_reason: Completed

title: [HIGH] fsci-cluster: silhouette/calinski_harabasz/davies_bouldin/adjusted_rand/normalized_mutual_info/homogeneity all silently return 0.0 on length mismatch AND adversarial label magnitudes (e.g., [0, 1_000_000_000]) trigger OOM on the contingency table — sklearn raises ValueError; we return 'random agreement' numerically
description:
Review of crates/fsci-cluster/src/lib.rs on 2026-04-22.

Seven public cluster-evaluation metrics silently fail-open on malformed input
by returning 0.0 (or empty Vec) instead of a typed error. Each returns f64 or
Vec<f64> directly (not Result), so the caller cannot distinguish 'this metric
computed a legitimate 0.0' from 'I silently dropped your invalid request.'

Sites:

    silhouette_score       (line 885)  if n < 2 || labels.len() != n { return 0.0; }
    calinski_harabasz_score(line ~947)  same pattern
    davies_bouldin_score   (line ~1009) same pattern
    adjusted_rand_score    (line 1072) if n != labels_pred.len() || n < 2 { return 0.0; }
    normalized_mutual_info (line 1122) same pattern with n == 0
    homogeneity_score      (line ~1179) same pattern
    (plus a variant in elbow_inertias that returns vec![0.0; n])

Each of these conflates multiple semantically-distinct error conditions into a
single '0.0' return:

1. Length mismatch between labels_true and labels_pred  -- INVALID INPUT (should error)
2. n < 2 or n == 0                                       -- EDGE CASE (metric undefined or trivially 1.0)
3. labels contains only one unique value                 -- EDGE CASE (metric undefined)

scipy/sklearn parity for these conditions:

    sklearn.metrics.adjusted_rand_score(labels_true=[0,1], labels_pred=[0])
    -> raises ValueError: Found input variables with inconsistent numbers of samples: [2, 1]

    sklearn.metrics.silhouette_score(X, labels_with_1_cluster)
    -> raises ValueError: Number of labels is 1. Valid values are 2 to n_samples - 1

    sklearn.metrics.adjusted_rand_score([0], [0])
    -> returns 1.0 (trivially perfect)

So fsci-cluster departs from both scipy and sklearn in two ways:
- Returns 0.0 instead of erroring on length mismatch (fail-open)
- Returns 0.0 instead of 1.0 for trivial n=1 case (returns wrong answer)
- 0.0 in ARI context means 'random agreement', so a test with typo'd labels
  lengths gets a nonsensical 'random' verdict with no indication of the bug.

Additional concerns in adjusted_rand_score / normalized_mutual_info:

- Line 1076-1077, 1126-1127: k1 = max(labels_true) + 1. Allocates a
  contingency table of size k1 * k2. Adversarial labels (e.g., [0, 1_000_000_000])
  trigger a 1e9 x 1e9 allocation -> OOM. No sanity check on label magnitude.

- Line 1076: uses .unwrap_or(0) after .max(), so an empty labels slice
  (unreachable here due to n < 2 check earlier but defensively visible)
  would produce k=1. Shallow assumption that labels cover a dense integer
  range 0..k.

Fix:

1. Change return type to Result<f64, ClusterError> (or Option<f64>) for all
   evaluation metrics. Return Err(ClusterError::InvalidArgument) on length
   mismatch. Return Err on single-cluster input (where metric undefined). Return
   Ok(1.0) for trivial n<=1 cases.

2. Add a bounded label-range check: iff max(labels) > some_reasonable_bound *
   n, error instead of allocating OOM. E.g., require max(labels) < 10 * n.

3. Alternatively, dense-rename labels (map each unique label to 0..k) before
   constructing the contingency table, removing the max-label OOM risk.

4. Add regression tests:
    ari_length_mismatch  -> must return Err (currently returns 0.0)
    ari_trivial_n1       -> must return 1.0 (currently returns 0.0)
    ari_adversarial_label_1e9 -> must Err or handle gracefully (currently OOM)

Related: s9tt (SignalError stringly-typed, 201 sites), wofb (StatsError 1
variant), gtcn (fsci-runtime assert_close family). This is the third crate
in the 'fail-open + weak error taxonomy' audit: ClusterError has 3 variants
but the metric functions don't use them at all (they return f64 directly).

The underlying theme: MetricError as a distinct category doesn't exist;
existing ClusterError variants aren't wired through the metric functions.
close_reason: Made cluster metric invalid inputs typed errors and dense-mapped contingency labels

title: Run the bandwidth-dominant CG phase in mixed precision
description: Change: execute the memory-bandwidth-dominant early CG iterations with f32 matrix/vector storage and f64 scalar reductions, then hand off to the existing f64 solver before final convergence so the true f64 residual contract remains authoritative. Hotspot: large CG saturates bandwidth at nine workers and streams matrix plus vector state 494 times. EV: impact 5 * confidence 3 * reuse 5 / effort 4 * friction 1 = 18.75, priority A. Adoption: large persistent CG only, gated by finite f32 representability; serial and full-f64 paths remain fallbacks. Budget: bounded f32 phase ending at a conservative residual floor or fixed iteration fraction; on stagnation, non-finite values, or insufficient progress, hand off immediately to f64. Expected loss: extra iterations or conversion can erase bandwidth gain; keep only with exact f64 true residual and material wall-time improvement. Calibration: live SciPy same invocation plus same-ELF full-f64 control. Isomorphism: iteration order and rounding change, so tolerance and solution agreement are proof obligations rather than bit identity. Target: at least 1.10x over full-f64 persistent CG, live-SciPy decided win, true residual at most 1.25 times rtol, solution relative L2 at most 0.05. Risk: f32 stagnation on ill-conditioned systems; counter with f64 handoff before declaring convergence. Repro: exact ELF, affinity, worker count, iterations, true residual, timing, and bootstrap CI. Rollback: disable mixed phase and use existing f64 persistent CG. Comparator: current f64 persistent CG and live SciPy.
close_reason: Rejected: mixed phase took 438.57 ms versus 443.57 ms for same-ELF f64 control (1.01x), while restart increased iterations from 494 to 559.

title: fsci-signal: normalize_filter silently propagates NaN/Inf in denominator
description: REVIEW MODE finding cross-reviewing the just-shipped normalize_filter (97630a4). The leading-zero scan uses v != 0.0 which is true for NaN, so first_nonzero returns the index of the first NaN; leading = NaN propagates through a_norm and b_norm producing all-NaN vectors with Ok status. Inf in a similarly produces NaN/0. Pre-fix: normalize_filter([1.0], [1.0, f64::NAN]) returns Ok with NaN-laden vectors. Should return a typed SignalError::InvalidArgument naming the failure. Fix: validate a contains only finite values up-front, before the scan.
close_reason: Added up-front non-finite guard to normalize_filter (just shipped 97630a4): pre-fix the leading-zero scan v != 0.0 returned true for NaN, so a leading NaN became the divisor and propagated NaN through both b_norm and a_norm with Ok status. Same for Inf. Now both a and b are validated for finite values and rejected with SignalError::InvalidArgument naming the offending field. Regression test normalize_filter_rejects_nonfinite_coefficients exercises 6 invalid combinations: NaN-mid-a, NaN-first-a, Inf-in-a, neg-Inf-first-a, NaN-in-b, Inf-in-b. fsci-signal --lib: 408 → 409 passing.

title: rch: stop ignored fsci-special bin entrypoints from breaking strict-remote sync
description: Strict-remote routing to hz2 failed closed with RCH-E410 because Cargo discovers crates/fsci-special/src/bin/check_erfcx_simd.rs locally while .gitignore excludes the entire src/bin directory, so the source entrypoint is absent on a fresh worker. hz1/ovh-a only succeed because stale copies happen to exist. Decide which bin entrypoints are real and track them, or remove their Cargo discovery with explicit owner permission; also format retained bins. Acceptance: a clean Rust worker receives every Cargo source entrypoint through RCH sync and cargo fmt --all -- --check does not see ignored scratch binaries. Do not delete any file without explicit owner permission.
close_reason:
RESOLVED at HEAD — both acceptance criteria met, verified directly. But the resolution has a side effect I am recording rather than closing over, because it breaks a sibling bead's reproduce command.

THE FAILURE MODE CANNOT RECUR. The bead describes RCH-E410 arising because "Cargo discovers crates/fsci-special/src/bin/check_erfcx_simd.rs locally while .gitignore excludes the entire src/bin directory, so the source entrypoint is absent on a fresh worker." At HEAD, crates/fsci-special/Cargo.toml line 5 sets autobins = false and the file declares no [[bin]] sections. Measured with cargo metadata: fsci-special discovers 0 bin targets. Cargo cannot discover check_erfcx_simd.rs, so there is no entrypoint to go missing on a fresh worker.

That is one of the two dispositions the bead sanctioned ("Decide which bin entrypoints are real and track them, or remove their Cargo discovery"). No file was deleted: 122 scratch files remain on disk in that directory, untracked and ignored, exactly as the bead's final line requires.

ACCEPTANCE 1 — "a clean Rust worker receives every Cargo source entrypoint through RCH sync":
  RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec -- cargo check -p fsci-special --all-targets
  -> Finished, no errors, no RCH-E410.
Every discoverable target (lib, the special_bench bench, tests) builds on a
remote worker under strict routing.

ACCEPTANCE 2 — "cargo fmt --all -- --check does not see ignored scratch binaries":
  cargo fmt --all -- --check  ->  exit 0, zero output lines.
The 122 ignored scratch bins are invisible to the formatter because they are not
Cargo targets.

THE SIDE EFFECT, and it matters. Exactly ONE file in that ignored directory is tracked in git: crates/fsci-special/src/bin/perf_cdf.rs. Someone force-added it, presumably because it is a real perf entrypoint rather than scratch. But autobins = false and no [[bin]] entry means it is NOT a Cargo target either:

  cargo check -p fsci-special --bin perf_cdf
  -> error: no bin target named `perf_cdf` in `fsci-special` package

So perf_cdf.rs is in the worst of both states: tracked as if real, undiscoverable as if scratch. It syncs to workers and can never be built there.

CONSEQUENCE FOR frankenscipy-e2ve2: that bead's reproduce command is
  ... cargo clippy -j2 --profile release-perf -p fsci-special --bin perf_cdf
      --features ndtri-isafloor-bench --no-deps -- -D warnings
which cannot run at HEAD for the reason above. When I triaged e2ve2 in SC74 I
substituted --lib and said so, calling the 323 errors "the library floor"; I did
not then know the original command was unrunnable rather than merely narrower.
Posting this to e2ve2 as well.

RECOMMENDED FOLLOW-UP (not done here, since it is an owner call about which
entrypoints are real): give perf_cdf.rs an explicit [[bin]] entry with a path, so
the one tracked entrypoint is buildable and e2ve2's gate becomes runnable —
without re-enabling autobins and re-exposing the other 121 scratch files. That is
the "decide which bin entrypoints are real and track them" half of this bead's
own instruction, applied to the single file that was already tracked.

BISPLREP PORT GROUNDWORK (cc, 2026-06-16) — turnkey for a focused turn.

SOURCES (curl'd from scipy v1.10.1 scipy/interpolate/fitpack/, sizes):
  surfit.f 414  fpsurf.f 681  fprank.f 237  fpback.f 32  fpdisc.f 44

Re-fetch any with: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/scipy/scipy/v1.10.1/scipy/interpolate/fitpack/<name>.f
(curl-to-disk + `sed -n A,Bp` is the way — WebFetch truncates files >~a few k lines.)

ARCHITECTURE: bisplrep(x,y,z,...) -> surfit (the iopt/s driver + workspace setup)
  -> fpsurf (the heavy 681-line core: part1 = adaptive knot determination by
     least-squares spline + add knots until fp<=s, with x/y axis swap to minimize
     bandwidth; part2 = smoothing-spline iteration on p via fprati root-find).
  fpsurf calls: fpback (back-subst), fpbspl (B-spline basis), fpgivs/fprota
  (Givens), fpdisc (discontinuity jumps for the smoothing penalty), fporde (order
  data points into panels), fprank (rank-deficient LSQ solve, 237 lines).

WHAT FSCI ALREADY HAS: fpknot (knot insertion helper). The 1-D FITPACK family
(splrep/splev/make_splrep/splprep/make_splprep) is COMPLETE, so the de Boor
basis (fpbspl), fpback, fpgivs/fprota equivalents very likely exist inline in
crates/fsci-interpolate/src — GREP and reuse before re-porting. fsci also has
SmoothBivariateSpline but with HEURISTIC knot placement (not fpsurf adaptive),
so its tck != scipy except the no-interior-knot (large-s) case. Full parity
REQUIRES the fpsurf adaptive knot loop + fprank.

ORACLE: scipy.special bisplrep IS reliable here (unlike spheroidal rad2) — verify
tck (tx,ty,c) + bisplev(xi,yi,tck) values to ~1e-6. bisplev is ALREADY shipped
on origin/main (orthopoly note: another agent added it). So this bead is really
just bisplrep (the fit).

PLAN: (1) grep fsci-interpolate for existing fpbspl/fpback/fpgivs/fprota; reuse.
(2) port fpdisc, fporde, fprank, fprpsp (small). (3) port fpsurf (the big one) +
surfit driver faithfully, 1-based->Rust. (4) bisplrep public fn returning
(tx,ty,c,kx,ky). (5) verify vs scipy bisplrep on smooth scattered data at a few
s values incl s=0 (interpolating) and s>0 (smoothing). EST: multi-hour, like the
rad2 port (~1300 Fortran lines). Probe bins under fsci-interpolate/src/bin may be
gitignored (they are in fsci-special) — check before relying on committing one.

title: [HIGH] conformance: NO case/fixture struct uses #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] — fixture typos (e.g., 'modee' instead of 'mode') are silently dropped, unknown fields accepted in all 13 families
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/ on 2026-04-22:

grep -rE 'deny_unknown_fields' crates/ returns ZERO hits. No case struct
across any family has #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]. This is serde's
default behavior: unknown fields during deserialization are silently
ignored.

Concrete implications:

1. Typos in fixture field names become no-ops. Examples:
     {'case_id': 'x', 'modee': 'Hardened', ...}  -- 'modee' ignored, mode
       defaults to Strict (or Default RuntimeMode), case runs in wrong mode.
     {'atol': 1e-10, 'rtol_': 1e-8}              -- 'rtol_' ignored,
       rtol defaults to configured fallback.
     {'expected': {'kind': 'scalar', 'vaIue': 3.14}}  -- 'vaIue' (capital
       I instead of lowercase l) silently dropped; value becomes None.

2. Copy-paste between fixture families accepts stray fields. An optimize
   case accidentally carrying spatial's 'dual_points' field deserializes
   successfully.

3. Version skew is silent: older readers accept newer schema's new
   fields and ignore them. Fine for backwards-compat, but masks
   intentional field additions.

Compounds with several prior beads:
- vh06 (schema_validation.rs never loads fixtures): no schema check
  would catch typos either, so BOTH defense layers are missing.
- ubkg (family string match): typo in 'mode' compounds with typo in
  'family' -- neither is caught at deserialization.
- 95ld (mode: String ignored): even without typo, 'Hardened' is no-op
  for 5 families. Combined with this, mode='Hardened' AND mode='Hardend'
  have IDENTICAL (zero) effect on Rust behavior for cluster/spatial/
  signal/stats/integrate.

Running sample: today, grep shows NO fixtures with unknown fields (all
13 FSCI-P2C-*.json conform to their family's canonical schema). But the
runtime contract allows future typos to slip through silently, which is
why fail-closed projects typically enforce deny_unknown_fields.

Fix:
1. Add #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] to every case struct:
     #[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
     #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]
     pub struct ClusterCase { ... }
   Same for SpatialCase, SignalCase, StatsCase, IntegrateCase,
   SpecialCase, LinalgCase, OptimizeCase, FftCase, ArrayApiCase,
   SparseCase, CaspCase, ValidateTolCase.
2. Add the attribute to every nested ExpectedOutcome struct.
3. Run cargo test --workspace; any fixture that was relying on a
   typo'd field being ignored will now fail at parse time -- fixable.
4. Optional: fixture regen tooling can start emitting explicit
   'schema_version' and runner can gate on version compatibility.

Related: vh06 (no fixture schema validation), ubkg (family substring
match), 95ld (mode String ignored), utus (P2C-016 schema divergence),
c7b4 (docstring inaccuracy).
close_reason: Added #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] to all 22 Case/PacketFixture structs in fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs. Typos like "modee" instead of "mode" or "vaIue" instead of "value" now fail fixture deserialization with a clear serde error rather than silently dropping the field. All family packet-runner tests pass except the pre-existing stats_packet_runner_passes failure (shapiro-wilk bug, orthogonal to this change).

title: [perf] Reuse rcond sign-vector buffers
description: Profile-backed after frankenscipy-whhck: remote hyperfine shows lu_factor 512 3 42 at 47.7 ms while lu_solve 512 3 42 remains 65.0 ms, isolating ~17 ms of post-factorization solve/rcond overhead. In fast_rcond_from_lu, each estimator iteration allocates sign_x via x.map(...) and sign_w via w.map(...). Lever: allocate sign vectors once and refill them in storage order each iteration, preserving sign rule, LU solve order, convergence thresholds, floating-point arithmetic, and warning/rcond behavior. title: [code-review] [HIGH] fsci-special lambertw_scalar(+inf) returns NaN instead of +inf
description: Review of dfa90ac (fix(fsci-special): lambertw_scalar initial guess for x < e) found a missed non-finite boundary. title: fsci-stats: port scipy.stats.boltzmann (truncated geometric)
description: Port scipy.stats.boltzmann as Boltzmann struct (truncated geometric, discrete). Two parameters lambda > 0 and N (positive integer). Support k = 0, 1, ..., N-1. Closed forms: pmf(k) = (1-e^(-lambda)) * e^(-lambda*k) / (1-e^(-lambda*N)); cdf(k) = (1-e^(-lambda*(k+1))) / (1-e^(-lambda*N)). Mean has closed form via geometric-series differentiation. Add adjacent to existing Poisson/Geometric ports. 3 anchor tests at scipy 1.17.1 tol 1e-12: pmf/cdf at 5 (lambda, N, k) anchors; ppf at 3 anchor points; cdf monotone within support.
close_reason: Ported scipy.stats.boltzmann as Boltzmann struct (truncated geometric, discrete). Two parameters lambda > 0 and N (positive integer u32). Support k in {0, 1, ..., N-1}. All formulas closed-form: pmf(k) = (1-e^(-lambda)) * e^(-lambda*k) / (1-e^(-lambda*N)); cdf(k) = (1-e^(-lambda*(k+1))) / (1-e^(-lambda*N)). Mean uses canonical 1/(e^lambda - 1) - N/(e^(lambda*N) - 1). Var via direct sum (N is bounded by definition). Used numerically-stable expm1 throughout to avoid catastrophic cancellation when lambda is small. 3 tests at scipy 1.17.1 tol 1e-12: pmf/cdf at 5 (lambda, N, k) anchors; pmf normalisation across 5 (lambda, N) tuples + cdf(N-1)=1 + pmf(N)=0 boundary; geometric limit metamorphic (Boltzmann(lambda, large_N).pmf approaches (1-e^(-lambda)) * e^(-lambda*k) which matches a shifted geometric distribution with p = 1-e^(-lambda)). fsci-stats --lib: 1116 -> 1119.

description:

workspace clippy command and has to hand-narrow to --lib, which is how a real
lint in a neighbouring target goes unnoticed.

lints are ordinary dead-code/unused-import and can just be cleaned.

comments.text:
RubyBeacon 2026-08-09, commit 2c6e53b66: CAUSE 1 CLEARED, cause 2 open. Bead stays open.

CAUSE 1 DONE. cargo clippy -p fsci-sparse --all-targets -- -D warnings now FINISHES CLEAN. It previously failed with the 8 errors this bead lists, across profile_gmres_arnoldi, perf_spsolve and the lib test target.

Fixes, each chosen to match what the lint actually asks:
- spsolve_triangular: gated the import to match its only use site, a function behind the sparse-incumbent-bench feature, rather than dropping it.
- laplacian_3d_cubic / laplacian_3d_cuboid: NOT DELETED. Their comment says they exist for the profile-first tensor campaign, i.e. they are fixture specs. Deleting a spec to silence dead_code is the exact mistake recorded against iit9c, so they carry an allow(dead_code) with the reason inline.
- type_complexity in profile_gmres_arnoldi and construct.rs: named type definitions (ArnoldiKernel, DiagsCase), which is the fix the lint requests, not an allow.
- needless_range_loop, 5 sites (linalg 4, ops 1): rewritten to zip/enumerate, preserving the index variables the assertion messages interpolate.
- The normalized-laplacian scaling loop in linalg.rs is LIBRARY code, not test code. The range-over-indptr form indexing the indices array became a direct slice iteration over that same range, an exactly equivalent transformation.
- ops.rs CSC reconstruction: kept the index form under a SCOPED allow WITH a written reason. That loop walks columns and scatters into a row-major buffer where the row index comes from the indices array and varies per entry, so there is no row iterator to borrow and an iterator rewrite would obscure the access pattern. One documented suppression, not a blanket allow.

A NINTH ERROR WAS HIDDEN BEHIND THE EIGHT. Once they stopped aborting the build, benches/sparse_bench.rs:750 surfaced an unnecessary usize-to-usize cast. Fixed. Worth knowing for the sibling beads (iit9c, wv42a, e2ve2, 023vy, 9fq10): their error counts are LOWER BOUNDS, because compilation stops at the first failing target and later targets are never linted.

EVIDENCE: clippy --all-targets -D warnings finishes with no errors. cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib gives 426 passed, 0 failed, 4 ignored, identical to before the edits -- which is what makes the loop rewrites safe to believe rather than merely plausible. cargo fmt --check exit 0.

CAUSE 2 UNTOUCHED, deliberately. The all-features arm still fails E0432 on GMRES_BATCH_FORCE_SEQUENTIAL, the LGMRES/QMR batch controls, ITERATIVE_BATCH_LAST_WORKERS and the CG controls. That is the same family as frankenscipy-vacuous-perf-toggles-qcuyy: perf harnesses driving levers that were removed. Resolving it means either restoring the implementations (qcuyy/ct8n2 work, and restoring bare statics that nothing reads would recreate the vacuous-toggle defect fixed earlier in 2e6d3a7e3) or deleting harness code. Neither is a lint fix, so it should not be done under a lint bead.

title: defect: ndimage order-3 reflect/nearest spline interpolation only ~1e-5 accurate vs scipy
description:
fsci_ndimage geometric transforms (affine_transform, rotate, shift, zoom, map_coordinates) with spline order>=2 and mode in {Reflect, Nearest} route through prefilter_spline_coefficients -> pad_array_mode + spline_coefficients_for_line (make_interp_spline, de Boor knot basis), evaluated by sample_interpolated via eval_bspline_basis_all. This path diverges from scipy.ndimage.

INVESTIGATION (probed affine_transform 5x5 vs scipy, orders 2-5):
- order=3 nearest: ~1e-6 abs, boundary-padding-limited. The padded line uses not-a-knot end conditions; the mismatch vs scipy's mode-specific spline boundary contaminates the interior by O(pole^PAD). Raising SPLINE_NEAREST_PAD 12->~24 drops it below 1e-12, but make_interp_spline is superlinear in line length (PAD=48 made a small test take 11s) so large PAD is not viable.
- order=3 reflect: ~1e-5 abs, PADDING-INDEPENDENT — a coordinate/offset bug, likely the half-pixel +0.5/-0.5 in map_reflect_coordinate interacting with coord_offsets, not boundary contamination.
- order=2 and order=4 (EVEN orders): structurally broken, ~0.3-1.4 abs error in both Reflect and Nearest — a de Boor even-order knot-placement bug in make_interp_spline/uniform_interpolation_knots.
- order=5: reflect ~2.6e-3; nearest padding-limited.

PROPER FIX: replace the de Boor path with scipy's recursive spline filter (spline_filter1d) — cardinal B-spline coefficients via the order-p poles with per-mode boundary initialization, reconstructed with the cardinal order-p B-spline kernel + a per-mode index fold; the same treatment already applied to Constant/Wrap order=3 (cubic_constant_wrap_coefficients + cardinal eval). Covers orders 2-5. Constant/Wrap order=3 and all order<=1 modes are already bit-exact and unaffected.
close_reason: Fixed: order-3 (cubic) spline interpolation under reflect and nearest is now bit-exact vs scipy. Root cause was the de Boor not-a-knot interpolating-spline path (pad-12 + make_interp_spline), whose end conditions differ from the mode's true boundary. Replaced with: reflect -> cubic_reflect_coefficients, the exact tridiagonal solve with the half-sample-reflect boundary (c[-1]=c[0], stencil (5/6,1/6) at the ends) = the exact infinite-reflect cubic spline (no truncated initial-condition sum); nearest -> edge-pad then the same exact reflect prefilter (matching scipy's nearest = edge-pad + reflect prefilter). sample_interpolated reconstructs with the cardinal cubic B-spline, folding support taps via half-sample mirror (reflect) / clamp (nearest). Golden test verifies <1e-12 vs scipy.ndimage.shift/affine_transform (observed ~1e-15). Orders 2/4/5 reflect/nearest tracked in the new follow-up bead.

title: fsci-stats: kstatvar(data, 2) uses normal-asymptotic formula instead of scipy's unbiased estimator
description:
fsci kstatvar at lib.rs:15197 returns 2*k2²/(n-1), labelled 'for normal' in the source comment. scipy.stats.kstatvar uses the general unbiased variance-of-k2 estimator:
  var(k_2) = (2 * N * k_2² + (N-1) * k_4) / (N * (N+1))
that doesn't assume normality.

REPLICATION (data=[1..10]):
  fsci  kstatvar(data, 2) = 18.6728
  scipy kstatvar(data, 2) = 7.0277
  diff = 11.65

n=1 path matches (var(k1) = k2/n) on all fixtures.

FIX: at lib.rs:15197, change the n=2 branch to:
  if nn < 4.0 { return f64::NAN; }
  let k4 = kstat(&filtered, 4);
  (2.0 * nn * k2 * k2 + (nn - 1.0) * k4) / (nn * (nn + 1.0))
notes: Fixed in same tick. Replaced normal-asymptotic 2*k2²/(N-1) with scipy's general unbiased estimator (2*N*k2² + (N-1)*k4)/(N*(N+1)) at lib.rs:15197+. fsci-stats kstatvar_variance_of_mean unit test still passes; diff_stats_kstat.rs (18 cases including kstatvar n=2 across 3 datasets) ships green at 1e-12 abs.

title: GAP: fsci-linalg qr_delete / qr_insert / qr_multiply / qr_update (0/4 → 4/4)
description:
Per fgxx audit, fsci-linalg lacks all four QR-update primitives:
qr_delete, qr_insert, qr_multiply, qr_update. These are essential for
incremental least-squares (online regression, Kalman filter recursive
update, recursive RLS).

Scope:
- Implement qr_delete(Q, R, k) — delete row k, return updated (Q', R').
- Implement qr_insert(Q, R, u, k) — insert row u at position k.
- Implement qr_multiply(Q, R, c) — apply Q to a vector / matrix.
- Implement qr_update(Q, R, u, v) — rank-1 update: A + u·vᵀ.

All four can sit on top of the existing qr() decomposition. Reference
algorithms: Daniel/Gragg/Kaufman/Stewart "Reorthogonalization and
stable algorithms for updating the Gram-Schmidt QR factorization"
(1976) — same approach scipy uses.

Acceptance:
- Public functions in fsci_linalg with rustdoc that links the

title: fsci-odr cov_beta/sd_beta underestimated: covariance_from_jacobian ignores beta-delta coupling
description:
fsci-odr/src/lib.rs::covariance_from_jacobian (around line ~1060-1090, called from run() at line 500) builds the parameter covariance from ONLY the first beta_len columns of the least-squares Jacobian:

  normal = sum_rows J[:, :beta_len]^T J[:, :beta_len]   (i.e. J_beta^T J_beta)
  cov_beta = res_var * inv(normal)
  sd_beta[i] = sqrt(cov_beta[i][i])

This drops the delta (x-correction) columns of the Jacobian, so it ignores the beta-delta coupling. ODRPACK/scipy.odr compute cov_beta as the beta-block of the inverse of the FULL weighted normal matrix, which is the inverse of the Schur complement
  S = J_beta^T J_beta - J_beta^T J_delta (J_delta^T J_delta)^-1 J_delta^T J_beta
(marginalizing out delta). Because S <= J_beta^T J_beta, the true cov_beta is LARGER, so fsci-odr UNDERESTIMATES the reported standard errors.

VERIFIED against scipy 1.17.1 (linear model y=B0*x+B1, x=0..6):
- scipy out.cov_beta diag = [0.07142, 0.92812]
- beta-only (X^T X)^-1 diag (what fsci computes) = [0.03571, 0.46434]
- ratio = 2.000  -> fsci sd_beta is ~sqrt(2)x too small for equal weights.
The ratio is STRUCTURAL, not a constant: with Data(we=1, wd=4) scipy/beta-only ratio becomes ~1.249. So it depends on weights + Jacobian coupling, confirming the missing Schur complement.

res_var itself (line 498: dof = n - p) is CORRECT (verified: scipy res_var = sum_square/(n-p), n=#observations). The bug is purely in the covariance/standard-error computation.

FIX SKETCH: form the full normal matrix from all Jacobian columns (beta + free delta), invert (or solve), and extract the upper-left beta_len x beta_len block; multiply by res_var. Equivalent to computing the Schur complement over the delta block. Ensure weights (we/wd) are reflected (they already are if result.jac is the weighted-residual Jacobian).

NOTE: there are currently NO ODR conformance tests (crates/fsci-conformance/tests has no diff_odr_*). Add a diff_odr harness asserting sd_beta/cov_beta against scipy.odr for explicit + implicit + weighted models as part of the fix.

Found in review-mode by cc-frankenscipy/OliveSnow 2026-06-01.
close_reason: Fixed covariance extraction to invert the full beta/delta normal matrix and added scipy.odr covariance conformance coverage

title: [stats] linregress lacks an exact scipy slope/intercept/rvalue/pvalue/stderr golden test
close_reason:
Closed 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey). Genuine gap, not a duplicate: linregress's
inference fields had no scipy golden anywhere on data with real scatter.

DEDUP VERIFICATION -- ten linregress tests exist and none pins the ask:
  - linregress_perfect_line and linregress_negative_slope fit EXACT lines
    (y = 2x+3, y = -1.5x+10). slope, intercept and rvalue are then true by
    construction rather than by the estimator being right; stderr is asserted
    only as < 1e-10 and pvalue only as < 1e-70. A perfect fit constrains the
    stderr and p-value formulas almost not at all.
  - linregress_with_noise uses INEQUALITIES throughout: |slope-3| < 0.01,
    rvalue > 0.999, pvalue < 1e-10. Nothing pinned.
  - linregress_too_few_points, linregress_constant_x,
    linregress_length_two_matches_scipy_inference_fields and
    linregress_constant_y_matches_scipy_undefined_inference all cover DEGENERATE
    inputs (n=1, n=2, constant x, constant y).
  - the three linregress_ci_* tests assert containment/width properties.
So stderr, intercept_stderr and pvalue had never been checked against a scipy
value on an ordinary regression.

ADDED: linregress_all_fields_match_exact_scipy_on_scattered_data. Eight points
with genuine residuals -- not an exact line, and not the alternating +/-0.01
perturbation the noise test uses -- so every field is determined by the
estimator rather than by the input's structure. All SIX returned fields pinned
to scipy 1.17.1 at 1e-12 RELATIVE (the values span 2e-5 to 1.4, so a single
absolute tolerance would be meaningless at one end):
    slope             1.094047619047619
    intercept         1.3833333333333342
    rvalue            0.9793974519122625
    pvalue            2.1526223055628845e-05
    stderr            0.09209342014915883
    intercept_stderr  0.385254416728045

Plus a dof discriminator: the p-value must be a two-sided t tail on n-2 = 6
degrees of freedom. t = slope/stderr = 11.879758806607985 gives
2.1526223055628855e-05 on 6 dof but 6.8027120927890005e-06 on 7 -- a factor of
~3.2 apart -- and the test asserts the result is not the n-1 value.

PROCESS NOTE, recorded because it nearly went in wrong: I first wrote that
discriminator with a GUESSED n-1 value (~1.06e-5, "roughly half"). Computing it
showed the real figure is 6.80e-6 and about 3.2x smaller, so both the number and
the characterisation were wrong. The assertion would still have passed, but it
would have been guarding against a number that does not occur -- a live
assertion pointed at nothing. Same class of unverified inference that produced
the incorrect first description of frankenscipy-6ozha. Both figures in the
committed test were computed.

RESULT: fsci PASSES all six fields at 1e-12 relative. No defect.

EVIDENCE via RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 rch exec, with `Compiling fsci-stats`
confirmed in every run log (per frankenscipy-eibro a remote green is not
evidence without it):
  - cargo test -p fsci-stats --lib -> 2071 tests, 2069 passed, 0 failed,
    2 ignored, remote exit=0.
  - TWO-ARM CONTROL: perturbing intercept_stderr by 1e-10 (rel 2.6e-10, above
    the 1e-12 tolerance) FAILS with "linregress intercept_stderr: got
    0.38525441672804284, scipy 0.385254416828045 (rel 2.596e-10)". That also
    shows fsci's value agrees with scipy to ~2e-15 relative. Restored.
  - cargo fmt -p fsci-stats -- --check: clean. Diff is one purely additive hunk,
    56 insertions, 0 deletions.

NOT TOUCHED: frankenscipy-3mp6z (linregress edge-case inference fields) remains
open and is a separate concern; this test deliberately uses non-degenerate data
so it neither depends on nor enshrines that behaviour.

title: Route toms748 through checked root evaluator
description: Code-first fallback from empty br ready. optimize::root::toms748 validates options and finite bracket endpoints but evaluates callbacks directly, unlike bisect/brentq/ridder. This can let non-finite callback values leak into sign/interpolation logic instead of using the strict/hardened OptError mapping. close_reason: Already satisfied; verified by source read at close time, not by new code. optimize::root::toms748 constructs RootEvaluator::new(&f, options) and evaluates every point through eval.evaluate(..) -- there is no direct callback invocation anywhere in the function, so non-finite callback values are mapped to OptError::InvalidArgument (Strict) / OptError::NonFiniteInput (Hardened) by the shared evaluator exactly as bisect/brentq/ridder do. Inline coverage exists: crates/fsci-opt/src/root.rs tests::toms748_rejects_non_finite_function_values asserts BOTH mode mappings on f(x) = NaN for x > 0.8 over bracket (0.1, 0.9). title: [parity-gap] non-integer complex jv/iv/kv/yv wrong at large |z| (200-term power series cancels)
description: complex_jv_scalar and complex_iv_scalar use a 200-term ascending power series for all z. For large |z| it truncates before convergence (peak term at k~|z|) and cancels (max term ~e^|z|), so complex jv/iv fail for |z|>~30 and the non-integer kv/yv built from I_+-v/J_+-v inherit it (kv nonint 12/40, yv nonint 7/40 bad on the probe grid). Fix: add the large-|z| Hankel/I asymptotics for complex jv/iv (analogous to the real jv/iv work goaov/4icoi) or Miller-style recurrence; the integer-order K/Y asymptotics already added in cbiky can be reused. Separately, integer yv near the negative-real-axis branch cut (arg~pi) is ~5e-4 off.
close_reason: Fixed in 67e1fad6: complex Hankel J asymptotic (with Re<0 reflection), I via J(iz), direct K asymptotic, gated |z|>max(15,v^2). jv/iv/kv 0/96, yv 1/96 vs scipy 1.17.1 (was 14/12/52/47). Remaining yv point is the integer neg-real-axis branch cut (wan3w).

title: Reuse a persistent Rayon pool across sparse matvec calls
description: Change: route the shared large-CSR matvec kernel through a persistent Rayon worker pool instead of opening a new std scoped team on every call. Hotspot: every GMRES, BiCGSTAB, CGS, eigsh, eigs, svds, and onenormest iteration currently spawns up to nnz-per-128K worker tasks anew; the CG persistent-team keep proved this lifecycle tax is material. EV: impact 5 * confidence 5 * reuse 5 / effort 2 * friction 1 = 62.5, priority A. Adoption: only the existing large-matrix parallel branch; serial thresholds and equal-row chunking stay unchanged. Budget: same nthreads and chunk count; Rayon global pool remains bounded by available parallelism. Expected loss: scheduler overhead or pool oversubscription can erase spawn savings; same-ELF scoped-thread switch is the fallback. Isomorphism: output rows remain disjoint and every row accumulates entries in identical CSR order, so matvec and solver values should be bit-identical. Target: at least 1.10x over per-call scoped workers on a repeated non-CG solver and a decided live-SciPy win with identical iterations and residual. Risk: nested Rayon callers or unexpected global pool size; counter with unchanged serial gate and scoped fallback. Repro: exact ELF, affinity, observed threads, live SciPy identity, iterations, residual, timings, and CI. Rollback: restore scoped branch as default. Comparator: current per-call std scoped team and live SciPy.

title: fsci-conformance: parity_report writer churns committed artifacts on every run
description: write_packet_report_artifacts in crates/fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs:10253 unconditionally writes parity_report.json with a fresh generated_unix_ms timestamp on every test run. Because parity_report.raptorq.json and parity_report.decode_proof.json are derived from the report bytes (hash + raptorq encoding of report_bytes), the timestamp churn cascades to all three sibling artifacts. Result: every test run modifies 3 committed files per packet, forcing periodic 'refresh parity reports' churn commits with no semantic content (8+ such commits in git log: 3e91c41, d9ec190, 66a1ab1, cf612d9, e83f039, a993042, ca44b8b, f78934a). Fix: make writer content-stable — if the existing on-disk parity_report.json deserializes and matches the new report modulo generated_unix_ms, reuse the on-disk bytes verbatim (preserves the old timestamp). Otherwise write fresh.
close_reason: Fixed parity_report writer churn in crates/fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs. write_packet_report_artifacts now reads the existing parity_report.json and parity_report.decode_proof.json before writing — if the only difference vs. the new value is the volatile timestamp (generated_unix_ms / ts_unix_ms), the on-disk bytes are reused verbatim. Because parity_report.raptorq.json is hash-derived from the report bytes, preserving them transitively stabilises the sidecar too. New regression test write_parity_artifacts_is_byte_stable_modulo_generated_unix_ms (1) writes report with ts=1000, captures bytes for all three artifacts, (2) writes same content with ts=2000 — asserts all three byte-identical, (3) writes content-changed report with ts=3000 — asserts parity_report.json changes. fsci-conformance --lib: 176 → 177 passing.

title: [parity-gap] owens_t(h,a) a>1 36% off: fixed 10-point GL misses peaked integrand
description: owens_t_scalar integrated T(h,a)=(1/2pi) int_0^a exp(-h^2(1+t^2)/2)/(1+t^2) dt with a FIXED 10-point Gauss-Legendre rule over [0,a]. For a>1 the integrand is sharply peaked near t=0 and 10 nodes miss it: owens_t(1,100) was 36% off (0.0508 vs 0.0793). Large h also lost ~0.7% to cancellation (owens_t(8,3)). Fix: reduce to h>=0,a>=0 via even-in-h/odd-in-a symmetry, then for a>1 apply Owen reflection T(h,a)=0.5 Phi(-h)+0.5 Phi(-ah)-Phi(-h)Phi(-ah)-T(ah,1/a) (1/a<1 lands in the accurate GL branch); the constant uses complementary Phi(-x) to avoid cancellation when Phi approx 1. Verified vs scipy 1.17.1: worst rel now ~5e-9 at owens_t(10,0.5) where the value is 4e-24 (absolutely negligible); all moderate cases <1e-13.
close_reason: Fixed: Owen reflection for a>1 (maps to 1/a<1 GL branch) + stable Phi(-x) constant + symmetry reduction. owens_t(1,100) 36% off -> ~3e-16; all moderate cases <1e-13. Committed a0b1df03.

title: fsci_integrate::cumulative_simpson diverges from scipy on higher-order / non-uniform inputs
description: The fsci_integrate::cumulative_simpson docstring claims to match scipy.integrate.cumulative_simpson for 1-D sampled data. However a direct comparison shows large divergence on non-quadratic integrands and on non-uniform grids: e.g., y=x^3+2x on x=[0,0.2,0.5,1.1,1.4,2.0,2.7,3.5] produces a max-abs diff of ~0.1 vs scipy; y=sin(x) on uniform pi-grid n=11 shows ~7e-4; y=exp(-x) on a non-uniform 9-grid shows ~1.3e-3. The fsci impl uses left/right interval splitting via local quadratics, but scipy uses a different windowing scheme. Probe via /tmp/cumsimp_compare.py — scipy itself is off from the exact cubic by tens of percent, confirming the schemes themselves differ. Either fix fsci to match scipy or amend the docstring + add an explicit semantics note. The conformance harness diff_integrate_cumulative_simpson is currently scoped to constant/linear/quadratic/two-point/three-point cases where Simpson is exact, so both agree by construction — broader parity is gated on resolving this.
close_reason: done

title: [MEDIUM] determinism: fsci-stats + fsci-opt use rand::rng() (thread-local, non-deterministic) in both TESTS (5 sites in fsci-stats) and PRODUCTION (2 sites in fsci-opt); tests are flaky and production rvs/optimize is non-reproducible without explicit seed
description:
Review of crates/fsci-* for rand::rng() (thread-local RNG) usage on 2026-04-22:

grep 'rand::rng()' results:
    crates/fsci-opt/src/lib.rs:1293  (production differential_evolution)
    crates/fsci-opt/src/lib.rs:1533  (production basinhopping or dual_annealing)
    crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:18653  (test: multivariate_normal_rvs_tracks_mean)
    crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:18688  (test: dirichlet_rvs_sum_to_one)
    crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:19633  (test: rvs_normal_sample_mean)
    crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:19645  (test: rvs_uniform_bounds)
    crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:19656  (test: rvs_exponential_positive)

Two classes of issue:

1. PRODUCTION non-determinism in fsci-opt (covered by 9n5j):
   When seed=None, differential_evolution + basinhopping + dual_annealing
   use rand::rng() thread-local. Stochastic optimizers produce DIFFERENT
   global minima across runs. Any consumer caching results or using them
   downstream gets non-reproducible behavior.

2. FLAKY TESTS in fsci-stats (5 test sites):
   Each test generates N samples using rand::rng() and asserts statistical
   properties (mean close to expected, samples in range, etc.).
   multivariate_normal_rvs_tracks_mean at line 18651 asserts:
       |empirical_mean - true_mean| < 0.08
   For 4000 samples from Normal(0, 1), std of sample mean ≈ 0.0158.
   Tolerance 0.08 is ≈ 5 sigma. Failure rate per axis ~6e-7, combined
   across 2 axes ~1.2e-6. Over thousands of CI runs, occasional false
   failures accumulate.

   dirichlet_rvs_sum_to_one at line 18688: tighter assertion
   (sum should be exactly 1 within 1e-10). This is an invariant of the
   algorithm (normalized gamma), not a statistical property -- should
   pass every time. OK in practice.

   rvs_normal_sample_mean at 19633: sample 1000 values, assert mean
   close to 0 within 0.1. std of mean = 1/sqrt(1000) ≈ 0.032. Tolerance
   0.1 ≈ 3 sigma. Failure rate ~0.27%. EXCEEDS quality_gates.toml
   max_flake_rate = 0.001 = 0.1%.

   rvs_uniform_bounds at 19645: assert samples are in [a, b]. Bounded
   by construction -- deterministic invariant. OK.

   rvs_exponential_positive at 19656: assert samples >= 0. Bounded
   invariant. OK.

Issues:
- 2 of 5 stats tests have statistical tolerances that will occasionally
  flake. Quality_gates declares max_flake_rate 0.001 but rvs_normal
  test has ~0.003 failure rate.
- Flake rate across all CI runs: at least 2 test cases that can fail
  by random chance, each with non-trivial probability.

Fix:
1. TESTS: replace rand::rng() with seeded StdRng::seed_from_u64(42)
   for deterministic test runs. Statistical assertions become exact.
   No flakes.
2. PRODUCTION: per 9n5j, add explicit seed requirement for stochastic
   optimizers in conformance path. Keep rand::rng() fallback for
   non-conformance user-facing API if desired.

Related: 9n5j (stochastic methods no fixture coverage), flaky-tests
quality_gates_max_flake_rate = 0.001 (quality_gates.toml line 27).
close_reason: Seeded 5 stats rvs tests with StdRng (commit a84a2fb).

title: [HIGH] cross-crate: AuditLedger has FOUR divergent Arc<Mutex<AuditLedger>> type aliases — fsci-runtime uses asupersync::sync::Mutex, three others use std::sync::Mutex; SharedAuditLedger and SyncSharedAuditLedger are NON-INTERCHANGEABLE
description:
Review of AuditLedger type aliases across fsci-* crates on 2026-04-22:

grep 'pub type .*AuditLedger\s*=' crates/ finds 4 declarations:

  crates/fsci-runtime/src/evidence.rs:179
      pub type SharedAuditLedger = Arc<Mutex<AuditLedger>>
      where Mutex = asupersync::sync::Mutex

  crates/fsci-fft/src/transforms.rs:105
      pub type SyncSharedAuditLedger = Arc<Mutex<AuditLedger>>
      where Mutex = std::sync::Mutex

  crates/fsci-integrate/src/validation.rs:8
      pub type SyncSharedAuditLedger = Arc<StdMutex<AuditLedger>>
      where StdMutex = std::sync::Mutex

  crates/fsci-linalg/src/lib.rs:11
      pub type SyncSharedAuditLedger = Arc<StdMutex<AuditLedger>>
      where StdMutex = std::sync::Mutex

Three distinct problems:

1. TYPE INCOMPATIBILITY
   asupersync::sync::Mutex<T> is a REAL struct (verified at
   /home/ubuntu/.cargo/registry/src/.../asupersync-0.2.5/src/sync/mutex.rs),
   not an alias for std::sync::Mutex. So:
       Arc<asupersync::sync::Mutex<AuditLedger>>   (SharedAuditLedger)
   is a DIFFERENT concrete type from:
       Arc<std::sync::Mutex<AuditLedger>>          (SyncSharedAuditLedger)

   A user passing fsci-runtime's SharedAuditLedger to fsci_linalg::solve
   (which expects SyncSharedAuditLedger per lib.rs:11) gets a compile
   error. The 'AuditLedger' protocol is fragmented into at least two
   incompatible synchronization primitives at the type level.

2. NAME COLLISION
   Three crates (fsci-fft, fsci-integrate, fsci-linalg) all define the
   SAME name 'SyncSharedAuditLedger' but in their own namespaces.
   They happen to resolve to the same underlying type
   (Arc<std::sync::Mutex<AuditLedger>>) -- but this is implementation
   detail. If fsci-linalg switched to parking_lot::Mutex, suddenly
   fsci-linalg::SyncSharedAuditLedger != fsci-fft::SyncSharedAuditLedger
   and importing the wrong one becomes a subtle bug.

3. NO SHARED PROTOCOL
   fsci-conformance's runner instantiates THREE separate ledgers per
   test run (lines 7735/7833/8337: integrate_sync_audit_ledger() +
   linalg_sync_audit_ledger() + fft_sync_audit_ledger()). Each writes
   its own audit trail. A single user-level operation that spans
   integrate->linalg->fft produces THREE disjoint audit JSONL files
   with no cross-reference. Audit-trail-completeness claim (per
   mhuk, egba) is compromised -- the trail is fragmented by crate
   boundaries, not just by test boundaries.

Fix options:
1. MINIMAL: rename all four aliases to distinct names (e.g.,
   RuntimeSharedAuditLedger, FftSyncAuditLedger, LinalgSyncAuditLedger,
   IntegrateSyncAuditLedger) so users see the divergence explicitly.
2. BETTER: centralize on ONE audit ledger protocol in fsci-runtime,
   using std::sync::Mutex (or parking_lot for perf). Remove asupersync
   dependency from the ledger path. Have fsci-fft/linalg/integrate

title: [CRITICAL][infra] rch served a STALE SOURCE snapshot — a clippy run reported line numbers from before a 65-line edit
description:
Observed 2026-08-16 (RainyPrairie). This is the DISTINCT failure that frankenscipy-eibro's closure explicitly listed as still uncovered: eibro proved the fleet does not serve a stale BINARY (9/10 workers, detector live on each), and named 'a worker whose SOURCE SYNC is behind' as the untested case. Here it is.

WHAT HAPPENED, on RCH_WORKER=vmi1293453, harness 'RCH_WORKER=vmi1293453 RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec -- cargo clippy -j 1 -p fsci-interpolate --lib --no-deps -- -D warnings':
1. Baseline run reported 33 errors with cited locations including lib.rs:2185 and lib.rs:7065.
2. I edited the tree: 5 mechanical lint fixes plus 13 blocks of 5 lines each inserted above functions in the SAME file (65 inserted lines). Verified on disk afterwards: 'grep -c repeat_n' = 2, 'grep -c allow(clippy::needless_range_loop, clippy::explicit_counter_loop)' = 13.
3. Re-ran the IDENTICAL command. It reported the SAME 33 errors, with the SAME pre-edit line numbers 2185 and 7065. After inserting 65 lines above them those numbers cannot still be correct.
4. Re-ran the IDENTICAL command AGAIN. 10 errors, with shifted locations (2730, 2814, 4672). This is the fresh snapshot.

So run 3 linted source that did not match the working tree. No local edit intervened between runs 3 and 4.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE BINARY CASE. A stale binary at least tends to produce an obviously repeated result. A stale SOURCE snapshot produces a plausible one: an agent who has just made a fix sees 'the same errors as before' and concludes their edit was wrong, or -- in the dangerous direction -- an agent who has just introduced a defect sees the pre-edit GREEN and banks it. eibro's own original report was exactly that second shape.

WHAT MADE IT DETECTABLE, and this is the reusable part: the edit shifted line numbers. Diagnostics that cite locations are self-checking against a stale snapshot in a way that a pass/fail count is not. An edit that changes only VALUES would have been invisible.

NOT DIAGNOSED: whether this is rsync raciness against concurrent writes (this checkout is edited by several agents continuously), an incremental-sync fingerprint that missed same-size writes, or a per-worker snapshot cache. The 'Sync completed' line appears in all three runs.

NEGATIVE CASE any fix must pass: after the fix, an edit made between two identical rch invocations must be visible in the second, demonstrated with a location-citing diagnostic (line numbers must move) and not merely with a pass/fail flip -- a flip can be produced by a stale binary too, which is a different bug.
notes:
2026-08-17 RainyPrairie -- CORRECTING MY OWN NOTE FROM EARLIER TODAY. I wrote that
the sync "appears to honour committed state and drop uncommitted modifications, at
least on this worker". The general form of that is REFUTED by evidence I already
had, and I should have caught it before writing it.

What each worker actually demonstrated:

  vmi1227854  build 1  saw the UNCOMMITTED edit -- it FAILED INSIDE panel_pool.rs:312
  vmi1227854  build 5  sees the COMMITTED edit  -- 6 tests, count 596 -> 602
  vmi1153651  builds 2-4  did NOT see the uncommitted edit, while holding older commits
  vmi1153651  with the edit COMMITTED  -- NEVER TESTED

vmi1227854 honoured an UNCOMMITTED edit perfectly well. So commit state is NOT the
discriminating variable; the WORKER is. vmi1153651 is stale in a way that
vmi1227854 is not, and my commit-state story was an over-inference from one
worker's behaviour that the other worker's behaviour already contradicted.

WHAT REMAINS ESTABLISHED, and it is the part that matters:
 - vmi1153651 served a snapshot missing source that was present in the working
   tree, and returned exit 0 three times having compiled none of it.
 - The freshness marker (test count 596 unchanged after adding a 6-test module) is
   what caught it. Exit status, absence of warnings, and the ELF sha would all have
   passed.

WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED:
 - Any mechanism. Whether vmi1153651 would now serve the COMMITTED edit is untested.
   The clean experiment is to force that specific worker and rebuild; I have not
   done it and am not claiming its result.

PRACTICAL ADVICE UNCHANGED, and it does not depend on the mechanism: verify
freshness from a property of the SOURCE UNDER TEST (test count for cargo test, a
printed source-derived marker for cargo run) rather than from exit status or an ELF
sha, because at least one worker in this fleet will hand you a green build of code
you did not write.

title: [MEDIUM] conformance: scipy_special_oracle.py uses bare except Exception — hides KeyboardInterrupt/MemoryError/SystemExit
description:
Review of scipy_special_oracle.py:237:

    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001

Issues:
1. Per PEP-8 / BLE001, bare Exception includes MemoryError, RecursionError, OSError — these typically indicate the oracle itself is broken (OOM, stack overflow in scipy, fd exhaustion), not a scipy domain error. Silently reporting status='error' for these makes conformance output unreliable on worker machines with different resource limits.
2. KeyboardInterrupt is a BaseException (not caught by Exception), so Ctrl-C still works — but SystemExit also derives from BaseException and is fine. Still, catching MemoryError as if it were a domain error is wrong.
3. The # noqa: BLE001 comment acknowledges the lint was suppressed without justification.

The current pattern means:
- Out-of-memory on an oracle worker → test 'errors' → Rust side sees status='error' → counts as a valid scipy domain error → conformance passes without actually having compared against scipy.

Ask:
1. Narrow the catch to: (ValueError, TypeError, FloatingPointError, OverflowError, ArithmeticError, ZeroDivisionError, RuntimeError).
2. Let MemoryError, RecursionError, OSError, ImportError propagate — these should kill the oracle process so CI fails visibly.
3. Remove the BLE001 suppression comment after narrowing.
4. Optional: add an 'error_class' field alongside 'error' so the Rust side can distinguish ValueError (domain error) from FloatingPointError (numerical issue).
close_reason: Narrow oracle exception catches across all scripts (commit bacfe70).

title: [HIGH] conformance: CASP executor hardcodes alpha=0.05, capacity=64/200 instead of reading from fixture — expected values silently depend on these magic numbers; changing defaults breaks conformance without fixture visibility
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs:2737-2779 on 2026-04-22:

execute_casp_case hardcodes several CASP runtime parameters instead of
reading them from the fixture case:

    line 2737:  PolicyController::new(case.mode, 64)       // capacity 64
    line 2756:  SolverPortfolio::new(case.mode, 64)        // capacity 64
    line 2775:  ConformalCalibrator::new(0.05, 200)        // alpha=0.05,
                                                           // capacity=200

CaspCase struct (line 4112+) has fields for case_id, mode, test_kind,
condition_signal, metadata_signal, anomaly_signal, condition_state,
observations. It does NOT have fields for capacity or alpha, so the
fixture has no way to vary these parameters even though they materially
affect CASP behavior.

Impact:

1. Hand-typed expected_outcome values in FSCI-P2C-008_runtime_casp.json
   (15 cases) are implicitly tied to 'when capacity=64 and alpha=0.05'.
   If fsci-runtime ever changes the default capacity for
   PolicyController / SolverPortfolio, or someone decides alpha=0.1 is
   a better default for ConformalCalibrator, every conformance case's
   expected action silently becomes wrong.

2. No test ever exercises non-default capacity/alpha behavior. If
   capacity=4 causes boundary bugs (e.g., ring-buffer wraparound), or
   if alpha=0.01 triggers a different fallback threshold, conformance
   never sees it.

3. ConformalCalibrator specifically: alpha is a statistical parameter
   (significance level). Cases ostensibly testing 'calibrator drift'
   but hardcoded to one alpha only exercise one significance threshold.
   The 'drift' detection behavior is entirely a function of alpha.

Fix:
1. Add optional fields to CaspCase:
       policy_capacity: Option<usize>,        -- defaults 64
       solver_capacity: Option<usize>,        -- defaults 64
       calibrator_alpha: Option<f64>,         -- defaults 0.05
       calibrator_capacity: Option<usize>,    -- defaults 200
2. execute_casp_case reads case.policy_capacity.unwrap_or(64), etc.
3. Extend FSCI-P2C-008_runtime_casp.json with at least one case
   exercising each non-default value (alpha=0.01, alpha=0.1,
   capacity=4, capacity=1024) to lock in non-default correctness.
4. Document defaults in fsci-runtime rustdoc so fixture authors know
   which values match current behavior.

Related: aqm6 (runner fragmentation), 37ip (no tolerance contract), ivg5
(self-check instead of oracle -- expected values are hand-typed for
specific magic numbers).
close_reason: Added 3 optional CaspCase fields (capacity, alpha, calibrator_capacity) threading through execute_casp_case. Defaults preserve legacy magic numbers (64/0.05/200) so existing 15 cases in FSCI-P2C-008 keep passing. Fixtures can now vary CASP ring-buffer capacity, ConformalCalibrator alpha, and calibrator history size to cover boundary behavior; previously these were unreachable from fixtures. casp_packet_runner_passes test still passes.

title: [optimize] Global optimization: differential_evolution, basinhopping
description:
## Goal
Implement global optimization algorithms. Local optimizers (BFGS, etc.) find the nearest local minimum, but many real problems have multiple local minima (molecular conformation, neural network training, engineering design).

## What to implement
- `differential_evolution(func, bounds)`: DE algorithm — population-based evolutionary optimizer. The most robust and commonly used global optimizer in SciPy. Requires only function evaluations (no gradients).
  - Parameters: strategy (best1bin, rand1bin, etc.), maxiter, popsize, tol, mutation, recombination, seed
  - Returns OptimizeResult with x, fun, success, nfev, nit
- `basinhopping(func, x0, minimizer_kwargs)`: basin-hopping algorithm — random perturbation + local minimization. Good for smooth functions with many local minima.
  - Parameters: niter, T (temperature), stepsize, minimizer_kwargs (passed to minimize)

## Why this matters
differential_evolution is the #1 most used global optimizer in SciPy. It works on black-box functions, handles box constraints naturally, and is embarrassingly parallelizable. basinhopping is preferred when a good local minimizer is available.

## Implementation approach
- DE: initialize random population within bounds → mutation (combine 3 random vectors) → crossover (mix with target) → selection (keep better) → iterate
- basinhopping: perturb x → local minimize → Metropolis acceptance criterion → iterate

## Dependencies
- Uses existing minimize() for basinhopping local steps
- Bounds struct from constraint infrastructure bead

## Testing requirements
- DE: Rastrigin function (many local minima) → finds global minimum near origin
- DE: Rosenbrock in 2D with bounds → converges to (1,1)
- basinhopping: multi-modal function → finds global minimum
- Population diversity: DE population explores broadly before converging
- Bounds respected throughout optimization
- At least 8 tests
close_reason: Implemented differential_evolution (best1bin/rand1bin strategies) and basinhopping (Metropolis + BFGS local) with 8 tests

title: [signal] Cross-correlation and auto-correlation: correlate, correlate2d

## Goal
Implement correlation functions essential for signal processing and time series analysis.

## What to implement
- `correlate(a, v, mode)`: Cross-correlation of two 1D arrays. mode="full"/"same"/"valid".
- `correlate2d(a, v, mode)`: 2D cross-correlation for image processing.

## Implementation approach
- correlate(a, v) = convolve(a, v[::-1]) — reverse v and convolve
- Use existing fftconvolve infrastructure for efficiency

## Testing requirements
- Auto-correlation peak at zero lag
- Cross-correlation of shifted signal peaks at correct lag
- correlate(a, a) symmetric
- At least 6 tests

So: an EFFICIENT real path changes last bits -> fails golden; an EXACT real replication must keep (sum_re*x)/(x*x), +0.0 flushes, etc. -> retains most of the work, unlikely Score>=2.0.
