title: [CRITICAL][linalg] eig can HANG FOREVER -- six .schur() sites use nalgebra's unbounded constructor (max_niter=0 means never give up)
description:
`eig` CAN HANG FOREVER. Found 2026-08-18 by diagnosing a metamorphic run that held this
project's only build slot for 96 minutes. NO BUILD was used to diagnose it.

## What happens

`crates/fsci-linalg/src/lib.rs` calls nalgebra's UNBOUNDED Schur constructor at six sites
(:6363, :6601, :7793, :7929, :9073, :9175), all of the form `matrix.clone().schur()`.

nalgebra 0.33.3 `src/linalg/schur.rs`:

```rust
pub fn new(m: OMatrix<T, D, D>) -> Self {
    Self::try_new(m, T::RealField::default_epsilon(), 0).unwrap()
}
```

and its own doc for `try_new`:

> `max_niter` — maximum total number of iterations performed by the algorithm. If this
> number of iteration is exceeded, `None` is returned. **If `niter == 0`, then the algorithm
> continues indefinitely until convergence.**

The loop guard is `niter += 1; if niter == max_niter { return None; }` (:257). With
`max_niter == 0`, `niter` is 1, 2, 3, … and never equals 0, so the guard can never fire. A
matrix on which the implicit-QR iteration does not converge spins forever. `eig` never
returns and cannot be interrupted by the caller.

## Evidence, four independent strands

1. **The test harness said so.** The metamorphic run's last line before it was killed:
   `test metamorphic::tests::linalg_svd_eig_relations::mr_eig_trace_identity_bounded has
   been running for over 60 seconds`.
2. **Two profiles 32 minutes apart are statistically identical** — `array_axcpy` 9.08% then
   9.71%, `Schur::do_decompose` 2.38% then 2.28%, same supporting symbols in the same
   proportions. Not slow progress; no progress.
3. **The work is bounded and tiny.** `mr_eig_trace_identity_bounded(n in 2usize..=8, seed in
   0u64..1000)` at `EIG_TRACE_CASES = 64` — at most 64 eigendecompositions of matrices no
   larger than 8×8, built by `make_diag_dominant`. That is milliseconds of work, even in a
   debug build. It ran for 96 minutes.
4. **The mechanism is in the dependency's source and doc**, quoted above, not inferred.

## Fix

Replace every `.schur()` with `Schur::try_new(m, eps, MAX_NITER)` for a finite `MAX_NITER`
and map `None` to a `LinalgError` (LAPACK's `dhseqr` returns `info > 0` for exactly this
case, so an error return is the scipy-faithful behaviour — scipy raises
`LinAlgError("eig algorithm did not converge")`). A bound of the LAPACK order (30·n) is a
reasonable starting point; the value should be justified in the row, not picked silently.

## Verify — and the must-hit arm is the hard part

- **MUST-HIT:** find the specific `(n, seed)` in `2..=8 × 0..1000` that hangs. It is
  reproducible by construction: `make_diag_dominant(n, seed)` is deterministic, so a bounded
  sweep calling `eig` under a per-case timeout will name it. That fixture then becomes the
  regression test, and it must FAIL (hang or error) before the fix and PASS after.
- **MUST-MISS:** a well-conditioned matrix must still decompose to the same values as
  before, bit-for-bit — the bound must not change results on inputs that already converged.
- Compare the failing fixture against live scipy: if scipy also fails to converge, our
  correct behaviour is to raise, matching it. If scipy converges and we do not, there is a
  SECOND defect underneath this one in the iteration itself, and the bound only converts a
  hang into an error rather than fixing it.

## Why this is P1 rather than a test annoyance

A public library function that never returns is worse than one that returns a wrong answer:
it cannot be caught, retried or timed out by the caller, and it takes the whole process with
it. It also silently blocks CI — this is what consumed 96 minutes of the project's single
build slot today, across at least three quiet measurement windows, while presenting as
"tests are slow".

## Related

`frankenscipy-jn3vu` argued the metamorphic suite is slow because of proptest case counts in
a debug build. That analysis stands for the rest of the suite but was measuring the WRONG
THING for this run: the dominant cost was not case count, it was a hang. Both can be true;
the jn3vu evidence comment should be read with that correction.
notes:
2026-08-18 RainyPrairie -- INCREMENT 6 (UNBUILT): fixed a defect in MY OWN previous
increment, found by reading further into eig rather than by testing it.

eig establishes LAPACK's eigenvector convention upstream: each complex vector rotated
so its LARGEST-MAGNITUDE COMPONENT IS REAL AND POSITIVE, then unit 2-norm. That is what
SciPy returns and what callers compare against elementwise.

My dgebak back-transform multiplies by the balancing transform, which changes the
component magnitudes -- so a DIFFERENT component becomes largest and the upstream
rotation no longer holds. I renormalized length and stopped, leaving a unit-norm vector
with an ARBITRARY PHASE: still a valid eigenvector, still satisfying A v = lambda v,
and no longer comparable to SciPy.

THE GENERAL LESSON, which is the part worth keeping: my residual test could NEVER have
caught this. Any phase rotation of a complex eigenvector is still an eigenvector, so
the defining relation holds regardless; and the vector is unit-norm either way, so a
norm check cannot see it. A test written against the DEFINING PROPERTY covers
correctness but not INTERFACE COMPATIBILITY -- and for a library whose purpose is to
match an incumbent, the convention is part of the contract and needs its own gate.

FIX: re-apply the same rotation in the same form as the upstream site, for conjugate
pairs only, then the shared-factor normalization the pair requires. Real columns keep
plain unit-norm scaling.

TEST: fixture mixes a genuine conjugate pair (+/- i) with a real pair ((5+/-sqrt5)/2),
badly scaled by an exact power-of-two similarity. Asserts the largest component of each
complex eigenvector is real AND positive (both halves -- satisfying only the first is

ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED 2026-08-18. Reproduced standalone, mechanism traced to source at every
step, and the incumbent's contrasting behaviour explained.

## Reproduced

`eig_sweep_probe` (one process per case, OS `timeout 2` as executioner) over the fixture
space the hung proptest draws from. PARTIAL — n=7,8 still running:

| n | timeouts | of |
|---|---|---|
| 2, 3, 4 | **0** | 1000 each |
| 5 | **25** | 1000 |
| 6 | **40+** | 1000 (in progress) |
| 7, 8 | pending | |

Zero non-timeout anomalies: no `ERR`, no unexpected exit codes. So the failure is purely
non-termination, not a wrong answer or a returned error. Controls passed: `(2,0)` OK
3.553e-15, `(8,999)` OK 3.695e-13, bad args → exit 2 so a timeout is distinguishable from a
usage failure.

**It starts at n=5.** n≤4 is clean across all 3000 cases.

## The discriminator is eigenvalue SPREAD, not degeneracy

| | spread (max−min real part) |
|---|---|
| HANG — (5,201) (5,213) (5,234) (6,319) (6,335) | 0.085 – 0.946 |
| PASS — (5,0) (5,1) (6,0) (6,1) | 2.49 – 2.99 |

Both groups contain EXACTLY repeated eigenvalues (`min|Δλ| = 0`), so degeneracy is not the
trigger. Tight clustering is. With the diagonal at 2n (10–12), the hanging cases have a
relative spread under ~8%.

## Mechanism, from source

1. `eig` → `matrix.clone().schur()` → `Schur::new(m)` → `try_new(m, eps, **0**)`.
2. nalgebra's own doc: *"If `niter == 0`, then the algorithm continues indefinitely until
   convergence."* The guard is `niter += 1; if niter == max_niter { return None }`, so with
   `max_niter == 0` it counts 1,2,3,… and can never fire.
3. `schur.rs:129` describes the algorithm as *"Implicit double-shift QR method"* — and that
   comment is **the only occurrence of the word "shift" in the entire file**. There is no
   exceptional-shift path and no stagnation detection. The shift always comes from the
   trailing 2×2.
4. A tightly clustered spectrum is the classic stagnation case for unmodified Francis
   double-shift QR: every shift is nearly equally poor, the subdiagonal does not decay, and
   deflation never triggers.
5. LAPACK's `dlahqr`/`dhseqr` inserts an **exceptional shift** every ~10 iterations for
   exactly this reason. That is why `scipy.linalg.eig` converges on **all 7000** fixtures
   (worst |Σλ.real − trace| = 8.527e-14) while ours hangs on 65+ of them.

Our own wrapper is NOT the loop: `eig`'s `while i < rows` block walk advances by 1 or 2 on
every path.

## What this means for the fix — the original proposal is insufficient

The bead first proposed bounding `max_niter`. That is necessary but **not sufficient**: it
converts a hang into an error, while scipy returns correct eigenvalues for the same matrix.
Shipping only the bound would trade a hang for a spurious failure on ~1% of a benign fixture
family. Options, cheapest first:

1. **Bound AND retry with a perturbed/exceptional shift** on non-convergence — mirrors what
   LAPACK does, keeps us in safe Rust, no new dependency.
2. **Fix the iteration**: add an exceptional-shift path to a vendored/own Schur. Larger, but
   it is the actual defect and `eig`/`eigvals`/`ordqz` all sit on it (six `.schur()` sites).
3. Bound only, and document `eig` as "may fail to converge on clustered spectra" — a real
   parity regression against scipy and NOT recommended; recorded so the option is visible.

A finite bound should ship regardless and immediately, because a library call that never
returns cannot be defended; but it must not be reported as closing this bead.

## Regression fixtures, ready to use

`(5, 201)`, `(5, 213)`, `(5, 234)`, `(6, 319)`, `(6, 335)` — deterministic via
`make_diag_dominant`, all hang today, all converge under scipy. A must-miss control is
`(5, 0)` / `(6, 0)`, which pass today and must keep passing bit-for-bit.

## Refuted along the way

My first hypothesis was that LAPACK BALANCES and nalgebra does not. **Refuted by
measurement**: worst condition number across the fixture space is 1.32 and the worst
row-norm ratio is 1.240 — balancing targets ratios ≫ 1, so there is nothing to balance.
Recorded because the next person will otherwise have the same idea.

CITATION CORRECTION 2026-08-18 — I quoted the WRONG nalgebra version in both comments above.

## What happened

I located nalgebra's source with `find ... -path "*nalgebra*/src/linalg/schur.rs" | head -1`
and got **0.33.3**. Four versions are unpacked in this registry (0.31.4, 0.33.3, 0.34.2,
0.35.0) and `head -1` picked one arbitrarily. `Cargo.toml` requires `nalgebra = "0.35"` and
`Cargo.lock` pins **0.35.0**, so every line number and quote in the two comments above came
from source that this project does not build.

Caught only because I went to check whether the probe could call `Schur` directly and read
the dependency line while doing it. Nothing about the earlier reasoning surfaced the error —
the 0.33.3 text was self-consistent and said what I expected, which is exactly why it read
as confirmation.

## Re-verified against 0.35.0, the version that actually builds

Every substantive claim survives:

- `Schur::new(m)` → `try_new(m, T::RealField::default_epsilon(), **0**)`. Unchanged.
- Doc on `try_new`: *"If `niter == 0`, then the algorithm continues indefinitely until
  convergence."* Unchanged.
- Guard: `niter += 1; if niter == max_niter { return None; }`. Unchanged, and still cannot
  fire when `max_niter == 0`.
- The word "shift" occurs **once** in the whole file, and there is no `exceptional` anywhere.
  So "no exceptional-shift path" is also true of 0.35.0.

One genuine DIFFERENCE, in our favour and worth knowing: 0.35.0's `delimit_subproblem` adds
an ABSOLUTE deflation threshold of `eps²` alongside the relative test, with a comment saying
it approximates LAPACK's `SMLNUM`. That is strictly MORE permissive than 0.33.3's
relative-only test, so it can only make deflation easier — it does not explain the hang, and
it means the hang persists despite a deflation improvement.

## Net effect on this bead

- The reproduction, the fixtures, the spread correlation, and the scipy comparison never
  depended on nalgebra's source at all. Unaffected.
- "Hang rather than error" is still explained by `max_niter = 0`, now verified in the right
  version.
- The RETRACTION above still stands on its own evidence: the numpy model refuted the
  exceptional-shift CAUSE independently of which nalgebra version I was reading.
- Only the line numbers in the two comments above are wrong. Read them as 0.35.0 facts,
  re-verified here, not as 0.33.3 citations.

## Rule for the next person

Resolve the dependency version from `Cargo.lock` BEFORE reading vendored source, and check
`ls` for multiple unpacked copies. A registry with four versions of a crate will hand you a
plausible, self-consistent, wrong file without any error.

"NEVER" vs "SLOWLY" SETTLED 2026-08-18 — it is NEVER. One build, df 54G immediately before.

## The question the timeout could not answer

A `timeout 2` kill proves the call did not finish in 2 seconds. It cannot distinguish a
non-terminating iteration from one that would converge after a huge but finite number of
sweeps, and the fix differs: slow convergence is a tuning problem, non-convergence is a
defect. So the probe gained a bounded mode calling `nalgebra::linalg::Schur::try_new(m, eps,
K)` directly, which returns `None` when the bound is exceeded.

## Observed — both arms, perfect discrimination

| fixture | K = 100,000 |
|---|---|
| (5,201) | **NOCONV** (also NOCONV at K=50 and K=1,000) |
| (5,213) | **NOCONV** |
| (5,234) | **NOCONV** |
| (6,319) | **NOCONV** |
| (6,335) | **NOCONV** |
| (5,0) control | CONV |
| (6,0) control | CONV |
| (8,999) control | CONV |
| (8,42) control | CONV |

Every known-hanging fixture fails to converge in 100,000 sweeps; every control converges.
`(5,201)` was additionally checked at K=10,000,000, where it exceeded a 60-second wall clock
still iterating.

## Why 100,000 is decisive rather than merely large

These are **5×5 and 6×6** matrices. A Francis double-shift QR iteration on a 5×5 converges in
of order 10–20 sweeps; LAPACK's `dlahqr` gives up at `30·max(10,n)` = 300 for n=5 and calls
that a failure. Surviving 100,000 sweeps without deflating is four orders of magnitude past
"slow" and roughly 300× past the incumbent's own patience threshold. This is
**non-convergence**, not tuning.

## Consequences for the fix

1. **A finite `max_niter` WILL fire.** It is not a theoretical guard — it converts a real,
   reproducible hang into a real, reproducible error on 3.29% of this fixture family. Ship
   it anyway: an unkillable hang cannot be defended and an error can at least be caught.
2. **The real fix must change the ITERATION, not its budget.** No bound recovers the
   eigenvalues scipy returns for these same matrices.
3. Together with the earlier refutations (balancing; exceptional-shift stagnation — a numpy
   Francis model converges on these fixtures in 7–13 iterations), the defect is localised to
   nalgebra's **implicit bulge chase**, the one part an explicit-shift model does not
   exercise. That is now the only surviving candidate, and it is reached by elimination plus
   this result rather than by elimination alone.

## Method note

The zsh gotcha that bit the first attempt: unquoted `$c` does NOT word-split in zsh (unlike
bash), so `probe $c 100000` passed "5 213" as a single argv and every case died in
`ParseIntError`. Visible only because the probe parses strictly and panics loudly — a probe
that silently defaulted a bad argument would have printed a full table of confident,
meaningless results.

`LinalgError::ConvergenceFailure { detail: String }` already exists at lib.rs:705, with the

returns `Result<_, LinalgError>`.

One helper, used at all 14 sites, so the bound and the error text live in a single place:

```rust
fn bounded_schur(m: DMatrix<f64>) -> Result<Schur<f64, Dyn>, LinalgError> {
    let n = m.nrows();
    nalgebra::linalg::Schur::try_new(m, f64::EPSILON, schur_max_niter(n))
        .ok_or_else(|| LinalgError::ConvergenceFailure {
            detail: format!("Schur iteration did not converge for a {n}x{n} matrix"),
        })
}
```

`schur_max_niter` should be justified by measurement, not chosen. A sweep of all 7000
fixtures at K = 300 (LAPACK `dlahqr`'s own `30·max(10,n)`) is running to establish whether
that bound falsely fails any case that legitimately converges. Pick the bound from that
result.

Bounding converts a hang into an error on the 3.29% of cases where scipy returns correct
eigenvalues. It is a strict improvement — nothing that succeeds today changes, and an
unkillable hang becomes a catchable error — but the parity gap remains open until the
iteration itself is fixed.

BOUND CHOSEN BY MEASUREMENT 2026-08-18 — LAPACK's own `30·max(10,n)` is PERFECTLY
DISCRIMINATING on this fixture family. Zero false failures across all 7000 cases.

## The experiment

The open question was whether a finite iteration budget would also fail cases that
legitimately converge — which would trade a hang for a spurious error on working inputs. So
the whole fixture space was swept twice: once unbounded (OS `timeout 2` as executioner), and
once at K = 300, which is LAPACK `dlahqr`'s budget `30·max(10, n)` for every n in this range.

| n | unbounded TIMEOUT | NOCONV at K=300 | false failures |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0 | 0 | **0** |
| 3 | 0 | 0 | **0** |
| 4 | 0 | 0 | **0** |
| 5 | 25 | 25 | **0** |
| 6 | 49 | 49 | **0** |
| 7 | 70 | 70 | **0** |
| 8 | 86 | 86 | **0** |
| **total** | **230** | **230** | **0** |

The two sets are identical, dimension by dimension. Every case that converges at all
converges within 300 sweeps; every case that fails at 300 also fails unbounded (and one was
separately shown still iterating at K = 10,000,000).

## Why this settles the bound

Adopting `30·max(10,n)` costs nothing measurable on this family: no input that works today
starts failing. It is also the incumbent's own threshold, so a caller comparing against
`scipy.linalg.eig` sees the same patience budget rather than one we invented. And
`f64::EPSILON` is exactly what `Schur::new` passes via `default_epsilon()`, so the arithmetic
is untouched — converging results stay bit-identical and only the cap is new.

## Limits of the claim, stated plainly

- The fixture family is `make_diag_dominant`, n ∈ 2..8. **Nothing here speaks to n > 8**,
  where the formula's `30n` growth kicks in above n = 10 and where convergence behaviour may
  differ. The bound is justified FOR THIS RANGE; a wider sweep would be needed to claim more.
- "Zero false failures" is a statement about 7000 specific matrices, not a proof. A different
  matrix family could in principle need more than 300 sweeps and would then regress from
  "slow but correct" to "error". LAPACK accepts exactly that risk with the same constant.
- This remains a ROBUSTNESS fix. It converts an unkillable hang into a catchable
  `ConvergenceFailure` on 3.29% of this family; it does NOT recover the eigenvalues SciPy
  returns for those same matrices. The non-convergence itself is still unexplained — two
  hypotheses refuted (balancing; exceptional-shift stagnation), with nalgebra's implicit
  bulge chase the surviving candidate.

The loop is `while end != start`, so every iteration has `subdim >= 2`. There are exactly two
branches, and only one of them can fail to advance:

**`subdim == 2` — CANNOT loop.** It attempts `compute_2x2_basis`; if the block has complex
eigenvalues that returns `None` and the block is correctly left as a 2×2 Schur block. Either
way control then reaches `if end > 2 { end -= 2 } else { break }`. **Unconditional progress.**
This branch is exonerated.

**`subdim > 2` — the only stagnation candidate.** It performs a Francis double-shift sweep and
then re-runs `delimit_subproblem(&mut t, eps, end)` with `end` UNCHANGED. If the sweep does not
shrink the trailing subdiagonal enough for the deflation test to fire, `start` and `end` come
back identical and the next iteration repeats with the same state. With `max_niter = 0` that
repeats forever.

So the hang is **numerical, not structural**: the control flow is sound and there is no
missing `end` decrement or off-by-one. Something about the sweep's effect on these matrices
fails to reduce the subdiagonal.

## What the shift selection actually is

Textbook Francis: the shift comes from the trailing 2×2 (`hnn`, `hmm`, `hnm`, `hmn`) via
`tra`/`det`, and the bulge axis is built from the leading 3×3 (`h11`, `h12`, `h21`, `h22`,
`h32`) at `start`. That matches what my numpy model used — and the model **converged on these
fixtures in 7–13 iterations**.

## Where that leaves the diagnosis

Two possibilities remain, and I cannot separate them by reading:

1. **The implicit bulge chase is buggy.** Explicit-shift QR and the implicit chase are
   mathematically equivalent only if the implicit Q reproduces the explicit one; a defect in
   the reflector application or its view bounds would break that. Note the sweep reflects rows
   `0..=end` and columns `m..dim` — correct for maintaining similarity on the FULL matrix
   while working on a submatrix, but exactly the sort of boundary condition where an error
   would be invisible on well-separated spectra and fatal on clustered ones.
2. **My model differs materially from nalgebra** in some way I have not identified, in which
   case its convergence proves less than I took it to.

## The test that would separate them, for whoever has a build slot

Instrument the real loop, not a model: print `niter`, `start`, `end`, and the trailing
subdiagonals each iteration for `(5,201)` under a bounded `try_new`. A subdiagonal that
**plateaus** at a fixed nonzero value implicates the deflation threshold; one that
**oscillates** implicates the bulge chase; one that **shrinks but never crosses** the
threshold means the bound is simply too tight for these matrices, which the 230/230 sweep
already argues against.

That is the same test named earlier on this bead, now with a narrowed prior: the control flow
is exonerated, so the answer is in the sweep's arithmetic.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
NEW LEAD 2026-08-18, freeze-compliant (python only, no build): the difference may be in the
HESSENBERG REDUCTION, not the QR sweep. Also contains a false alarm of mine, recorded.

## The observation

`scipy.linalg.hessenberg(make_diag_dominant(5,0))` has subdiagonals

    [1.000e+00, -8.882e-16, 2.220e-16, 2.220e-16]

against a deflation threshold of `eps*(|t_nn|+|t_mm|)` = 4.663e-15. **Three of the four
subdiagonals are already at machine epsilon before any QR iteration runs.** These matrices
are diagonal ~2n with off-diagonals in [-0.5, 0.5], so the reduction alone very nearly
triangularises them. `delimit` correctly collapses the problem to a 2x2 and the loop exits in
**zero** iterations.

## Why that matters

If the input to the QR loop is already near-triangular, the loop has almost nothing to do and
cannot plausibly stagnate for 100,000 sweeps. So the interesting question moves UPSTREAM:
**nalgebra runs its own Hessenberg reduction (`hess`) before the loop; scipy runs LAPACK's.**
If nalgebra's reduction leaves materially larger subdiagonals on these matrices, the QR
iteration faces a real problem where scipy's faces none — and that would explain both the
hang and why every explicit- and implicit-shift model I have written converges immediately.

**This is a hypothesis, not a finding.** I have not compared the two reductions; doing so
needs nalgebra's `Hessenberg` on the same fixture, which needs a build.

## The false alarm, recorded because it nearly cost the lead

My implicit-chase model reported the PASS controls "converging in 0 iterations" and I
immediately called the controls failed and the run void — 0 iterations looked impossible. It
is correct. I was applying the right instinct (check the controls before believing the
result) to the wrong target, and had I stopped there I would have discarded the observation
that actually matters. Checking WHY the control looked wrong is what turned it into a lead.

## Model caveats, stated so nobody over-reads it

My implicit chase mirrors nalgebra's shift and axis construction but **omits the 2x2
`compute_2x2_basis` decoupling** and improvises the axis-rebuild bounds. It converged on the
hanging fixtures in 3-4 iterations. Combined with the explicit-shift model's 7-13, that is two
independent reimplementations converging where nalgebra does not — suggestive, but both are
MY code, and the shared assumption they make is scipy's Hessenberg input.

## Concrete next test, for whoever has a slot

Print the subdiagonals of **nalgebra's** `Hessenberg::new(m).unpack_h()` for `(5,201)` and
compare against `scipy.linalg.hessenberg` on the same matrix. If nalgebra's are materially
larger, the defect is in the reduction and the QR loop is a victim. That is cheaper than
instrumenting the sweep and should be tried first.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
THE ARGUMENT FOR MY HESSENBERG LEAD IS REFUTED — 2026-08-18, same day, python only, no build.

## What I argued last turn

That scipy's Hessenberg reduction leaves these matrices *already near-triangular*, so the QR
loop "has almost nothing to do and cannot plausibly stagnate", and therefore nalgebra's own
reduction must be producing something materially different.

## What the data actually shows

Subdiagonals of `scipy.linalg.hessenberg` on the fixture set, counting how many fall below
the deflation threshold `eps*(|t_i+1,i+1| + |t_i,i|)`:

| fixture | negligible / total | largest subdiagonal |
|---|---|---|
| HANG (5,201) | 1 / 4 | 5.980e-01 |
| HANG (5,213) | 1 / 4 | 5.813e-01 |
| HANG (5,234) | 1 / 4 | 5.838e-01 |
| HANG (6,319) | 3 / 5 | 6.771e-01 |
| HANG (6,335) | 2 / 5 | 7.551e-01 |
| PASS (5,0) | 3 / 4 | 1.000e+00 |
| PASS (6,0) | 4 / 5 | 1.118e+00 |
| **PASS (8,999)** | **0 / 7** | **1.986e+00** |

**Near-triangularity does not predict hang versus pass.** `(8,999)` is the LEAST triangular
fixture in the set — zero negligible subdiagonals out of seven — and it converges. The hanging
fixtures are *more* triangular than that, and each still has real work for the loop (largest
subdiagonal ~0.6).

## The mistake

I observed near-triangularity on `(5,0)` — a **PASS** case — and generalised it to the hanging
ones without checking. The observation was true of the matrix I looked at and false as a
description of the failures. Every hanging fixture has a substantial subdiagonal, so
"the loop has nothing to do" is simply not the situation.

## What survives and what does not

- **DOES NOT survive:** the motivation. There is no longer a reason to expect nalgebra's
  reduction to be the differentiator, and the "compare the two reductions first, it's cheaper"
  advice loses its basis.
- **STILL UNTESTED, now unmotivated:** whether nalgebra's Hessenberg output differs from
  LAPACK's on these inputs. Someone with a slot could still check it cheaply, but it should no
  longer be described as the leading candidate.
- **UNAFFECTED:** the control-flow exoneration (only the `subdim > 2` branch can stagnate),
  and the two model results (explicit shifts converge in 7–13 iterations, implicit chase in
  3–4). The instrumentation test on the real loop remains the way to settle this.

Recorded rather than quietly dropped, because a lead with a refuted motivation still sitting
in the record reads as a priority. This is the fourth hypothesis on this bead to fail —
balancing, exceptional-shift stagnation, the "root cause" retraction, and now this — and the
pattern is consistent: each was a plausible mechanism proposed before the cheap check that
could kill it.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
COORDINATION NOTE 2026-08-18 — an untracked `crates/fsci-linalg/src/hessenberg_qr.rs` has
appeared in the shared tree (21 KB, unwired, self-declared UNBUILT). I did not write it and
have NOT touched, staged or modified it. Two items in its header need reconciling with
evidence already on this bead, and I am raising them rather than editing someone else's file.

## 1. The nalgebra version citation is wrong — and it is MY error being inherited

The header cites **nalgebra 0.33.3** `src/linalg/schur.rs:129`. `Cargo.lock` pins **0.35.0**;
0.33.3 is one of four copies unpacked in this registry and is not what builds. I made exactly
this mistake earlier on this bead (`find … | head -1` picked 0.33.3) and corrected it — so
this is very likely my wrong citation propagating.

The conclusion survives: I re-verified against 0.35.0 that `Schur::new` still passes
`max_niter = 0`, and that "shift" appears once in the file with no exceptional-shift branch.
So the CLAIM is true of the built version; only the reference is wrong. Worth fixing to
0.35.0 before it propagates further.

## 2. The module's stated MECHANISM is contradicted by a recorded refutation

The header argues: a tight cluster makes the trailing-2x2 shift barely move the iteration, it
recomputes the same shift, and cycles without deflating — "which is why LAPACK converges where
nalgebra spins."

That is the exceptional-shift stagnation hypothesis. **I proposed it on this bead, committed
it as ROOT CAUSE, and then retracted it**, because a numpy Francis double-shift model using
the same trailing-2x2 shift selection **converges on the hanging fixtures in 7-13 iterations**,
and adding exceptional shifts every 10 sweeps changed nothing. A second model mirroring
nalgebra's IMPLICIT bulge chase converged in 3-4.

**I am not claiming the module is wrong.** My models are my own code, both consumed scipy's
Hessenberg input, and I separately refuted my own reasoning about that input. LAPACK's
approach is battle-tested regardless of whether my model reproduces the failure. But the
module's premise and the bead's recorded evidence currently disagree, and that should be
resolved rather than left for a reader to trip over:

- If the exceptional shift fixes the hanging fixtures when compiled, my refutation was wrong
  and should be marked so — that would be a clean, decisive result.
- If it does NOT fix them, the module is correct LAPACK-parity work that does not address
  sez4r, and the bead should say so before anyone routes `eig` to it.

Either way the named fixtures settle it: `(5,201)`, `(5,213)`, `(5,234)`, `(6,319)`,
`(6,335)` must converge, and `(5,0)`, `(6,0)`, `(8,999)`, `(8,42)` must still converge to
bit-identical values.

## 3. Not a criticism of the work

The header does several things right that are worth preserving: it states the LAPACK
constants are QUOTED from the published routine rather than read from a vendored file, it
scopes itself to eigenvalues, and it declares UNBUILT and unwired so it changes no behaviour
until someone routes to it deliberately. That is the correct posture for freeze-time code.

title: [fft] Multi-dimensional real FFT: rfft2, irfft2, rfftn, irfftn
description:
## Goal
Complete the FFT module with N-dimensional real FFT variants used in image processing.

## What to implement
- rfft2(x): 2D real FFT (applies rfft along last axis, fft along first)
- irfft2(x): Inverse 2D real FFT
- rfftn(x): N-dimensional real FFT
- irfftn(x): Inverse N-dimensional real FFT

## Implementation approach
- rfft2: compose existing rfft + fft along different axes
- rfftn: generalize to N dimensions via axis-by-axis transforms

## Testing requirements
- rfft2 round-trip: irfft2(rfft2(x)) ≈ x for real input
- Parseval's theorem for 2D
- At least 6 tests
close_reason: Already implemented: rfft2, irfft2, rfftn, irfftn all present with full implementations.

title: [stats] KsTwoBign.sf uses default 1-cdf -> KS-test p-value underflows to 0 in the tail (scipy gives 3.86e-22 at x=5)
close_reason: Already fixed (no prior BLOCKER comment on this one, so verified from scratch). KsTwoBign's sf lives in 'impl ContinuousDistribution for KsTwoBign' and sums the large-x Kolmogorov survival series 2*sum (-1)^(k-1) exp(-2k^2x^2) DIRECTLY above KSTWOBIGN_THRESHOLD, falling back to 1-cdf only below it where the cdf is near 0 and nothing cancels. The source comment records why this matters beyond precision: sf IS the KS-test asymptotic p-value, so the deep tail is exactly where significant results live. Regression coverage is tests::kstwobign_sf_tail_match_scipy. RE-MEASURED live: kstwobign sf(0.5)=0.9639452436648751, sf(1.5)=0.022217962616525127, sf(3)=3.045995948942526e-08, sf(5)=3.8574996959278356e-22 -- all four match, the last being this bead's named 3.86e-22. TWO-ARM CONTROL: scipy's own 1-cdf on the same deep-tail point returns exactly 0.0 while its sf returns the finite value, so the bug class the override prevents is demonstrated, not assumed. Here: 1-kstwobign.cdf(5.0) == 0.0 in scipy itself. Test re-run green with 'Compiling fsci-stats' in the log.

title: [special] airy Ai/Bi negative-x series cancels at large |x| (~5e-5 at x=-12); asymptotic fix regresses derivatives
description: airy(x) for x in [-12,6) uses Maclaurin series; Ai/Bi cancel for large |x| (Ai(-12) ~5e-5 vs mpmath). Moving the series->asymptotic bound (and extending the oscillatory asymptotic L/M to 6 terms, u5/u6) fixes Ai/Bi to ~6e-9, BUT the 4-term derivative asymptotic N/O has a ~zeta^-4 residual (~1e-6) so it REGRESSES Aip/Bip (series gives ~1e-9 there). Clean fix needs EITHER correcting the N/O derivative coeffs to ~1e-9 OR a hybrid (asymptotic Ai/Bi + series Aip/Bip in the seam). Verified coeffs u5=5391411025/46438023168, u6=5849680962125/20061226008576 (work for L/M). Reverted to avoid the derivative regression. The Aip 'worst 9.8e-6 at -11.5' in probes is a near-zero-of-Ai' artifact, not a real bug.
close_reason: Shipped: 6-term asymptotic L/M + crossover -12->-9. Ai/Bi ~6e-9 vs mpmath (was 5e-5), derivs ~1e-6 (was ~1e-4 series cancellation); no regression. The 'series deriv good' was a near-zero artifact. Commit pushed above.

title: [sparse][conformance] sparse_nnz and sparse_count_nonzero have identical bodies — scipy's .nnz vs .count_nonzero distinction is collapsed (84bf20f91 fix lost to revert churn)
description:
Found by RusticCarp 2026-08-04, surfaced by fixing frankenscipy-5i3a9 (the metamorphic_tests target had never compiled, so its 56 tests had never run).

DEFECT: sparse_nnz and sparse_count_nonzero have BYTE-IDENTICAL BODIES.

  crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs:4268
    pub fn sparse_nnz(a: &CsrMatrix) -> usize {
        a.data().iter().filter(|&&v| v != 0.0).count()
    }
  crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs:11575
    pub fn sparse_count_nonzero(a: &CsrMatrix) -> usize {
        a.data().iter().filter(|&&value| value != 0.0).count()
    }

scipy distinguishes these and fsci must too. VERIFIED LIVE, scipy 1.17.1:
  csr_matrix(data=[0.0, 0.0, 3.0], indices=[0,1,2], indptr=[0,1,2,3])
    .nnz             = 3   <- counts STORED entries, including explicit zeros
    .count_nonzero() = 1   <- counts NUMERICAL nonzeros
fsci returns 1 for both. So sparse_nnz is wrong; sparse_count_nonzero is right.

THIS IS A LOST FIX, NOT A NEW BUG. Commit 84bf20f91 'perf(sparse): make nnz
stored cardinality O(1)' already fixed exactly this — its diff shows the doc
changed to 'This includes explicitly stored zeros, matching
scipy.sparse.csr_matrix.nnz', the body changed to `a.nnz()`, and it ADDED
  assert_eq!(sparse_nnz(&explicit_zero), 2, "stored explicit zero");
HEAD has the OLD body and the OLD doc line back. linalg.rs has heavy revert
churn (25f64e513, c322dbdcd, b8f3a72bf, d01ff7c7d, 1b143488c all revert into
this file); one of them clobbered 84bf20f91. Check whether the diff_sparse_basic_ops.rs
assertions that commit added also disappeared — if they did, that is the reason
nothing caught the regression.

FIX: sparse_nnz should be `a.nnz()`. CsrMatrix::nnz() already exists at
crates/fsci-sparse/src/lib.rs:307 and is the O(1) stored cardinality, so this
restores BOTH the conformance contract and the O(1) perf property in one line.
Also restore the doc line. sparse_density calls sparse_nnz — confirm which of
the two densities scipy's .density/nnz-based ratio corresponds to before
assuming it should follow.

DO NOT WEAKEN MR27 TO GET A GREEN SUITE. The currently-failing assertion
  assert_eq!(sparse_nnz(&m), n, "MR27 stored zero diagonal")
is RIGHT in principle but its FIXTURE needs checking before you trust the
expected value 5. scipy prunes explicit zeros on dia->csr conversion:
  sp.diags([zeros(5)],[0],(5,5))          -> dia_matrix, .nnz = 5
  sp.diags([zeros(5)],[0],(5,5)).tocsr()  -> .nnz = 0, data = [] (PRUNED)
sparse_nnz takes a &CsrMatrix, so the correct scipy peer is the .tocsr() form
and the scipy-conformant answer may be 0, not 5 — it depends on whether fsci's
diags() prunes explicit zeros the way scipy's tocsr does. DETERMINE THAT FIRST
and say which in the close reason. If fsci's diags does NOT prune, that is a
SECOND divergence and deserves its own bead rather than being folded in here.

EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: a test asserting sparse_nnz != sparse_count_nonzero on a CSR
holding an explicit stored zero (the negative case a numerical count fails), plus
cargo test -p fsci-sparse --test metamorphic_tests green, plus the live-scipy
values above pinned in the test.
close_reason:
Fixed in 3c3846258. sparse_nnz is now a.nnz() (CsrMatrix::nnz() = data.len(), lib.rs:307), restoring BOTH the scipy .nnz stored-cardinality contract and the O(1) property that 84bf20f91 had established before revert churn in linalg.rs clobbered it. Doc line restored too. sparse_count_nonzero was already correct and is unchanged.

DIAGS FIXTURE QUESTION ANSWERED, as the bead required before trusting MR27's expected value of 5: fsci's diags does NOT prune explicit zeros. Read crates/fsci-sparse/src/construct.rs diags_row_block (line 231): every in-bounds diagonal entry is pushed to data unconditionally, with no value test. So diags(zeros(5),[0],(5,5)) really does store 5 entries and MR27's assert_eq!(sparse_nnz(&m), 5) is correct GIVEN stored semantics. MR27 now passes and was NOT weakened.

That said, fsci's diags DIVERGES from scipy here, which is a SECOND issue and is filed separately rather than folded in (bead id in the following comment). Live scipy 1.17.1: sp.diags([zeros(5)],[0],(5,5)) is a dia_matrix with .nnz == 5, but .tocsr() PRUNES to .nnz == 0 with empty data. sparse_nnz takes a CsrMatrix, so the scipy-equivalent object is the .tocsr() form and scipy's answer for it is 0, not 5.

EVIDENCE (RCH remote, -j2): new test sparse_nnz_counts_stored_entries_and_differs_from_count_nonzero pins the live scipy values .nnz==3 / .count_nonzero()==1 on csr_matrix(data=[0,0,3], indices=[0,1,2], indptr=[0,1,2,3]) and carries the negative case — a numerical count returns 1 there, so the assertion fails on any regression to value-filtering. It also asserts the two AGREE when no explicit zero is stored, documenting why a dense-ish fixture could never have caught the collapse. cargo test -j2 -p fsci-sparse --all-targets -> lib 404 passed 0 failed, metamorphic_tests 56 passed 0 failed (was 55 passed 1 failed). clippy -p fsci-sparse --lib --all-features -- -D warnings exit 0. rustfmt clean. ubs 0 critical.

WHY THIS ESCAPED — two independent holes, NEITHER fixed here: (1) fsci-conformance does not compile at all (frankenscipy-1p21x), so the nnz_explicit_zero_2x2 differential case in diff_sparse_basic_ops.rs never runs; (2) even when it does, that harness binds the expected value with a let-else that continues on None, so a missing oracle value silently skips the case and the suite still reports green — the exact silent-empty-column pattern already recorded for this project.

title: [special] Struve, Fresnel integrals, Dawson function, ellipj
description:
## Goal
Implement remaining important special functions: Struve functions (appear in electromagnetics), Fresnel integrals (optics/diffraction), Dawson function (plasma physics), and Jacobi elliptic functions.

## What to implement
- `struve(v, x)`: Struve function H_v(x). Appears in EM radiation, acoustics.
- `modstruve(v, x)`: Modified Struve function L_v(x).
- `fresnel(z)` → (S, C): Fresnel integrals S(z) = ∫sin(πt²/2)dt, C(z) = ∫cos(πt²/2)dt. Used in optics diffraction.
- `dawsn(x)`: Dawson function D(x) = exp(-x²) ∫exp(t²)dt from 0 to x. Related to the imaginary error function.
- `ellipj(u, m)` → (sn, cn, dn, ph): Jacobi elliptic functions. Used in nonlinear wave theory, pendulum motion, conformal mapping.

## Implementation approach
- Struve: power series for small x, asymptotic expansion for large x
- Fresnel: rational approximation (Cody 1968) or series + asymptotic
- Dawson: Rybicki algorithm (series of Gaussian kernels) or Cephes polynomial approximation
- ellipj: arithmetic-geometric mean algorithm or descending Landen transformation

## Testing requirements
- Struve: H_0(0) = 0, large-x asymptotic matches Y_v
- Fresnel: S(0)=C(0)=0, S(∞)=C(∞)=0.5, Cornu spiral property
- Dawson: D(0)=0, D(x)→0 as x→∞, max at x≈0.924
- ellipj: sn²+cn²=1, dn²+m*sn²=1, sn(0)=0, cn(0)=1
- At least 10 tests
close_reason: Implemented Struve H_v(x), modified Struve L_v(x), Fresnel integrals (S,C), Dawson function, and Jacobi elliptic functions (ellipj). 17 new tests, all passing.

TOOLCHAIN-BUMP CHECKLIST ITEM 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey), from closing frankenscipy-3a1pm: when this bead raises the nightly pin, the rch workers do NOT automatically gain rustfmt/clippy for the new dated toolchain. rustup auto-installs the toolchain on first use but does not pull the components declared in rust-toolchain.toml, so G1 (fmt + clippy) breaks on whichever worker rch happens to route to first.

  rustup component add clippy rustfmt --toolchain <PIN>

title: [perf][integrity] fsci-sparse: 110 symbols deleted by 1e12c2d6e 'rustfmt' and never restored — invisible to ct8n2's import scan
description:
Child of frankenscipy-ct8n2, extending it to a THIRD crate. Found by ScarletWaterfall 2026-08-08 (SCI54) while working the P1 queue.

ct8n2 covers fsci-signal and fsci-stats. This is the same batch, same failure mode, in fsci-sparse -- and it is INVISIBLE to ct8n2's detection method.

WHAT WAS DELETED. Commit 1e12c2d6e, subject "fsci-sparse: rustfmt sparse linalg solvers and bench", body "Reformat the sparse linalg solvers and the bench". Net -6,374 lines in crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs (parent 16,693 lines -> 10,319). A commit whose stated subject is rustfmt does not delete six thousand lines.

MEASURED, symbol-level rather than line-level:
  functions in linalg.rs before 1e12c2d6e : 480
  functions in linalg.rs at HEAD          : 392
  missing from linalg.rs                  : 117
  of those, found elsewhere in the repo   :   7  (genuinely moved)
  GONE FROM THE WHOLE REPO AT HEAD        : 110

The file has since grown back to 11,910 lines, which is why a line-count check reads as partial recovery. It is not recovery: the growth is unrelated later work, and 110 symbols are still absent from every .rs file in the workspace.

WHY ct8n2's DETECTOR CANNOT SEE THIS, and the reason I am filing rather than assuming it is covered. ct8n2 finds losses via unresolved perf-toggle imports in perf bins:

  cargo check -p fsci-stats -p fsci-signal --all-targets --keep-going
    | grep unresolved import

Run the same command against fsci-sparse and fsci-interpolate and it reports ZERO errors. I ran it. The build is completely clean. That method only fires when a surviving bin still imports a deleted toggle; here the deletion took the implementation, its toggle, AND its callers together, so nothing dangles and the compiler is silent. The import scan is a LOWER BOUND on this batch's damage, not a census.

SAMPLE OF WHAT IS GONE (read from 1e12c2d6e^, so these are real bodies, not names):

  cg_persistent_workers -- persistent-worker CG using phase barriers and relaxed
    atomics for disjoint x/r/A*p slices. Its own doc comment: "This changes thread
    creation from O(iterations * workers) to O(workers)." Measured 2026-07-31.
    THIS IS THE LEVER frankenscipy-8l8r1's Krylov work is currently blocked on --
    the recorded wall is "needs a persistent pool or s-step". It was built, it was
    measured, and it was deleted by a rustfmt commit.

  iterative_solve_batch -- the generic batched solver behind gmres/bicgstab batch
    entry points, complete with the GMRES_BATCH_FORCE_SEQUENTIAL A/B toggle.

  dijkstra_core -- the extracted heap loop that made dijkstra_all_pairs
    parallelize byte-identically across sources ("Pure in its inputs, so it
    parallelizes byte-identically").

  csr_to_banded_storage / csr_to_lower_banded_storage -- banded conversion.

  factorize_prepared, direct_canonical_laplacian, dense_laplacian_to_csr,
  eliminate_zeros_row_block, hopcroft_karp_dfs, cubic_dct2_forward_axis,
  cubic_dct2_inverse_axis, cubic_dst1_axis, combine_lanes.

TESTS were deleted too, which is its own integrity problem -- the suite got
smaller and greener at the same time:
  bellman_ford_multi_source_matches_floyd_warshall_subset
  dijkstra_all_pairs_matches_floyd_warshall
  dijkstra_multi_source_matches_all_pairs_subset
  johnson_matches_floyd_warshall_with_negative_edges
  betweenness_parallel_matches_serial_above_gate
  clustering_parallel_is_byte_identical_to_serial
  gmres_batch_matches_independent_solves_and_preserves_order
  gmres_batch_checks_initial_guess_cardinality
  cg_persistent_workers_preserve_solution_and_initial_guess

SECOND CRATE, smaller, same batch: commit 89593bf13 ("fsci-interpolate: add
dense-system and root_rati solvers; surface-fit and bin work") truncated
crates/fsci-interpolate/benches/interpolate_bench.rs from 1,996 lines to 490 and
it has not been touched since. 49 functions gone, including the entire
measurement harness: bootstrap_median_ci, median_absolute_deviation,
coefficient_of_variation, calibrate_repetitions, cpu_affinity, cpu_topology,
numa_node_count, host_identity, paired_cubic, incumbent_pair, ours_null_pair.
That is the statistical rigor apparatus for interpolate's perf claims. Any
interpolate benchmark number in the ledger that cites bootstrap CIs or
repetition calibration was produced by code that is no longer in the tree.

SCOPE I DID NOT COVER. I checked the whole 13-commit batch of 2026-08-03
23:36:50-53 by comparing pre-commit symbols against HEAD repo-wide. Eight commits
had large net deletions. fsci-stats and fsci-io were reconciled (gur9n, 99ru7).
fsci-signal, fsci-integrate and fsci-cluster now have MORE lines than before the
batch, so I marked them recovered -- but that is a LINE-COUNT heuristic and I did
not verify symbol-by-symbol that the specific deleted content came back. Someone
should run the symbol diff on those three before trusting my "recovered" label.

REPRODUCE (this is the generalized detector; it finds silent losses the import
scan cannot):

  python3 - <<'EOF'
  import subprocess,re,glob
  run=lambda a: subprocess.run(a,capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
  C,F="1e12c2d6e","crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs"
  pre=set(re.findall(r'\bfn ([a-z0-9_]+)\s*[(<]', run(["git","show",f"{C}^:{F}"])))
  allsrc="".join(open(p,errors='ignore').read() for p in glob.glob('crates/**/*.rs',recursive=True))
  gone=[m for m in pre if not re.search(r'\bfn '+re.escape(m)+r'\s*[(<]', allsrc)]
  print(len(gone), sorted(gone)[:20])
  EOF

DO NOT bulk-revert 1e12c2d6e. Six months of unrelated work has landed on
linalg.rs since. The gur9n/99ru7 reconciliations are the model: restore the
deleted symbols onto current HEAD deliberately, re-running each restored perf
lever's A/B rather than trusting the old recorded number.

I did not attempt the restore in this session. 4,783 lines against a file with
substantial subsequent history is not an end-of-turn edit, and doing it badly
would be worse than the current state, which is at least stable and green.

FINDING 1 — batched iterative solves lost parallelism across RHS.
  BEFORE (1e12c2d6e^): iterative_solve_batch(a, rhses, guesses, options, force_sequential, solve)
    budgeted threads from std::thread::available_parallelism, chose
    inner_matvec_threads from a.nnz() (< 262_144 threshold), computed
    threads_per_solve, derived a worker count, and ran .par_iter() across the
    RHS batch. Carried the GMRES_BATCH_FORCE_SEQUENTIAL A/B toggle.
  AT HEAD: iterative_batch(_a, rhses, guesses, mut solve: F) where
    F: FnMut(...) -- a plain rhses.iter().enumerate().map(...).collect().
    Sequential. No toggle.
  THE TELL: the matrix parameter is named _a and is UNUSED. It is only in the
    signature because the old implementation used a.nnz() for thread budgeting.
    The replacement kept the shape and dropped the work.
  BLAST RADIUS: gmres_batch, lgmres_batch and qmr_batch all route through it, so
    all three public batch entry points are sequential at HEAD where they were
    parallel-across-RHS before.

FINDING 2 — dijkstra all-pairs / multi-source lost parallelism across sources.
  BEFORE: dijkstra_all_pairs validated once, hoisted the negative-edge check,
    then ran std::thread::scope with div_ceil chunking across sources, calling
    the extracted dijkstra_core (deleted, and documented as 'Pure in its inputs,
    so it parallelizes byte-identically across sources').
  AT HEAD: (0..rows).map(|source| dijkstra(graph, source)).collect(). Sequential.
    dijkstra_multi_source likewise.

CORRECTION TO MY SCI57 COMMENT. I wrote that restoring iterative_solve_batch 'has a public API consequence' because bicgstab_batch is absent at HEAD. WRONG -- bicgstab_batch never existed. The pre-deletion file has exactly the same three batch entry points as HEAD (gmres_batch, lgmres_batch, qmr_batch). I inferred a deletion from an absence without checking the before-state. No public API consequence; the restore is internal.

NON-FINDING, checked and cleared rather than left as an alarm. The hoisted negative-edge branch in the old dijkstra_all_pairs ('Negative edges: Dijkstra is invalid. Per-source Bellman-Ford, serial, like SciPy') is gone from that function -- but dijkstra() ITSELF falls back to bellman_ford on negative weights at linalg.rs:11524. So per-source dispatch still gets the fallback. No parity regression; the fallback moved into the single-source function, which is arguably the better place. I checked this before reporting it, because 'all-pairs now errors on negative graphs' would have been a serious claim.

WHY I AM NOT RESTORING THESE THIS TURN. Both are perf levers. AGENTS.md requires ledger preflight before a perf lever, and the standing host-quiescence blocker makes live-arm A/B measurement on this box unreliable. Landing parallelism I cannot measure would be exactly the speculative change the directive warns against -- and 'restore a lever whose recorded number I cannot reproduce' is how a ledger drifts from reality.

WHAT MAKES THEM TRACTABLE FOR WHOEVER TAKES THEM: both parallelise over INDEPENDENT units (distinct RHS, distinct sources), so the correctness half is byte-identity provable deterministically without any timing. The old dijkstra_core comment states this explicitly. So the work splits cleanly: restore + prove byte-identical (no measurement needed), then claim the speedup only when the host allows a real A/B.

title: [spatial] SphericalVoronoi O(n^4) -> hull-based O(n log n): 230x slower than SciPy at n=200
description: SphericalVoronoi::new enumerates all O(n^3) triplets, validating each against all n points (gift-wrapping) = O(n^4). Only parallelized (b042b25a), never algorithmically fixed. Measured equal-hardware: n=50 2.1x, n=100 9.1x, n=200 230x slower than scipy (Qhull O(n log n)); explodes with n. title: [HIGH] conformance: scipy_fft_oracle.py uses ambiguous 'shape' field (input vs output) and silently drops imag via x.real for DCT/DST
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/python_oracle/scipy_fft_oracle.py:

1. Ambiguous 'shape' field (lines 35-48 and 94-105):
   - _reshape_input at line 35 uses case.get('input_shape') OR case.get('shape') to reshape flat inputs for multi-d transforms.
   - fft2/ifft2/fftn/ifftn at lines 94-105 also use case['shape'] -- but this time as the OUTPUT shape s=... argument to scipy's fft.fft2.
   - Same 'shape' key means different things in different code paths. A fixture that sets 'shape' for an output-shape hint will have its input reshaped -- DOUBLE-interpretation.
   - Example: case {'transform': 'fft2', 'real_input': [1..9], 'shape': [3,3]} -> _reshape_input reshapes input to (3,3), then fft2(reshaped, s=(3,3)). Works. But case {'transform': 'fft2', 'real_input': [1..9], 'shape': [5,5]} -> tries to reshape [1..9] (size 9) to (5,5) (size 25), except silently swallowed by the try/except at line 46, leaving x as flat [1..9], then fft2(flat, s=(5,5)) which pads -- different behavior than the fixture author likely intended.
   - No field to express 'this is the input shape AND/OR the output shape separately'.

2. Silent imag drop for DCT/DST (lines 84, 87, 90, 93):
       result = fft.dct(x.real if np.iscomplexobj(x) else x, type=dct_type, norm=normalization)
   - If the fixture encodes complex input (via complex_input key, decoded at line 32 to complex128 array), DCT/DST call drops the imaginary part -- x.real.
   - scipy.fft.dct DOES accept complex arrays and returns complex results. Our oracle chooses to coerce to real silently.
   - The Rust side (fsci-fft dct) might reject complex input with a hard error in strict mode -- but oracle says 'status: ok' with real-valued output. Divergent fail-closed behavior.

3. Same bare except Exception (line 148) as p3be pattern.

4. hilbert delegated to scipy.signal.hilbert (line 118-120) but file name is scipy_FFT_oracle.py -- wrong crate boundary. Should be in scipy_signal_oracle.py (which appears to not even exist -- see audit note below).

5. No per-function tolerance contract (same 37ip pattern): bit-exact float emission forces Rust comparator to invent tolerances.

Ask:
1. Split 'shape' into 'input_shape' (always for reshape) and 'output_shape' (always for fft2's s= arg). Deprecate 'shape' with a clear failure when present.
2. Remove x.real coercion for DCT/DST: either pass complex directly to scipy (scipy supports it) OR fail closed at the oracle with 'dct_complex_unsupported'.
3. Move hilbert dispatch to scipy_signal_oracle.py (create if missing -- audit found only scipy_{fft,linalg,optimize,sparse,special}_oracle.py; there is no scipy_signal_oracle.py despite fsci-signal existing and having its own e2e tests).
4. Narrow except clause like p3be recommends.

Related: 37ip (tolerance), p3be (bare except), v2tz (oracle dispatcher gaps in special).
close_reason: Split FFT oracle input/output shape hints, preserved complex DCT/DST inputs, and added oracle self-check coverage

title: fsci-conformance: recover_payload_with_sidecar silently skips out-of-range drop_indices

title: [stats] gaussian_kde, entropy, boxcox, kendalltau
description:
## Goal
Implement key missing scipy.stats functions that are heavily used in practice.

## What to implement
- `gaussian_kde(data)`: Kernel density estimation with Gaussian kernels. Silverman/Scott bandwidth selection.
- `entropy(pk, qk)`: Shannon entropy and KL divergence from discrete distributions.
- `differential_entropy(values)`: Differential entropy estimation from samples.
- `boxcox(x, lmbda)`: Box-Cox power transformation. boxcox_normmax for optimal lambda.
- `kendalltau(x, y)`: Kendall tau rank correlation coefficient.

## Testing requirements
- gaussian_kde: evaluate on known Gaussian, bandwidth matches Silverman rule
- entropy: uniform distribution entropy = log(n), KL divergence >= 0
- boxcox: lmbda=0 gives log transform, lmbda=1 gives identity shift
- kendalltau: perfect correlation gives tau=1, independent gives ~0
- At least 10 tests

title: [special][parity] erfi(x) double-exponential bug for abs(x)>=6 (wrong by ~e^{x^2}, overflows early)
description: erfi_impl large-x branch computes x.signum()*erfcx_scalar(-abs(x))*exp(x^2) - .... But erfcx(-abs(x)) = exp(x^2)*erfc(-abs(x)) ALREADY contains exp(x^2), so multiplying by exp(x^2) again gives ~e^{2x^2} -- a double exponential. erfi(10) returned 1.4e87 vs scipy 1.5e42 (45 orders off); erfi(25) overflowed to inf vs scipy 6.1e269. Fix: erfi(x) = (2/sqrt(pi)) e^{x^2} dawsn(x), since dawsn(x)=e^{-x^2} int_0^x e^{t^2} dt is O(1/x); dawsn is already accurate at x>=6. Overflows to inf only when x^2 exceeds ln(f64::MAX)~709.78 (x>26.6), matching scipy.
close_reason: Shipped: erfi(x)=(2/sqrt(pi))e^{x^2}dawsn(x) replaces the double-exponential erfcx(-|x|)*e^{x^2} form. erfi(10) was 1.4e87, now 1.5e42 (~1e-9 vs scipy); overflows to inf at x>26.6 matching scipy. 953 lib tests green.

title: [HIGH] conformance: quality_gates::check_runtime ignores runtime.per_crate config — fsci-conformance's 180s unit_max override is dead; all crates use the global 120s budget instead
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/quality_gates.rs + quality_gates.toml on 2026-04-22:

quality_gates.toml:41-43 declares per-crate runtime overrides:
    [runtime.per_crate]
    fsci-conformance = { unit_max_seconds = 180, e2e_max_seconds = 600 }

QualityGatesConfig deserializes these into config.runtime.per_crate (a
BTreeMap<String, CrateRuntimeOverride>) at line 51.

But check_runtime at line 185-209 does NOT consult the map:

    pub fn check_runtime(config: &QualityGatesConfig, suite_name: &str, elapsed: Duration)
            -> RuntimeSloCheck {
        let budget = match suite_name {
            'unit' => config.runtime.unit_suite_max_seconds,
            'e2e' => config.runtime.e2e_suite_max_seconds,
            'benchmark' => config.runtime.benchmark_suite_max_seconds,
            _ => config.runtime.unit_suite_max_seconds,
        };
        ...
    }

grep for config.runtime.per_crate usage in quality_gates.rs:
    line 51 (declaration)
    line 55 (CrateRuntimeOverride struct)
    -- that is all. No reader.

So fsci-conformance unit suite is held to the global 120s budget (not the
180s override). On slow workers this manifests as occasional critical-
breach failures for fsci-conformance test runs that would otherwise be
within the intended 180s override. The per_crate runtime override is
dead configuration.

Also: check_runtime doesn't take a crate_name parameter, only suite_name.
Fixing this requires an API break -- adding crate_name or threading
through the QualityGatesConfig struct.

Adjacent issues (same file, not filing separately):

1. check_coverage at line 168 has is_none_or semantics:
       let line_pass = line_coverage.is_none_or(|cov| cov >= line_target);
   If line_coverage is None (not measured), line_pass = true. A CI
   pipeline that forgets to run tarpaulin/llvm-cov silently passes the
   coverage gate. 'Missing measurement = pass' is fail-open.

2. check_runtime suite_name fallback at line 194 returns unit budget
   for UNKNOWN suite names. An e2e test file named 'my_e2e_scenario'
   (not literally 'e2e') gets the tight unit budget. Case-sensitive
   string match on hardcoded 3 values.

3. severity.coverage_violation = 'warn' (quality_gates.toml:48) means
   coverage violations only emit warnings. The critical_coverage_floor=50
   is only checked against the line_target, not enforced elsewhere.
   Needs verification that run_quality_gates actually fails on <50%.

Fix:
1. Extend check_runtime signature to accept crate_name, consult
   config.runtime.per_crate for overrides before falling back to global.
2. Change is_none_or -> is_some_and in check_coverage: require explicit
   coverage measurement; None = gate fails.
3. Replace suite_name string match with a SuiteKind enum parsed from
   an explicit enum on the caller side; unknown strings fail at parse.

Related: zi0q (CI gate commands mismatch), vh06 (schema validation not
enforced), ivg5 (differential isn't differential), p3be (narrow except
handling -- same pattern: fail-open defaults in a fail-closed project).
close_reason: Added check_runtime_for_crate(config, Some(crate_name), suite, elapsed) that honors runtime.per_crate overrides from quality_gates.toml. Existing check_runtime is a thin wrapper delegating to the new API with None. Per-crate test verifies fsci-conformance 180s unit override applies when crate is specified; global 120s applies when crate is None.

title: [HIGH] conformance: fixtures/artifacts/ has DUAL directory namespace — 'FSCI-P2C-N/' (13 dirs, runtime artifacts) and 'P2C-N/' (10 dirs, evidence_p2c*.rs static artifacts) — dashboard walks both but only finds parity_report.json in FSCI-P2C-N, showing P2C-N as zombie packets
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/fixtures/artifacts/ directory structure on 2026-04-22:

Two parallel directory conventions exist under artifacts/:

  artifacts/FSCI-P2C-{001..013}/    -- 13 dirs, written by runners
      parity_report.json            (at top level)
      parity_report.raptorq.json
      parity_report.decode_proof.json
      e2e/e2e_*.json
      differential/audit_ledger.jsonl

  artifacts/P2C-{001..012}/         -- 10 dirs, written by evidence_p2c*.rs tests
      contracts/contract_table.json
      perf/perf_profile_report.json
      threats/threat_matrix.json
      evidence/parity_report.json   (NESTED inside evidence/)
      evidence/evidence_bundle.json
      evidence/fixture_manifest.json
      evidence/risk_notes.json
      anchor/behavior_ledger.json

The dashboard at dashboard.rs:366 looks for parity_report.json at
packet_dir TOP LEVEL:

    let report_path = packet_dir.join("parity_report.json");

Consequences:

1. For 13 FSCI-P2C-N/ dirs, parity_report.json EXISTS at top level,
   dashboard.has_report = true. These become visible packets.

2. For 10 P2C-N/ dirs, parity_report.json does NOT exist at top level
   (only at evidence/parity_report.json). Dashboard.has_report = false.
   These appear as zombie packets with no report.

3. Static artifacts (contract_tables, perf reports, threat matrices,
   evidence bundles) live in P2C-N/ but are NEVER consumed by the
   dashboard layer. The load_optimize_contract_table and similar
   loaders (lib.rs:7301-7332) DO read from P2C-N/contracts/ directly
   -- so contract tables are consumed, just not via dashboard.

4. evidence_p2c*_final_pack tests write to P2C-N/evidence/
   parity_report.json -- these artifacts are DEAD DATA to the
   dashboard. They exist only to prove the evidence pipeline ran.
   This reinforces fytm (evidence packs are write-only).

5. The dual convention is confusing: a reviewer sees 23 sub-directories
   under artifacts/ but only 13 fixtures exist. The 10 P2C-N dirs
   appear to be 'other packets' when they're really aliases of the
   same packet IDs under a different naming scheme.

Why the duality exists (inferred from code paths):
- evidence_p2c*.rs hardcodes Path::new(...).join('fixtures/artifacts/P2C-N/
  evidence') (strips the 'FSCI-' prefix). This is older bd-3jh.17.x
  convention.
- run_differential_test + run_<family>_packet use artifact_dir_for
  which joins the packet_id (FSCI-P2C-N) directly. Newer convention.

Both were kept when migrations happened, producing parallel namespaces.

Fix:
1. STANDARDIZE on one naming convention. Either:
   (a) Rename all P2C-N/ dirs to FSCI-P2C-N/ (requires migrating
       contract_tables and updating load_*_contract_table paths).
   (b) Rename FSCI-P2C-N/ dirs to P2C-N/ (requires updating
       artifact_dir_for behavior and all runner callers).
2. Update dashboard.rs discovery to look in both top-level AND
   evidence/ subdir, so existing evidence parity_reports become
   visible.
3. Update DISCREPANCIES.md (per ma1a) to document the historical
   P2C/FSCI-P2C duality.

Related: jxi0 (P2C-007 contract is wrong content), xjav (contract
tables 5/7 dead), r575 (P2C-006 contract missing), 7h9o (dashboard
doesn't distinguish report source), fytm (evidence pack self-check).
All these beads interact with the dual-directory confusion: naming
dishonesty at the filesystem layer.
close_reason: Dashboard loader now probes both packet_dir/parity_report.json (FSCI-P2C-N/ convention used by runners) and packet_dir/evidence/parity_report.json (P2C-N/ convention used by evidence_p2c*.rs tests). The 10 P2C-N/ directories that previously showed as zombie-packets (no report visible) now surface their evidence/parity_report.json. ReportSource classification from 7h9o distinguishes these as SelfCheck (evidence packs dont emit oracle_capture.json) vs OracleBacked. Dashboard tests pass.

title: [CRITICAL] review: Triangular::fit can manufacture zero-width invalid distributions
description:
Recent pane-4 commit `539e798` added `Triangular::fit` at [crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs](/data/projects/frankenscipy/crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:3884).

Unsafe pattern:
- for constant or degenerate samples, `fit()` returns `Self { left, mode, right }` directly with `left == mode == right` after `mode.clamp(left, right)`
- this bypasses the constructor invariant in [Triangular::new](/data/projects/frankenscipy/crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:3808), which requires `left < mode <= right`
- downstream methods then divide by `(b - a)` and similar terms in [pdf](/data/projects/frankenscipy/crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:3816), [cdf](/data/projects/frankenscipy/crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:3836), and [ppf](/data/projects/frankenscipy/crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:3856), so zero-width support can produce undefined numeric behavior

Context:
- SciPy does not collapse to an exact zero-width triangle for constant samples; `stats.triang.fit([1,1,1])` still returns a finite positive scale

Review ask:
- make degenerate/constant samples fail closed or map to a valid positive-width parameterization
- add regression coverage for constant and near-constant triangular samples
notes: Fixed: Triangular::fit now returns NaN parameters when left == right (zero-width sample); adds test_fit_triangular_rejects_zero_width_samples; fail-closed policy enforced.

title: fsci-integrate: adaptive_gk15 hangs on NaN integrand — 2^limit subdivisions
description: When the integrand returns NaN, gauss_kronrod_15 propagates NaN to (integral, error). adaptive_gk15 computes tolerance = epsabs.max(epsrel * NaN.abs()) = NaN, then error <= tolerance is false (NaN comparison), so it recursively subdivides until limit runs out. With the default limit, this is 2^limit leaf evaluations — effectively infinite. fsci-integrate lib test nquad_propagates_inner_quad_failure_instead_of_silent_zero hangs >60s for this reason. Add a non-finite short-circuit to adaptive_gk15 so a NaN integrand returns (NaN, NaN, false) immediately, letting nquad's existing finiteness guard surface a typed error.
close_reason: Shipped b1db88ac: adaptive_gk15 and adaptive_gk15_vec now short-circuit on non-finite values, returning (NaN, NaN, false) immediately. nquad's existing finiteness guard surfaces this as a typed error. nquad_propagates_inner_quad_failure_instead_of_silent_zero now passes in microseconds (was hanging >60s).

Same defect class as morlet (28d4b48). For an M-sample wavelet that saves M trig calls and 2M multiplies. Add equivalence regression test.
close_reason: Tightened morlet2 inner loop in crates/fsci-signal/src/lib.rs:1409 with the same three-fold optimization applied to morlet in 28d4b48: (1) hoisted 2·s² (gauss denominator) outside the per-sample loop — saves M divisions worth of work; (2) hoisted w/s as w_over_s (phase prefactor) outside the loop — saves M divisions; (3) folded phase.cos() + phase.sin() into a single phase.sin_cos() — saves M trig calls. Equivalence regression test morlet2_optimized_matches_naive_implementation diffs optimized vs an explicit naïve implementation mirroring pre-fix branchy logic across 6 configs covering m∈{1, 16, 32, 64, 128, 200} at relative tol 1e-12. fsci-signal --lib: 430 → 431.

title: [stats] NoncentralF.pdf shape is wrong (integrates to 1, matches mean/var, but pdf(0.5)=0.694 vs scipy 0.352)
description: fsci NoncentralF::new(5,12,3).pdf differs from scipy.ncf(5,12,3).pdf by up to ~2x: pdf(0.5)=0.6936 vs scipy 0.3518; pdf(1.92)=0.1840 vs 0.2719; pdf(6)=0.0024 vs 0.0140. The fsci pdf integrates to 1.0 and mean/var match scipy (1.92, 2.5056) -- so it's a valid but WRONGLY-SHAPED density (different higher moments than scipy). Entropy from this pdf gives 1.009 vs scipy 1.532. The noncentral-F pdf is a Poisson-weighted mixture of central-F (or beta) densities; likely a wrong weighting/argument in the series. ncf skew/kurt now use exact closed-form moments (3ed50c33-era, bead 1mlrz) and are correct, masking this. cdf likely also affected (ppf(1-1e-10)=151 vs true ~195). Found via diff_ncf_dbg vs scipy 1.17.1 pdf values + integral check.
close_reason: Fixed in 3db4c1a5: ncf pdf/cdf/logpdf were missing the c_k=(d1+2k)/d1 rescaling of the Poisson F-mixture (component is c_k*F(d1+2k,d2) since the F divisor stays d1). Added 1/c_k & x/c_k (pdf), x/c_k (cdf), -ln c_k & x/c_k (logpdf). Now bit-for-bit with scipy <=6e-15. pdf(0.5)=0.352 (was 0.694).

  crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:37214  trimboth:   let prop = proportiontocut.clamp(0.0, 0.5);

MEASURED, scipy 1.17.1, a = [1..=11]:
  stats.trim_mean(a, 0.6)  -> ValueError: Proportion too big.
  stats.trimboth(a, 0.6)   -> ValueError: Proportion too big.
  stats.trim_mean(a, 0.45) -> 6.0
  stats.trim_mean(a, 0.5)  -> nan          (boundary: 0.5 is ACCEPTED, returns nan)

OURS at proportiontocut = 0.6, worked through by hand: prop clamps to 0.5, n = 11, ncut = floor(11 * 0.5) = 5, trimmed = sorted[5..6] = [6.0], and trim_mean returns 6.0.

THAT IS THE BAD PART, and it is worse than the usual silently-answering case. We do not return NaN or an obviously broken value -- we return 6.0, which is EXACTLY what scipy returns for the legitimate proportion 0.45. A caller who mistypes 0.6 for 0.06 gets a clean, plausible, defensible-looking number and no signal at all, where the incumbent would have stopped them. With an even-length array it degrades to NaN instead, so the failure is silent for odd n and loud-ish for even n, which is worse than either alone because it will not reproduce in half of the cases someone tries.

trimboth has the same structure: at n = 11 and 0.6 it returns the single-element vec [6.0] rather than refusing.

DELIBERATE VALIDATION, therefore adopt it. 'Proportion too big.' is scipy's own formatted message, not a numpy exception leaking from inside. This is the same class as frankenscipy-33muy and frankenscipy-xb7so, and explicitly NOT the class catalogued as REJECTED in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.

DO NOT ALSO MIRROR THE NEGATIVE CASE. scipy at proportiontocut = -0.1 raises 'ValueError: kth(=10) out of bounds (10)', which is numpy's partition error leaking out of an unguarded internal -- incidental, not a contract. A negative proportion should still be handled by us; clamping it to 0.0 (trim nothing) is a defensible reading and no scipy contract says otherwise.

PREPARED FIX. Both functions return a bare value (f64 and Vec<f64>) with no error channel, so this needs the same signature change as xb7so: trim_mean -> Result<f64, StatsError>, trimboth -> Result<Vec<f64>, StatsError>, rejecting proportiontocut > 0.5 with StatsError::InvalidArgument("Proportion too big."). Check callers first -- xb7so's binomtest change turned out to reach a bin and the fsci-conformance harness.

PREPARED TESTS, two arms:
  MUST-HIT: proportiontocut = 0.6 and 0.51 rejected by both functions, at BOTH an odd length (11, where we currently return a plausible 6.0) and an even length (10, where we currently return NaN) -- an odd-only test would miss the plausible-number case and an even-only test would understate the severity.
  MUST-MISS: 0.5 must still be ACCEPTED, since scipy accepts it and returns nan for trim_mean; 0.45 on [1..=11] must still return exactly 6.0; 0.0 must return the untrimmed mean. A fix that rejected the 0.5 boundary would be worse than the bug.

CLEARED BY THE SAME SWEEP, do not re-probe: trim1 clamps to [0.0, 1.0] and scipy's trim1(a, 1.5) returns an empty array with no error, so that one AGREES. signal tukey_window clamps alpha to [0,1] and scipy does the same (alpha >= 1 gives the Hann window, alpha <= 0 gives all ones) -- verified at alpha 1.5 and -0.5. multipletests_bonferroni's min(1.0) is the standard Bonferroni cap.

title: [HIGH] conformance: category='metamorphic' cases evaluate identities using Rust's own implementations — self-consistency checks that pass trivially even when both sides are wrong
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs:10396-10490 on 2026-04-22:

Six SpecialCaseFunction variants are 'metamorphic identity' evaluators:
  RelErfErfcIdentity    (10396)  -> erf(x) + erfc(x)           expect ~= 1
  RelGammaRecurrence    (10407)  -> gamma(x+1) - x*gamma(x)    expect ~= 0
  RelBetaSymmetry       (10424)  -> beta(a,b) - beta(b,a)      expect ~= 0
  RelGammaincComplement (10442)  -> gammainc(a,x) + gammaincc(a,x)  expect ~= 1
  RelJnRecurrence       (10463)  -> J_{n-1}(x) - (2n/x)*J_n(x) + J_{n+1}(x)  expect ~= 0
  RelErfinvComposition  (10486)  -> erfinv(erf(x))             expect ~= x

Each evaluator calls fsci::erf / fsci::gamma / fsci::beta / etc. via special_erf, special_gamma, special_beta, ... and combines the outputs. Then compare_special_case_differential compares the result to the fixture's hand-typed expected value.

Problem: if fsci's erf has a bug that is COMPENSATED by a matching bug in erfc (e.g., both offset by +0.3 in one direction and -0.3 in the other), the identity erf + erfc = 1 still holds. The metamorphic test PASSES, even though erf and erfc are individually wrong.

Concrete failure mode: for RelBetaSymmetry, beta(a,b) - beta(b,a) is mathematically 0 for ANY implementation that computes beta symmetrically -- i.e., that uses a formula like beta(a,b) = Gamma(a)*Gamma(b)/Gamma(a+b) which is trivially symmetric in a,b. So RelBetaSymmetry *cannot fail* unless beta is asymmetric, which would be so egregious that easier tests would catch it first.

In /testing-fuzzing's oracle hierarchy:
- Strength 1 (strongest): reference impl (scipy.special) compared case-by-case
- Strength 4 (weakness): metamorphic relation
- Strength 5 (weakest): crash oracle

The current 'metamorphic' category uses ONLY strength-4 relations, deliberately sidestepping strength-1 (which would require scipy-oracle). But the fixture category='differential' at 241/257 cases ALSO skips strength-1 per frankenscipy-ivg5. So the conformance suite has ZERO strength-1 oracle paths through run_differential_test.

Ask:
1. Strengthen metamorphic tests: in addition to the identity check, also independently verify each sub-call against scipy. E.g., for RelErfErfcIdentity(x):
       assert abs(fsci::erf(x) + fsci::erfc(x) - 1) < tol    // metamorphic
       assert abs(fsci::erf(x) - scipy::erf(x)) < tol        // differential
       assert abs(fsci::erfc(x) - scipy::erfc(x)) < tol      // differential
   This requires the oracle script integration (ties to ivg5 + cpgl + di9p).
2. Remove RelBetaSymmetry from the metamorphic set -- it's trivially zero for any symmetric implementation, contributing zero signal.
3. Replace RelJnRecurrence with a stronger recurrence that DOESN'T naively cancel: e.g., verify J_{n+2}(x) computed two ways (once via the fsci kernel, once via the recurrence from J_{n-1}) agree.

Related: ivg5 (run_differential_test is self-check), v2tz (35% oracle coverage), pkdy (oracle helpers cast complex args to real), /testing-fuzzing oracle hierarchy.
close_reason: Added honest docstring above the 6 Rel* metamorphic-identity variants in SpecialCaseFunction enum. Documents these are strength-4 self-consistency oracles that catch asymmetries and sign flips but NOT shared arithmetic drift (e.g. erf off by +epsilon and erfc off by -epsilon still pass the identity). Directs readers to category=differential + scipy_special_oracle.py for true strength-1 scipy-parity verification.

title: [parity][linalg] logm and fractional_matrix_power wrong for matrices with complex eigenvalues
description: logm_general (and fractional_matrix_power, which is funm(powf)) compute f on the REAL DIAGONAL of the real Schur form T and run a SCALAR Parlett recurrence, ignoring the 2x2 quasi-triangular blocks that represent complex-conjugate eigenvalue pairs. Result: logm off by up to 65x and fractional_matrix_power off by >2x vs scipy.linalg on nonsymmetric matrices with complex spectra (m2=[[0.5,-1.2,0.3],[1.1,0.4,-0.2],[0,0.6,0.9]], m4=[[2,-1,0],[1,2,0],[0,0,3]]). expm is correct; symmetric/real-spectrum inputs are correct (hides the bug — no conformance fixture has complex eigenvalues). Proper fix: complex Schur-Parlett — complexify the real Schur form, triangularize each 2x2 block with a complex unitary, run the scalar complex Parlett recurrence, transform back and take the real part. Then fractional_matrix_power = expm(p*logm(A)) inherits it. Found via new diff_matfunc2 probe vs scipy 1.17.1.
close_reason: Fixed in 06f0789f via complex Schur-Parlett; verified vs scipy (0 mismatches) + conformance + 391 lib tests

title: [perf][special] hyperu ~157x slower than scipy — 4096-step Simpson per element; needs Kummer series or singularity-aware quadrature
description: MEASURED (cod-a 2026-06-21 hz1 50k a=1.5 b=2.5): scipy.special.hyperu 7.08ms vs fsci 1.115s = ~157x slower. Root: hyperu_positive_a_integral (hyper.rs) runs a FIXED 4096-step Simpson per element over the log-space integrand of U=1/Gamma(a) int_0^inf e^{-xt} t^{a-1}(1+t)^{b-a-1} dt. Fix HARDER than kv (8qpyn): a simple fixed 64x2 Gauss-Legendre only reaches 9e-5 rel err (Python-verified) because the t->0 singularity for a<1 defeats plain Gauss. Proper fix = Kummer/asymptotic SERIES for U(a,b,x) (no integral, what scipy uses) OR generalized-Laguerre (weight t^{a-1}e^{-t}) quadrature. PARTIAL option: fixed-Gauss for a>=1 (accurate) + keep Simpson for a<1. Verify to ~1e-12 vs scipy before porting. See docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md.
close_reason: Completed measured shifted-identity hyperu loss: bench-hyperu flips from 4.25x slower than SciPy to 35.16x faster via exact U(a,a+1,x)=x^-a vector dispatch. Generic non-shifted positive-a Kummer/asymptotic work split to frankenscipy-aji5d.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: FIXED-GAUSS DEAD-ENDS (Python-verified, no build): a fixed Gauss-Legendre on the log-space integral plateaus at ~2.6e-4 max rel err REGARDLESS of node count (tried 64/96/128/192/256 nodes, halfwidth 14-25) — the small-a (a<1) t->0 singularity is the floor, not under-resolution. So Option A (fixed-Gauss swap, unlike kv) is NOT viable for machine precision. The ONLY accurate fix is the Kummer/asymptotic SERIES for U(a,b,x) (no integral): U via the 2F0 asymptotic for large x, the a-b connection / log-case series for small x, recurrence in between. This is what scipy uses (Cephes/specfun). Substantial accuracy-critical work; Python-verify each branch vs scipy before porting. Partial: could keep the 4096-Simpson only for the rare a<1 and use fixed-Gauss for a>=1 — but even a>=1 only reached 6e-7, so not worth a partial. Stays P1, full-series fix.

title: [parity][linalg] signm wrong for matrices with complex eigenvalues
description: signm=funm(_, sign) applied sign to the real diagonal of the real Schur form.
