title: [signal] gauspuls accepts zero center frequency like SciPy
description: Code-first fallback from empty br ready and stale cod-b residue. SciPy signal.gausspulse(..., retquad=True, retenv=True) accepts fc=0 and returns unit in-phase/envelope with zero quadrature, while fsci_signal::gauspuls rejects fc=0 as invalid. Allow finite non-negative fc, keep negative/non-finite rejection, and lock inline parity coverage. code-first, batch-test pending
close_reason:
Closed 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey), bulk reconciliation under frankenscipy-5ucdi. VERIFIED ALREADY IMPLEMENTED, both halves, with SciPy measured.

SCIPY (1.17.1): gausspulse(t, fc=0) is ACCEPTED and returns [1., 1.]; gausspulse(t, fc=-1) RAISES ValueError('Center frequency (fc=-1.00) must be >=0.'). So the contract is fc >= 0, not fc > 0.

FSCI matches exactly: gauspuls at crates/fsci-signal/src/lib.rs:13702 guards with '!(fc >= 0.0 && fc.is_finite())' -- the >= admits zero while still rejecting negatives and non-finites. It also guards bw > 0 and bwr < 0 alongside.

COVERAGE: gauspuls_zero_center_frequency_matches_scipy at :27839, calling gauspuls(&[0.0, 0.1], 0.0, 0.5, -6.0).expect("zero fc") -- the acceptance is asserted directly, which is the only way to cover an ACCEPT-shaped contract.

NAMING NOTE for anyone searching: scipy spells it gausspulse (double s, trailing e) and it lives in scipy.signal; this bead and fsci's Result-returning entry point both spell it gauspuls. fsci ALSO has a separate gausspulse at :2406 returning a bare Vec. Searching scipy's spelling in fsci, or fsci's in scipy, finds nothing -- I initially got AttributeError from scipy.signal.gauspuls. Nothing to implement.

title: [parity][special] elliprj negative-p Cauchy principal value returns NaN, scipy computes finite
description: fsci_special::elliptic::elliprj returns NaN for p<0 ("Cauchy-PV branch — deferred for now"), but scipy.special.elliprj computes the finite Cauchy principal value (e.g. elliprj(1,2,3,-1)=-0.0932404524386764). Implement via Carlson 1995 / Boost negative-p reduction: sort x<=y<=z, q=-p, pmy=(z-y)(y-x)/(y+q), pn=pmy+y, RJ = (pmy*RJ(x,y,z,pn) - 3*RF(x,y,z) + 3*sqrt(xyz/(xz+pn*q))*RC(xz+pn*q, pn*q))/(y+q). p==0 stays NaN; two-or-more zeros stays inf. Verified vs scipy 1.17.1 over 2000 cases, max relerr 1.2e-15.
close_reason: Fixed in 55d44396: elliprj p<0 Cauchy PV via Carlson/Boost reduction; verified vs scipy 1.17.1 over 2000 cases (max relerr 1.2e-15), 8 elliprj + 106 elliptic tests pass.

Eliminate all 16 stub sites with real implementations or explicit errors.

2. Tests cover each replaced stub
3. No downstream crate broken by the changes

## Serves Project Goal

ArrayAPI is the foundation layer. Stubs here create hidden landmines for every module that uses it.

title: [parity-gap] hyperu(a,b,x) a<0 non-int, b non-int, large x: connection formula cancels catastrophically
description: For a<0 non-integer and b non-integer, hyperu_scalar uses the Gamma-weighted connection formula U = c1 M(a,b,x) + c2 x^{1-b} M(a-b+1,2-b,x). Both 1F1 terms grow like e^x while U is recessive (~x^{-a}), so at large x they cancel catastrophically: hyperu(-0.5,-1.5,50) returned -3.16e8 vs scipy 7.21, and -5.3e74 at x=200. Breakdown onsets near x=18-20 and worsens. Fix: try the cancellation-free DLMF 13.7.3 asymptotic U ~ x^{-a} sum (a)_k (a-b+1)_k (-1/x)^k / k! with optimal truncation first; accept when its smallest-term floor is below 1e-7 rel, else fall back to the small-x-accurate connection formula. 288-case (a,b,x) grid now 0 mismatches vs scipy 1.17.1 (a in [-3.5,1.5], x in [2,200]). Cases where a-b+1 is a nonpositive integer were already clean (one connection term has a 0 Gamma coefficient).
close_reason: Fixed in 467daa6b: DLMF 13.7.3 large-x asymptotic (cancellation-free) tried before the connection formula, accepted when its optimal-truncation floor is <1e-7 rel. 288-case grid 0 mismatches vs scipy 1.17.1 (was -3e8/-5e74 at x=50/200).

title: [HIGH] conformance: scipy_optimize_oracle.py references undefined 'shifted_quadratic' objective; _get_objective silently returns lambda: NaN for unknown names; _get_root_function same pattern
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/python_oracle/scipy_optimize_oracle.py:

1. 'shifted_quadratic' orphan (line 178):
   - _get_jacobian_and_hessian maps 'shifted_quadratic' to (_shifted_quadratic_grad, _shifted_quadratic_hess) which ARE defined at lines 81-91 and are the mathematically CORRECT derivatives of f(x)=(x0-1)^2 + 4*(x1+2)^2.
   - But the _get_objective map (line 151-171) has NO entry for 'shifted_quadratic'. It only has 'scaled_quadratic' which points to _scaled_quadratic -- a function with the SAME formula but MISMATCHED derivatives (see frankenscipy-pqka).
   - Root-cause hypothesis: a rename scaled_quadratic <-> shifted_quadratic was started but left incomplete. The 'correct' derivative helpers now exist under the 'shifted' name while the broken derivatives are under 'scaled'.

2. Silent NaN fallback (line 172):
       return objectives.get(name, lambda x: float('nan'))
   - If the Rust conformance case specifies objective='shifted_quadratic' (or any typo / unknown name), scipy.optimize.minimize receives a function returning NaN everywhere.
   - With jac hint present (for trust-exact), scipy iterates with NaN function values and non-NaN gradients -> returns garbage x / fun / nit / nfev.
   - The oracle writes status='ok' with those garbage numbers -- Rust side then has to 'match' garbage.

3. Same pattern in _get_root_function (line 201):
       return funcs.get(name, lambda x: float('nan'))
   - Unknown root-function names silently become 'find root of NaN', which scipy reports as not-converged or raises.

Fix:
1. Decide which of scaled_quadratic / shifted_quadratic is canonical. Either:
   (a) Delete _shifted_quadratic_grad/hess and fix _scaled_quadratic_grad/hess (the pqka fix), OR
   (b) Add _shifted_quadratic objective function and remove _scaled_quadratic* entirely.
2. Change _get_objective fallback to RAISE KeyError(f'unknown objective: {name}') instead of lambda NaN. Same for _get_root_function. Fail-closed doctrine demands unknown names fail the oracle, not manufacture 'ok' responses.
3. Add a test asserting every key in _get_jacobian_and_hessian has a matching entry in _get_objective (schema consistency gate).

Related: pqka (mismatched grad/hess for scaled/translated), m9jp (stirling2 formula error -- analogous class of bug), p3be (bare except hides cascading errors).
close_reason: Completed

title: [perf][harness] nine *_many harnesses still fail-closed on absolute host quiescence and have never produced a ratio
description:
SPLIT OFF FROM THE TRUNCWEIBULL CONVERSION (PeachSummit, 2026-08-16), which is the template.

WHAT IS WRONG. Nine live-incumbent harnesses call a fail-closed `require_host_wide_quiescence(phase)`
that returns `Err` when ANY single CPU exceeds `HOST_QUIESCENCE_MAX_BUSY = 0.20` over a 400 ms
window. On a shared 64-way box with a dozen concurrent agents that condition is never met, so the
harness aborts before it measures anything. The effect is not rigour; it is that these binaries have
established live-SciPy incumbent arms and NO ratio against them.

```
crates/fsci-stats/src/bin/perf_truncweibull_scipy.rs   -- CONVERTED, use as the template
crates/fsci-stats/src/bin/perf_normality_many_scipy.rs
crates/fsci-opt/src/bin/perf_minimize_many_scipy.rs
crates/fsci-opt/src/bin/perf_curve_fit_many_scipy.rs
crates/fsci-opt/src/bin/perf_newton_many_scipy.rs
crates/fsci-opt/src/bin/perf_root_many_scipy.rs
crates/fsci-integrate/src/bin/perf_quad_many_scipy.rs
crates/fsci-integrate/src/bin/perf_dblquad_many_scipy.rs
crates/fsci-integrate/src/bin/perf_tplquad_many_scipy.rs
crates/fsci-sparse/src/bin/perf_gmres_job_vs_scipy.rs
```
`perf_sparse_nnz.rs` and `perf_sparse.rs` already return a bool and sample rather than abort --
check them, do not assume.

THE SUBSTITUTION IS A DESIGN, NOT A RELAXATION, and the ledger side of it was already amended on
2026-08-15 by RosePelican: `scripts/ledger_preflight.py` admits
`host_wide_quiescence_<phase>=NOT_CERTIFIED(host_mean_busy=N)` ONLY for a row that also carries
same-invocation A/A nulls, because the null DETECTS the contention that quiescence tried to exclude
in advance, and does it by measuring the interference that actually occurred rather than asserting
in advance that none would. Every harness listed above already interleaves independent A/A nulls per
round, so each already carries the detector that makes the NOT_CERTIFIED form admissible. Only the
harness side is outstanding.

MEASURED SUPPORT for dropping the ABSOLUTE bound specifically (docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md,
2026-08-16, six splu balanced-square runs): the busiest sample on record, a saturated box at
`host_mean_busy=0.988`, produced the TIGHTEST A/A null of any run (0.0053); the quietest at 0.135
produced the loosest that still passed (0.0198). Absolute load and null failure are ordered
INVERSELY in that data. A load-DELTA criterion did not reproduce there either, so do NOT add one --
the null is the gate.

RECIPE, exactly as applied to `perf_truncweibull_scipy.rs`:
1. rename `require_host_wide_quiescence` -> `report_host_wide_quiescence` (the name was the bug).
2. accumulate `total_busy_fraction` alongside `maximum_busy_fraction`; `host_mean_busy = total / cpus`.
3. keep printing `=clear` when no CPU exceeds the limit -- clear is still the strongest form and a
   row that can claim it should.
4. otherwise print, and RETURN `Ok`:
   `host_wide_quiescence_<phase>=NOT_CERTIFIED(host_mean_busy=N) sampled_cpus=.. maximum_busy_fraction=.. busy_cpu_count_above_limit=.. limit=.. gate=same_invocation_A/A_nulls busy_cpus=<cpu:pct,..>`
   The NOT_CERTIFIED spelling is matched by `HOST_WIDE_QUIESCENCE_NOT_CERTIFIED_RE`; do not reformat it.
5. do NOT touch the null gate, the bootstrap-median CI, the 2x null margin, parity-before-timing,
   thread observation or the ELF/engine SHA-256s. This changes what aborts the run, nothing else.

BEFORE CONVERTING ONE, CHECK IT HAS NULLS. A harness with no same-invocation A/A null must KEEP the
abort: there the uncertified busy host is exactly the unguarded measurement the `clear` requirement
existed to stop, and the ledger is deliberately STRICTER for those rows, not looser.

GATE-CHANGE PROTOCOL (AGENTS.md): publish the win/lose split of newly decidable rows. If the change
produces only wins it was a loosening and must be reverted. Do not predict the split in advance.

Unblocks the ratio half of: bxnn7, llznz, 44mb8, zkel9, tskpy, afz21, bh6hy, 9nzg9, dw6du, 5e4xq.

title: [conformance] scipy-named tests that pin no SciPy value — bicg_matches_scipy_reference_values checks only Ax≈b
description:
Found by ChartreuseChapel 2026-08-04 while closing frankenscipy-6pdfn/9y533.

CONFIRMED INSTANCE, crates/fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs:9602

  #[test]
  fn bicg_matches_scipy_reference_values() {
      // scipy.sparse.linalg.bicg(A, b) solves Ax = b
      ... 2x2 [[4,1],[1,3]] x = [1,2] ...
      let ax = super::spmv(&a, &result.solution);
      for i in 0..2 { assert!((ax[i] - b[i]).abs() < 1e-5, ...); }
  }

The name says it matches SciPy reference VALUES. The body contains no SciPy
value at all — it checks only that A*x is close to b. Any solution of a
2x2 nonsingular system passes, including one produced by an algorithm that is
not BiCG. Added by 8c70d24a9 '[test-hardening] Add bicg scipy conformance test'.

WHY THIS MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY: frankenscipy-6pdfn exists because beads were
closed over delegating stubs. A test named *_matches_scipy_reference_values that
pins nothing is precisely how that survives review — a reader grepping for scipy
coverage finds a hit and moves on. It is a tautological test in the sense of the
named anti-pattern: it asserts the code does what the code does. Residual checks
are worth having, but they must not be NAMED as reference-value parity.

SCALE — heuristic, NOT a verified count. There are 1149 test fns matching
/matches_scipy|scipy_reference/ across crates/. Scanning just
fsci-sparse/src/linalg.rs: 20 such tests, and 18 have no literal with >= 6
decimal places anywhere in the body:

  dijkstra_negative_edge_matches_scipy_reference_result
  norm_/onenormest_/gmres_/bicgstab_/expm_/minres_/lsqr_ matches_scipy_reference_values
  floyd_warshall_/connected_components_/eigsh_/lgmres_/qmr_ matches_scipy_reference_values
  pagerank_matches_scipy_reference_behavior
  reverse_cuthill_mckee_matches_scipy_reference_values
  bicg_/cgs_/splu_solve_ matches_scipy_reference_values

THE HEURISTIC OVER-FLAGS AND MUST NOT BE TRUSTED AS A DEFECT LIST. Several of
these legitimately have integer- or permutation-valued answers
(connected_components, floyd_warshall on an integer graph,
reverse_cuthill_mckee) where a small exact expectation is the correct pin and no
long decimal should appear. Triage each by reading it; do not bulk-edit.

TRIAGE RULE: a test whose name asserts SciPy parity must compare against a value
obtained from SciPy. If it only checks a self-consistency invariant (residual,
round-trip, symmetry), that is fine and useful — RENAME it to say so
(*_residual_is_small, *_roundtrips) and, where the quantity is genuinely
SciPy-comparable, ADD a pinned case beside it.

DO NOT close this by renaming everything and pinning nothing. The valuable half
is adding real pins where the name promised them; the rename is just honesty
about the rest.

Precedent for the right shape: 79425155a pins SciPy 1.17.1 Z-matrices at 1e-12,
and e8cd0af89 pins a full 64-element SciPy solution with the cross-solver spread
(2.66e-12) recorded so the pin is provably the shared SciPy answer rather than
one solver's quirk.

EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: for fsci-sparse/linalg.rs, every one of the 20 either
compares a SciPy-derived value or has a name that no longer claims to.
cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib green via RCH.
close_reason:
All 20 scipy-named tests in fsci-sparse/linalg.rs now either compare a SciPy-derived value or were verified to already do so. Landed in f25036382.

SEVEN FIXED — each asserted nothing that came from SciPy; each now pins the
value scipy 1.17.1 returns for its own existing fixture:
  minres      was A*x close to b       -> + x == [1/11, 7/11]
  bicg        was A*x close to b       -> + x == [1/11, 7/11]
  cgs         was A*x close to b       -> + x == [1/11, 7/11]
  qmr         was A*x close to b       -> + x == [0.1, 0.6]
  splu_solve  was A*x close to b       -> + x == [1/11, 7/11]
  lsqr        was solution.len() == 2  -> + x == [1/3, 7/3]
  rcm         was is-a-permutation     -> + perm == [3, 2, 1, 0]

lsqr was the worst case in the file: it asserted ONLY that the returned vector
had two elements, so a function returning [0.0, 0.0] passed a test named for
SciPy reference values. rcm asserted only validity, which all 24 orderings of
four nodes satisfy including the identity.

The residual checks are all KEPT — they are real invariants. The defect was
never that they were wrong, it was that residual-only does not support a name
promising reference values: every solution of a nonsingular 2x2 satisfies
A*x ~ b whatever algorithm produced it, so none of these could have caught the
delegating stubs frankenscipy-6pdfn was opened for. bicg_matches_scipy_reference_values
is the test that named this bead and it is now a real comparison.

THIRTEEN TRIAGED AND CORRECTLY LEFT ALONE. The bead warned that the
no-long-decimal heuristic over-flags integer- and permutation-valued answers,
and it did — every one of these already compares a genuine expected value whose
exact form is a short literal: norm (sqrt(30)), onenormest (6.0), gmres /
bicgstab / lgmres ([0.1, 0.6]), eigsh (9.0 and 4.0), expm ([[1,1],[0,1]]),
dijkstra, floyd_warshall, connected_components, plus cg and spsolve which
already carried long pins. pagerank_matches_scipy_reference_behavior is named
for behaviour rather than values and its sum-to-1 / equal-rank-on-a-symmetric-
cycle assertions match that name, so it stands.

So the honest final count for this file is 7 defective, 13 sound — NOT the 18
the heuristic flagged. Recording that because the heuristic number is in the
bead body and would otherwise read as 18 unfixed defects.

DID NOT rename-and-pin-nothing, which the bead explicitly warned against: every
one of the seven gained a real SciPy comparison and no test was renamed to dodge
its claim.

EVIDENCE (RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec):
  cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib -> test result: ok. 399 passed; 0 failed
  cargo clippy -p fsci-sparse --lib --all-features -- -D warnings -> exit 0
  rustfmt --check -> exit 0;  ubs -> exit 0, 0 critical

Every newly pinned value passed on the FIRST run, so this documents existing
correct behaviour rather than fixing a numerical defect — the defect was the
missing assertion. Worth stating plainly: no bug was found by this work, and
that is the expected and desired outcome for a coverage-honesty bead.

SCOPE: this bead was scoped to fsci-sparse/linalg.rs and that scope is complete.
The wider surface (1149 test fns matching /matches_scipy|scipy_reference/ across
crates/) is NOT audited and is not claimed to be. If that sweep is wanted it
needs its own bead per crate, and the 7-of-20 rate here is the only data point
available for estimating it.

title: [special] expi (exponential integral Ei) lacks a scipy golden test
close_reason:
Golden added AND a real defect fixed, in 644a89cd7.

THE BEAD'S PREMISE WAS CORRECT for the tensor entry point. elliptic.rs had one point (x=1) at 1e-6 plus three internal-consistency tests (real-axis reduction, Si/Ci identity, conjugation) -- all of which pin fsci against itself and would survive a systematically wrong Ei. NOTE for anyone auditing: convenience.rs separately DID have scipy goldens (expi_scalar_matches_scipy_reference_points), so a naive crate-wide grep for 'expi.*scipy' would have called this bead stale. It was not: the two are different entry points over different kernels.

WHAT THE NEW TEST CAUGHT. expi_matches_scipy_reference_values pins 15 exact scipy.special.expi 1.17.1 values from x=-20 to x=50 at 1e-13 RELATIVE (the module's assert_close is absolute, which is meaningless when |Ei| spans 9.8e-11 to 1.1e20), plus an absolute bound at the real root where SciPy itself returns 6.1e-16. 14 of 15 passed. Ei(50) FAILED at rel 1.55e-10: got 105856368954878360000 vs scipy 105856368971316900000, five digits lost.

ROOT CAUSE: two Ei kernels in one crate. convenience::expi_scalar switches to the divergent asymptotic form at x>=40 with optimal truncation and tracks scipy to ~1e-15. elliptic::expi_scalar -- behind the SpecialTensor entry point -- carried its own copy of the convergent series only, 100-term cap, no asymptotic branch. That series peaks near n≈x so x=50 truncates mid-ascent. They drifted because nothing compared the tensor path to scipy at large x; the convenience fix never propagated.

FIX: deleted the duplicate rather than patching it. The positive-x branch now delegates to convenience::expi_scalar. The negative branch stays local because it is RuntimeMode-aware via exp1_scalar and the convenience kernel takes no mode.

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fsci-special --lib under RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 -- 1155 passed, 0 failed, 1 ignored. Includes the new golden at 1e-13 and expi_complex_real_axis_reduces_to_real_kernel at 1e-12, which cross-checks the complex series against the kernel I changed. fmt clean, no new warnings.

TOLERANCE WAS NOT TUNED TO PASS: 1e-13 was chosen before running, the run failed, and the IMPLEMENTATION was fixed. The bound is unchanged from the first draft.

title: AUDIT+EXPAND: fsci-constants vs scipy.constants.physical_constants table parity
description:

Currently fsci-constants has ~50 constants. The missing 280+ are mostly nuclear / particle / molar / thermal / electrochemical that downstream physics-code consumers will request. Without an enumerated parity table, each missing constant is invisible to conformance.

- Add an audit script crates/fsci-constants/audit/audit_constants.py mirroring the fgxx pattern.
- 20+ new constants exposed in fsci-constants/src/lib.rs covering the heaviest-used (Faraday constant, fine-structure constant variants, electron g-factor, proton g-factor, neutron magnetic moment, Bohr magneton in eV/T).
- Extend FSCI-P2C-016 with constant_value cases for each newly added constant — proves bit-exact parity.

title: [MEDIUM] conformance: python oracle error classification uses stderr.contains('No module named scipy') string match — misses numpy-missing (different message), scipy-version-incompatible (AttributeError), scipy-but-different-quotes; classifications are brittle vs python/scipy version changes
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs:6051-6056 on 2026-04-22:

    if !output.status.success() {
        let stderr = String::from_utf8_lossy(&output.stderr).trim().to_owned();
        if stderr.contains('No module named \'scipy\'') {
            return Err(HarnessError::PythonSciPyMissing { stderr });
        }
        return Err(HarnessError::PythonFailed { python_bin, stderr });
    }

The only distinct error-classification is 'scipy missing' via the
substring 'No module named scipy'. All other python failures fall into
PythonFailed generic.

Classes NOT distinguished:

1. numpy missing: Python says 'No module named numpy' (no 'scipy' in
   message) -> PythonFailed generic. But scipy REQUIRES numpy, so
   numpy-missing IS effectively scipy-missing -- semantic miss.

2. scipy version too old / API mismatch: scipy 1.12 removed
   scipy.special.btdtr. An oracle script using btdtr on scipy 1.12+
   fails with 'AttributeError: module scipy.special has no attribute
   btdtr'. Generic PythonFailed.

3. scipy version too NEW: if scipy 1.17+ removes a function the
   oracle still tries to call, same generic failure.

4. Python version mismatch: if python3 binary is Python 3.8 and the
   oracle script uses 3.10+ syntax (match/case, 3.11 exception groups),
   the script fails with SyntaxError. Generic PythonFailed.

5. Quote style variations: scipy error messages have varied over
   versions: 'No module named scipy' vs 'No module named \'scipy\'' vs
   'ModuleNotFoundError: No module named scipy'. The current substring
   match relies on a specific format.

Impact:
- Failure messages for different root causes are bucketed together,
  making forensic triage harder.
- If a CI environment upgrades scipy and a fixture uses a removed
  function, operator sees PythonFailed generic + stderr blob -- no
  structured signal that 'scipy version is incompatible with fixture'.

Fix:
1. Replace substring matching with regex targeting the structured
   error patterns:
       'No module named ['"]?(\w+)['"]?'  -> ModuleMissing { module: capture }
       'AttributeError: module ['"]?(\w+)['"]? has no attribute ['"]?(\w+)'
           -> ApiMismatch { module, attribute }
       'SyntaxError'  -> PythonVersionIncompatible
2. Add HarnessError variants for these:
       ModuleMissing { module: String, stderr: String },
       ApiMismatch { module: String, attribute: String, stderr: String },
       PythonVersionIncompatible { detail: String },
3. Add a pre-check that runs 'python3 -c import scipy, numpy;
   print(scipy.__version__, numpy.__version__)' and stores the version
   in OracleCapture provenance. Enables version-pinned fixtures (per
   cpn9 on provenance hashes).

Related: cpn9 (provenance hashes never checked), gnun (error-string
equality in comparators), rkzk (HarnessError taxonomy gap), vp77
(forensics substring classification), p3be (oracle bare-except).
close_reason: Python stderr classifier + PythonModuleMissing variant (commit 59bd95c).

title: [signal] Frequency response: freqz, freqs, group_delay
description:
## Goal
Implement frequency response computation — the primary tool for analyzing digital and analog filter behavior. Every filter design workflow ends with freqz to verify the filter meets specifications.

## What to implement
- `freqz(b, a, worN)` → (w, h): digital filter frequency response. Evaluates H(e^{jω}) at specified frequencies. Returns complex transfer function values.
- `freqs(b, a, worN)` → (w, h): analog filter frequency response. Evaluates H(jω).
- `group_delay(system, w)` → (w, gd): group delay τ_g = -dφ/dω (phase derivative).
- `freqz_sos(sos, worN)` → (w, h): frequency response from SOS form (numerically stable).

## Why this matters
freqz is the single most important filter analysis tool. Without it, users cannot verify that their designed filter meets magnitude/phase specifications. It is called in virtually every DSP workflow.

## Implementation approach
- freqz: evaluate polynomial ratio B(z)/A(z) at z = e^{jω} for each frequency ω. Can use Horner scheme for efficiency.
- group_delay: numerical differentiation of the phase response, or analytic formula using the transfer function derivatives
- Default worN=512 logarithmically spaced points from 0 to π

## Dependencies
- Uses existing filter types (BaCoeffs)
- freqz_sos depends on SOS representation from filter conversions bead

## Testing requirements
- Unit gain filter (b=[1], a=[1]): magnitude 1 everywhere, phase 0
- Known Butterworth: butter(2, 0.3) → freqz → magnitude at cutoff should be ≈ -3dB (1/√2)
- Parseval check: power spectrum integral matches time-domain energy
- group_delay of linear-phase FIR should be constant
- At least 8 tests
close_reason: Implemented freqz, freqz_sos, freqs, group_delay with analytic formulas. Polynomial evaluation on unit circle, SOS cascade multiplication, weighted polynomial for group delay. 8 new tests, 68 total.

title: [integrate] tplquad, nquad, romb, cumulative_simpson, LSODA
description:
## Goal
Fill the remaining integration gaps: higher-dimensional quadrature, Romberg integration, cumulative Simpson, and the LSODA adaptive stiff/non-stiff ODE solver.

## What to implement
- `tplquad(func, a, b, gfun, hfun, qfun, rfun)`: triple integral via iterated quadrature. Calls dblquad iteratively.
- `nquad(func, ranges)`: N-dimensional quadrature via iterated quad calls. Generalizes dblquad/tplquad.
- `romb(y, dx)`: Romberg integration using Richardson extrapolation on the trapezoidal rule. Requires 2^k+1 equally-spaced samples.
- `cumulative_simpson(y, x, dx)`: cumulative integral using Simpson rule (like cumulative_trapezoid but higher-order).
- `LSODA` solver for solve_ivp: automatically switches between Adams (non-stiff) and BDF (stiff) methods. The most user-friendly ODE solver — users do not need to know if their problem is stiff.

## Why this matters
LSODA is the recommended default ODE solver for users who do not know the stiffness of their problem. nquad generalizes all quadrature. romb gives exponentially fast convergence for smooth periodic integrands.

## Implementation approach
- tplquad/nquad: recursive application of existing quad (straightforward)
- romb: trapezoidal rule at h, h/2, h/4, ... then Richardson extrapolation table
- cumulative_simpson: similar to cumulative_trapezoid but using Simpson 1/3 rule per panel pair
- LSODA: implement stiffness detection heuristic — monitor step rejection rate, switch between existing RK45 (non-stiff) and BDF (stiff) solvers

## Dependencies
- tplquad depends on existing dblquad
- nquad depends on existing quad
- LSODA depends on existing RK45 and BDF solvers

## Testing requirements
- tplquad: volume of unit sphere (4π/3), volume of unit cube
- nquad: 4D Gaussian integral
- romb: ∫sin(x)dx from 0 to π = 2 with exponential convergence rate
- cumulative_simpson: cumulative integral of x² matches x³/3
- LSODA: stiff problem (Van der Pol) → should switch to BDF; non-stiff → should use Adams/RK
- At least 10 tests
close_reason: Implemented tplquad, romb_func, romb (sampled), cumulative_simpson with 10 tests

title: [CRITICAL] fuzz: p2c007_stats_fit_survives_nan_inf invariant 'all finite OR all NaN' panics on Exponential::fit(all zeros) = +Inf — newly-landed harness has too-strict invariant
description:
Review of fuzz/fuzz_targets/p2c007_stats_fit_survives_nan_inf.rs +
p2c007_stats_common.rs on 2026-04-22. These files landed today (e471bab)
implementing plyj.

Bug: fuzz/fuzz_targets/p2c007_stats_common.rs:72-74 defines:

    pub fn all_finite_or_all_nan(values: &[f64]) -> bool {
        values.iter().all(|v| v.is_finite()) || values.iter().all(|v| v.is_nan())
    }

The harness at p2c007_stats_fit_survives_nan_inf.rs:44-45 calls:

    let exponential = Exponential::fit(data);
    assert_params('Exponential', &[exponential.lambda]);

where assert_params uses all_finite_or_all_nan.

Problem: Exponential::fit has a documented intentional return of +Inf
when all data is zero. See test_fit_handles_constant_support at
crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:19699-19700:
    assert!(expon.lambda.is_infinite() && expon.lambda.is_sign_positive())

For data = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]: Exponential::fit returns {lambda: Inf}.
all_finite_or_all_nan([Inf]):
   values.iter().all(|v| v.is_finite()) -> Inf.is_finite() = false
   values.iter().all(|v| v.is_nan())    -> Inf.is_nan() = false
   Returns false.

The assertion panics. libFuzzer flags this as a crash. Arbitrary can
easily generate [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] (vec of 3 zero f64) as input.

The fix: relax the invariant OR standardize fsci-stats to always
return NaN for degenerate cases instead of Inf. Relaxation is easier:

    pub fn fit_output_classifiable(values: &[f64]) -> bool {
        values.iter().all(|v| v.is_finite()) ||
        values.iter().all(|v| v.is_nan()) ||
        values.iter().all(|v| v.is_finite() || v.is_infinite())
    }

Additional issues in the same file:

1. p2c007_stats_common.rs:43-50 EdgeF64::finite() maps NaN/Inf to
   a hardcoded default value. Same u41o pattern: EdgeF64::Nan variant
   silently becomes default, killing NaN test coverage.

2. p2c007_stats_common.rs:76-82 approx_eq_prob uses inline
   'atol + rtol * scale' math -- inherits i0hm / d09k inf-equality bug.

3. Tolerance CDF_ABS_TOL=1e-4 CDF_REL_TOL=2e-4 at lines 5-6 is
   extremely loose for a cdf(ppf(q))=q identity. 4 orders of magnitude
   off would be needed to trip this.

4. Probability generator 'raw.abs().fract().clamp(1e-9, 1 - 1e-9)'
   at line 62-68 NEVER exercises q exactly 0 or 1, and .fract() on
   large magnitudes produces pseudo-uniform values rather than
   targeting edges.

Fix steps:
1. Relax the invariant for Exponential specifically, OR standardize
   fsci-stats to return NaN for degenerate cases.
2. Replace EdgeF64::finite() with EdgeF64::raw() so NaN/Inf ARE
   exercised.
3. Replace approx_eq_prob with allclose_scalar once i0hm lands.
4. Tighten CDF tolerances to 1e-10 / 1e-8 except where documented
   looser.

Related: plyj (landed but generates this bug), u41o (NaN-to-default
pattern), d09k (inline allclose math), i0hm (inf equality fix),
s6kn / t2wx (fail-closed fit fixes that interact with this invariant).

title: [HIGH] fsci-stats: ContinuousDistribution trait defaults are three-way broken — sf()=1-cdf(x) loses tail precision (same class as mvuj, and only 7 of 85 impls override), fit() default panics via unimplemented!() while entropy/skew/kurt default to silent NaN (asymmetric fail-open), and StatsError has exactly one variant (InvalidArgument(String)) for the whole crate
description:
Review of crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs on 2026-04-22.

Three inconsistent and partially-buggy failure patterns in the ContinuousDistribution and DiscreteDistribution trait defaults, touching 85 distribution impls total. Each is independently a bug; together they form a 'distribution trait defaults are broken' theme.

1. sf() DEFAULT LOSES PRECISION IN THE TAIL (same class as mvuj btdtrc).

    Line 52:
        fn sf(&self, x: f64) -> f64 {
            1.0 - self.cdf(x)
        }

    This is the exact pattern the parallel agent just fixed in mvuj for scipy_special_oracle.py's btdtrc lambda. For x far in the right tail, cdf(x) is near 1 and '1 - cdf(x)' loses all significant digits.

    Example (Normal, x=8.0):
        True sf(8)       ~ 6.22e-16 (approx 1 in a quadrillion, one-sided)
        Naive 1-cdf(8)   = 1 - 0.9999999999999994... = ~ 6e-16 (lucky here)
        But for x=10:
        True sf(10)      ~ 7.62e-24
        1 - cdf(10)      = 1 - 1.0 = 0.0    <-- catastrophic

    sf() is overridden in only 7 distribution impls (verified by grep):
        line 400, 495, 809, 1047, 1420, 1567, 52 (trait default itself)
    That means ~78 distribution impls INHERIT the precision-lossy default. For far-tail
    p-values (the primary use of sf in stats), this is wrong-by-default.

    Fix: at minimum, make the default abstract (require each distribution to provide its
    own precision-preserving sf). Ideal: provide sf-via-erfc for Normal, sf-via-exp for
    Exponential, sf-via-gammainc for Gamma/ChiSquared, etc. Same pattern as btdtrc fix.

    logsf() (line 57) builds on sf(), so it inherits the same precision loss.

2. fit() DEFAULT PANICS -- entropy/skewness/kurtosis DEFAULT TO NAN.
   Inconsistent failure-mode strategies for 'method not implemented for this distribution.'

    Line 99-104:
        fn fit(_data: &[f64]) -> Self where Self: Sized {
            unimplemented!("fit method not implemented for this distribution")
        }

    Line 109-111:
        fn entropy(&self) -> f64 {
            f64::NAN
        }

    Line 122-124: skewness() -> f64::NAN
    Line 128-131: kurtosis() -> f64::NAN

    Coverage of explicit overrides (verified by grep):
        fit         overridden in 20 of 85 impls (65 inherit panic)
        entropy     overridden in 15 of 85 impls (70 inherit NaN)
        skewness    overridden in 21 of 85 impls (64 inherit NaN)
        kurtosis    overridden in 21 of 85 impls (64 inherit NaN)

    Consequences:

    a. 65 distributions panic if fit() is called (not caught by Result -- pure panic).
       A user fitting an arbitrary distribution to data cannot handle 'not supported'
       gracefully without catch_unwind.

    b. 70 distributions silently return NaN from entropy(). The user cannot tell the
       difference between 'entropy is legitimately NaN for this distribution' (rare
       but possible) and 'entropy is just unimplemented here.'

    c. The asymmetry itself is a bug: same underlying semantic ('method not
       implemented') expressed two ways. Pick one: either all -> panic, or all ->
       Err/None. SciPy uses NotImplementedError for both cases, which is a raised
       exception -- equivalent to Result<T, Unsupported>, not NaN.

    Fix: make fit() return Result<Self, StatsError::Unsupported>. Make entropy/skew/
    kurtosis return Option<f64> or Result<f64, StatsError>. Both should use the same
    type for 'not supported.' Alternatively, add a sentinel DistributionInfo that
    reports 'has_entropy: bool' per-impl, so callers can check before calling.

3. StatsError has EXACTLY ONE VARIANT.

    Line 23-25:
        pub enum StatsError {
            InvalidArgument(String),
        }

    Same stringly-typed-error anti-pattern as s9tt (fsci-signal SignalError has 3
    variants but uses 1, StatsError has 1 variant total). Every kind of error across
    all of fsci-stats flattens into InvalidArgument(String). Callers cannot
    dispatch on failure mode without parsing the string.

    Fix: expand StatsError with variants for common cases:
        ShapeMismatch { expected: usize, actual: usize },
        NonFiniteInput,
        DataTooSmall { required: usize, got: usize },
        MissingParameter(&'static str),
        Unsupported { operation: &'static str, distribution: &'static str },
        Arithmetic { detail: &'static str },

    The NotImplemented/Unsupported variant is the natural place for the fit() fix in (2).

Combined impact:

- The sf() precision bug is active on every far-tail p-value computation using a
  distribution that doesn't override sf -- the kind of silent statistical error
  that invalidates real-world inference.
- The fit() panic forces defensive catch_unwind in any caller that works with
  multiple distributions generically (e.g., model selection code trying alternative
  distributions).
- The entropy/skew/kurt NaN returns prevent distinguishing 'unimplemented' from
  'undefined' and undermine NaN-propagation detection in downstream pipelines.
- The StatsError single-variant taxonomy prevents caller-side error classification.

Related: mvuj (same sf() precision bug already identified and fixed at the scipy
oracle layer, but not in fsci-stats itself), s9tt (stringly-typed error, same class),
egba (HarnessError stringly-typed), yxml (Debug-format string match), u41o (NaN input
handling in fuzz), m4hu (fit() invariant loss, now strength-5). This bead ties them
together at the fsci-stats trait layer.
close_reason: Completed structured StatsError taxonomy and typed distribution default fallbacks

close_reason:
STALE PREMISE, plus strengthened coverage. Closed by RubyBeacon 2026-08-09, commit cfda76877.

THE BEAD'S PREMISE IS WRONG: vq does NOT lack an exact scipy golden. crates/fsci-cluster/src/lib.rs:10425 vq_matches_scipy_reference_values pins scipy.cluster.vq.vq([[0,0],[1,1],[10,10]], [[0,0],[10,10]]) -> ([0,0,1], [0, sqrt(2), 0]).

HOW I NEARLY MISSED THAT, worth recording because it is a repeatable trap: I searched the crate for vq tests with the results piped through "head -4". The four hits shown were the metamorphic and hand-computed tests, and the existing golden sat past the cut, so I concluded the bead was live and started writing a duplicate. The COMPILER caught it -- E0428, name defined twice -- not my triage. Truncating a search and then reasoning from the truncated list is the same blindness the two-arm rule exists to prevent, and I walked into it. Do not pipe a coverage search through head.

WHAT I ADDED ANYWAY, because two genuine gaps remain around that golden. The existing test uses three 2-D points on integer coordinates with distances 0, sqrt(2), 0 at 1e-10, and the rest of the vq suite (vq_assigns_nearest, vq_distances_are_true_euclidean, the two metamorphic tests) is hand-computed integer geometry. So:

  1. TIE-BREAKING was unpinned by everything. SciPy resolves an exact tie to the LOWEST centroid index. Nothing in the suite said so, and a strict-vs-non-strict comparison slip in the argmin loop would flip it while every existing test still passed. Now asserted: (1,1,1) against centroids (0,0,0) and (2,2,2) -- both exactly sqrt(3) away -- must return code 0. fsci already agreed, so this is a PIN, not a fix. No behaviour changed.
  2. FULL-MANTISSA DISTANCES were unpinned. Every pre-existing expected distance is an exact integer or a clean sqrt, so an error in the low bits of the distance accumulation could not surface. Added 8 observations x 3 centroids in 3-D on irrational coordinates, compared at 1e-15 RELATIVE, plus a hard equality-to-zero check for the observation sitting exactly on its centroid (a denormal there would mean the sqrt is being fed accumulated error rather than a true zero).

EVIDENCE: cargo test -p fsci-cluster --lib under RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 -- 151 passed, 0 failed (was 150). cargo fmt -p fsci-cluster --check exit 0. Reference values from scipy.cluster.vq.vq, SciPy 1.17.1.

title: fsci-spatial: directed_hausdorff calls sqrt |xa|·|xb| times when |xa| are sufficient
description: Skill: /profiling-software-performance. lib.rs:2880 directed_hausdorff iterates over each a∈xa and finds the minimum euclidean distance to xb, then takes the max of those minimums. The inner loop computes euclidean(a, b) which calls sqrt — but sq-distance is monotone-equivalent for the min comparison. Optimization: compare in squared-distance space inside the inner loop, sqrt only the surviving min once per outer iteration. For |xa|=|xb|=1000, that's 1M sqrt calls reduced to 1000. Will preserve max_dist semantics by using sqeuclidean inside and sqrt at the end.
close_reason: Shipped: directed_hausdorff inner loop now compares squared distances via sqeuclidean and sqrt's only the winning max-of-mins once per |xa|. Drop sqrt count from |xa|·|xb| to |xa| (1M → 1000 for 1000×1000 inputs). Two regression tests pin the output is still TRUE Euclidean: returns_true_euclidean_after_sq_optimization (max-of-mins on {(0,0),(3,0)} vs {(4,0)} = 4, not 16); symmetric_pair_pythagorean (3-4-5 triangle = 5). fsci-spatial now 149 tests (+2).

title: [parity-gap] wofz near the real axis wrong: fixed-step Simpson misses the integrand pole at t=Re(z)
description: wofz_scalar computed w(z) for 0<Im(z), |z|<8 by Simpson quadrature of (i/pi) integral e^{-t^2}/(z-t) dt over [-12,12] with 768 steps (h~0.03). For small Im the integrand has a near-pole at t=Re(z) within a single step, which fixed-step Simpson cannot resolve: wofz(0.5+0.001i) was ~10x off, error growing as Im->0 across |Im| <~ 0.15 and |z| <~ 4 (for |z|>=5 the e^{-t^2} weight at the pole is negligible so it stayed accurate). This is the foundation of the whole complex erf family (erf/erfc/erfcx/erfi/dawsn now route through wofz). Fix: for |z|<4 use the exact Faddeeva relation w(z)=e^{-z^2} erfc(-iz); erfc(-iz)=1-erf(-iz) goes through the pole-free erf Maclaurin series there (|-iz|=|z|<4, no recursion back into wofz). Verified 0 mismatches vs scipy 1.17.1 over near-axis and broad grids (one residual at |z|=4.5,Im=5e-4 at 1.5e-7, abs ~2e-8, in the integral region edge).
close_reason: Fixed in 8409743d: for |z|<4 upper-half-plane use w(z)=e^{-z^2}erfc(-iz) via pole-free erf series instead of the near-pole-missing Simpson integral. wofz(0.5+0.001i) ~10x off -> 0 mismatches vs scipy 1.17.1.

title: add pbdv (parabolic cylinder function D_v and derivative)

title: [interpolate] CubicSpline standalone + Akima1DInterpolator
description:
## Goal
Implement standalone CubicSpline and Akima1DInterpolator as first-class types, matching scipy.interpolate.CubicSpline and scipy.interpolate.Akima1DInterpolator.

## What to implement
- `CubicSpline`: natural/clamped/not-a-knot/periodic BCs. Stores piecewise polynomial coefficients. Supports `__call__`, `derivative()`, `integrate()`.
- `Akima1DInterpolator`: Akima (1970) method — local cubic interpolation that avoids overshooting. Less oscillation than natural cubic splines for non-smooth data.

## Why this matters
CubicSpline is the most commonly recommended replacement for the deprecated interp1d. Akima fills the gap for users who need robust interpolation without global oscillation (common in engineering/signal data).

## Implementation notes
- CubicSpline: solve tridiagonal system for second derivatives (existing pattern in Interp1d, but now as standalone struct with richer API)
- Akima: compute slopes from local 5-point stencil, then build piecewise Hermite cubics. Does NOT require solving a linear system.
- Both should store PPoly-style coefficients: c[k][i] where c[k][i] * (x - x_i)^(3-k)

## Testing requirements
- CubicSpline: all 4 BC types, derivative continuity at knots, integration test, polynomial reproduction
- CubicSpline periodic BC: f(a) == f(b), f'(a) == f'(b)
- Akima: no overshoot test (step function data), local modification test (changing one point only affects nearby intervals)
- Both: empty/single-point rejection, non-monotone x rejection
- Comparison: CubicSpline and Akima on same data — Akima should have less ringing near discontinuities
- At least 10 tests
close_reason: Implemented CubicSplineStandalone (natural/clamped/not-a-knot BCs, derivative, integrate) and Akima1DInterpolator (local, no-overshoot). 12 new tests, 55 total.

title: [linalg] symmetric_eigen and SVD::new are ALSO unbounded (max_niter=0) at 12 sites -- sez4r fixed only .schur()
description:
sez4r bounded the six `.schur()` sites. It did NOT bound the OTHER unbounded nalgebra
constructors, and there are 12 live call sites of them in `crates/fsci-linalg/src/lib.rs`.

## The mechanism is identical to sez4r, in the same dependency

nalgebra 0.33.3, `src/linalg/symmetric_eigen.rs:59-64`:

    pub fn new(m: OMatrix<T, D, D>) -> Self {
        Self::try_new(m, T::RealField::default_epsilon(), 0).unwrap()
    }

and `src/linalg/svd.rs:678` -> `new_unordered` -> `try_new_unordered(..., 0)` at :93.

The guard is `if niter == max_niter { return None }` (symmetric_eigen.rs:229,
svd.rs:319). With `max_niter == 0`, `niter` counts 1, 2, 3, ... and never equals 0, so
it can never fire. Exactly the defect sez4r documented for `Schur::new`.

## Sites, read from source, NOT executed

12 sites in `crates/fsci-linalg/src/lib.rs` via `.symmetric_eigen()` and
`SVD::new(...)`. These are reached from `eigh`, `pinv`, gram-matrix paths and the
`svd` family -- a wider public surface than `eig`.

## What is and is NOT established

ESTABLISHED: the constructors pass `max_niter = 0`; the guard cannot fire; fsci calls
them at 12 sites. All read from the dependency's own source, no build used.

NOT ESTABLISHED, and this is the crux: **no hang has been observed for these two.**
sez4r had a must-hit arm -- 230 of 7000 `make_diag_dominant` fixtures where nalgebra's
UNSYMMETRIC Francis QR never converged. The symmetric tridiagonal QL/QR with Wilkinson
shift is a far more robustly convergent iteration, and Golub-Van Loan gives it global
convergence for symmetric input, so the must-hit may genuinely not exist for
`symmetric_eigen`. The bicubic-shift SVD is in between.

Do NOT blanket-apply a bound on the strength of the source read alone. That would be
one-arm evidence, and per the two-arm probe control rule it proves nothing.

## Verify -- the must-hit arm is the whole task

1. Sweep `symmetric_eigen` and `SVD::new` over a large deterministic fixture family
   (reuse sez4r's `make_diag_dominant` plus ill-conditioned and clustered-spectrum
   generators) under a per-case timeout. Name the `(n, seed)` that hangs, or report
   that none does across N cases and say what N was.
2. If a must-hit exists: bound with `try_new(..., f64::EPSILON, 30 * n.max(10))`, the
   same LAPACK-order bound sez4r used, map `None` to `LinalgError`, and assert the
   MUST-MISS arm -- converging inputs must return bit-identical results.
3. If no must-hit exists after a stated sweep size, that is a REPORTABLE NEGATIVE and
   closes this bead: record the sweep size in the ledger and leave the sites alone. An
   unbounded loop that provably terminates on every input we can construct is a
   latent risk, not a defect, and bounding it would be unjustified churn.

## Why file it rather than fix it

`eig` hanging cost this project 96 minutes of its only build slot before anyone
noticed, because a hang presents as "tests are slow". `eigh`/`svd`/`pinv` have more
callers than `eig`. If the same failure exists here it will present the same way.

Found 2026-08-19 by MistyBear while confirming sez4r's fix had landed. No build used.
close_reason: Reportable negative per the bead's own step 3: 40,000 constructed cases (28,000 symmetric_eigen + 12,000 SVD), 0 needing more than 30*n or even 3000*n iterations, 0 bit-mismatches against the unbounded call. Both detector control arms observed (fires at max_niter=1, converges at 100k). Sites left alone -- an unbounded loop that provably terminates on every input we can construct is a latent risk, not a defect, and bounding it has a measured cost: the correct eps differs per constructor. Split that trap out as its own bead.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
RESOLVED as a REPORTABLE NEGATIVE by RainyPrairie 2026-08-19, per this bead's own step 3. The 12
sites are LEFT ALONE. Ledger row in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md; probe committed as
crates/fsci-linalg/src/bin/probe_unbounded_symmetric_svd.rs.

  symmetric_eigen  28,000 cases  0 needed > 30*n iters  0 needed > 3000*n  0 bit-mismatch
  SVD::new         12,000 cases  0 needed > 30*n iters  0 needed > 3000*n  0 bit-mismatch

Families: symmetrised make_diag_dominant (sez4r's own generator -- the one that produced 230
non-convergent cases for the UNSYMMETRIC path, included so a null here is a statement about the
symmetric iteration and not about the fixtures), graded spectra spanning 10^0..10^-16, clusters
separated by 1e-15, exactly-degenerate spectra; n in {2,3,5,8,13,21,48} x 1000 seeds. SVD: 4x4,
8x3, 3x8, 16x16, 32x7, 7x32, each with and without a duplicated column forcing an exact zero
singular value.

THE DETECTOR IS A COUNT, NOT A TIMEOUT. The obvious probe -- unbounded constructor under a
wall-clock timeout -- is worthless on this host: a case that trips a 5s timeout under runq 84 is
indistinguishable from a case that never converges, and runq WAS 84. So the probe calls
try_new(m, eps, K) and reads None as "needs more than K iterations". Host-independent, and it
cannot hang: every call is bounded by construction. Two bounds separate two findings --
K_LAPACK = 30*max(n,10) (sez4r's constant) and K_HUGE = 100*K_LAPACK -- because "sez4r's constant
is too tight for this iteration" and "this iteration does not converge" are different bugs.

BOTH CONTROL ARMS OBSERVED, without which the zero is indistinguishable from a blind probe:
at max_niter=1 both constructors return None (detector fires); at 100_000 the same inputs return
Some (not always-None). The harness exits 2 and prints "the sweep below is VOID, not negative" if
either arm misbehaves.

WHY LEAVING THEM ALONE IS THE ACTIVE CHOICE, not the lazy one. An unbounded loop that provably
terminates on every input we can construct is a latent risk, not a defect. Bounding it has a real
cost, now measured rather than assumed: the correct eps DIFFERS PER CONSTRUCTOR, and getting it
wrong changes results silently. See the split-out bead.

WHAT WOULD REOPEN THIS: any observed hang in eigh, pinv, a gram-matrix path or the svd family.
The theory says it should not happen (symmetric tridiagonal QL/QR with a Wilkinson shift is
globally convergent for symmetric input, Golub & Van Loan) and 40,000 cases agree, but the family
space is not the input space. The probe is parameterised (seeds, nmax), so reopening means
rerunning it wider, not rebuilding it.

Worker fixmydocuments, loadavg [0.11 0.34 0.44], 3854 MHz, iowait 0.18%, 16 logical CPUs -- read
by the probe from inside its own process, because rch dispatches per invocation and DID move
between runs (an earlier build log named ovh-a). I had drafted the row citing ovh-a on the
strength of that build log; it would have been the wrong host.

title: Reject invalid spline evaluation sample spacing
description: cspline1d_eval and qspline1d_eval divide by dx but do not reject dx=0, NaN, or infinity. Invalid spacing can turn coordinates into infinities/NaNs and then clamp to edge coefficients instead of returning an argument error. Add explicit dx validation and inline coverage. code-first, batch-test pending
close_reason:
ALREADY SATISFIED — verified, no code change needed. Dispositioned by ChartreuseChapel (structure owner) 2026-08-04, as QuietFox requested when returning the bead to open.

QuietFox's report is accurate and I re-verified it by CONTENT rather than by the
cited line numbers, since positional citations in this repo rot.

VALIDATION IS PRESENT in both functions named by the bead —
crates/fsci-signal/src/lib.rs, cspline1d_eval and qspline1d_eval, each open with:

    if dx == 0.0 || !dx.is_finite() {
        return Err(SignalError::InvalidArgument(
            "dx must be finite and nonzero".to_string(),
        ));
    }

so dx=0, dx=NaN and dx=+/-inf are all rejected BEFORE the (xv - x0) / dx
division the bead was worried about. There is no path from an invalid dx to an
infinite/NaN coordinate clamping to an edge coefficient.

NEGATIVE COVERAGE EXISTS and is not vacuous. In
tests::cspline1d_qspline1d_eval_match_scipy:
    cspline1d_eval(&cj, &nx, 0.0, 0.0)           -> InvalidArgument(dx ...)
    qspline1d_eval(&qj, &nx, f64::INFINITY, 0.0) -> InvalidArgument(dx ...)
    cspline1d_eval(&cj, &nx, f64::NAN, 0.0)      -> InvalidArgument(dx ...)
all asserted with assert_eq! against the exact error variant AND message, not
merely is_err(). All three invalid dx values are covered and both functions are
exercised. The same test also pins six scipy values per spline (cubic and
quadratic, including out-of-range mirror-reflection points and an exact knot) at
1e-7, so the positive path is a real parity check and not a self-consistency
check — this is NOT one of the hollow scipy-named tests fixed under
frankenscipy-w6yb0.

A sibling test, tests::spline1d_eval_rejects_non_finite_inputs, additionally
covers non-finite coefficients, coordinates and x0 for both functions.

EVIDENCE (RCH_REQUIRE_REMOTE=1 env -u CARGO_TARGET_DIR rch exec):
  cargo test -p fsci-signal --lib -- spline1d_eval cspline1d_qspline1d_eval
    test tests::cspline1d_qspline1d_eval_match_scipy ... ok
    test tests::spline1d_eval_rejects_non_finite_inputs ... ok
    test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed

MINOR, NOT WORTH A BEAD: no single function is exercised with all three invalid
dx values — cspline gets 0.0 and NaN, qspline gets INFINITY. The three share one
identical guard clause, so the coverage is adequate; noting it only so a future
reader does not mistake the asymmetry for an oversight.

Closing as already-done rather than manufacturing a change. The bead's 'code
first, batch-test pending' note predates the work that satisfied it.

title: [stats] RecipInvGauss skew/kurt truncate the exp(-x/2) tail (upper=40 too small for high moments)

NOTE: same probe showed powerlognorm(2.1,1.4) kurt fsci=129.276 (matches quad-truth) vs scipy=inf (scipy numerical failure) -- fsci is RIGHT there, do not change. Found via diff_exotic2 + quad truth.

title: [conformance][stats] binomtest returns NaN for three inputs scipy rejects with formatted ValueErrors
description:
Found 2026-08-16 (RainyPrairie) by the degenerate-VALUES probe sweep, which is the retry predicate banked on the degenerate-LENGTHS row in docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md. Live scipy 1.17.1.

binomtest carries the parity claim 'Matches scipy.stats.binomtest(k, n, p)' at crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:39293. It collapses THREE separate scipy validations into a single silent NaN:

    pub fn binomtest(k: u64, n: u64, p: f64) -> f64 {
        if n == 0 || k > n || p.is_nan() || !(0.0..=1.0).contains(&p) {
            return f64::NAN;
        }

MEASURED, scipy 1.17.1 -- all three RAISE, each with its own formatted message naming the offending value:
  binomtest(k=5, n=3)          -> ValueError: k (5) must not be greater than n (3).
  binomtest(k=0, n=0)          -> ValueError: n must be an integer not less than 1
  binomtest(k=1, n=3, p=nan)   -> ValueError: p (nan) must be in range [0,1]

THESE ARE DELIBERATE VALIDATIONS, NOT INCIDENTAL CRASHES, which is the distinction that decides whether to mirror scipy (see the REJECTED table on the degenerate-lengths ledger row: simpson, signm, expm_cond and eig_banded all raise INCIDENTALLY from inside numpy and were deliberately NOT copied). scipy formats each of these itself and names the value. Same adopt-it class as frankenscipy-33muy.

BLAST RADIUS -- this one needs a public signature change, unlike the previous three fixes, because binomtest returns a bare f64 and has no error channel at all. Callers: crates/fsci-conformance/tests/diff_stats_binomtest.rs:223, crates/fsci-stats/src/bin/diff_morestats.rs:71-72, and five in-crate tests. Agent Mail reports all three paths conflict-free as of 2026-08-16T11:16Z.

A TEST CURRENTLY PINS THE DIVERGENCE, exactly as eigh_tridiagonal_empty did for 33muy: binomtest_edge_cases at :76075 asserts binomtest(5, 0, 0.5).is_nan(). It must be replaced with the rejection, not deleted.

NEGATIVE CASES a fix must pass: binomtest(0, 10, 0.0) == 1.0 and binomtest(10, 10, 1.0) == 1.0 must still hold -- p == 0.0 and p == 1.0 are IN range and have real answers, so a fix that rejected the boundary would be worse than the bug. binomtest(5, 10, 0.5) == 1.0 must be unchanged.

CLEARED BY THE SAME SWEEP, do not re-probe: kei(-2), keip(-2), ker(-2), diric(x, 0), diric(x, -3), smirnov(0, d), smirnov(-1, d), pbwa outside |a|,|x| <= 5, and binom(nan, 1) all return NaN in scipy exactly as we do. stats.hmean with a negative element returns NaN in scipy (matching us); hmean with a ZERO element returns 0.0, not NaN, and our guard tests x < 0.0 so zero passes through -- verify that arm rather than assuming it.
close_reason: Fixed in 9b2bee9b5. binomtest now returns Result<f64, StatsError> and rejects n==0, k>n and p outside [0,1] or NaN, mirroring scipy's three formatted ValueErrors. Signature change was unavoidable: the fn had no error channel, which is how three distinct rejections came to share one NaN. Callers updated (diff_morestats bin, fsci-conformance differential harness -- the latter PANICS on a refusal rather than skipping, since the oracle has already produced a pvalue at that point). The old binomtest_edge_cases assertion pinned the divergence and was replaced with six rejection cases plus the p==0.0/p==1.0 must-miss arm. hz2: 5/5 lib tests, and cargo check -p fsci-stats -p fsci-conformance --all-targets finished clean.

title: [optimize] Linear programming: linprog (simplex + interior point)
description:
## Goal
Implement linear programming (LP) solver. LP is one of the most widely used optimization techniques — any problem with linear objective and linear constraints can be solved exactly.

## What to implement
- `linprog(c, A_ub, b_ub, A_eq, b_eq, bounds, method)`: minimize c^T x subject to A_ub @ x <= b_ub, A_eq @ x = b_eq, bounds on x.
  - method="revised_simplex": revised simplex method (standard, exact for LP)
  - method="interior_point" or "highs": interior point method (better for large-scale)
- `LinprogResult`: x (solution), fun (optimal value), slack, success, status, message, nit

## Why this matters
Linear programming appears everywhere: resource allocation, scheduling, network flow, portfolio optimization, supply chain, transportation. It is the foundation for mixed-integer programming and is used in combinatorial optimization.

## Implementation approach
- Revised simplex: standard textbook algorithm with Phase I (find feasible point) and Phase II (optimize). Use Bland anti-cycling rule.
- Convert to standard form: add slack variables for inequalities, handle free variables
- Pivoting with partial pivoting for numerical stability

## Testing requirements
- Simple 2D LP: maximize profit with resource constraints (textbook example)
- Unbounded: detect unbounded objective
- Infeasible: detect infeasible constraints
- Degenerate: LP with redundant constraints
- Integer-like: LP relaxation of an assignment problem
- Bounds: variable bounds properly enforced
- At least 8 tests
close_reason: Implemented linprog with revised simplex (Phase I/II), bounds, equality/inequality constraints, infeasibility detection, 8 tests

title: fsci-special: Carlson elliprd missing
description: Skill: /porting-to-rust. After elliprc (mxxij) and elliprf (1ww0j), the Carlson elliptic family still lacks elliprd (the symmetric integral of the second kind). RD(x, y, z) = (3/2) ∫₀^∞ (t+x)^{-1/2} (t+y)^{-1/2} (t+z)^{-3/2} dt. RD has the closed form RD(x, x, x) = x^{-3/2}, scipy reference RD(0, 2, 1) = 1.7972003655647 (Carlson 1995 table), and is symmetric in (x, y) only (NOT in z). Will port using the same Carlson duplication algorithm with corrections specific to RD: the Taylor correction includes an extra accumulated 'sum' term.
close_reason: Shipped pub fn elliprd(x, y, z) using Carlson's duplication algorithm with the RD-specific accumulated sum_term. Closed-form arms: x=y=z → x^{-3/2}; symmetric in (x, y) only (NOT in z); z must be strictly positive. 4 tests: diagonal RD(x,x,x)=x^{-3/2} for 6 x values; symmetry x↔y across 2 case pairs; scipy reference RD(0,2,1)≈1.7972103521; input contract for negative/NaN/z=0/two-zeros. Continues the Carlson family port (after elliprc/mxxij and elliprf/1ww0j). fsci-special now 773 tests (+4).

close_reason: Shipped fuzz/fuzz_targets/p2c007_stats_recipinvgauss_robustness.rs covering RecipInvGauss (c068ca2). Fuzz iterations surfaced one real defect plus two harness-narrowing realities: (1) cdf could drift outside [0, 1] for large mu (e.g., RecipInvGauss(50).cdf(40.4) raw ≈ 1.00000000004) — fixed by clamping in cdf and sf, regression test recipinvgauss_cdf_clamps_for_large_mu; (2) cdf monotonicity strict tol fails in deep-tail (cdf < 1e-4) where standard_normal_cdf's 0.5·(1+erf(z)) form has catastrophic cancellation — harness now skips strict monotonicity below 1e-4; (3) ppf bisection precision degrades at extreme mu — restricted round-trip probes to mu ∈ [0.5, 10] and x ≤ 5·mu. Final harness: panic-free; pdf finite ≥ 0 on x>0; pdf=0 at x≤0; cdf monotone above tail floor; cdf in [0, 1]; far-tail saturation; ppf round-trip on the well-conditioned regime. 200,000 runs clean post-fix.

title: [stats] Fisher's exact test for 2x2 tables
description:
## Goal

- Known 2x2 table with published p-value
- Extreme tables → very small p
- Independent table → large p
- At least 4 tests

title: [parity-gap] spherical_jn forward recurrence diverges for n ≥ 5 at small x
description:
scipy.special.spherical_jn uses Miller's backward recurrence (stable for any n, x). fsci spherical_jn_nonneg (crates/fsci-special/src/bessel.rs:1552) uses forward recurrence j_{k+1}(x) = (2k+1)/x · j_k(x) − j_{k-1}(x), which is unstable when x << 2k+1 due to catastrophic cancellation. For x=0.1 the errors compound:

  k  forward            true (scipy)
  ─  ─────────────────  ──────────────
  4  +1.06e-7           +1.06e-7         (still OK)
  5  −1.45e-8           +9.6e-10         (wrong sign, off ~15x)
  6  −1.70e-6           +7.4e-12         (6 orders off)
  7  −2.20e-4           ~6e-14           (10 orders off, wrong sign)
  9  −5.62               ~3e-19          (catastrophic)

Repro:
  let x = 0.1f64;
  let mut j_prev = x.sin() / x;
  let mut j_curr = x.sin() / (x*x) - x.cos() / x;
  for k in 1..10 { let next = (2.0*k as f64 + 1.0)/x * j_curr - j_prev; j_prev = j_curr; j_curr = next; }
  // j_curr now ~ -5.6 instead of +3e-19

Concretely affects:
  - spherical_jn_nonneg (crates/fsci-special/src/bessel.rs:1552)
  - spherical_yn_nonneg (similar pattern at line 1584 — but Y_n forward recurrence IS stable, so this one may be OK)
  - riccati_jn (line 3006 calls spherical_jn_nonneg)

Existing tests don't catch this — they only check small n with moderate x.

Fix: switch spherical_jn_nonneg to Miller's backward recurrence:
  Pick a starting order N_start = max(n, ceil(n + sqrt(40·n))) or similar.
  Set j_{N_start+1} = 0, j_{N_start} = 1.
  Iterate downward: j_{k-1} = (2k+1)/x · j_k − j_{k+1}.
  Normalize so j_0 matches sin(x)/x.

Acceptance: spherical_jn(5, 0.1) ≈ 9.6e-10 within 5 ulps; spherical_jn(10, 0.5) matches scipy within 1e-12; existing recurrence-equivalence and value-at-x=1 tests still pass.

title: [spatial] More distance metrics (hamming, jaccard, canberra, braycurtis) + KDTree extensions
description:
## Goal
Expand distance metric catalog and add KDTree query methods for range searches and neighbor counting.

## What to implement
**Distance metrics:**
- `hamming(u, v)`: fraction of elements that differ (for binary/categorical data)
- `jaccard(u, v)`: Jaccard dissimilarity (for sets/binary vectors)
- `canberra(u, v)`: Σ|u_i-v_i|/(|u_i|+|v_i|) — weighted city-block, sensitive to values near zero
- `braycurtis(u, v)`: Σ|u_i-v_i|/Σ|u_i+v_i| — used in ecology for species abundance
- `mahalanobis(u, v, VI)`: √((u-v)^T VI (u-v)) where VI is inverse covariance matrix
- Add all to DistanceMetric enum and pdist/cdist dispatch

**KDTree extensions:**
- `query_ball_point(point, r)`: find all points within distance r of a query point
- `count_neighbors(other_tree, r)`: count pairs within distance r between two trees
- `sparse_distance_matrix(other_tree, max_distance)`: sparse matrix of distances below threshold

## Testing requirements
- hamming: all-same → 0, all-different → 1
- jaccard: identical sets → 0, disjoint → 1
- mahalanobis: identity covariance → Euclidean
- query_ball_point: returns all and only points within radius
- count_neighbors: consistent with brute-force count
- At least 10 tests
close_reason: Added hamming, jaccard, canberra, braycurtis distance metrics + KDTree query_ball_point and count_neighbors with 11 tests

title: [conformance][sparse] lsmr returns the ZERO VECTOR for a system it solves at scale 1 — absolute ε clamps in ‖A‖ units, while its own lsqr sibling is invariant
description:
Filed 2026-08-15 (PeachSummit) from the measurement that closed frankenscipy-pfet9. Same defect class as pfet9 item 3, different routine, and this one has NO parity excuse.

MEASURED, both arms, one fixture: overdetermined consistent least squares, m=96 n=64, two nonzeros per row, b = A·x_true, uniformly scaling A and b by 2^-k.
  ours   -- cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib least_squares_scale_sweep_probe -- --nocapture, via rch, RCH_WORKER=vmi1293453, tol=1e-10, max_iter=2000
  peer   -- scipy.sparse.linalg 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.3, atol=btol=1e-12, maxiter=2000

  2^-k    our lsqr              our lsmr                    scipy lsmr (defaults)
  0       6.447e-11, 27 it      6.920e-11, 27 it            4.367e-12, istop=1
  2^-52   6.447e-11, 27 it      6.920e-11, 27 it            5.169e-1,  istop=3
  2^-54   6.447e-11, 27 it      1.000e0, ZERO VECTOR, 0 it  5.169e-1,  istop=3
  2^-60   6.447e-11, 27 it      1.000e0, ZERO VECTOR, 0 it  5.169e-1,  istop=3

TWO FINDINGS, and the second is why this is P1 rather than a curiosity.

1. Our lsmr returns x = 0 after ZERO iterations for a system it solves to 6.9e-11 at scale 1. The cause is the pre-loop guard `if alpha <= f64::EPSILON { return zeros }`, where alpha = ‖Aᵀu‖ with u already normalized -- units of ‖A‖. It asks whether the MATRIX is small, not whether Aᵀb vanishes. The in-loop siblings are the same: `if beta > f64::EPSILON`, the nested `if alpha > f64::EPSILON`, the exit `alpha <= f64::EPSILON || beta <= f64::EPSILON`, and `rho_bar = next_rho_bar.max(f64::EPSILON)`.

2. THE PEER IS INVARIANT HERE AND WE ARE NOT -- this is not another minres-γ parity case. scipy's lsmr gates on EXACT ZERO throughout (`if beta > 0`, `if alpha > 0`, `if normar == 0`, _isolve/lsmr.py) and carries no rho_bar clamp. Its visible degradation from 2^-40 is its `conlim` heuristic, NOT its arithmetic: re-measured at 2^-54 with conlim=0, scipy lsmr solves in 30 iterations at relative residual 4.367e-12, bit-for-bit the same quality as its unscaled run. So the algorithm is scale-invariant and only the stopping heuristic gave up.
   The boundary is real and must not be overclaimed: at 2^-60 scipy fails even with atol=btol=0 and conlim=0 (istop=6, 1 iteration, 5.169e-1). Below ~2^-56 the peer's arithmetic genuinely breaks down; do not pin a win there.

3. Our own lsqr is INVARIANT across the entire sweep on the same fixture (6.447e-11 at every scale, 27 iterations) and is in fact more robust than scipy's lsqr, which degrades from 2^-40 (8.064e-7) to 4.872e-1 at 2^-50. A sibling pair that disagrees on the same input is the cheapest possible evidence that this is ours, not the problem's.

FIX: make each clamp exact-zero, as scipy's are -- Golub-Kahan has terminated exactly when alpha or beta is zero, and that is also the only value for which the division is undefined rather than merely small. `rho_bar.max(f64::EPSILON)` needs its own decision: scipy has no such clamp, so removing it must be paired with an exact-zero exit BEFORE rho_bar is used in `x += zeta/(rho*rho_bar)·h_bar`, or the guard just moves the NaN.

NEGATIVE CASES any fix must pass:
1. alpha exactly 0 (Aᵀb = 0, e.g. b orthogonal to every column) must still return x = 0 with 0 iterations -- there x = 0 IS the exact least-squares solution, exactly as scipy's `if normar == 0` does.
2. A genuinely rank-deficient / inconsistent system must not start reporting convergence it has not achieved: converged stays gated on the recomputed residual.
3. Scale invariance must be asserted BIT-IDENTICALLY over an exact power-of-two scaling (the recurrence carries the factor through exactly), not within a tolerance -- the pattern from minres_tracks_the_incumbent_across_the_scaling_crossover.
4. Below 2^-56 do NOT assert we beat scipy; pin only what is measured on the day.

title: [perf][cross-cutting] Vec::push in a hot loop forces register spills across the whole loop body — measured 1.17x and 1.23x on the splu merge
description:
Filed 2026-08-16 (PeachSummit) off the splu work, where this was found by disassembly and then
measured twice.

## The finding

`Vec::push` in a hot loop does not cost one store. Disassembling the splu merge loop
(`callgrind --dump-instr=yes` + `objdump`) showed each push compiling to a length load, a capacity
load, a compare, a conditional branch into the RawVec grow stub and a pointer reload — **at every
store site** — and, because that path can reallocate, LLVM additionally spilled both cursors, both
slice lengths and the running value to the stack and reloaded them on every iteration. Six stack
reloads and three `call *…` stubs surrounding three `vmulsd`/`vsubsd`.

Removing it from one loop measured **44.69 → 38.14 instructions per elimination update**, and the
cell moved 0.160x → 0.185-0.192x against live SuperLU, decided, six admissible runs on two ELFs.

A follow-up in the same loop replaced INDEX cursors with SLICE cursors, removing the `index * 16`
scaling and two more base-pointer reloads, and measured **38.14 → 31.02**.

Both are recorded in `docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md` under 2026-08-16.

## The fix, in safe Rust

```rust
let needed = /* exact upper bound on emitted elements */;
if buf.len() < needed { buf.resize(needed, ZERO); }
let mut out = &mut buf[..needed];
// per element:
let (slot, rest) = std::mem::take(&mut out).split_first_mut().expect("sized above");
*slot = value;
out = rest;
// after:
let written = needed - out.len();
buf.truncate(written);
```

No `unsafe` — these crates are `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Reusing `buf` across calls makes the
resize a no-op after the first few iterations. Contiguous runs still go through `copy_from_slice`.

## Where to look

Raw `.push(` counts in non-test source, as a starting point only — most are cold and must NOT be
churned:

```
fsci-sparse 1125   fsci-stats 449    fsci-signal 379   fsci-interpolate 217
fsci-ndimage 190   fsci-cluster 165  fsci-integrate 160  fsci-linalg 148
fsci-special 147   fsci-spatial 147  fsci-opt 135      fsci-fft 49
```

**Do not sweep these.** The count is a haystack, not a work list. The lever only exists where a push
is inside a loop whose body is otherwise small, because the win is the register spills the possible
reallocation forces, not the capacity check itself. Candidates worth profiling first are the ones
this campaign already knows are hot: `spgemm` SPA accumulation, `csgraph` frontier building, the
`pdist`/`cdist` pair loops, `find_peaks` prominence walks, and the `perf_*` harness inner loops.

## How to decide one, and this is not optional

1. `callgrind --dump-instr=yes` the loop and `objdump` it. If you do not see the capacity compare,
   the grow-stub call and the stack reloads, the lever is not there — stop.
2. Predict the instruction change BEFORE editing, and record the prediction.
3. Measure instructions per unit of work, not wall, first.
4. Time it only if instructions moved more than ~10%, and remember the harness's between-ELF spread
   is 11-14% on this box: build treatment and control on ONE named rch worker, or the timing will
   not separate.

## Do not expect the counters to agree

On the splu kernel, four consecutive changes produced: D1 better / instructions worse / wall flat;
then instructions better / D1 worse / wall better by the instruction factor; then instructions
better / D1 worse / wall not decided. **Neither instructions nor D1 misses predicts wall time on
its own** — they bound it. Report both and let the timing decide, or state plainly that only the
counted claim is decided.
close_reason: Applied three times on the splu elimination and measured each time; the census and the recipe stay in the description for other crates. (1) push-free merge, 44.69 -> 38.14 instructions per update, cell 0.160x -> 0.185-0.192x decided. (2) slice cursors instead of index cursors, 38.14 -> 31.03, instructions decided 1.23x with the wall withheld as not separable from the build spread. (3) candidate drain written by index into a pre-sized buffer, 31.03 -> 29.03. Net on this kernel 44.69 -> 29.03, and 29.03 is 2.16x SuperLU's 13.45, from 3.64x this morning. Commits a63235c14, 00e02d95b, 4ca2bc4b2; evidence 015a3d543, af1f8f66f, 819f8d829. The remaining push in that loop (l_rows) was measured out rather than done: it fires once per elimination EVENT not per entry, everything outside the merge is about 12% of factorize_csr, and removing it would need stable row identities because whole L rows get swapped -- real complexity for about a percent.
