title: [perf][sparse] merge the splu row in place from the back — memcpy is 19% of the process and the copy-back is the source
description:
Split off frankenscipy-9nw95 2026-08-16 (PeachSummit). The target is measured, the two cheap
alternatives are already refuted, and the cost this design must answer is stated up front.

## The measured target

`__memcpy_avx_unaligned_erms` is **19% of process instructions** on the cubic cell — 1,292,898,732
against `factorize_csr`'s 4,575,048,595 at side=12, 37 factorizations. `_int_malloc` adds another
184,836,059.

The dominant source is the **copy-back**: `apply_sorted_pivot_tail` builds the merged row in a
shared `scratch` and then copies it into the row's own storage. That copy is deliberate and is
already justified — it replaced a `mem::swap` that made the output buffer a different allocation on
every call, and it took the D1 **write**-miss rate from **10.8% to 1.8%** against SuperLU's 1.0%.
So the copy cannot simply be deleted; the write-locality it buys has to be preserved.

Already refuted, do not re-try:
- borrowing the pivot tail instead of copying it (`split_at_mut`) — memcpy moved **0.8%**
- block-advancing the non-matched merge branches — instructions moved **0.6%**
- sorting the candidate list for a monotone header walk — D1 read went **7.2% -> 7.5%**

## The design: merge in place, from the back

A merge's output is never longer than `live_len + tail_len`. So if the row's arrays are extended to
`len + tail_len` and the merge writes **descending** from the far end, the write cursor is always
ahead of both read cursors and no unread input is ever clobbered. This is the standard in-place
merge-from-the-back argument, and it removes the scratch buffer and the copy-back together while
keeping every write inside the row's own storage — which is the property that made the copy-back
work in the first place.

Cancellation to exactly zero makes the result shorter. That needs no compaction at the time: the
row already carries a `start` window, so a shorter result is simply a larger `start`.

Sketch:

```
let need = live_len + tail_len;
row.cols.resize(row.cols.len() + tail_len, 0);      // extend, do not allocate a second buffer
row.vals.resize(row.vals.len() + tail_len, 0.0);
let mut w = row.cols.len();                          // exclusive write cursor, descending
let mut l = old_len;                                 // exclusive, over the live target
let mut r = tail_len;                                // exclusive, over the tail
while l > lo && r > 0 { ... write the LARGER column at w-1, decrement ... }
row.start = w;                                       // whatever is left of the front is dead
```

## The cost it has to answer, stated now

Arrays grow by `tail_len` on every merge and `start` only advances, so **storage is monotonically
increasing** and must be compacted on some schedule. Compaction is itself a memcpy, so this design
only wins if the schedule is amortized well below one compaction per merge — e.g. compact row `r`
when `start > len / 2`, which is O(1) amortized per element but needs measuring rather than
assuming. If the compaction traffic approaches the copy-back traffic it replaces, the design is a
wash and should be reported as one.

## Verify this way, and measure both numbers

1. `__memcpy_avx_unaligned_erms` instructions, **not** the aggregate — the aggregate mixes the
   copy-back with every other copy in the process.
2. The D1 **write**-miss rate at the same time. A back-merge writes into the row's own storage, so
   if the write-miss rate rises above ~2% the design has lost the thing it was meant to keep, and
   that is a rejection even if memcpy falls.
3. `_int_malloc`, because `resize` on a row that has no spare capacity reallocates; if malloc rises
   to meet the memcpy that fell, nothing was gained.

Bit-identity is testable throughout: `sorted_rows_are_bit_identical_to_the_hashed_reference` runs
the retained hash-backed elimination and the shipping one in the same binary and compares
`row_perm`, `fill_perm`, L and U exactly. A back-merge changes the ORDER in which entries are
written but not the value written to any `(row, col)`, so it must keep passing unchanged. If it
does not, the merge has a real bug, not a tolerance question.

Also re-run the shape diagnostic afterwards, since it reports the fraction of merges taking the
in-place fast path and a back-merge should not change that fraction:
`cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib merge_shape -- --ignored --nocapture`

## Budget

Needs at least two build-and-measure cycles. `/data` has been oscillating between 58G and 63G
against a 58G floor; check `df -h /data` and skip below 60G.
notes:
=== STATUS 2026-08-16 (PeachSummit): ANALYSIS COMPLETE, IMPLEMENTATION DELIBERATELY NOT STARTED ===
Evidence 401675453 (share series), 9483f2402 (cache baseline), 3d8fcbbe2 (per-call-site split).
All three taken BUILD-FREE on ELF 9b2bc0fb. `br update --notes` REPLACES; history has the rest.

--- 1. THE GATE IS PASSED ---

Per-call-site split of memcpy inside factorize_csr at side=16, by caller instruction address,
identified from the disassembly by OPERAND WIDTH (Vec<u32> scales length by 4, Vec<f64> by 8):

  0x5eac1  copy-back vals   20,538,552 calls  3,247,774,596 Ir  42.96%
  0x5e763  copy-back cols   20,538,552        1,936,718,472     25.62%
  0x5e3c1  in-merge run     20,829,816        1,882,196,033     24.90%
  0x5e67e  remainder cols   20,538,552          267,437,258      3.54%
  0x5e6d9  remainder vals   20,538,552          226,360,154      2.99%

COPY-BACK ALONE = 5,184,493,068 Ir = 68.57% of memcpy = 15.13% of factorize_csr inclusive. That
clears the ~10% decidability threshold. Step 3 is unlocked.

Line tables were NOT needed to get this. release-lines (94cbeefc3) stays for cases where operand
widths do not discriminate, but do not spend a build on it for THIS bead.

--- 2. WHY I STILL DID NOT WRITE THE BACK-MERGE ---

Working the design's cost identity out on paper first, because it has a wash case and it is cheap to
find on paper and expensive to find after a build.

Merging descending into arrays extended by tail_len, with w the write cursor and l the target read
cursor, the gap g = w - l starts at tail_len and moves as:
    tail-only element WRITTEN        g -= 1
    matched element written          g unchanged
    target-only element written      g unchanged
    matched element CANCELS to zero  g += 1
    tail-only element with zero delta g unchanged
So at exhaustion g = tail_len - (tail-only written) + (cancelled).

THE LEFTOVER MOVE. When the tail is exhausted, the target elements still at [lo, l) must end at
[w-(l-lo), w). If g > 0 they have to be MOVED -- a memmove that is exactly the kind of copy this
bead exists to remove. The move length is (l - lo) = THE NUMBER OF TARGET COLUMNS STRICTLY BELOW THE
SMALLEST TAIL COLUMN.

So the lever's payoff is NOT 15.13%; it is 15.13% MINUS that leftover move, and if the target
routinely carries a long prefix below the tail's first column, the design is a wash.

--- 3. THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDES IT, AND IT NEEDS NO NEW CODE ---

MergeShape (cfg(test), already in linalg.rs) counts `target_only` -- merge steps where a target
column has no tail partner. target_only == 0 implies the leftover prefix is empty and the back-merge
moves NOTHING; a small target_only bounds the move directly.

When builds are permitted, the FIRST thing to run is the existing diagnostic, not an implementation:
    cargo test -p fsci-sparse --lib merge_shape -- --ignored --nocapture
Read target_only against merges (555,096 merges per factorization at side=16, measured) and runs
(1.014 runs per merge -- so a merge almost always contains exactly ONE coincident run).

  target_only near 0     -> back-merge moves ~nothing, implement it, expect most of the 15.13%
  target_only comparable
  to run_elements        -> the leftover move approaches the copy it replaces: WASH, report and drop

PRIOR, stated so it can be wrong: the in-place fast path requires live_cols[0] == tail_cols[0], and
it fires often, which suggests the first columns usually coincide and the prefix is usually short.
That is an inference from a related predicate, NOT a measurement of target_only, and it is exactly
what the run above checks.

--- 4. THEN, AND ONLY THEN ---

Implement behind its own toggle DEFAULTING OFF (unproven levers do not change shipping behaviour),
with a bit-identity test: a back-merge changes the ORDER writes happen in, never the value written to
any (row, col), so sorted_rows_are_bit_identical_to_the_hashed_reference must pass UNCHANGED.
Acceptance is JOINT: memcpy Ir down past ~10%, D1mw rate no worse than ~2%, DLmw DOWN not merely
moved (baseline 594,964 = 66.97% of all LL write misses), and _int_malloc not risen to meet the
memcpy that fell.
close_reason: REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT (not abandoned) -- the design was built, proven correct, and measured 3.41x SLOWER than the copy-back it replaces (305.10 ms vs 89.40 ms; bootstrap-median CIs [0.4662,0.4765] vs [0.1404,0.1445], disjoint; in-run SciPy control flat at 41.85/43.00 ms so not host drift). Toggle proven live both directions from inside the process (hits=48/toggle_reads=48 on, hits=0/48 off). Correctness passed first: splu_back_merge_is_bit_identical_to_the_scratch_merge compares row_perm/fill_perm/L/U as raw bits across the toggle. MECHANISM: with target_only=0 the merge consumes every live target element, so the survivor sits at the FAR END and the dead prefix is nearly the whole row -- the start>len/2 compaction rule then fires almost every merge, so each merge pays a zero-filling resize, often a realloc, the descending merge, AND a compaction that IS the copy-back reintroduced. One copy removed, two added. TRANSFERABLE LESSON: target_only=0 was the WRONG GATE -- it passed honestly and the design still lost, because the cost that killed it was the storage schedule the gate never looked at. A gate that checks one of two costs licenses nothing. NOT REFUTED: the target stands -- the copy-back is still 15.13% of the factorization, 44.42% of writes, 66.97% of LL write misses. RETRY PREDICATE (do not re-open without it): bound the compaction traffic first via a per-call-site memcpy count on a built binary, requiring compaction instructions below the 5,184,493,068 the copy-back costs. Sizing every row once from a symbolic bound dodges the schedule entirely but that is the arena rewrite, frankenscipy-u7biq, not this bead. Ledger: docs/NEGATIVE_EVIDENCE.md, row '2026-08-16 - PeachSummit (cc)' on the back-merge A/B. Closed 2026-08-18 during a build freeze on this project's slot; no build was spent to reach this conclusion.

title: [stats] rankdata tie methods (average/min/max/dense/ordinal) lack a combined scipy golden test
close_reason:
Closed 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey). The combined five-method test exists; its input
is sorted, which erases the one rule that makes `ordinal` different.

DEDUP VERIFICATION: rankdata_methods_match_scipy already covers all five tie
methods (average/min/max/dense/ordinal) against scipy values -- this bead's
literal ask -- so it is not repeated. rankdata_dense_min_max_match_scipy_
reference and rankdata_matches_scipy_reference_values add more of the same.

THE GAP: every one of those uses input that is ALREADY SORTED ASCENDING
([1,2,2,3,3,3] and [1,2,2,4]). Four of the five methods are order-insensitive by
construction, so sorted input costs them nothing. `ordinal` is not: it breaks
ties by position in the ORIGINAL array. On sorted input its answer is trivially
[1,2,3,4,5,6] -- which is exactly what you also get from an implementation that
sorts first and then hands out consecutive ranks in SORTED order. That is a
completely different rule that happens to agree on sorted data, so the existing
tests cannot tell the two apart.

title: [HIGH] integrate/quad: quad/quad_vec/cubature epsabs/epsrel NaN pass the < 0.0 reject branch — same fail-open class as i9vw, spread across 3 more sites; adaptive refinement returns converged=false with arbitrary partial sum instead of rejecting at input
description:
Review of crates/fsci-integrate/src/quad.rs on 2026-04-22, companion to frankenscipy-i9vw.

Three additional sites in quad.rs have the same NaN-fail-open pattern as validation.rs:

    Line 228  (quad):           if options.epsabs < 0.0 || options.epsrel < 0.0 { reject }
    Line 282  (quad_vec):        if options.epsabs < 0.0 || options.epsrel < 0.0 { reject }
    Line 1479 (cubature):        if options.atol   < 0.0 || options.rtol   < 0.0 { reject }

Each check fails open for NaN because NaN < 0.0 is false in IEEE 754. A caller passing epsabs=NaN, epsrel=NaN, atol=NaN, or rtol=NaN gets no QuadInvalidTolerance error.

Downstream behavior is then dictated by the adaptive refinement tolerance check at quad.rs:330:

    let tolerance = epsabs.max(epsrel * integral.abs());

With NaN inputs:
  - epsabs = NaN: `NaN.max(x)` in Rust returns x (f64::max treats NaN as smaller).
    So tolerance = epsrel * integral.abs(). If epsrel is also NaN, tolerance = NaN.
  - The recursion continues while `error >= tolerance`. With tolerance = NaN, all
    comparisons return false; loop terminates at the recursion depth limit and
    returns whatever partial sum was accumulated with converged=false.

So with NaN tolerances: quad/quad_vec returns Ok with converged=false and an integral
value that is WHATEVER the adaptive splitter happened to compute at the limit cap.
A caller reading result.integral without checking result.converged gets potentially
meaningful-looking numbers from a request that should have been rejected at input.

Inconsistency in the same file: cubature_bounds_check (line 1474-1496) CORRECTLY
uses `!value.is_finite()` for cubature points at line 1490. The author knew the
right predicate. The shallow `< 0.0` check was used for atol/rtol inconsistently.

Fix (paralleling i9vw):
1. Replace each `options.foo < 0.0` with `!options.foo.is_finite() || options.foo < 0.0`
   (and Inf epsabs/epsrel may be legit -- decide per SciPy's behavior), OR better:
   add explicit is_nan check:

       if options.epsabs.is_nan() || options.epsrel.is_nan() {
           return Err(IntegrateValidationError::QuadInvalidTolerance {
               detail: "tolerances must not be NaN".to_string(),
           });
       }
       if options.epsabs < 0.0 || options.epsrel < 0.0 {
           ... (existing)
       }

2. Add regression tests for each entry point:
    quad(f, 0.0, 1.0, QuadOptions { epsabs: NaN, ... })         => Err
    quad_vec(f, 0.0, 1.0, QuadOptions { epsrel: NaN, ... })     => Err
    cubature(f, a, b, CubatureOptions { atol: NaN, ... })       => Err

3. Consider unifying under a single helper validate_quad_tolerance that's called from all
   three entry points; 3-way duplication of the predicate invites drift.

Related: i9vw (the solve_ivp path; same class of bug in validate_{first_step,max_step,tol}),
95ld (string mode fields for integrate), mhuk (audit ledger gap).
close_reason: All three sites (quad.rs:228 / 282 / 1479) already gate on is_nan() before the < 0.0 strict compare. Grep confirms. Already-fixed, no code change needed.

title: [MEDIUM] conformance: build_replay_command in e2e.rs:665 builds shell command by string interpolation without shell-escaping packet_id/scenario_id/artifact_root — malicious or typo'd fixture ID with shell metacharacters can inject commands when an operator copy-pastes
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/e2e.rs:665-676 on 2026-04-22:

    fn build_replay_command(config, packet_id, scenario_id) -> String {
        format!(
            'cargo run -p fsci-conformance --bin e2e_orchestrator -- --artifact-root {} --packet {} --scenario {}',
            config.artifact_root.display(),
            packet_id,
            scenario_id,
        )
    }

This builds a shell command by direct string interpolation. No
shell escaping is applied to packet_id, scenario_id, or artifact_root.

Call context: build_replay_command is called from run_single_scenario
at line 335 with discovered.packet_id (from fixture JSON) and
scenario.scenario_id (from fixture JSON). These are written into
events.jsonl as the replay_command field, intended for an operator
to copy-paste into a terminal when debugging a failed scenario.

Threat model:

1. Operator copy-paste is TRUSTED -- the operator reads the command
   before running it. So auto-execution is not the attack vector.

2. BUT if packet_id or scenario_id contains shell metacharacters
   (spaces, ';', '|', '&&', '', backticks), the copy-pasted
   command breaks or executes unintended operations. A fixture with:
       scenario_id: 'scenario_01; rm -rf /tmp/stuff'
   produces a replay command that, when pasted, runs the rm -rf.

3. Current fixtures use sanitized IDs (a-z, 0-9, _, -). No malicious
   IDs today. But the runtime contract permits future fixtures to
   contain anything, including accidental shell metacharacters like
   unicode quotes or typos.

4. Fail-closed doctrine demands defenses at serialization layers, not
   just at consumption. A replay command that the operator expects
   to be a SAFE string is actually a partially-attacker-controlled
   payload once written to events.jsonl.

Additional observations:

1. sanitize_path_component at line 678 IS applied to scenario_id for
   the scenario_dir_name (line 315) but NOT for the replay command.
   Two different escaping conventions for the same raw value within
   the same module.

2. artifact_root.display() for non-UTF-8 paths may produce lossy
   output. On Linux paths are bytes, not necessarily UTF-8.

Fix:
1. Emit replay command as a JSON array of arguments, not a shell string:
       replay_command: ['cargo', 'run', '-p', 'fsci-conformance', ...,
                        '--packet', packet_id, '--scenario', scenario_id]
   Tools like jq or Python subprocess.run(..., shell=False) consume
   this safely. Human can manually concatenate with copy-paste awareness.
2. Alternative: use the shlex crate (or manual escaping) to
   shell-quote each argument before interpolation. Requires adding
   shlex as a dependency.
3. Add a test that generates a replay command with a scenario_id
   containing a space + semicolon, asserts the command is either
   escaped correctly OR rejected at emit time.

Related: nub7 (deny_unknown_fields permits typos), gnun (error-string
equality anti-pattern), similar class: trusting string interpolation
of potentially-untrusted content.
close_reason: Shell-quoted replay command args (commit 527585e).

description:

    pub fn run_smoke(config: &HarnessConfig) -> HarnessReport {
        let fixture_count = fs::read_dir(&config.fixture_root)

            .into_iter()

        HarnessReport {
            suite: 'smoke',
            oracle_present: config.oracle_root.exists(),
            fixture_count,
            strict_mode: config.strict_mode,
        }
    }

What run_smoke actually does:
1. Count entries (files + dirs) in fixture_root directory.
2. Check if oracle_root path exists (doesn't exec python, just filesystem check).
3. Report strict_mode flag.

What run_smoke does NOT do:
- Load any fixture file
- Parse any fixture JSON
- Call any fsci-* function
- Execute any Rust scientific logic
- Invoke any scipy oracle
- Compare any output against any reference

The test at tests/smoke.rs (15 lines):

    fn smoke_report_is_stable() {
        let cfg = HarnessConfig::default_paths();
        let report = run_smoke(&cfg);
        assert_eq!(report.suite, 'smoke');
        assert!(report.fixture_count >= 1);
        assert!(report.oracle_present);
        let fixture_path = cfg.fixture_root.join('smoke_case.json');
        assert!(Path::new(&fixture_path).exists());
    }

Assertions:
1. suite field is literally 'smoke' -- hardcoded at line 1546.
2. fixture_count >= 1 -- fixtures/ has 14+ files; trivially passes.

4. fixture_path exists -- filesystem presence check.

Impact:

- A critical regression in any fsci-* function that would be caught

2. linprog with revised simplex method
3. differential_evolution global optimizer
4. root() / fsolve() multivariate root finding (hybrd/hybrj methods)
5. linear_sum_assignment (Hungarian algorithm)
6. Unit tests + conformance fixtures for each
7. FEATURE_PARITY.md updated

## Serves Project Goal

differential_evolution and linprog are #3 and #4 on the highest-impact missing list. Constrained optimization is the most-requested missing capability.

title: Implement Bounds, LinearConstraint, NonlinearConstraint types
description:
## What

Implement the three constraint types needed for constrained minimize(): Bounds (per-variable box constraints), LinearConstraint (A @ x ≤ b), NonlinearConstraint (lb ≤ c(x) ≤ ub). Wire into existing minimize() dispatcher so that BFGS/L-BFGS-B/etc. can accept constraints.

## Why

Without constraint types, minimize() can only solve unconstrained problems. L-BFGS-B already supports bounds internally but there's no Bounds type to pass them through.

## Implementation Notes

- Bounds: Vec<(Option<f64>, Option<f64>)> with validation
- LinearConstraint: matrix A, vectors lb/ub, keep_feasible flag
- NonlinearConstraint: function c(x), vectors lb/ub, jacobian option
- Wire Bounds into L-BFGS-B minimize path
- For linear/nonlinear constraints: needed by trust-constr or SLSQP (future), but define the types now

## Tests

- Bounds validation (lb ≤ ub)
- minimize with L-BFGS-B + bounds produces constrained solution
- LinearConstraint construction and validation
notes: All three constraint types already implemented in types.rs: Bounds, LinearConstraint, NonlinearConstraint with full validation and helper methods
close_reason: already implemented in fsci-opt/types.rs: Bounds, LinearConstraint, NonlinearConstraint

title: Implement linprog (revised simplex)
description:
## What

Implement linprog(c, A_ub, b_ub, A_eq, b_eq, bounds) — linear programming solver. Primary method: revised simplex. Standard form: minimize c^T x subject to A_ub @ x ≤ b_ub, A_eq @ x = b_eq, bounds.

## Why

#4 highest-impact missing function across all of FrankenSciPy. LP is foundational for operations research, economics, and network optimization.

## Implementation Notes

- Revised simplex method: maintain basis inverse factorization, price/ratio test/pivot
- Preprocessing: convert inequality constraints to equalities with slack variables
- Phase I (artificial variables) for finding initial basic feasible solution
- Phase II: optimize
- Return: optimal x, optimal value, status (optimal/infeasible/unbounded), number of iterations
- Consider also implementing interior-point (HiGHS-style) as future enhancement

## Tests

- Classic 2-variable LP → known optimal vertex
- Infeasible problem → status=infeasible
- Unbounded problem → status=unbounded
- Degenerate LP (cycling protection)
- Comparison against hand-solved examples from textbooks
close_reason: linprog already implemented in fsci-opt (verified in reality-check)

title: Implement differential_evolution (global optimizer)
description:
## What

Implement differential_evolution(func, bounds) — stochastic global optimization via differential evolution. Parameters: strategy, maxiter, popsize, tol, mutation, recombination, seed, polish.

## Why

#3 highest-impact missing function across all of FrankenSciPy. The go-to global optimizer when gradient-free optimization is needed over a bounded search space.

## Implementation Notes

- Population: popsize × ndim matrix of candidates within bounds
- Mutation: best1bin, rand1bin, currenttobest1bin strategies
- Crossover: binomial with recombination probability
- Selection: greedy — keep better of trial vs. target
- Polish: optional local minimize (L-BFGS-B or NM) on best result
- Convergence: when std(population values) < tol or maxiter reached
- Seed parameter for reproducibility

## Tests

- Rosenbrock 2D → finds (1,1) within tolerance
- Rastrigin 2D → finds global minimum (not just local)
- Ackley function → global minimum
- Converges faster with polish=true
- Reproducible with fixed seed
close_reason: differential_evolution already implemented in fsci-opt (verified in reality-check)

title: Implement root() and linear_sum_assignment()
description:
## What

1. root(fun, x0, method) — multivariate root finding. Methods: hybr (Powell's hybrid/MINPACK), lm (Levenberg-Marquardt).
2. linear_sum_assignment(cost_matrix) — Hungarian algorithm for optimal assignment.

## Why

root/fsolve is needed for equation solving. linear_sum_assignment is needed for matching problems in combinatorics, tracking, and scheduling.

## Implementation Notes

- root (hybr): Newton's method with dogleg trust-region for robustness. Compute Jacobian via finite differences if not provided.
- root (lm): Levenberg-Marquardt for nonlinear least-squares formulation of root finding.
- linear_sum_assignment: Jonker-Volgenant variant of Hungarian algorithm, O(n³). Handle rectangular cost matrices by padding.

## Tests

- root: f(x) = [x[0]²+x[1]-1, x[0]+x[1]²-1] → two solutions
- linear_sum_assignment: 3×3 known-answer cost matrix
- linear_sum_assignment: rectangular matrix
- linear_sum_assignment: negative costs
notes: Already implemented in fsci-opt

title: fsci-stats: pin RDist ≡ shifted symmetric Beta metamorphic identity
description: Pin the textbook metamorphic identity RDist(c) ≡ 2·Beta(c/2, c/2) − 1. The R-distribution is the linearly-shifted symmetric Beta: if Y ~ Beta(c/2, c/2), then 2Y − 1 ~ RDist(c). Equivalent: RDist(c).cdf(x) = Beta(c/2, c/2).cdf((x + 1)/2) and RDist(c).pdf(x) = Beta(c/2, c/2).pdf((x + 1)/2) / 2 (Jacobian). Pin pdf+cdf agreement at multiple (c, x) values.

If Y ~ Beta(c/2, c/2), then 2Y − 1 ~ RDist(c). cdf relation: RDist.cdf(x) = Beta(c/2, c/2).cdf((x+1)/2). pdf relation: RDist.pdf(x) = Beta(c/2, c/2).pdf((x+1)/2)/2 (Jacobian). Test sweeps 5 c-values × 7 x-values comparing cdf at tol 1e-12 and pdf at relative 1e-10. title: [stats] NoncentralT.ppf wrong at extreme quantiles — bisection converges on abs cdf tol 1e-10 (same size as q)
description: nct(10,5).ppf(1e-10)=-12.96 vs scipy -1.81 (cdf(-12.96)=3e-18, not 1e-10). The nct ppf has a custom bisection whose convergence check is (cdf_mid-q).abs()<1e-10. The cdf itself is accurate (cdf(-1.81)=1.009e-10 matches scipy). Fix: drop the cdf-abs-tol exit, converge on bracket width (hi-lo)<=1e-13*max(|mid|,1) like the shared ppf_bisection. title: [code-review] fftconvolve 'valid' mode panic risk on a.len() == b.len() == 0
description:
Reading fftconvolve at crates/fsci-fft/src/helpers.rs:154-206 with a /modes-of-reasoning correctness lens: the early return 'if a.is_empty() || b.is_empty() { return Ok(vec![]); }' protects most empty cases, but the 'valid' branch at line 193-202 unconditionally subtracts (b.len() - 1) from a usize when a.len() >= b.len(). If both are empty by some reachable code path that bypasses the early return (currently impossible, but the early-return guard is the only defense), the subtraction would underflow.

P1 because the safety relies on the early return being placed BEFORE any path that touches len()-1; ride-along refactor opportunity to express the constraint at the type level via NonZeroUsize or a debug_assert!(b.len() > 0) at the start of the 'valid' arm.

Acceptance: add debug_assert!(!a.is_empty() && !b.is_empty()) at the top of 'valid' and 'same' arms so any future regression that moves the early-return loses out cleanly under cargo test, not in production.

title: Implement remaining distribution moments: Gompertz, LogLaplace, Mielke, FrechetR
description:
## Context (REVISED after re-audit)
GenLogistic is already implemented. Remaining distributions with NaN moments that have
computable formulas or can use numerical integration:

## Scope
All changes in crates/fsci-stats/src/lib.rs:

1. **Gompertz::mean()** (line ~3425) — Formula: mean = -(1/c)·e^c·Ei(-c) where Ei is the
   exponential integral. Use fsci_special::expi_scalar. Note: for Gompertz distribution
   with parameter c, mean = (1/c)·exp(c)·E₁(c) where E₁ is the exponential integral.
   Available via fsci_special::exp1_scalar or expi_scalar.

2. **Gompertz::var()** (line ~3429) — Compute via numerical integration:
   E[X²] = ∫₀^∞ x²·c·exp(x)·exp(-c·(exp(x)-1)) dx, then var = E[X²] - mean².
   SciPy uses generic numerical integration. We can use adaptive trapezoidal
   quadrature on [0, 20] (tail decays rapidly).

3. **LogLaplace::var()** (line ~3321) — Formula: var = E[X²] - mean² where
   E[X²] = c²/((c-2)(c-1)²) when c > 2. Guard: NaN when c ≤ 2.
   mean = c²/(c²-1) when c > 1 (already implemented).

4. **Mielke::mean()** (line ~3360) — Formula: mean = k·Γ(1+1/k)·Γ(s-1/k)/Γ(s)
   when k·s > 1. Guard: return INFINITY when k·s ≤ 1.
   Need to check Mielke struct fields.

5. **Mielke::var()** (line ~3364) — var = E[X²] - mean² where
   E[X²] = k·Γ(1+2/k)·Γ(s-2/k)/Γ(s) when k·s > 2. Guard: NaN when k·s ≤ 2.

6. **FrechetR::var()** (line ~3518) — Formula: Γ(1-2/c) - Γ(1-1/c)² when c > 2.
   Same structure as InvWeibull. Guard: NaN when c ≤ 2.
   mean = -Γ(1-1/c) when c > 1 (already implemented).

## Dependencies
- fsci_special::expi_scalar (exists at convenience.rs:1115) for Gompertz
- ln_gamma (already used throughout) for LogLaplace, Mielke, FrechetR

## Testing Requirements
- Unit tests: Gompertz(0.5), Gompertz(1.0), Gompertz(3.0) mean/var vs SciPy
- Unit tests: LogLaplace(3.0), LogLaplace(5.0) var vs SciPy; LogLaplace(1.5) var = NaN
- Unit tests: Mielke(k,s) mean/var for ≥3 valid param combos vs SciPy
- Unit tests: FrechetR(3.0), FrechetR(5.0) var vs SciPy; FrechetR(1.5) var = NaN
- Edge cases: parameters at boundary of moment existence
- Verify var() ≥ 0 for all valid parameters

## Validation
```
cargo test -p fsci-stats -- gompertz
cargo test -p fsci-stats -- log_laplace
cargo test -p fsci-stats -- mielke
cargo test -p fsci-stats -- frechet
```
close_reason: All distribution moments (Gompertz, LogLaplace, Mielke, FrechetR) are fully implemented with SciPy-verified tests. 6/6 tests pass.

close_reason:
Closed 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey) by filling the real remaining gap, not by re-adding covered ground.

PARTIALLY-ALREADY-COVERED, verified before writing anything (three sibling beads --
efgsn, 6o0i4, bti46 -- turned out to be pure duplicates, so I checked first):

the final bin's imaginary part must be non-zero -- plus rfft/fft bin agreement.

title: [audit][FLEET] STANDING RULE: two-arm probe control — no count is reportable without a must-hit AND a must-miss case; plus the stale byte-identity doc audit
description:
Found by RusticCarp 2026-08-06 while implementing frankenscipy-5f06d. Corrected in the same commit; filed because the CLASS of error matters more than this instance.

WHAT HAPPENED. I classified all 53 undriven toggles by the contract in their doc comment, then wrote an exact to_bits() A/B gate for the 41 that claimed byte-identity. logsumexp FAILED it: at n = 100_000, serial gives 23.242200846466424 and parallel 23.242200846466545.

THAT WAS NOT A LEVER DEFECT. It was a STALE DOC. The static's doc said the parallel arm 'materialises the heavy exp via an order-preserving parallel map ... then sums serially over that Vec in index order. Byte-identical.' The code does not do that — it computes per-thread partial sums with no intermediate Vec and folds them, which reassociates. The function's OWN INLINE COMMENT has said 'within per-op ULP tolerance (parallel reorder)' all along, and even explains that the materialise-then-sum path was replaced because the alloc plus serial reduction dominated at large n.

So the implementation was correctly changed and correctly commented INSIDE the function, while the toggle's doc comment — the thing a classifier or a reader reaches for first — kept advertising the old contract.

FIXED: the doc now states the within-ULP contract, names the replaced implementation, and cites the measured drift. The gate was moved to a per-op ULP bound scaled by n. The bound was NOT invented to make a red test green — the lever's real contract was recovered from its own inline comment and the doc was corrected to match.

WHY THIS NEEDS ITS OWN BEAD. My 41/12 classification was built from these doc comments, so at least one entry was wrong and there may be more. Two independent sources of truth exist per lever — the static's doc and the inline comment in the gated function — and they can disagree silently. Anywhere they do, the doc is the one people trust and the code is the one that ships.

WORK: for each of the remaining toggles, compare the static's doc claim against the inline comment in the function it gates, and against what the code actually does. Flag every disagreement. A cheap first pass: grep for statics whose doc says byte-identical while the gated function's body contains a chunked/partial/fold reduction, an unrolled multi-accumulator sum, or any per-thread combine.

This also means frankenscipy-5f06d's 41/12 split should be treated as PROVISIONAL until that audit runs. An exact gate that fails is the cheapest detector for it, which is an argument for continuing to apply exact gates first and letting them find the stale docs.

EVIDENCE TO CLOSE: every toggle's doc contract matches its implementation, with any corrections made to the DOC (or the code, if the code is the thing that is wrong) and never to a test bound.
notes:
2026-08-16 RainyPrairie — AUDIT RUN, reading only (no build; /data freeze). The doc-vs-implementation audit this bead asks for is now DONE for every exactness claim in the tree. Three results, and the first one revises this bead's premise.

(1) THE POPULATION IS NOT WHAT THIS BEAD ASSUMES. Fleet-wide there are 350 `pub static` perf toggles (133 in fsci-stats alone). Only EIGHT carry an exactness claim in the static's doc with no tolerance caveat. The other 342 state no accuracy contract at all, and many carry no doc line whatsoever — fsci-stats DISCRETE_PPF_MANY_FORCE_SERIAL (:9323), TRIANGULAR_FIT_FUSE_DISABLE (:13442), GENNORM_LOGPDF_FORCE_SERIAL (:23423), NEFF_FUSE_DISABLE (:25400) and a long tail of the same shape are bare statics.

That matters for how this bead is framed. It says "two independent sources of truth exist per lever — the static's doc and the inline comment in the gated function — and they can disagree silently". For 342 of 350 there is only ONE source: the inline comment. A doc that says nothing cannot disagree with the code, so the silent-disagreement hazard is real but far rarer than feared; the commoner hazard is a lever with NO stated contract, where a reader has nothing to check the code against and no classifier can recover one. frankenscipy-5f06d's 41/12 split therefore cannot have been derived from static docs alone, and should still be treated as provisional — but for this reason, not the one recorded there.

(2) ALL EIGHT EXACTNESS CLAIMS AUDITED; SEVEN HOLD, ONE IS FALSE.
  - fsci-linalg CHOL_PANEL_TRSM_FORCE_SERIAL (:5430), CHOL_PANEL_TRSM_PAR_MACS_OVERRIDE (:5512), EIGH_INVITER_FORCE_SERIAL (:12582), MATMUL_MACS_GATE_OVERRIDE (:18842): the parallel arms split over independent output units (4-row-aligned TRSM chunks, one eigenvector column per index, matmul output tiles) or change only a thread-count threshold. No float reduction is reassociated by the split, which is the specific hazard this bead was opened on. Claims hold.
  - fsci-spatial SPATIAL_BOOL_POPCOUNT_DISABLE (:1626): integer (in)equality counts. Exact by construction.
  - fsci-ndimage NDIMAGE_ZOOM_SEPARABLE_DISABLE (:9762) and fsci-stats STATS_CROSS_PRESORT_DISABLE (:44447): precompute-once vs recompute-per-use of the same values, same summation order. Claims hold on reading.
  - fsci-stats BRUNNERMUNZEL_MATRIX_PRESORT_DISABLE (:44150): FALSE. Filed as frankenscipy-m3eja with a prepared fix. The two arms differ by Err vs Ok on ragged input, because the toggle branch returns before the equal-length validation — and the validation is itself wrong for a two-sample test. Note the shape of the miss: the disagreement is not float drift at all, it is a VALIDATION-ORDERING difference. This bead's suggested first-pass grep (chunked/partial/fold reductions) would never have found it. Anything that returns early on one arm can skip a check the other arm applies; that is the second pattern worth grepping for.

(3) NEW, AND THE MOST ACTIONABLE PART: TWO OF THE EIGHT CLAIMS ARE ASSERTED BY NOTHING. NDIMAGE_ZOOM_SEPARABLE_DISABLE and SPATIAL_BOOL_POPCOUNT_DISABLE are driven ONLY by perf bins — perf_shift_sep, perf_affine_sep, perf_pdist_jaccard, perf_bool_popcount. Those are timing harnesses. Neither toggle has a cfg(test) A/B anywhere, so their byte-identity claims have never once been checked, and per this bead's own argument an exact gate is the cheapest detector of a stale doc. The other six all have to_bits assertions near their drivers. Filed separately as the concrete follow-up.

REMAINING TO CLOSE. The eight exactness claims are adjudicated. What is NOT done, and is the larger job this audit uncovered, is the 342 toggles with no stated contract: each needs its contract recovered from the code and written into the doc. That is a different and much bigger task than the one this bead describes, and it should probably be scoped as its own bead rather than silently expanding this one.

comments.text:
SECOND CONFIRMED INSTANCE — this is a pattern, not a one-off. RusticCarp 2026-08-06, found by the heavy-fixture gate batch (d7d2d912b).

SOFTMAX_FORCE_SERIAL, same shape as logsumexp:
  static doc  : 'fans the order-preserving maps across cores for large inputs. Byte-identical.'
  inline commt: 'below the gate ... keep the EXACT serial fold (byte-identical), above it within
                 per-op ULP tolerance (parallel reorder, propagated through the divide-by-sum map)'
  measured    : n = 1_500_000 gives 1.7897196667740724e-9 serial vs 1.789719666774089e-9 parallel

THE MECHANISM IS NOW CLEAR AND IT PREDICTS WHERE ELSE TO LOOK. In both cases the doc was TRUE WHEN WRITTEN and became false later:
  - softmax's doc describes the order-preserving MAPS being parallelised. The
    SUM was parallelised afterwards, above its own separate 1<<20 gate, and the
    doc was never revisited.
  - logsumexp's doc describes a materialise-then-sum-in-index-order
    implementation. That implementation was REPLACED by per-thread partials, and
    the doc kept describing the old one.

So the failure mode is not sloppiness at authoring time. It is a SECOND parallelisation landing on a function that already had a documented byte-identical toggle, where the author updated the inline comment next to the code they touched and left the static's doc alone.

THAT GIVES A TARGETED SEARCH, cheaper than reading all 53 docs:
  find levers whose gated function contains MORE THAN ONE parallel construct, or
  whose function has its own second size gate distinct from the toggle's. Those
  are the ones where a later parallelisation can have outrun the doc. Both
  confirmed instances have exactly that signature — softmax has a map gate
  (700_000/thread) AND a sum gate (1<<20); logsumexp has the toggle plus an
  internal 1<<16.

SCORE SO FAR: two of two float-sum levers examined had stale byte-identity docs. Levers whose parallel arm merges INTEGER counts or reduces with min/max (histogram family, par_max_fold, rsh) all passed their exact gates, and passed for a structural reason — associativity — rather than by luck. The suspicion should concentrate on FLOAT REDUCTIONS, not on parallel maps.

Practical note: an exact gate remains the cheapest detector, and it costs nothing to apply it first even to a lever you suspect is tolerance-class. Both finds came free that way.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
STANDING CHECK — READ FIRST. THE CHECK APPEARS TO PASS BECAUSE IT NEVER LOOKED.

Three independent instances of one failure shape have now been found in this repo within a single session. In every one, a verification reported success while examining nothing, and the output was indistinguishable from a genuine pass:

  1. PIPE EXIT STATUS. `sometool ... | tail -20; echo $?` reports TAIL's status,
     always 0. The bash fix does not help here either: in this fleet's zsh
     `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` expands to the EMPTY STRING (the array is `$pipestatus`
     and it is 1-indexed), so the "fixed" form printed a blank and proved
     nothing.

  2. STALE BYTE-IDENTITY DOCS. Two levers (logsumexp, softmax) documented a
     byte-identical A/B contract that their own implementations had stopped
     honouring. Reading the doc — the obvious way to "check" the contract —
     returned a confident wrong answer. Only executing an exact gate found it.

  3. NAMING-SENSITIVE PROBE. My undriven-toggle sweep matched toggles by a
     guessed suffix pattern. Against fsci-sparse it found 23 statics where a
     naming-agnostic pass found 25 — it MISSED TWO. It happened to report the
     right conclusion (0 undriven), but a regex matching NOTHING would have
     reported "0 undriven" just as cheerfully, and looked identical.

THE RULE, and it is one line:

  BEFORE TRUSTING ANY COUNT OR ANY PASS, PROVE THE PROBE MATCHES SOMETHING —
  run it against a case you KNOW should hit, and confirm it hits.

Two controls, both cheap, both mandatory for anything used as evidence:

  POSITIVE CONTROL — does the probe fire when it should? Run the grep/regex/gate
  against a known-present instance. A sweep that returns "0 problems" is only
  meaningful once you have watched it return a non-zero count on a case you
  planted or already know about. Prefer naming-agnostic probes (every
  `pub static`, every `^error`) over pattern-guessed ones; where a pattern is
  unavoidable, cross-check it once against the agnostic form and report the
  delta.

  NEGATIVE CONTROL — does the probe fail when it should? Already in use for the
  build gates: when re-verifying the clippy claims, fsci-stats correctly returned
  exit 101 with 25 errors while the clean crates returned 0. Without that arm,
  "everything passed" and "nothing was checked" are the same observation.

COROLLARY, which is why this belongs on the audit bead specifically: prefer a
check that EXECUTES the thing over one that READS ABOUT it. Instance 2 is the
sharp case — the doc said byte-identical, the code was not, and no amount of
careful reading would have found it. An exact gate cost nothing and found two.
That is the strongest argument for this bead's method: apply exact gates first
and let them surface the disagreements.

CONSEQUENCE FOR EXISTING NUMBERS: every undriven-toggle count I have reported
from the suffix-pattern sweep is a LOWER BOUND — frankenscipy-5f06d's 53/134 and
the six-crate sweep on frankenscipy-ct8n2 included. They are being re-run
naming-agnostically; until that lands, do not treat them as complete, and in
particular do not treat "only fsci-stats is affected" as established.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
ADDENDUM TO THE STANDING CHECK — the two controls must be stated TOGETHER, and here is why.

While writing that check I built a probe in four attempts. Version 2 matched EVERYTHING and reported 0 undriven toggles across all seven crates — a perfect clean sweep, entirely false. MY POSITIVE CONTROL PASSED ON IT.

That is the gap: a positive control only proves the probe is not BLIND. It is satisfied by a probe that says yes to everything, which is exactly the failure mode that produces a reassuring number. What caught v2 was the NEGATIVE control — asserting that a toggle I know is ungated is STILL reported undriven.

So the rule as written above needs both arms held together, never one:
  POSITIVE — does it fire when it should?     catches BLINDNESS
  NEGATIVE — does it stay silent when it should?  catches BLANKET-MATCHING
A probe that fails either one is not evidence, and the two failures look nothing alike: blindness under-reports, blanket-matching over-reports, and both print a clean-looking number.

Instances of the pattern now stand at six, the last two in my own tooling, back to back, while writing the check about it. Every wrong version produced a plausible count and none of them errored. That is the honest measure of how easy this failure is.

comments.text:
======================================================================
STANDING RULE — TWO-ARM PROBE CONTROL. READ BEFORE REPORTING ANY NUMBER.
FLEET-LEVEL FINDING, not a frankenscipy one.
======================================================================

A COUNT OR A PASS IS NOT REPORTABLE UNLESS THE PROBE HAS BEEN RUN AGAINST
BOTH A CASE THAT MUST HIT AND A CASE THAT MUST MISS, AND BOTH ARMS WERE
OBSERVED. Not reasoned about. Run, and seen.

  POSITIVE ARM — run it against a known hit.  Catches BLINDNESS: the probe
                 matches nothing, or misses a spelling. UNDER-reports.
  NEGATIVE ARM — run it against a known miss. Catches BLANKET-MATCHING: the
                 probe matches everything. OVER-reports — AND PASSES THE
                 POSITIVE ARM.

ONE ARM PROVES NOTHING. The two failures look nothing alike, and both print a
clean-looking number.

WHY THIS IS STATED SO FLATLY. Building the undriven-toggle probe for this bead
took FOUR attempts. Two produced confidently wrong answers. EVERY WRONG VERSION
PRODUCED A PLAUSIBLE COUNT AND NONE OF THEM ERRORED.

  v1  matched the literal `NAME.store`. Blind to a driver bound through a
      reference — reported as undriven two toggles that had just been gated by

  v2  treated everything after the first `#[cfg(test)]` as test code. In a 90k

      *** THE POSITIVE CONTROL PASSED ON v2. ***
  v3  used the last `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`. Too narrow; several such blocks
      exist across files. Positive control failed, caught immediately.
  v4  counts references that are not the declaration, not a comment, and not the
      `NAME.load` gate site. Both arms pass. This is the version behind the
      current number.

Only the NEGATIVE arm caught v2, and v2 is the dangerous one: a probe that says
yes to everything reports perfect coverage and is indistinguishable from success.

MECHANICAL FORM — encode both arms as asserts INSIDE the probe so it refuses to
print a number when either fails:

    assert KNOWN_HIT  not in reported_problems,  "positive: probe is blind"
    assert KNOWN_MISS     in reported_problems,  "negative: probe matches all"

comments.author: RusticCarp
comments.text:
FINDING WITH A DENOMINATOR: THE STALE-DOC CLASS BOUNDARY IS REAL, NOT ASSUMED. RusticCarp 2026-08-06.

This bead's whole point is that a byte-identity claim is a hypothesis. After
seven slices of frankenscipy-5f06d there is now enough population to say WHERE
the hypothesis fails, with the denominator, rather than just listing casualties.

  29 perf levers gated by this bead (32 statics touched, minus 3 that were only
     PINNED to isolate a sibling: COV_MATRIX_FORCE_SERIAL, NORMAL_EQ_FORCE_SERIAL,
     DESCRIBE_FUSE_DISABLE).

   7 of the 29 have an arm that REASSOCIATES A FLOAT SUM — folds per-thread or
     per-chunk partials rather than one left fold in index order:
       LOGSUMEXP  SOFTMAX  DIFFERENTIAL_ENTROPY  PEARSONR  PEARSONR_MEAN
       DESCRIBE_REDUCE  HMEAN_W_FUSE
   5 of those 7 had a STALE DOC.  (The 2 that did not — PEARSONR and
     DESCRIBE_REDUCE — documented their tolerance correctly from the start.)

  22 of the 29 do not reassociate a float sum: integer histogram/scatter merges,
     min/max folds, order-preserving maps folded serially in index order, strided
     gathers and transposed builds, presort hoists, pass fusion, mean hoists.
   0 of those 22 had a stale doc. All 22 passed an EXACT to_bits() gate, so this
     is 22 green exact gates, not 22 unexamined levers.

  5/7 vs 0/22. Five for five, the stale docs were float sums split across chunks
  and nothing else was.

WHY THE DENOMINATOR IS THE RESULT AND THE FIVE DOCS ARE NOT. Five stale docs is a
list of repairs. 5/7 against 0/22 is a CLASS BOUNDARY, and it is what lets a
reader treat the remaining exact-claim levers in fsci-stats — all sorts, ranks,
discrete maps and hoists — as structurally safe rather than merely unexamined.
That is a claim about work NOT yet done, which is only licensed by the zero in
the denominator of the other class.

THE MECHANISM BEHIND THE BOUNDARY, which is why it should generalise past
fsci-stats: a float sum is the only one of these shapes whose PARALLELISATION
CHANGES ITS RESULT. Integer merges, min/max, and write-once gathers can be
parallelised without touching the contract, so a later parallel split lands on
them silently and correctly. A float sum cannot, so every later split invalidates
a byte-identity claim written before it — and the claim lives in a doc comment
nobody recompiles. That is the yq1k8 mechanism stated as a predicate rather than
an anecdote.

OPERATIONAL FORM, cheap enough to run anywhere: when auditing byte-identity
claims in a numeric crate, sort the backlog by "does any arm reassociate a float
sum" and take that class FIRST. Do not spend fixture budget evenly.

THE PREDICTION WAS TESTED WHERE IT COULD FAIL, WHICH IS WHY IT COUNTS. After four
of four float-sum levers came back stale, the next slice was chosen to be the
remaining float reductions (MEAN_W_FUSE, HMEAN_W_FUSE, F_ONEWAY_FUSE,
DESCRIBE_REDUCE) rather than the safe sorts and ranks. HMEAN_W was the fifth
stale doc and DESCRIBE_REDUCE was the first correct one — a confirmation and a
counterexample from the same slice. Taking the safe class instead would have
produced green tests and no information.

TWO LIMITS ON THIS, STATED SO IT IS NOT OVER-READ:
 1. n = 29 from ONE crate. The mechanism should generalise; the ratio should not
    be quoted as a rate.
 2. "0 of 22" means no stale doc SURVIVED an exact gate on the fixtures used. For
    the levers whose two arms are arithmetically identical by construction
    (pass fusion, mean hoists), a green exact gate cannot distinguish "the arms
    agree" from "the toggle was ignored" — no observation can, for that shape.
    The 7 drifting levers are stronger in this one respect: a disagreement is
    reachable only if the alternate arm actually ran, so they prove their own
    fan-out.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text: NEW EVIDENCE FOR THIS RULE 2026-08-08 (TopazOsprey): the two-arm requirement caught a stale-binary false green, filed as frankenscipy-eibro. Sequence: a new fsci-stats golden test passed remotely; I then edited one golden constant to be wrong by ~2e-6 relative against a 1e-9 tolerance and re-ran the IDENTICAL rch command, which still reported "1 passed; 0 failed"; a third run landed on a different worker, actually compiled, and failed as predicted (rel 1.985e-6, exit 101). So run 2 executed a binary built from pre-edit source. Without the must-miss arm the original green would have been recorded as evidence and nobody would have learned the binary was stale. This is the strongest concrete case yet that a lone must-hit proves nothing here: it can be green because the code is right, OR because the code under test was never built.

title: [capability][linalg] eigh_tridiagonal has no value-range selection (scipy select=v)
description:
Landed 2026-08-16 (RainyPrairie), completing the scipy `select` surface for eigh_tridiagonal started in frankenscipy-0y08i.

scipy.linalg.eigh_tridiagonal supports select='a' (all), 'i' (index range) and 'v' (value range). 0y08i added the index form; this adds the value form, so the surface is complete for the tridiagonal entry point.

eigh_tridiagonal_subset_by_value(d, e, (vl, vu), eigvals_only, options) selects the HALF-OPEN interval vl < lambda <= vu, matching scipy, and refuses a decreasing or NaN range the way scipy does (its message: "select_range must be a 2-element array-like in nondecreasing order") rather than silently swapping the bounds.

An empty selection is an ANSWER, not an error: it returns an empty spectrum with an n x 0 eigenvector block. Callers scanning a spectrum in abutting windows depend on that, and the half-open convention is what makes such a scan visit each eigenvalue exactly once.

Because the spectrum is ascending the matching eigenvalues are contiguous, so this delegates to eigh_tridiagonal_subset rather than duplicating eigenvector logic -- the cluster and inverse-iteration fallbacks are identical on both entry points by construction, not by convention.

description: scipy.stats.truncpareto(b, c) is missing in fsci-stats. title: [perf][cluster] parallelize GMM EM E-step across data points (ordered slots, byte-identical); per-point logp/lse independent
description: LEVER (byte-identical via the proven ordered-slots pattern, used ~15x this campaign — csr_matvec/silhouette/lombscargle/kmeans2-assign): the gaussian_mixture (and _full) EM E-step computes resp[i][c] and the per-point log-likelihood lse[i] INDEPENDENTLY for each data point i (gaussian density + log-sum-exp). Currently serial with a single hoisted logp buffer (frankenscipy-5ufms). PLAN: parallelize across i with resp.chunks_mut() into ordered slots, each thread carrying its OWN logp scratch (the 5ufms hoist becomes per-thread) and writing lse into an ordered Vec; after the parallel scope, total_ll = lse.iter().sum() in point order. Byte-identical: each resp[i] is point-independent (same values, same slot), and total_ll is the SAME ordered sum of the SAME lse values (serial reduce after, preserving order). The M-step accumulation Σ resp[i][c]·x[i][j] is a reduction that reorders under naive parallelism -> KEEP IT SERIAL (it's O(n·d), less dominant than the E-step's gaussian evals). Gate on n·k·d work like the other parallel kernels. BENCH TARGET: cluster_bench bench_gmm (frankenscipy-rhdcs, k3/n1000) + scale n to 10000+; expect ~Nx on the E-step. GUARD: gaussian_mixture_recovers_separated/correlated_gaussians conformance tests (must stay byte-identical). NEEDS the benchmark wave to confirm the work-gate threshold + that thread-spawn overhead doesn't dominate at small n. Filed rather than done blind because the EM-loop + resp-reuse + per-thread-buffer interaction wants test verification.

title: PARITY: fsci-interpolate CubicSpline boundary-condition coverage (natural/clamped/not-a-knot/periodic/tuple)
description:
fsci-interpolate ships CubicSpline but only smoke-tests the natural-BC path. scipy.interpolate.CubicSpline supports five boundary-condition modes:
  - natural        (second derivative = 0 at both ends)
  - clamped        (first derivative specified at both ends, e.g. 0)
  - not-a-knot     (default; third derivative continuous across the second knot)
  - periodic       (y, y', y'' match at endpoints)

- Tolerance contract: 1e-10 absolute for natural / not-a-knot, 1e-9 for clamped / periodic (slight numerical sensitivity), exact endpoint match for periodic.

title: [HIGH] conformance: SpecialExpectedOutcome::ErrorKind comparison uses format!('{:?}', kind) string match — breaks when Debug repr changes (enum variants grow fields) AND conflates fixture-schema DomainError with genuine domain violations
description:
Review of crates/fsci-conformance/src/lib.rs:10997-11006 on 2026-04-22:

    (SpecialExpectedOutcome::ErrorKind { error }, Err(actual)) => {
        let observed_kind = format!('{:?}', actual.kind);
        let pass = observed_kind == *error;
        ...
    }

Problems:

1. Debug-format coupling. Rust's Debug repr is NOT a stable string contract. If FsciSpecialErrorKind::DomainError grows to DomainError { detail: String }, the Debug output changes from 'DomainError' to 'DomainError { detail: "..." }'. All 10 adversarial cases (case.category == 'adversarial') using expected.kind='error_kind' + expected.error='DomainError' silently flip pass -> fail without any actual behavior change.

2. Inconsistency with Class comparator. At 10987-10989 the ValueClass comparison uses typed enum equality (observed_class == *class). The ErrorKind comparator should mirror this pattern: compare typed enums, not Debug strings. The Class path is the right pattern; the ErrorKind path regresses to the string-compare anti-pattern documented in gnun.

3. Masks fixture-schema bugs. Per frankenscipy-04jy, special_invalid_fixture_error mints FsciSpecialErrorKind::DomainError for ANY argument-count mismatch (191 sites). So a fixture like:
       case_id: 'adv_gamma_pole_hardened_error'
       function: 'gamma'
       args: [-2.0, 3.0, 1.0]   # typo: should be [-2.0]
       category: 'adversarial'
       expected: {kind: 'error_kind', error: 'DomainError'}
   would:
   - enter execute_special_case at 10509 (actually gamma takes 1 arg, not covered there; use a 1-arg fn)
   - actual handler sees wrong arity, returns special_invalid_fixture_error (DomainError kind)
   - compare_special_case_differential sees observed_kind='DomainError'
   - matches expected='DomainError' -> PASS
   - claim 'verified gamma fails closed on pole' even though we hit an arity check before touching gamma
   The test is lying about what it verified.

Fix:
1. Introduce a typed comparison path. Parse expected.error into FsciSpecialErrorKind (perhaps via FromStr or a lookup table) and compare enum vs enum:
       let expected_kind: FsciSpecialErrorKind = error.parse()
           .map_err(|_| (false, format!('unknown error kind: {error}'), None, None))?;
       let pass = actual.kind == expected_kind;
2. Separate fixture-schema errors from domain errors (ties to 04jy) -- a fixture-schema error should make the case UNJUDGEABLE (per ihex), not match a DomainError expectation.
3. Mirror the Class comparator pattern at 10987.

Related: gnun (error-string equality anti-pattern), 04jy (DomainError overloaded for fixture-schema), ihex (both-errored = pass amplification), tfd7 (metamorphic self-consistency is strength-4 without strength-1 cross-check).

title: [parity-gap] airy Ai'(-x)/Bi'(-x) oscillatory N-series sign error: 6e-5 vs scipy
description: oscillatory_coefficients in crates/fsci-special/src/airy.rs built the derivative even-series N = sum (-1)^k v_2k / zeta^2k as 1 - |v2|/zeta^2 + |v4|/zeta^4. But the DLMF v_k are intrinsically negative for k>=1 (v_k = -(6k+1)/(6k-1) u_k), so the (-1)^k and that intrinsic sign combine to a NET POSITIVE: N = 1 + |v2|/zeta^2 + |v4|/zeta^4. The wrong sign left a +2|v2|/zeta^2 (about zeta^-2) residual in BOTH Ai'(-x) and Bi'(-x) for the asymptotic branch |x|>=12: rel 5.8e-5 at x=-15, 2.5e-5 at -20, 7.3e-6 at -30, while Ai/Bi were fine at 1e-10. The closed yz8s7 Wronskian fix did NOT catch this because the symmetric N error cancels in Ai*Bip - Aip*Bi = 1/pi. Fix: flip the sign to N = 1 + v2 iz2 + v4 iz4. Verified vs scipy 1.17.1: residual drops to under 1e-7 across x in [-15,-100]. Golden test airy_negative_x_derivatives_match_scipy tightened from 1e-4 abs to 2e-6 rel.
close_reason: Fixed: flipped N even-series sign to 1+|v2|/zeta^2+|v4|/zeta^4 in oscillatory_coefficients; Ai'/Bi'(-x) now match scipy 1.17.1 to <1e-7 on the asymptotic branch (was 6e-5). Committed e8e92625.

title: [code-review] periodogram_simple uses fft on complex-promoted real input — should use rfft
description:
fsci-fft's periodogram_simple at crates/fsci-fft/src/helpers.rs:231 takes a real signal x: &[f64], allocates a complex_input: Vec<(f64, f64)> twice the size, runs the full complex fft (which produces N complex outputs), then keeps only the first N/2+1 bins. This is two unnecessary costs on a real-input hot path:

  1. Allocation: complex_input doubles the input footprint (N (f64, f64) pairs vs N f64).
  2. Compute: fft computes N complex bins, but symmetry says only N/2+1 are independent for real input.

scipy.signal.periodogram uses rfft internally. fsci-fft already has rfft (line 444 of transforms.rs); switching periodogram_simple to call rfft directly halves the FFT work and removes the intermediate Vec.

P1 because periodogram is a common hot path in spectral analysis. Acceptance: periodogram_simple stops allocating the complex_input Vec; calls rfft(x) directly; produces identical (within f64 precision) output to the current implementation; existing tests still pass.

title: [MEDIUM] fsci-linalg: solve_circulant silently zeros out near-singular FFT-space modes (|λ|²<1e-30) instead of raising — produces wrong 'solution' that doesn't satisfy Cx=b for singular/ill-conditioned circulants; scipy.linalg.solve_circulant raises LinAlgError by default via singular='raise'; no input finiteness check either
description:
Review of crates/fsci-linalg/src/lib.rs on 2026-04-23.

solve_circulant (line 4308-4348) silently zeros out near-singular frequency
components rather than raising LinAlgError, producing wrong answers for
singular or ill-conditioned circulant systems.

Problematic code (line 4330-4342):

    let fft_x: Vec<(f64, f64)> = fft_b
        .iter()
        .zip(fft_c.iter())
        .map(|(&(br, bi), &(cr, ci))| {
            let denom = cr * cr + ci * ci;
            if denom < 1e-30 {
                (0.0, 0.0)                                  // <-- silent singularity mask
            } else {
                ((br * cr + bi * ci) / denom, (bi * cr - br * ci) / denom)
            }
        })
        .collect();

Analysis:

A circulant matrix C has FFT-space diagonalization C = F^* diag(λ) F, where
λ_k = FFT(c)[k]. Solving Cx = b becomes x̂_k = b̂_k / λ_k.

When λ_k ≈ 0, the system is singular (or nearly so). The code silently sets
x̂_k = 0 in that case, producing a 'solution' that fails to satisfy Cx = b
when b̂_k ≠ 0. This is a classic 'return wrong answer silently on singular
input' bug.

Scipy comparison:
- scipy.linalg.solve_circulant has two extra parameters:
    tol: float, default 1e-16 * max(|eigenvalues|)
    singular: 'raise' (default) or 'lstsq'
  With singular='raise', raises scipy.linalg.LinAlgError when any |λ_k|
  falls below tol.
  With singular='lstsq', computes least-squares solution using 0 for the
  null-space modes.
- Our implementation is silently a 'lstsq'-mode solver with tol fixed at
  sqrt(1e-30) ≈ 3e-16 of the eigenvalue magnitude squared. No 'raise' mode,
  no user-configurable tolerance.

Impact:

1. Users migrating from scipy see different behavior: scipy raises on
   singular input (default); our impl silently returns a wrong solution.

2. The 'wrong' solution satisfies C * x ≈ P_range(C) * b (projection of b
   onto range of C), not Cx = b. For users expecting exact solution, this
   is a correctness bug.

3. Detection requires checking ||Cx - b|| afterward, which users shouldn't
   have to do for a solve function that's advertised as a 'solver.'

4. NaN fall-open: if cr or ci is NaN (which shouldn't happen given earlier
   NaN validation at the solve entry points, but solve_circulant doesn't
   have any own validation), denom = NaN, NaN < 1e-30 is false, takes
   else branch, divides by NaN, output NaN silently. No input validation
   on the circulant vector c.

Additional concerns in solve_circulant:

a. No validation that c is finite. Line 4308 is:
       pub fn solve_circulant(c: &[f64], b: &[f64]) -> Result<Vec<f64>, LinalgError>
   No mode parameter. No check_finite parameter. No Hardened-mode path.
   Other solve functions (solve, solve_triangular, solve_banded) take
   SolveOptions with mode and check_finite. Inconsistent API.

b. Divergence threshold 1e-30 is on denom = |λ|² not |λ|. So the cutoff
   is at |λ| ≈ 1e-15, close to machine epsilon for 1.0-scale matrices.
   For small-scale matrices this is far too permissive; for large-scale
   it's too strict. Scipy scales tol by max |eigenvalue|.

Fix:

1. Add a `tol` parameter (or use a default based on max|eigenvalue|):
       let max_lambda_sq = fft_c.iter().map(|&(cr, ci)| cr*cr + ci*ci).fold(0.0, f64::max);
       let tol = 1e-28 * max_lambda_sq;  // or parameterized

2. Detect singularity and raise:
       if denom < tol {
           if br*br + bi*bi > tol * tol * max_b_sq {
               return Err(LinalgError::SingularMatrix);
           }
           (0.0, 0.0)  // only if b̂_k is also zero
       }

3. Add SolveOptions-based variant for scipy-parity mode control:
       pub fn solve_circulant_with_options(..., options: SolveOptions) -> ...

4. Validate c and b for finiteness at function entry.

Regression tests:
    let c = vec![1.0, -2.0, 1.0];  // circulant with eigenvalue 0 (λ[1] = 1 - 2*e^{2πi/3} + e^{4πi/3} = 0 for certain c)
    let b = vec![1.0, 0.0, 0.0];   // b̂ not in range of C
    let x = solve_circulant(&c, &b);
    assert!(x.is_err());  // currently returns Ok with wrong answer

Related: l15l (procrustes silent divergence via Newton-Schulz), wofb
(fsci-stats sf precision loss), n240 (cluster metrics silent 0.0),
42z1 (mmread DoS), 1dpl (RBF silent NaN). Pattern: functions that should
signal computational failure but instead return degraded-quality output.
close_reason: Fail-closed on singular solve_circulant (commit 818d02d).

title: [conformance][linalg] ldl silently returns a 7% wrong factorization for a well-conditioned matrix below scale 2^-46 — absolute pivot floor, and the existing test tolerance cannot see it
description:
Filed 2026-08-15 (PeachSummit), found by pointing the frankenscipy-pfet9 / xs7i2 harness at fsci-linalg. Same defect class, worse consequence: this one returns a WRONG ANSWER with no error at all.

SITE: crates/fsci-linalg/src/lib.rs, in `pub fn ldl`, 'if d_vec[j].abs() < f64::EPSILON * 1e3' (2.22e-13, ABSOLUTE). When it fires the routine zeroes the rest of that column of L and continues, so the caller gets an Ok(LdlResult) that does not reconstruct A.

MEASURED, both arms, same closed-form fixture: n=8 symmetric, a[i][i] = 6 + 0.5*(i%3), a[i][j] = -1/(1+|i-j|) off-diagonal, cond(A) = 1.733, uniformly scaled by 2^-k. Relative reconstruction error of L·D·Lᵀ against A.
  ours -- cargo test -p fsci-linalg --lib ldl_scale_sweep_probe -- --nocapture, via rch, RCH_WORKER=vmi1227854
  peer -- scipy.linalg.ldl 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.3

  2^-k    scipy ldl      ours          our min|d|
  0       8.474e-17      1.269e-16     5.901e0
  2^-40   8.474e-17      1.269e-16     5.367e-12
  2^-44   8.474e-17      1.269e-16     3.354e-13
  2^-46   8.474e-17      7.143e-2      8.527e-14   <<< silently wrong from here down
  2^-50   8.474e-17      7.143e-2      5.329e-15
  2^-60   8.474e-17      7.143e-2      5.204e-18

SciPy is exactly scale-invariant here -- 8.474e-17 at every scale including 2^-60, where its own min|d| is 5.118e-18 -- because it PERMUTES (Bunch-Kaufman) rather than clamping. There is no parity defence for this one.

SECOND FINDING, and the reason the bead says the tolerance cannot see it: the test helper `verify_ldl_reconstruction` asserts '(sum - aij).abs() < 1e-10', an ABSOLUTE bound. At 2^-46 the matrix entries are order 1e-13, so a 7.1% relative error is about 7e-15 absolute and the assertion passes VACUOUSLY. Any new test must assert the RELATIVE reconstruction error, and the old helper should be reviewed for the same reason -- this is the vacuously-true-contract hazard in live form.

FIX DIRECTION: the precedent this repo already set (frankenscipy-4u7vp, quoted in pfet9) is a pivot floor relative to the factor's largest diagonal, which is what update_solution now does. Applying it here means comparing |d_j| against EPSILON*1e3*max|a_ii| computed once, which keeps the guard's purpose -- do not divide by a numerically-zero pivot -- while making the question scale-free.

NEGATIVE CASES any fix must pass:
1. A genuinely singular matrix (an exactly zero pivot) must still take the skip branch rather than dividing.
2. The factorization of a WELL-SCALED matrix must be unchanged byte-for-byte; capture the fingerprint on the parent commit and assert it after, as frankenscipy-pfet9 item 2 did.
3. The scale-invariance assertion must be RELATIVE (or bit-identical over an exact power-of-two scale). An absolute reconstruction bound proves nothing here, per the second finding above.

NOT IN SCOPE, worth its own bead: our ldl does no permutation at all ('no permutation for simplicity' in the source), while scipy returns a perm and pivots. That is a separate and larger conformance gap; this bead is only about the scale-dependence of the existing guard.

SIBLING SITES found in the same sweep, unmeasured, each an absolute epsilon on a dimensioned quantity in fsci-linalg/src/lib.rs: :6293 and :6529 't_mat[(i+1,i)].abs() > f64::EPSILON * 100.0' (Schur 2x2 block classification -- decides real vs complex eigenvalues), :7701 'beta.abs() <= f64::EPSILON' in ordqz_selected (generalized eigenvalue selection; a scaled B makes every eigenvalue unselected), :13388 'r[(idx,idx)].abs() <= f64::EPSILON' (QR rank test), and fsci-opt/src/minimize.rs:2055/:2102/:2165 on gradient and direction norms. Measure before touching any of them -- pfet9 item 3 is the standing reminder that half of a suspected clamp family can turn out to be parity.
notes:
DONE 2026-08-15 (PeachSummit).

FIXED: the pivot floor in fsci-linalg ldl is now relative to the largest diagonal of A -- 'f64::EPSILON * 1e3 * largest_diagonal' -- the form frankenscipy-4u7vp established for update_solution. Paired with an explicit 'd_vec[j] == 0.0' arm, which is NOT redundant: a hollow-diagonal matrix leaves the relative floor at zero and '0.0 < 0.0' is false, so the relative test alone would have divided by exactly the pivot the guard exists to catch. That arm has its own test.

RED first, worker vmi1227854, harness cargo test -p fsci-linalg --lib ... --nocapture via rch: relative reconstruction error of L·D·Lᵀ vs A was 1.269e-16 through 2^-44, then 7.143e-2 at 2^-46, 2^-50 and 2^-60 -- returned as Ok, no error, on a matrix of condition number 1.733. Incumbent on the identical closed-form fixture (scripts/scipy_scale_probe.py, section 'ldl under scaling'): scipy.linalg.ldl 1.17.1 reconstructs to 8.474e-17 at EVERY scale including 2^-60, where its own min|d| is 5.118e-18. No parity defence; scipy permutes rather than clamping.

PROBES: ldl_reconstructs_the_matrix_at_every_scale_the_incumbent_does (relative error < 1e-14 at seven scales, plus no pivot skipped); a_well_scaled_ldl_is_untouched_by_the_relative_pivot_floor (negative case 2 -- byte-for-byte equality against a reference LDL carrying the OLD absolute floor, compared in the same build rather than against a stored golden, with a second arm at 2^-46 asserting the two REFERENCE and CURRENT arms genuinely differ so the comparison cannot pass vacuously); ldl_still_skips_a_pivot_that_is_actually_zero (negative case 1, including the hollow-diagonal case).

SECOND FINDING CONFIRMED AND ACTED ON: the pre-existing helper verify_ldl_reconstruction asserts an ABSOLUTE '(sum-aij).abs() < 1e-10'. At 2^-46 this fixture's entries are order 1e-13, so the 7.1% relative error is ~7e-15 absolute and that assertion passes over it without noticing. The new tests use a RELATIVE reconstruction error (helper ldl_relative_reconstruction_error) for exactly this reason. The old helper is left in place for the well-scaled tests that use it; re-auditing it is not this bead.

Gates: fsci-linalg --lib 535 passed / 0 failed (vmi1153651), 12/12 ldl tests including the pre-existing ldl_matches_scipy_reference_values (vmi1293453), clippy -p fsci-linalg --lib -D warnings clean (hz2), fmt clean, ubs 0 critical.
HONEST GATE NOTE: 'cargo clippy -p fsci-linalg --all-targets -D warnings' is RED, and was already red before this change -- the findings are in perf bins (perf_are, perf_band_tri) and crates/fsci-linalg/src/cossin.rs, none of which this change touches. Verified no finding falls in either edited range (lib.rs 6007-6036, 33517-33710). Not fixed here and not claimed as clean.

STILL OPEN, sibling sites listed in the description and NOT measured: lib.rs :6293/:6529 Schur 2x2 classification, :7701 ordqz_selected beta test, :13388 QR rank test, and fsci-opt minimize.rs :2055/:2102/:2165. Each needs its own incumbent measurement before anyone touches it -- pfet9 item 3 is the standing reminder that half of a suspected clamp family can be parity.
close_reason: Pivot floor made relative to the largest diagonal (4u7vp form) plus an explicit zero arm; RED (7.143e-2 reconstruction error at 2^-46, vmi1227854) observed first, now < 1e-14 at every scale scipy handles; probes ldl_reconstructs_the_matrix_at_every_scale_the_incumbent_does, a_well_scaled_ldl_is_untouched_by_the_relative_pivot_floor, ldl_still_skips_a_pivot_that_is_actually_zero; 535 passed / 0 failed.

title: fsci-stats: metamorphic — Kappa3(a=1) ≡ Lomax(c=1)
description: Kappa3(a=1) is algebraically identical to Lomax(c=1): both have pdf = (1+x)^(-2) and cdf = 1 - 1/(1+x) = x/(1+x). Pin this in fsci-stats lib as kappa3_a1_matches_lomax_c1 across 8 x-values [0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 100], asserting max abs diff < 1e-13 for both pdf and cdf. Catches future drift in either Kappa3 or Lomax that would break this identity (and they SHOULD remain identical at this point in parameter space).
close_reason: Added kappa3_a1_matches_lomax_c1 metamorphic test in fsci-stats lib. Drives 8 x-values [0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 50, 100] and asserts max abs diff < 1e-13 for both pdf and cdf between Kappa3(a=1) and Lomax(c=1). The identity is exact: both reduce to pdf=(1+x)^(-2), cdf=x/(1+x). Catches future drift in either family that would break this structural equivalence. fsci-stats --lib: 1103 -> 1104.

title: [perf][fft] REJECT: parallel fwht butterfly is memory-bandwidth-bound (1.67x ceiling) + 3x regression at gate
description: Profiled+measured reject. fwht (transforms.rs:1868) is a plain serial Hadamard butterfly with no parallel machinery. Parallelized each stage's disjoint 2^h blocks across cores (chunks_mut + thread::scope, one barrier/stage, byte-identical: single add/sub per cell, no reduction; in-bench .to_bits() assert green). Same-process A/B (serial_reference vs gated-parallel): n=2^20 5.85ms->17.31ms 0.34x (3x REGRESSION from per-stage spawn over cheap add/sub work), n=2^22 64.5ms->51.0ms 1.27x, n=2^24 318ms->191ms 1.67x. The butterfly is add/sub = cheapest-possible per-element op ⇒ memory-bandwidth-bound (~1.67x ceiling even at 128MB), and log2(n) per-stage barriers over trivial work regress badly below the gate. This is the cheap-op parallelization anti-pattern (work-gate must scale with per-element OP COST, not flop count). Not worth a fussy high gate for a niche transform. REVERTED, shipped nothing.
close_reason: Measured reject: bandwidth-bound 1.67x ceiling + 3x regression at gate; cheap-op parallel anti-pattern. Reverted.

title: Add E2E conformance tests for stub-remediation: moments, interpolation, BDF Newton
description:
## Context
As stubs are remediated across fsci-stats, fsci-ndimage, and fsci-integrate, we need
E2E conformance tests to verify correctness against SciPy reference values with full
forensic logging per ARTIFACT_TOPOLOGY.md.

## Scope

### 1. E2E stats moments verification (e2e_stats.rs scenarios 11-14)
Add scenarios to crates/fsci-conformance/tests/e2e_stats.rs:

- **e2e_011_closed_form_moments**: Verify Burr12, InvWeibull, TukeyLambda,
  GenHalfLogistic mean/var against SciPy reference values (multiple parameter combos)
- **e2e_012_special_function_moments**: Verify GenLogistic, Gompertz mean/var
  against SciPy reference values
- **e2e_013_piecewise_integral_moments**: Verify CrystalBall, Argus, ExponWeibull
  mean/var against SciPy reference values
- **e2e_014_tukey_lambda_analytical**: Verify TukeyLambda analytical PDF values
  and CDF/PPF roundtrip accuracy

### 2. E2E ndimage interpolation (new test file)
Create crates/fsci-conformance/tests/e2e_ndimage.rs:

- **e2e_001_shift_interpolation**: Compare shift with orders 0,1,3 to SciPy
- **e2e_002_zoom_interpolation**: Compare zoom with orders 0,1,3 to SciPy
- **e2e_003_rotate_interpolation**: Compare rotate with orders 0,1,3 to SciPy
- **e2e_004_map_coordinates**: Compare map_coordinates with orders 0,1,3 to SciPy

### 3. E2E BDF Newton (add to existing integrate tests)
- **e2e_bdf_stiff_convergence**: Van der Pol μ=1000, verify convergence with
  Newton where functional iteration would fail

### Output format
All E2E tests emit topology-compliant artifacts:
- events.jsonl (one JSON line per step)
- summary.json (pass/fail + replay command)
- Under fixtures/artifacts/FSCI-P2C-{NNN}/e2e/runs/{run_id}/{scenario_id}/

## Testing Requirements
- All new scenarios must pass with all_pass = true
- Forensic logs must capture: parameter values, computed moments, reference values,
  absolute error, relative error, tolerance used, pass/fail per step
- Reference values should be hardcoded from SciPy (not computed at test time)

## Dependencies
Depends on: all other beads in this series (moments, interpolation, BDF)

## Validation
```
cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test e2e_stats
cargo test -p fsci-conformance --test e2e_ndimage
cargo test -p fsci-conformance
```

title: [parity-gap] jn_zeros / yn_zeros fail for moderate-to-large order n
description:
scipy.special.jn_zeros(100, 1) returns ~108.836; fsci jn_zeros(100, 1) returns ~120.8 (the McMahon asymptotic guess), missing the true zero by ~12 units. Same defect in yn_zeros.

Root cause: McMahon's asymptotic expansion (DLMF 10.21.19) μ=(4k+2n−1)π/4 is accurate when k>>n, not when n is moderate-to-large. For n=100, k=1, McMahon gives initial ≈ 120.83 but the true first zero of J_100 is ≈ 108.84. The current adaptive bracket-expansion (radius 1, then 8× ±0.3) only reaches ±3.4 from the initial — far too narrow to catch the true zero. The function falls through to 'keep the asymptotic guess' (crates/fsci-special/src/bessel.rs:3160), silently returning a wrong answer.

Repro:
  let zeros = fsci_special::jn_zeros(100, 1);
  let val = fsci_special::jn(100, zeros[0]);  // |val| should be near 0
  // Currently val ≈ J_100(120.83) which is large, NOT a zero.

Existing tests miss this because they only cover n ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3} (crates/fsci-special/src/bessel.rs:4155-4168).

Fix options:
  1) Replace McMahon with Olver/Tricomi expansion (DLMF 10.21.40):
       j_{n,1} ≈ n + 1.85575 n^(1/3) + 1.03315 n^(−1/3) − ...
     valid for the small-k, large-n regime.
  2) Use a piecewise initial guess: McMahon when k > n/2, Olver otherwise.
  3) Widen the adaptive expansion to ±20 with verification that the bracket
     brackets a sign change before bisection.

Acceptance: jn(n, jn_zeros(n, k)[k-1]) is < 1e-6 in absolute value for at
least n ∈ {0, 5, 20, 100} and k ∈ {1, 5, 20}; same for yn_zeros.
